But that this last supposition is a mistake, the very next <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> except one affirms us: for we are there told, that "when the thousand years are expired, Satan shall be loosed out of his prison, and shall go out to deceive the nations which are in the four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of the earth;" and we have no reason to believe that he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a> have such power or such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> in "the new heavens and the new earth wherein dwelleth righteousness." For this and other reasons, which our limits will not permit us to enumerate, the most judicious critics contend, that the prophecies of the millennium point, not to a resurrection of martyrs and other just men to reign with Christ a thousand years in a visible kingdom upon earth, but to that state of the Christian church, which, for a thousand years before the general judgment, will be so pure and so widely extended, that, when compared with the state of the world in the ages preceding, it may, in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of scripture, be called a resurrection from the dead. In support of this interpretation they quote two passages from St Paul, in which a conversion from Paganism to Christianity, and a reformation of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, is called a resurrection from the dead:—"Neither yield ye your members as instruments of unrighteousness unto sin; but yield yourselves unto God as those that are alive from the dead." And again, "Wherefore he saith, Awake thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall give thee <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>." It is likewise to be observed, that in all the descriptions of the resurrection and future judgment which are given us at such length in the gospels and epistles, there is no mention made of a first and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SECOND">second</a> resurrection at the distance of a thousand years from each other. There is indeed an order in the resurrection: for we are told, that "every <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAN">man</a> shall rise in his own order; Christ the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, afterwards they that are Christ's at his coming, &c." But were the millenarian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a> well founded, the words should rather have run thus: "Christ the first fruits, then the martyrs at his coming, and a thousand years afterwards the residue of mankind. Then cometh the end, &c." These arguments strongly incline us to believe, that Millenium by the reign of Christ and the saints for a thousand years upon earth, nothing more is meant, than that before the general judgment the Jews shall be converted, genuine Christianity be diffused through all nations, and mankind enjoy that peace and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> and precepts of the gospel are calculated to confer on all by whom they are sincerely embraced. Our Saviour's own account of his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> is, that from a small beginning it will increase to the full <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a>. The millennium therefore is to be considered as the full effect of the Christian principles in the hearts of men, and over the whole world; and the divines who have treated of this subject endeavour to prove, that this is to be expected from the facts which have already existed, and from the importance of the Christian doctrine. 1. The gradual progress of Christianity is no objection to this fact. This is similar to the progress and advancement from less to greater perfection in everything which possesses vegetable or animal life. The same thing is observed in the arts, in civilization, in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a>, and in individuals—and why should it not be admitted to have <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in religion? There is indeed a general principle on which a gradual progression, both in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> and moral world, is founded. The Almighty never employs supernatural means where the thing can be accomplished by those which are natural. This idea is of the most general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> through the whole of the present system of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. The possibility of another <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> could easily be admitted; but in this <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CASE">case</a> there would be a total <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> of every <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> of the works of God or of man that we are acquainted with. In the same manner, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the religion of Christ had been irresistible, it would have totally altered its natural consequences. It was necessary, therefore, from the present condition of man, as an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a>, intelligent, and accountable being, that means should be employed; and wherever means are employed, the effects produced must be gradual, and not instantaneous. 2. Though the progress of a divine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REVELATION">revelation</a> be gradual, yet it is to be expected, from the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> and compassion of God, that it will still be advancing in the hearts of men, and over the world. In the first age of the church, the word of God, supported by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a>, and by the animated zeal of men, who spoke what they saw and heard, grew and prevailed. In this case supernatural means were necessary, because the prejudices of the world could not be subdued without them. It was the first watering of a plant which you afterwards leave to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEW">dew</a> of heaven. Miracles at the same time were employed only as the means of conviction; and they were not <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a>, because in this case they would have become a constant and irresistible principle, incompatible with the condition of man as a reasonable <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGENT">agent</a>. After this power was withdrawn, there were many ages of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a> in the Christian church. But what is necessary to be established on this subject is, not that the progress of Christianity has never been interrupted, but that on the whole it has been advancing. The effects of this religion on mankind, in proportion as it was received, were immediate and visible: It destroyed the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> superstition of idol-worship; it abolished the practice, which was general in the heathen world, of reducing to the lowest state of servitude the greatest part of our brethren: it softened the horrors of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WAR">war</a> even when the vices of mankind made defense necessary: it entered into social and private life; and taught men benevolence, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>, and mercy. It is in these blessed effects that we can observe the progress of Christianity even to this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>. Superstition and idolatry were soon engrained on the stem which our Saviour planted in the world; but the simplicity of the gospel has been gradually undermining the fabric of superstition; and the men who are most nearly interested in the deceit are now almost ashamed to show their faces in the cause. The practice of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a> has, generally speaking, been extinguished in the Christian world; yet the remains of it have been a disgrace to the Christian name, and the professors of that religion have now begun to see the inconsistency. War is not only carried on with less animosity, and less havoc of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; but men begin to cultivate more generally, and to delight in, the arts of peace. The increasing spirit of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> and benevolence, of which it were easy to give unexampled instances in the present age, is a decided <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of the increasing influence of Christianity. At the same time, if, instead of these general principles, we were to descend to private examples of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-INFIDELITY">infidelity</a> or of wickedness, it would be easy to bring proofs in support of an opposite opinion; but the reasoning would by no means be equally conclusive; for if the general principles by which <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> is regulated be more liberal and merciful, it is evident that there is more goodness in a greater <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of the human <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-RACE">race</a>. Society is nothing more than a collection of individuals; and the general tone, especially when it is on the side of virtue, which almost in every instance opposes the designs of leading and interested men, is a certain <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> of the private spirit. To show that this reformation is connected with Christianity, it is unnecessary to state any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> between the influence of heathen and the influence of Christian principles; between civilization as depending on the powers of the human understanding, and on the efficacy of the word of God. The whole of this controversy may be appealed to an obvious fact, viz. that as any nation has come nearer to the simplicity of the gospel in the standard of its worship, it has been more possessed of those national virtues which we have ascribed to the influence of Christianity. This fact is worth a thousand volumes of speculation on this subject. 3. A revelation sanctioned by God, for a benevolent purpose, will be expected to produce effects corresponding to the wisdom which gave it, and to the purpose for which it is employed. It may be gradual; but it will be increasing, and it must increase, to the full harvest. He that has begun the good <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> will also finish it. It is reasonable to expect this illustrious success of the gospel, both from the nature of the thing, and from the prophecies contained in the sacred scriptures. The precepts of the gospel, in their genuine sense, are admirably calculated for the peace and welfare both of individuals and society. The greatest liberality of mind, the greatest generosity of temper, the most unbounded <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LOVE">love</a>, and the greatest indifference to the accumulation of this world's <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, if they glowed from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a> to breast, and operated with equal force on all men, would be productive of equal good and happiness to all. We are scarcely able to perceive the force of this at first view, because the deceit and imposition which yet exist in the world, prevent the operation of the best principles even in the best hearts. But in proportion to the improvement of mankind, what is their real <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>, and what are the real objects of happiness, will gradually unfold. The contempt of vice will be greater in proportion to the fearfulness of it: for one villain gives countenance and support to another, just as <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-IRON">iron</a> sharpeneth iron. This opens to our view another fact connected with the practice of Christianity, namely, that the nearer it arrives to its perfect state, it will be the more rapid in its progress. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOLINESS">holiness</a> will be more visible; and, in the strong language of the prophet, "the earth shall bring forth in one day, and a nation shall be born at once." This future perfection of the gospel is consistent with its nature and importance. We can scarcely believe that means so admirably adapted to the reformation of mankind should be without their effect; and if the most difficult part be already accomplished, we have no reason to apprehend that the scheme will not be completed. This fact is also clearly the subject of ancient prophecy. For "thus saith the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>," I will extend peace to her like a river, and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> of the Gentiles like a flowing stream. And it shall come to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a>, from one Sabbath to another, and from one new <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MOON">moon</a> to another, shall all <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> come to worship before me, saith the Lord. Violence shall be no more heard in thy land, wasting nor destruction within thy border; but thou shalt call thy walls <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-SALVATION">salvation</a>, and thy gates praise." (H. lx. 18.) Without entering more minutely on the prophecy already quoted from chap. xx. of the book of Revelation, it is sufficient to observe, that Dr <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WHITBY">Whitby</a>, in his treatise on the millennium at the end of his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMENTARY">commentary</a>, proves, in the clearest manner, from the spirit of the passage and the similarity of the expressions with those of other prophets, that it refers to a state of the church for a thousand years, which shall be like life from the dead. The commencement of this period is connected with two events; the fall of antichrist, and the conversion of the Jews. The latter of these events must be considered as a key to all the prophecies concerning the millennium. As the Jews were the ancient people of God, and as their conversion is to be the previous step to the general knowledge of Christianity, the prophecies of the millennium have a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> relation to this important event. We have already observed, that God never interposes with miraculous power to produce what can be effected by natural means; and from what we know of human nature, we cannot but perceive that the conversion of the Jews will powerfully operate to the general conversion of mankind. Freed from those prejudices which now make them the objects of hatred in all nations, and fired with that zeal by which new converts are always actuated, they will preach the gospel with a fervour of which we, who have <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a> been blest with its rays, can hardly form a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONCEPTION">conception</a>; and, by their present <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISPERSION">dispersion</a> over the whole earth, they will be enabled to adapt their instructions to every individual of the human race. human race in the language of his fathers. Indeed, if they are not at some future period to be employed by <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a> for this purpose, it is difficult, if not impossible, to give any reason for their dispersed state and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> existence. Just now it must be confessed that they are the most implacable enemies of the Christian name; but their conversion is not on that account more unlikely or improbable than were events which have taken place of nearly equal importance a very few years ago. On the whole, the perfection of Christianity is a doctrine of reasonable <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a> to the church; and it is impossible for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADVOCATES">advocates</a> for natural religion to deny, that unlimited obedience to its precepts is consistent with the purest state of liberty and of happiness. This is the only millennium which the prophets and apostles, as we understand them, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> to the saints; but as men figuring in the very first ranks of learning have thought otherwise, we would not be too confident that our interpretation is just. Such of our readers as wish for further information, will find it in the works of Mr Mede, bishop Newton, Dr Whitby, and Dr Gill; and to those matterly writers we refer them for that satisfaction which in such an article as this cannot be given.

MILLEPEDES

Pages 34-34
or wood-louises, in zoology; a species of Oniscus. These insects are found in cellars, under stones, and in cold moist places; in the warmer countries they are rarely met with. Millepedes have a faint disagreeable smell, and a somewhat pungent, sweetish, nauseous taste. They have been highly celebrated in suppressions of urine, in all kinds of obstructions of the bowels, in the jaundice, weakness of sight, and a variety of other disorders. Whether they have any just title to these virtues is greatly to be doubted; thus much is certain, that their real effects come far short of the character usually give them.

MILLEPORA

Pages 34-34

in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a name by which Linnaeus distinguishes that genus of lithophytes, of a hard structure and full of holes, which are not stellate <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> radiated, and whose animal is the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HYDRA">hydra</a>, in which it differs from the madrepora, and comprehending 14 different <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>. In the millepora the animal which forms and inhabits it occupies the substance; and it is observed that the millepora grow upon one another; their little animals produce their spawn; which attaching itself either to the extremity of the body already formed, or underneath it, gives a different form to this production. Hence the various shapes of the millepora, which is composed of an infinite <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of the cells of those little insects, which all together exhibit different figures, though every particular cellula has its essential form, and the same dimensions, according to its own species.

MILLIARE

Pages 34-34
or Milliarium, a Roman mile, which consisted of 100 paces, milia passus, whence the name.

MILLION

Pages 34-34

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARITHMETIC">arithmetic</a>, the sum of ten hundred thousand, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> a thousand times a thousand. See Arithmetic.

MILLO

Pages 34-34

a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> of mount <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ZION">Zion</a> at its extremity; and therefore called Millo of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DAVID">David</a> (2 Chron. xxxii.), taken in with the wall that encompassed mount Zion. Uncertain whether Beth-Millo, (Judges ix. 20.) denotes a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it did, it lay near Sechem.

MILLOT

Pages 34-37

of the French academy, was born at Besançon <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1726, and was for some <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> a Jesuit. He was consecrated for the pulpit, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to preach after he left the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>: But the weakness of his <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>, his timidity, and the awkwardness of his manner, not permitting him to continue in this profession, he relinquished it, although he had preached Advent sermons at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VERSAILLES">Versailles</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LENT">Lent</a> sermons at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LUNEVILLE">Luneville</a>. The Marquis de Felino, minister of Parma, instituted an historical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> for the benefit of the young <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>; and, at the desire of M. le Duc de Nivernois, he gave the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of it to the Abbé Millot. The minister having occasioned a kind of rebellion among the people by some innovations which he had made in the state, the Abbé continued attached to the interests of his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PATRON">patron</a>, and would not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> him till the storm was blown over. When he was told that he would lose his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a> by this conduct, he replied, "My place is with a virtuous persecuted <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAN">man</a> who has been my benefactor; and that I shall never lose." At length, having filled the historical chair with <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> approbation, he returned to France, and was appointed preceptor to M. le Duc d'Enghien. In this situation he died, A.D. 1785, aged 59. The Abbé Millot did not shine in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>; he was <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLD">cold</a> and reserved in his manner; but everything he said was judicious, and exactly in point. D'Alembert said, that of all his acquaintance the Abbé Millot had the fewest prejudices and the least pretension. He composed several works, which are digested with great care, and written in a pure, simple, and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> style. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> are, 1. Éléments de l'Histoire de France, depuis Clovis jusque à <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIV. 3 vols in 12mo. The author, selecting the most curious and important facts, has suppressed every thing foreign to the subject; and has not only arranged the materials in their proper order, but chosen them with the greatest judgment. Querlon thought this the best <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABRIDGMENT">abridgment</a> which we have of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of France, and preferred it to that of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">President</a> Henault. 2. Éléments de l'Histoire d'Angleterre, depuis son origine sous les Romains, jusqu'à George II. 3 vols 12mo. In this valuable abridgment, the author satisfies, without tiring, his readers. It is all that is necessary for those who wish to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> a general knowledge of the English history, without entering minutely into its particular parts. 3. Éléments de l'Histoire Universelle, 9 vols. 12mo. A certain critic maintains, that this <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> is merely a counterfeit of Voltaire's general history. But this censure is altogether unjust. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> history in this work is wholly composed by the Abbé Millot; and, no less than the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a>, discovers his abilities in the choice of facts, in divesting them of useless circumstances, in relating them without <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a>, and in adorning them with judicious reflections. 4. L'Histoire... Milo, a celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATHLETE">athlete</a> of Crotona in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. His father's name was Diotimus. He early accustomed himself to carry the greatest burdens, and by degrees became a prodigy of strength. It is said that he carried on his shoulders a young bullock, four years old, for above forty yards; and afterwards killed it with one blow of his fist, and ate it up in one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>. He was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> times crowned at the Pythian games, and six at the Olympian. He presented himself a seventh time; but no one had the courage <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> boldness to enter the lists against him. He was one of the disciples of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PYTHAGORAS">Pythagoras</a>; and to his uncommon strength, it is said, the learned preceptor and his pupils owed their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>: The pillar which supported the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> of the school suddenly gave way; but Milo supported the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, and gave the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> and his auditors time to escape. In his old <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, Milo attempted to pull up a tree by the roots, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> it. He partly effected it; but his strength being gradually exhausted, the tree when half clefled re-united, and his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> remained pinched in the body of the tree. He was then alone; and, being unable to disentangle himself, he was devoured by the wild beasts of the place, about 500 years before the Christian era. Milo (T. Annius), a native of Lanuvium, who attempted to obtain the consulship at Rome by intrigue and seditious tumults. Clodius the tribune opposed his views; yet Milo would have succeeded but for the following event: As he was going into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, attended by his wife and a numerous retinue of gladiators and servants, he met on the Appian <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ROAD">road</a> his enemy Clodius, who was returning to Rome with three of his friends and some domestics completely armed.—A quarrel arose between the servants. Milo supported his attendants, and the dispute became general—Clodius received many severe wounds, and was obliged to retire to a neighbouring cottage. Milo pursued his enemy in his retreat, and ordered his servants to dispatch him. The body of the murdered tribune was carried to Rome, and exposed to public view. The enemies of Milo inveighed bitterly against the violence and barbarity with which the sacred person of a tribune had been treated. Cicero undertook the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of Milo; but the continual clamours of the friends of Clodius, and the sight of an armed soldiery, which surrounded the seat of judgment, so terrified the orator, that he forgot the greatest part of his arguments, and the defence he made was weak and injudicious.—Milo was condemned, and banished to Massilia. Cicero soon after sent his exiled friend a copy of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORATION">oration</a> which he had prepared for his defence, in the form in which we have it now; and Milo, after he had read it, exclaimed, O Cicero, hadst thou spoken before my accusers in these terms, Milo would not be now eating figs at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MARSEILLES">Marseilles</a>. The friendship and cordiality of Cicero and Milo were the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a> intimacy and familiar intercourse. It was to the successful labours of Milo that the orator was recalled from banishment, and restored to his friends. Milo, (anciently <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-MELOS">Melos</a>), an <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the Archipelago, about 50 miles in circumference, with a harbour, which is one of the largest in the Mediterranean. The principal town is of the same name as the island, and was prettily built, but abominably nasty; the houses are two stories <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, with flat roofs; and are built with a sort of pumice-<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, which is hard, blackish, and yet very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>. This island was formerly rich and populous. From the earliest times of antiquity it enjoyed pure <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>. The Athenians, not being able to persuade the Melians to declare in their favour in the Peloponnesian <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WAR">war</a>, made a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> upon the island, and attacked them vigorously. In two different expeditions they failed of their purpose: but returning with more numerous forces, they laid siege to Melos; and, obliging the besieged to surrender at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a>, put to the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> all the men who were able to bear arms. They spared only the women and children, and these they carried into <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of cruelty puts <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> to the blush, and disgraces the Athenian name. But war was then carried on with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of wild rage, unexampled in the present times. Republics know not how to <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a>, and always carry their vengeance to an extravagant height. When Lysander, the Lacedemonian general, came to give <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAW">law</a> to the Athenians, he expelled the colony which they had sent to Melos, and re-established the unfortunate remains of its original inhabitants. This island lost its liberty when Rome, aspiring to the empire of the world, conquered all the isles of the Archipelago. In the partition of the empire, it fell to the share of the eastern emperors, was governed by particular dukes, and was at last conquered by Soliman II. Since that <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, it has groaned under the yoke of Turkish despotism, and has lost its opulence and splendor. At the commencement of the present century, it boasted of 17 churches, and 11 chapels, and contained more than 20,000 inhabitants. It was very fertile in corn, wine, and fruits; and the whole space from the town to the harbour, which is nearly two miles, was laid out in beautiful gardens. M. Tournefort, who visited it in the year 1700, gives a fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of it. "The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, being constantly warmed by subterranean fires, produced almost without interruption plentiful crops of corn, barley, cotton, exquisite wines, and delicious melons. St Elias, the finest <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> in the island, and situated on the most elevated spot, is encircled with <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITRON">citron</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CEDAR">cedar</a>, and fig trees. Its gardens are watered by a copious <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>. Olive trees, of which there are but few in the other parts of the island, grow in great numbers around this monastery. The adjacent vineyards afford excellent wine. In a word, all the productions of the island are the very best of their kinds; its partridges, quails, kids, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAMBS">lambs</a>, are highly valued, and yet may be bought at a very cheap price." Were M. Tournefort to return to Milo, M. Savary assures us, he would no longer see the fine island which he has described. "He might still see <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a>, in the form of feathers, and fringed with silver thread, hanging from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a> of the caverns; pieces of pure sulphur filling the cliffs of the rocks; a variety of mineral <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>; hot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a>, (though these are now only a set of small dirty caves); the same subterraneous fires which in his days warmed the bottom of the earth, and were the cause of its extraordinary fertility: but instead of 5000 Greeks, all paying the capitation tax (a), he would now find no more than about 700 inhabitants on an island 18 leagues in circumference. He would figh to behold the finest lands lying uncultivated, and the most fertile valleys converted into marshes; of the gardens scarcely a vestige left; three-fourths of the town in ruins, and the inhabitants daily decreasing. In short, during the last 50 years, Milos has assumed a quite different appearance. The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a>, which the Turks propagate everywhere, has cut off one part of its inhabitants; the injudicious administration of the Porte, and the oppressive extortions of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Pacha, have destroyed the rest. At present, for want of hands, they cannot cut out a free channel for their waters, which stagnate in the valleys, corrupt, and infect the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> with their putrid exhalations. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-SALT">salt</a> marshes, of which there are numbers in the island, being equally neglected, produce the same effects. Add to these inconveniences, those sulphureous exhalations which arise all over the island, and by which the inhabitants of Milos are afflicted with dangerous fevers during three-fourths of the year. Perhaps they may be obliged to forsake their country. Every countenance is <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a>, and livid; and none bears any marks of good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>. The prudent traveller <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a> be careful to spend but a very short time in this unwholesome country, unless he chooses to expose himself to the danger of catching a fever. To <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> over-night, or to spend but one day in the island, is often enough to occasion his being attacked with that distemper. "Yet (continues our author) a judicious and enlightened <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> might expel those evils which ravage Milos. Its first care would be to establish a lazaret, and to prohibit vessels whose crews or cargoes are infected with the plague from landing. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANALS">Canals</a> might next be cut, to drain the marshes, whose exhalations are so pernicious. The island would then be re-peopled. The fulphureous vapours are not the most noxious. These prevailed equally in ancient times, yet the island was then very populous. M. Tournefort, who travelled through it a time less distant from the period when it was conquered by the Turks, and when they had not yet had time to lay it waste, reckons the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of its inhabitants (as we have said) at about 20,000. The depopulation of Milos is therefore to be ascribed to the delapidation of the Porte, and its detestable <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol18.html#article-POLICE">police</a>." The women of Milos, once so celebrated for their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, are now fallow, unhealthy, and disgustingly ugly; and render themselves still more hideous by their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUTHERLAND">Sutherland</a>'s dres, which is a kind of loose jacket, with a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WHITE">white</a> p. 146 coat and petticoat, that scarcely covers two-thirds of their thighs, barely meeting the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-STOCKING">stocking</a> above the knee. Their hind <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> hangs <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the back in a number of plaits; that on the fore-part of the head is combed down each side of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FACE">face</a>, and terminated by a small stiff curl, which is even with the lower part of the cheek. All the inhabitants are Greeks, for the Turks are not fond of trusting themselves in the small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>; but every <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> the captain <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASHAW">bashaw</a> goes round with a squadron to keep them in subjection, and to collect the revenue. When the Russians made themselves masters of the Archipelago during the late war, many of the islands declared in their favour; but being abandoned by the peace, they were so severely mulcted by the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GRAND">Grand</a> Signior, that they have professed a determination to remain perfectly quiet in future. As the Turks, however, do not think them worth a garrison, and will not trust them with arms and ammunition, all those which the Russians may choose to invade will be obliged to submit. The two <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POINTS">points</a> which form the entrance of the harbour, crowding each other, render it imperceptible until you are <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to it. Thus, while you are perfectly secure within it, you find great difficulty in getting out, particularly in a northerly <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>; and as no trade is carried on except a little in corn and salt, Milos would scarcely ever be visited, were it not that, being the first island which one makes in the Archipelago, the pilots have chosen it for their residence. They live in a little town on the top of a high rock, which, from its situation and appearance, is called the Caffle.—Partridges still abound in this island; and are so cheap, that you may buy one for a charge of powder only. The peasants get them by standing behind a portable screen, with a small aperture in the centre, in which they place the muzzle of their piece, and then draw (a) Grown up men are the only persons who pay the capitation tax. Therefore, by adding to the number of 5000 who paid the tax, the women, boys, and girls, we find that Milos, in the days of Tournefort, contained at least 20,000 souls. Miltiades the partridges by a call. When a sufficient number are collected, they fire among them, and generally kill from four to seven at a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a>; but even this method of getting them is so expensive, from the scarcity of ammunition, that the people can never afford to shoot them, except when there are gentlemen in the island, from whom they can beg a little powder and shot. Milo is 60 miles <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of Candia; and the town is situated in E. Long. 25° 15'. N. Lat. 36° 27'. MILSTONE. See MILLSTONE.

MILT

Pages 37-37
or Milt; in href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL">natural history, the soft roe in fishes; thus called from its yielding, by expression, a whitish juice resembling milk. See ROE. The milt is properly the seed or spermatic part of the male fish. The milt of a carp is reckoned a choice bit. It consists of two long whitish irregular bodies, each included in a very thin fine membrane. M. Petit considers them as the testicles of the fish wherein the seed is preserved; the lower part, next the anus, he takes for the vesicule seminales.

MILTHORP

Pages 37-37

a port-town of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WESTMORELAND">Westmoreland</a>, at the mouth of the Can, five miles from <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KENDAL">Kendal</a>. It is the only <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>; and goods are brought hither in small vessels from Grange in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LANCASHIRE">Lancashire</a>. Here are two <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a>. It has a market on Friday, and a fair on Old May-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>; and there is a good <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-STONE">stone</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> over the river Betha, which runs through the town.

MILTIADES

Pages 37-38

an Athenian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a>, son of Cypselus. He obtained a victory in a chariot <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-RACE">race</a> at the Olympic games. He led a colony of Athenians to the Cheroneus. The causes of this appointment are striking and singular. The Thracian Dolonci, harassed by a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WAR">war</a> with the Abysynthians, were directed by the oracle of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DELPHI">Delphi</a> to take for their <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">king</a> the first <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAN">man</a> they met in their return home, who invited them to come under his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> and partake his entertainments. This was Miltiades, whom the appearance of the Dolonci, with their strange arms and garments, had struck. He invited them to his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, and was made acquainted with the commands of the oracle. He obeyed; and when the oracle of Delphi had approved a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> the choice of the Dolonci, he departed for the Cheroneus, and was invested by the inhabitants with sovereign power. The first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> he took was to stop the further incursions of the Abysynthians, by <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> a strong wall across the Isthmus. When he had established himself at home, and fortified his dominions against foreign invasion, he turned his arms against Lampacus. His expedition was unsuccessful; he was taken in an ambush, and made prisoner. His friend Croesus king of Lydia was informed of his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a>, and procured his release. He lived few years after he had recovered his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>. As he had no issue, he left his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> and possessions to Stefagoras the son of Cimon, who was his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> by the same mother. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of Miltiades was greatly honoured by the Dolonci, and they regularly celebrated festivals and exhibited shows in commemoration of a man to whom they owed their greatness and preservation. Miltiades, the son of Cimon, and brother of Stefagoras mentioned in the preceding article, was Miltiades, some time after the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of the latter, who died without issue, sent by the Athenians with one ship to take possession of the Cheroneus. At his arrival Miltiades appeared mournful, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> lamenting the recent death of his brother. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> inhabitants of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> visited the new governor to console with him; but their confidence in his sincerity proved fatal to them. Miltiades seized their persons, and made himself <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> in Cheroneus. To strengthen himself, he married Hegesipyle, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Olorus the king of the Thracians. His triumph was short. In the third year of his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, his dominions were threatened by an invasion of the Scythian Nomades, whom <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DARIUS">Darius</a> had some time before irritated by entering their country. He fled before them; but as their hostilities were of short <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>, he was soon restored to his kingdom. Three years after, he left Cheroneus; and set sail for <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, where he was received with <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> applause. He was present at the celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MARATHON">Marathon</a>; in which all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> officers ceded their power to him, and left the event of the battle to depend upon his superior abilities. He obtained an important victory over the more numerous forces of his adversaries. Some time after, Miltiades was intrusted with a fleet of 70 ships, and ordered to punish those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> which had revolted to the Persians. He was successful at first; but a sudden report that the Persian fleet was coming to attack him, changed his operations as he was besieging Paros. He raised the siege, and returned to Athens. He was accused of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TREASON">treason</a>, and particularly of holding correspondence with the enemy. The falsity of these accusations might have appeared, if Miltiades had been able to come into the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>. But a wound which he had received before Paros detained him at home; and his enemies, taking advantage of his absence, became more eager in their accusations, and louder in their clamours. He was condemned to death; but the rigour of his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> was retarded on the recollection of his great services to the Athenians, and he was put into prison till he had paid a fine of 50 talents to the state. His inability to discharge to great a sum detained him in confinement; and his wounds becoming incurable, he died a prisoner about 489 years before the Christian era. His body was ransomed by his son Cimon; who was obliged to borrow and pay the 50 talents, to give his father a decent <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BURIAL">burial</a>.—The accusations against Miltiades were probably the more readily believed by his countrymen, when they remembered how he made himself absolute in Cheroneus; and in condemning the barbarity of the Athenians towards a general, who was the source of their <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> prosperity, we must remember the jealousy which ever reigns among a free and independent people, and how watchful they are in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> which they see wrested from others by violence. Cornelius Nepos has written the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of Miltiades the son of Cimon; but his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> is incongruous and unintelligible, from his confounding the actions of the son of Cimon with those of the son of Cypselus. Greater reliance is to be placed on the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NARRATION">narration</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a>, whose veracity is confirmed, and who was indisputably better informed and more capable of giving an account of the the life and exploits of men who flourished in his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> and of which he could see the living monuments. Herodotus was born about six years after the famous battle of Marathon; and C. Nepos, as a writer of the Augustan age, flourished about 450 years after the age of the father of history.

MILTON

Pages 38-40

the most illustrious of the English poets, was descended of a genteel family, seated at a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of their own name, viz. Milton, in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OXFORDSHIRE">Oxfordshire</a>. He was born <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 9, 1608, and received his first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> under the care of his parents, assisted by a private <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a>. He afterwards passed some <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> at St Paul's school, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONDON">London</a>; in which <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CITY">city</a> his father had settled, being engaged in the business of a scrivener. At the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 17, he was sent to Christ's <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>; where he made a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> progress in all parts of academical learning; but his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> delight was in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>. In 1628, he proceeded bachelor of arts, having performed his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> for it with great applause. His father designed him for the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>; but the young <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to the muse was so strong, that it became impossible to engage him in any other pursuits. In 1637, he took the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of arts; and having now spent as much time in the university as became a person who determined not to engage in any of the three <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PROFESSIONS">professions</a>, he left the college, greatly regretted by his acquaintance, but highly displeased with the usual method of training up youth there for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>; and being much out of humour with the public administration of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> affairs, he grew dissatisfied with the established form of church-<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, and disliked the whole <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of education practised in the university. His parents, who now dwelt at Horton, near Colnbrook, in Buckinghamshire, received him with unaltered affection, notwithstanding he had thwarted their views of providing for him in the church, and they amply indulged him in his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of retirement; wherein he enriched his mind with the choicest flores of Grecian and Roman literature: and his poems of Comus, L'Allegro, Il Penseroso, and Lycidas, all wrote at this time, would have been sufficient, had he never produced any thing more considerable, to have transmitted his fame to latest posterity. However, he was not so absorbed in his studies as not to make frequent excursions to London; neither did so much excellence <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> unnoticed among his neighbours in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, with the most distinguished of whom he sometimes chose to relax his mind, and improve his acquaintance with the world as well as with books. After five years spent in this manner, he obtained his father's permission to travel for farther improvement.—At <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> he became acquainted with the celebrated Hugo Grotius; and from thence travelling into <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, he was everywhere cared for by persons of the most eminent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> and learning. Upon his return home, he set up a genteel academy in Aldergate-street.—In 1641, he began to draw his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PEN">pen</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of the Presbyterian party; and the next year he married the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Richard Powell, Esq., of Forest-Hill in Oxfordshire. This lady, however, whether from a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> on account of party, her father being a zealous royalist, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> some other cause, soon thought proper to return to her relations; which so incensed her husband, that he resolved never to take her again, and wrote and published several tracts in defence of the doctrine and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> of divorce. He even made his addresses to another lady; but this incident proved the means of a reconciliation with Mrs Milton. In 1644, he wrote his Tract upon Education; and the restraint on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of the press being <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, he wrote boldly and nobly against that restraint. In 1645, he published his juvenile poems; and about two years after, on the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his father, he took a smaller <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">High</a> Holburn, the back of which opened into <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a>'s-Inn Fields.—Here he quietly prosecuted his studies, till the fatal catastrophe and death of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I.; on which occasion he published his <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TENURE">Tenure</a> of Kings and Magistrates, in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JUSTIFICATION">justification</a> of the fact. He was now taken into the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the commonwealth, and made Latin secretary to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of state, who resolved neither to write to others abroad, nor to receive any answers, except in the Latin tongue, which was <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to them all. The famous news papers coming out about the same time, our author, by command, wrote and published his Iconologia the same year. It was also by order of his masters, backed by the reward of 1000l. that, in 1651, he published his celebrated piece, entitled Pro Populo Anglicano Defensio. "A Defence of the People of England, in answer to Salmasius's Defence of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">King</a>?" which performance spread his fame over all <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>.—He now dwelt in a pleasant house, with a garden, in Petty France, Westminster, opening into St James's <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PARK">Park</a>. In 1652, he buried his wife, who died not <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a> after the delivery of her fourth child; and about the same time he also lost his eye-sight, by a quinta ferentia, which had been growing upon him many years. Cromwell took the reins of government into his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> in the year 1653; but Milton still held his office. His leisure-hours he employed in prosecuting his studies; wherein he was so far from being discouraged by the loss of his sight, that he even conceived hopes this misfortune would add new vigour to his genius; which, in fact, seems to have been the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CASE">case</a>.—Thus animated, he again ventured upon matrimony: his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SECOND">second</a> lady was the daughter of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WOODSTOCK">Woodstock</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HACKNEY">Hackney</a>: she died in childbirth about a year after. On the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEPOSITION">deposition</a> of the protector, Richard Cromwell, and on the return of the long parliament, Milton being still continued secretary, he appeared again in print; pleading for a farther reformation of the laws relating to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>; and, during the anarchy that ensued, he drew up several schemes for re-establishing the commonwealth, exerting all his faculties to prevent the return of Charles II. England's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESTINY">destiny</a>, however, and Charles's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a>, prevailing, our author chose to consult his safety, and retired to a friend's house in Bartholomew-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CLOSE">Close</a>. A particular prosecution was intended against him; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> esteem to which his admirable genius and extraordinary accomplishments entitled him, had raised him so many friends, even among those of the opposite party, that he was included in the general amnesty. This storm over, he married a third wife, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, daughter of Mr Minshall a Chehire gentleman; and not long after he took a house in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTILLERY">Artillery</a> Walk, leading to Bunhill-Fields. This was his last stage: here he sat <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DOWN">down</a> for a longer continuance than he had been able to do anywhere; and though he had lost his fortune (for every thing belonging to him went to wreck at the Restoration), he did not lose his <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for literature, but continued his studies with almost as much ardour as ever; and applied himself particularly to the finishing his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>, the Paradise Lost; one of the noblest poems that ever was produced by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> genius.—It was published in 1667, and his Paradise Regained came out in 1670.—This latter work fell short of the excellence of the former production; although, were it not for the transcendent merit of Paradise Lost, the second <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> would doubtless have stood foremost in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of English epic poems. After this he published many pieces in prose; for which we refer our readers to the edition of his Historical, Poetical, and Miscellaneous Works, printed by Millar, in 2 vols 4to, in 1753. In 1674, this great <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAN">man</a> paid the last debt to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> at his house in Bunhill-fields, in the 66th year of his age; and was interred on the 12th of November, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCEL">chancel</a> of St Giles's, Cripplegate.—A decent monument was erected to his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>, in 1737, in Westminster <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a>, by Mr Benfon, one of the auditors of the imprest.—As to his person, it was remarkably handsome; but his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> was tender, and by no means equal to his incessant application to his studies.—Though greatly reduced in his circumstances, yet he died worth £1500 l. in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, beside his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a> goods.—He had no son; but left behind him three daughters, whom he had by his first wife. Milton, the name of several places in England; particularly, Milton, or Middleton, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DORSETSHIRE">Dorsetshire</a>, south-west of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLANDFORD">Blandford</a>, near the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ROAD">road</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DORCHESTER">Dorchester</a>, 114 miles from London. It is chiefly noted for its abbey, built by King Athelstan. The church stands near the south side of the abbey. It is a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and magnificent pile of Gothic <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, and contains several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> monuments. Here is an alms-house for six people, who have 12s. a-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a>, and three yards of cloth for a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GOWN">gown</a>, one <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of shoes and stockings, and 10s. each on St Thomas's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> yearly. Here is a free-school, and a market on Tuesdays. Milton, in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>, near Sittinbourn and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> of Sheppey, 6 miles <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west of Faversham, and 40 from London. It is also called Middleton from its situation near the middle of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>, i.e., from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEPTFORD">Deptford</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DOWNS">Downs</a>. The kings of Kent had a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> here, which was castellated, and stood below the church; but was burnt down in Edward the Confessor's time by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-EARL">Earl</a> Godwin, &c. Its church stands near a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MILE">mile</a> off. On approaching the town up the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>, by the East-Swale, it seems hid among the creeks: yet it is a large town; and has a considerable market on Saturdays, and a fair on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 24. The oysters taken hereabouts are the most famous of any in Kent. This town is governed by a portreeve, chosen yearly on St James's-day, who supervises the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WEIGHTS_AND_MEASURES">weights and <a class</a>="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> all over the hundred of Milton. Milton, in Kent, a mile on the east side of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GRAVESEND">Gravesend</a>, was incorporated with it in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> Elizabeth, by the name of the portreeve, jurats, and inhabitants of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of Gravesend and Milton. King Henry VIII. raised a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PLATFORM">platform</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLOCK">block</a>-house here, for the defence both of this town and Gravesend, and the command of the river. It has a fair Jan. 25. MILVIUS Molvius, or Mulvius, Pons; a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> on the Tiber, built by Emilius Scaurus the censor, in the time of Sylla, at two miles distance from the city, on the Via Flaminia, and repaired by Augustus. From this bridge the ambassadors of the Allobroges were brought back to Rome, by Cicero's management, and made a discovery of Catiline's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSPIRACY">conspiracy</a> (Sallust). Near it Maxentius was defeated by Constantine (Eutropius). Now called Ponte <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MOLE">Mole</a>. Milvius, in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">ornithology</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of Falco. Mimi, Mimes, in the ancient <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a>, were buffoons or mimics, who entertained the people by taking off certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, using such gestures as suited the persons or subjects they represented. There were on the Roman stage <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> performers of this kind called mima. The word is derived from mimauai, I imitate. Some of the mimi acted their parts to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> of the tibia; these they called mimauai. Mimi were also a kind of farces or ludicrous comedies, generally performed by one person. They had no acts, nor any exordium.—The mimi were introduced upon the Roman stage long after comedy and tragedy had arrived at their full perfection. The <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTOR">actor</a> wore no mask, but smeared his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FACE">face</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOOT">soot</a>, was dressed in lambkin, wore garlands of ivy, and carried a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASKET">basket</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> and herbs, in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a>, and diverted the audience with apish tricks and ridiculous dances. This was the state of the mimi soon after their first introduction; but they underwent many alterations, which it would take up too much room to relate, and which are not of sufficient importance to justify a detailed account. See Pantomimes. Mimesis, in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a>, the imitating the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> and gestures of another person. Minnermus, an ancient poet and musician, flourished about the beginning of the 6th century B.C. He was of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SMYRNA">Smyrna</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> with Solon. Athenaeus gives him the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of pentameter <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>. His elegies, of which only a few fragments are preserved, were so much admired in antiquity, that Horace preferred them to those of Callimachus. He composed a poem of this kind, as we learn from Paulanias, upon the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> fought between the people of Smyrna and the Lydians, under Gyges. He likewise was author of a poem in elegiac verse, quoted by Strabo, which he entitled Nanno, and in which we may suppose he chiefly celebrated a young and beautiful girl of that name, who, according to Athenaeus, was a player on the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FLUTE">flute</a>, with whom he was enamoured in his old age. With respect to love matters, according to Propertius, his verses were more valuable than all the writings of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>. Pluris in amore <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-VALET">valet</a> Minnermi versus Homero. Lib. i. Eleg. 9. v. 11. And Horace bears testimony to his abilities, in describing that seducing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>: Si Minnermus uti cenat, sine amore jocisque Nil est jucundum, vivas in amore jocisque. Epift. VI. Lib. i. v. 65. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a>, as wise Minnermus said, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">Life</a> unblest with love and joy Ranks us with the senseless dead, Let these gifts each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> employ. Alluding to some much admired <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> of this Greek poet, which have been preserved by Stobaeus. Tis the bliss, tis the joy, tis the peace, tis the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a>, &c. What is life and all its <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a>, If love and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> be denied? Snatch, snatch me hence, ye fates, whene'er The am'rous bliss I cease to share. Oh let us crop each fragrant flow'r While youth and vigour give us pow'r; For frozen age <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a> soon destroy The force to give or take a joy; And then, a prey to pain and care, Detected by the young and fair, The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>'s blest beams will hateful grow, And only shine on scenes of wo.

MIMOSA

Pages 40-40

the sensitive plant: A genus of the polygamia order, belonging to the monoecea class of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 33d order, Lomentaceae. The hermaphrodite calyx is quinquedentate; the corolla quinquefid; there are five <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> more stamens, one <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PISTIL">pistil</a>, and a legumen: The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MALE">male</a> calyx is quinquedentate; the corolla quinquefid; with five, ten, or more stamens.

MINA

Pages 47-47
or MANEH, a species of money, which properly signifies one part or ounce. It is observed that this word occurs only in the books of Kings, Chronicles, Ezra, and Ezekiel. This prophet (xlv. 12.) tells us, that the minah or maneh was valued at 60 shekels, which in gold make of our English money about £4 pounds, and in silver almost seven pounds. Thus for the Hebrew maneh. But the Greek or Attic mina, which is probably that mentioned in the books of the Maccabees and in the New Testament, is valued at 100 drachmae, or about 21. 17 s. sterling. There was also a lesser mina, which was valued at 75 drachmae.

MINAGNGHINIM

Pages 47-47

a pulsatile <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> of music, among the Hebrews, which was a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TABLE">table</a> of wood, fitted with a handle; over this table was stretched an <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-IRON">iron</a> chain, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> hempen <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CORD">cord</a>, passing thro' balls of wood or braids, which struck against the table, when the instrument was shook, and occasioned a clear <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOUND">sound</a>, which might be heard at a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> distance. See Kircher's <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of it in Plate CCCXIV.

MINCHA

Pages 47-47

in the Jewish customs, offerings of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MEAL">meal</a>, cakes, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> biscuits, made in the temple of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>. The Seventy have sometimes preferred this word in their translation; but instead of mincha they read manaa, which doubtless was the received <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRONUNCIATION">pronunciation</a> in their <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a>. We find manaa in the same <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, in Baruch i. 10. Levit. ii. 3. &c. See the Greek of Jerem. xvii. 26. Dan. ii. 46. 2 Kings viii. 5, 9, xvi. 7. xx. 12. 2 Chron. vii. 7. Nehem. xiii. 5, 9, &c.

MINCHING-HAMPTON

Pages 47-47

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-GLOUCESTERSHIRE">Gloucestershire</a>, 20 miles from Bath and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BRISTOL">Bristol</a>, and near 90 from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, with a market on Tuesdays, and two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> is pretty <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, being bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the Stroud, and on the south by the brook Avoning; and has 12 hamlets belonging to it, with a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMON">common</a> called Amberley. Here is a good large rectory <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, built in form of a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>, and worth 200l. a-year. Near it are very large <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAMPS">camps</a>, with deep trenches; and near <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DUNKIRK">Dunkirk</a> in this parish are fulling <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a>.

MINCIUS

Pages 47-47

a river of the Transpadana; running from, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> rather transmitted through, the Lacus Benacus, from <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NORTH">north</a> to south, into the Padus; but originally rising in the Rhaetian <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a>. Now Mincio or Menzo, running through the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MANTUA">Mantua</a> into the Po.

MINDANOA

Pages 47-48
or MAGINDANAO, a large island of Asia in the East Indies, and one of the Philippines; Vizaghi, 160 miles in length, and 120 in breadth. The interior parts contain several chains of lofty mountains, between which are extensive plains, where vast herds of cattle roam at large in the most delicious pastures. Several deep valleys also intersect, as it were, certain parts of the country, through which, during the rainy season, vast torrents pour from the mountains, and force their impetuous way to the sea. The rains and vapours which lodge in the plains diffuse themselves into meandering rivulets, and, collecting a variety of small streams in their course, approach the sea in the form of considerable rivers.—The sovereign of Magindanao is a powerful prince, and has several inferior chiefs, who acknowledg... acknowledge him as their head. Nevertheless, there are others of them who refuse submission to him, and are consequently in a continual state of war; so that peace, at least, does not appear to be one of the blessings of this island. The Spaniards, indeed, assert their right to the entire dominion of Magindanao; but it is mere assertion; for though they have forts, &c., on the island, it is by no means in a state of subjection to their nation. The air is esteemed salubrious, particularly in the vicinity of the sea. The heat there is not, in any degree, so intense as might be expected in a country which is situated on the very verge of the torrid zone. The prevalence of the easterly winds, in that part of the coasts which is washed by the Pacific Ocean, renders the air cool and pleasant, the trade-wind blowing incessantly on its shores. It acts, indeed, with so much power as to sweep the whole breadth of the island; and though in its passage it loses much of its strength, it retains a sufficient degree of force to afford refreshing breezes to the inhabitants of the western shore. The interior parts are much colder, from a very cloudy atmosphere, which frequently hangs over the summits of the mountains in thick and humid vapours. The soil, which is very exuberant, is suited to the cultivation of the whole vegetable tribes. Rice is produced in the greatest abundance; a peck, or 133 pounds, may be purchased for a Spanish dollar. Every part of the island abounds with buffaloes, cows, hogs, goats, &c. It affords also great variety of fowls, and a species of duck, whose head is of a fine scarlet colour. Here are also a small breed of horses, remarkable for their spirit. The natives, however, principally employ buffaloes in the various branches of husbandry and agriculture. The city of Magindanao is situated on the southeast side of the island, has a river capable of admitting small vessels, and carries on a considerable trade with Manila, Sooloo, Borneo, and the Moluccas. Their exports are rice, tobacco, beeswax, and spices; in return for which they receive coarse cloths of Coromandel, China ware, and opium. The village or town of Samboangan is situated on the banks of a small rivulet, which empties itself immediately into the sea, and is agreeably shaded by groves of cocoa-trees. The number of its inhabitants are about 1000, among which are included the officers, soldiers, and their respective families. In its environs there are several small look-out houses, erected on posts of twelve feet high, in all of which a constant guard is kept; so that it appears as if the Spaniards were in a continual state of enmity with the natives. The houses are built of those simple materials which are of very general use in the eastern seas. They are erected on posts, and built of bamboo, covered with mats; the lower apartments serve for their hogs, cattle, and poultry, and the upper ones are occupied by the family."

MINDEN

Pages 48-48
