It makes a venerable and majestic <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, even in its present state of decay, having in it a large Gothic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>, some other churches and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a>, the governor's <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, and an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a>, which is no contemptible pile.—There are in it 600 houses, which, before the seat of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> and the courts of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> were removed to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MAHON">Mahon</a>, were fully inhabited; and there are still more gentlemen's families here than in all the rest of the island. It hath a port commodious enough for the vessels employed in the trade of this country, which, though in the possession of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> power, is less than it formerly was. It is still, in the style of our officers, the best <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> (and there are none bad) in the country; and if there was a civil government, and the place made a free port, the best judges are of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> it would very soon become a flourishing place again; and the fortifications, if it should be found necessary, might then also be easily restored and improved. The termino of Fererias is the next, a narrow slip reaching from sea to sea, and the country little cultivated; it is therefore united to Mercadal. In this last termino stands Mont-toro in the very centre of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a>, and the highest ground, some say the only mountain in it; on the summit of which there is a convent, where even in the hottest months the monks enjoy a cool air, and at all times a most delightful prospect. About six miles north from Mont-toro stands the castle that covers Port Fornelles, which is a very spacious harbour on the east side of the island. There are in it shoals and foul ground, which, to those who are unacquainted with them, render it difficult and dangerous; yet the packets bound from Mahon to Marfeilles frequently take shelter therein; and while the Spaniards were in possession of the isle, large ships and men of war frequented it. At a small distance from this lies another harbour called Adaia, which runs far into the land; but being reputed unsafe, and being so near Fornelles, is at present useless. The country about it is, however, said to be the pleasantest and wholesomest spot in the island, and almost the only one plentifully supplied with excellent spring-water; so that the gardens are well laid out, and the richest and finest fruits grow here in the highest perfection. Adaia is the next termino, in which there is nothing remarkable. remarkable but the capital of the same name, well situated on an eminence, in a pleasant and tolerably cultivated country. The termino of Mahon, at the south-east end of the island, is at present the most considerable of them all, containing about 60,000 English acres, and nearly one-half of the inhabitants in Minorca. The town of Mahon derives its name from the Carthaginian general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGO">Mago</a>, who is universally allowed to be its founder.—It stands on an eminence on the west side of the harbour, the ascent pretty steep. There are in it a large <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, three convents, the governor's palace, and some other public edifices. It is large, but the streets are winding, narrow, and ill-paved. The fortres of St <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> stands near the entrance of the harbour, which it covers, is very spacious, of great strength, with subterranean works to protect the garrison from bombs, large magazines, and whatever else is necessary to render it a complete fortification, and hath a numerous and well-disposed <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a>. Port Mahon is allowed to be the finest harbour in the Mediterranean, about 90 fathoms wide at its entrance, but within very large and safe, stretching a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> or more into the land. Beneath the town of Mahon there is a very fine quay, one end of which is reserved for the ships of war, and furnished with all the accommodations necessary for careening and refitting them; the other serves for merchantmen. On the other side the harbour is <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MOLA">Mola</a>, where it is generally agreed a fortres might be constructed which would be impregnable, as the castle of St Philip was esteemed before we took it, and bestowed so much money upon it, that, though some works were erected at Cape Mola, it was not judged proper to proceed in the fortifications there at a fresh expense; at least this is the only reason that hath been assigned. Minorca was taken by the Spaniards during the American war, and is now in their possession.

MINORS

Pages 177-177
or FRIERS MINOR, an appellation which the Franciscans assume, out of shew of humility; calling themselves freres minorés, i.e. lesser brothers, and sometimes minorites. There is also an order of regular minors at Naples, which was established in the year 1588, and confirmed by Sixtus V.

MINOS

Pages 177-177

a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a>, son of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EUROPA">Europa</a>. He flourished about 1432 years before the Christian era. He gave laws to his subjects, which still remained in full force in the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a>, about 1000 years after the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LEGISLATOR">legislator</a>. His <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> and moderation procured him the appellation of the favourite of the gods, the confident of Jupiter, and the wife legislator, in every <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>; and, according to the poets, he was rewarded for his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-EQUITY">equity</a> after death with the office of supreme and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> judge in the infernal regions. In this capacity he is represented sitting in the middle of the shades, and holding a sceptre in his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. The dead plead their different causes before him; and the impartial judge shakes the fatal urn, which is filled with the destinies of mankind. He married Ithona, by whom he had Lycaetes, who was the father of Minos II. Minos II. was a son of Lycaetes, the son of Minos I. and king of Crete. He married Pasiphae, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Sol and Perseis, and by her he had many children. He increased his paternal dominions by the conquest of the neighbouring <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>; but showed himself cruel in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WAR">war</a> which he carried against the Athenians, who had put to death his son <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANDROGEUS">Androgeus</a>. He took <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-MEGARA">Megara</a> by the treachery of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SCYLLA">Scylla</a>; and not satisfied with victory, he obliged the vanquished to bring him yearly to Crete <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> chosen boys and the same <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of virgins to be devoured by the Minotaur. This bloody tribute was at last abolished when <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THESEUS">Theseus</a> had destroyed the monster. When Daedalus, whose industry and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> had fabricated the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LABYRINTH">labyrinth</a>, and whose imprudence in afflicting Pasiphae in the gratification of her unnatural desires, had offended Minos, fled from the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of his confinement with wings, and arrived safe in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>; the incensed monarch pursued the offender, resolved to punish his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-INFIDELITY">infidelity</a>. Cocalus, king of Sicily, who had hospitably received Daedalus, entertained his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> guest with dissembled friendship; and, that he might not deliver to him a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAN">man</a> whose ingenuity and abilities he so well knew, he put Minos to death. Minos died about 35 years before the Trojan war. He was father of Androgeus, Glaucus, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEUCALION">Deucalion</a>; and two daughters, Phaedra and Ariadne. Many authors have confounded the two Minoes, the grandfather and the grandson; but <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>, Plutarch, and Diodorus, prove plainly that they were two different persons.

MINOTAUR

Pages 177-177

a celebrated monster, half a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAN">man</a> and half a bull, according to this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> of Ovid, Semibovemque virum, semivirumque bovem. It was the fruit of Pasiphae's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMOUR">amour</a> with a bull. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MINOS">Minos</a> refused to sacrifice a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WHITE">white</a> bull to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol7.html#article-NEPTUNE">Neptune</a>, an animal which he had received from the god for that purpose. This offended Neptune, and he made Pasiphae the wife of Minos enamoured of this fine bull, which had been refused to his altars. Daedalus prostituted his talents in being subservient to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>'s unnatural desires; and by his means, Pasiphae's horrible passions were gratified, and the Minotaur came into the world. Minos confined in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LABYRINTH">labyrinth</a> this monster, which convinced the world of his wife's lasciviousness, and reflected disgrace upon his family. The Minotaur usually devoured the chosen young men and maidens which the tyranny of Minos yearly exacted from the Athenians. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THESEUS">Theseus</a> delivered his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> from this tribute, when it had fallen to his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a> to be sacrificed to the voracity of the Minotaur; and by means of Ariadne, the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>, he destroyed the monster, and made his escape from the windings of the labyrinth.—The fabulous <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a> of the Minotaur, and of the infamous <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> of Pasiphae with a favourite bull, has been often explained. Some suppose that Pasiphae was enamoured of one of her husband's courtiers called Taurus; and that Daedalus favoured the passions of the queen, by suffering his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> to become the retreat of the two lovers. Pasiphae some <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> after brought twins into the world, one of whom greatly resembled Minos and the other Taurus; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> resemblance of their countenance with that of their supposed fathers, originated their name, and consequently the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FABLE">fable</a> of the Minotaur.

MINOW

Pages 177-177

a very small <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of cyprinus, so well known that it needs no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>.

MINSTREL

Pages 178-179

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TERM">term</a> for a finger and instrumental performer. The word minstrel is derived from the French menestrier, and was not in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> here before the Norman conquest. It is remarkable, that our old monkish historians do not use the word citharaedus, cantator, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> the like, to express a minstrel in Latin; but either mimus, histrio, joculator, or some other word that implies jesture. Hence it should seem that the minstrels set off their singing by mimicry or <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a>; or, according to Dr <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BROWN">Brown</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a>, united the powers of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-MELODY">melody</a>, poem, and dance. The Saxons, as well as the ancient Danes, had been accustomed to hold men of this profession in the highest reverence. Their skill was considered as something divine, their persons were deemed sacred, their attendance was solicited by kings, and they were everywhere loaded with honours and rewards. In short, poets and their art were held among them in that rude admiration which is ever shown by an ignorant people to such as excel them in intellectual accomplishments. When the Saxons were converted to Christianity, in proportion as letters prevailed among them, this rude admiration began to abate, and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> was no longer a peculiar profession. The poet and the minstrel became two persons. Poetry was cultivated by men of letters indiscriminately, and many of the most popular rhymes were composed amidst the leisure and retirement of monasteries. But the minstrels <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> a distinct order of men, and got their livelihood by singing verses to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARP">harp</a> at the houses of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a>. There they were still hospitably and respectfully received, and retained many of the honours shown to their predecessors the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARDS">Bards</a> and Scalds. And indeed, though some of them only recited the compositions of others, many of them still composed songs themselves; and all of them could probably invent a few stanzas on occasion. There is no doubt but most of the old heroic ballads were produced by this order of men. For although some of the larger metrical romances might come from the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PEN">pen</a> of the monks or others, yet the smaller narratives were probably composed by the minstrels who sang them. From the amazing variations which occur in different copies of these old pieces, it is evident they made no scruple to alter each other's productions, and the reciter added or omitted whole stanzas according to his own fancy or convenience. In the early ages, as is hinted above, this profession was held in great reverence among the Saxon tribes, as well as among their Danish brethren. This appears from two remarkable facts in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, which show that the same arts of music and song were equally admired among both nations, and that the privileges and honours conferred upon the professors of them were <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to both; as it is well known their customs, manners, and even <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, were not in those times very dissimilar. When <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">King</a> Alfred the Great was desirous to learn the true situation of the Danish <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, which had invaded his realm, he assumed the dress and character of a minstrel; and taking his harp, and only one attendant (for in the earliest times it was not unusual for a minstrel to have a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> to carry his harp), he went with the utmost security into the Danish <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>. Minstrel! And though he could not but be known to be a Saxon, the character he had assumed procured him a hospitable reception; he was admitted to entertain the king at <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, and stayed among them <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a> enough to contrive that assault which afterwards destroyed them. This was in the year 878. About 60 years after, a Danish king made use of the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISGUISE">disguise</a> to explore the camp of King Athelstan. With his harp in his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and dressed like a minstrel, Anlaff king of the Danes went among the Saxon tents, and taking his stand near the king's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAVILION">pavilion</a>, began to play, and was immediately admitted. There he entertained Athelstan and his lords with his singing and his music; and was at length dismissed with an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> reward, though his songs must have discovered him to have been a Dane. Athelstan was saved from the consequences of this stratagem by a soldier, who had observed Anlaff <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BURY">bury</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> which had been given him, from some scruple of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>. This occasioned a discovery. From the uniform procedure of both these kings, it is plain that the same <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of entertainment prevailed among both peoples, and that the minstrel was a privileged character among both. Even as late as the reign of Edward II. the minstrels were easily admitted into the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> presence, as appears from a passage in Stow, which also shows the splendor of their appearance. "In the year 1316, Edward II. did solemnise his feast of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PENTECOST">Pentecost</a> at Westminster, in the great <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HALL">hall</a>; where sitting royally at the table with his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEERS">peers</a> about him, there entered a woman adorned like a minstrel, sitting on a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> trapped, as minstrels then used, who rode round about the tables, showing <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PASTIME">pastime</a>; and at length came up to the king's table, and laid before him a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LETTER">letter</a>, and forthwith <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> her horse, saluted every one, and departed."—The subject of this letter was a remonstrance to the king on the favours heaped by him on his minions, to the neglect of his knights and faithful servants. The messenger was sent in a minstrel's <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>, as what would <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> an easy admission; and was a woman concealed under that habit, probably to disarm the king's resentment: for we do not find that any of the real minstrels were of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SEX">sex</a>; and therefore conclude this was only an artful contrivance peculiar to that occasion. In the 4th year of Richard II. John of Gaunt erected at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TETBURY">Tetbury</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STAFFORDSHIRE">Staffordshire</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COURT">court</a> of minstrels, with a full power to receive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> from the men of his profession within five neighbouring counties, to enact laws, and determine their controversies; and to apprehend and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARREST">arrest</a> such of them as should refuse to appear at the said court, annually held on the 16th of August. For this they had a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a>, by which they were empowered to appoint a king of the minstrels, with four officers, to preside over them. These were every year elected with great <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a>; the whole form of which is described by Dr Plot: in whose <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a>, however, they seem to have become <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> musicians. Even so late as the reign of King Henry VIII. the reciters of verses or moral speeches learnt by heart, intruded without ceremony into all companies; not only Minstrel only in taverns, but in the houses of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> themselves. This we learn from Erasmus, whose argument led him only to describe a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of these men who did not sign their compositions; but the others that did, enjoyed without doubt the same privileges. We find that the minstrels continued <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>; in whose time they had lost much of their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, and were sinking into contempt and neglect. Yet still they sustained a character far superior to any thing we can conceive at present of the fingers of old ballads. When <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> Elizabeth was entertained at Killingworth castle by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEICESTER">Leicester</a> in 1575, among the many devices and pageants which were exhibited for her entertainment, one of the personages introduced was that of an ancient minstrel, whose appearance and dress are so minutely described by a writer there present, and gives us so distinct an idea of the character, that we shall quote the passage at <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a>. "A person very meet seemed he for the purpose, of a xlv. years old, appalled partly as he would himself. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a> off: his head seemingly rounded tonsilwife: fair-kembled, that, with a sponge daintily dipt in a little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPON">capon</a>'s grease, was finely smoothed, to make it shine like a mallard's wing. His <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARD">beard</a> snugly shaven: and yet his shirt after the new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRIM">trim</a>, with ruffs fair starched, flecked and glistering like a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of new shoes, marbled in good order with a setting slick, and strut, 'that' every ruff stood up like a wafer. A side [i.e. long] <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GOWN">gown</a> of Kendale green, after the freshness of the year now, gathered at the neck with a narrow gorget, fastened afore with a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WHITE">white</a> clasp and a keeper <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> up to the chin; but easily, for <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, to undo when he lift. Seemingly begirt in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RED">red</a> caddis girdle: from that a pair of capped <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHEFFIELD">Sheffield</a> knives hanging at two sides. Out of his bosom drawn from a lappet of his napkin edged with a blue <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LACE">lace</a>, and marked with a D for Damian; for he was but a bachelor yet. "His gown had side [i.e. long] sleeves down to mid-leg, slit from the shoulder to the hand, and lined with white cotton. His <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DOUBLET">doublet</a>-sleeves of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> worked: upon them a pair of pointes of tawny chambel laced along the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WRIST">wrist</a> with blue threaden pointes. A wealt towards the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of fustian-a-napes. A pair of red <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>-stockings. A pair of pumps on his feet, with a crofs cut at his toes for corns; not new indeed, yet cleanly blackt with foot, and shining as a foaming <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HORN">horn</a>. "About his neck a red ribbon suitable to his girdle. His harp in good <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> dependent before him. His wreft tyed to a green lace and hanging by: under the gorget of his gown a fair flaggon chain, (<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PEWTER">pewter</a> for) silver, as a squire Minstrel of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-MIDDLESEX">Middlesex</a>, that travelled the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> this <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> season, unto fair and worshipful mens houses. From his chain hung a feutecheon, with metal and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, resplendent upon his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>, of the ancient arms of Islington." —This minstrel is described as belonging to that village. We suppose such as were retained by noble families wore their arms hanging down by a silver chain as a kind of badge. From the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> of Squire Minstrel above, we may conclude there were other inferior orders, as Yeomen Minstrels, or the like. This minstrel, the author tells us a little below, "after three lowly courtesies, cleared his <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> with a hem ... and wiped his lips with the hollow of his hand for 'filing his napkin; tempered a string or two with his wreft; and, after a little warbling on his harp for a prelude, came forth with a solemn song, warranted for <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> out of King <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTHUR">Arthur</a>'s acts, &c." Towards the end of the 16th century, this class of men had lost all <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a>, and were sunk too low in the public <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that in the 39th year of Elizabeth a statute was passed by which "minstrels, wandering abroad," were included among "rogues, vagabonds, and sturdy beggars," and were adjudged to be punished as such. This <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> seems to have put an end to the profession, for after this time they are no longer mentioned.

MINT

Pages 180-180

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-MENTHA">MENTHA</a>. MINTURNÆ, a town of Campania between Sinnæssa and Formiae. It was in the marshes in this neighbourhood that Marius concealed himself in the mud to avoid the partizans of Sylla. The people condemned him to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEATH">death</a>; but when his <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> alone had terrified the executioner, they showed themselves compassionate and favoured his escape.

MINUET

Pages 180-180

a very graceful kind of dance, consisting of a couse, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> step, and a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a>; it begins with a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a>, and its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> is triple. The <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of the minuet seems generally to be ascribed to the French, and particularly to the inhabitants of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Poitou. The word is said by Menage and Furetiere to be derived from the French menu <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> menu, "small, or little;" and in strictness signifies a small pace. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-MELODY">melody</a> of this dance consists of two strains, which, as being repeated, are called reprises, each having eight or more bars, but never an odd <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> is three crotchets in a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAR">bar</a>, and is thus marked $\frac{3}{4}$, though it is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> performed in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> $\frac{3}{8}$. Walther speaks of a minuet in Lully's <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OPERA">opera</a> of Roland, each strain of which contains ten bars, the sectional number being 5; which renders it very difficult to dance.

MINUTE

Pages 180-181

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a>, the 60th <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of a circle. Minute of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">Time</a>, the 60th part of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>. Minute, in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, usually denotes the 60th, sometimes the 30th, part of a module. See Architecture. Minute is also used for a short memoir, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> sketch of a thing taken in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>. MINUTIUS Felix. See Felix. MINYÆ, a name given to the inhabitants of Orchomenos in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BOEOTIA">Boeotia</a>, from Minyas <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">king</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. Orchomenos the son of Minyas gave his name to the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the country; and the inhabitants still retained their original appellation, in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a> to the Orchomenians of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCADIA">Arcadia</a>. A colony of Orchomenians passed into Thessaly and settled in Iolchos; from which circumstance the people of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and particularly the Argonauts, were called Minyæ. This name they received, according to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of some, not because a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of Orchomenians had settled among them, but because the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> and noblest of them were descended from the daughters of Minyas. Part of the Orchomenians accompanied the sons of Codrus when they migrated to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-IONIA">Ionia</a>. The descendants of the Argonauts, as well as the Argonauts themselves, received the name of Minyæ. They first inhabited <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LEMNOS">Lemnos</a>, where they had been born from the Lemnian women who had murdered their husbands. They were driven from Lemnos by the Pelasgi, about 1160 before the Christian era, and came to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LACONIA">Laconia</a>, from whence they passed into Calliste with a colony of Lacedemonians. Miquelets, a name given to the Spaniards who inhabit the Pyrenean <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> on the frontiers of Arragon and Catalonia, and live by robbing.

MIQUELON

Pages 181-181

a small <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> off the southwest <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> May in Newfoundland, ceded to the French by the peace of 1763, for drying and curing their fish. W. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 54° 30' N Lat. 47° 22'. MIRABILIS. Marvel of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PERU">Peru</a>: A genus of the monogynia order, belonging to the pentandra class of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking with those of which the order is doubtful. The corolla is funnel-shaped above; the calyx inferior; the nectarium globular, containing the germin. The most remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> are, 1. The jalappa, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMON">common</a> marvel of Peru. It has a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, thick, fleshy root; an upright, thick, jointed stalk, dividing and branching numerously, widely, and erectly, a yard or more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>; garnished with <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, opposite leaves; and all the branches and shoots terminated by numerous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> in clusters, of different colours in the varieties. Of this there are varieties with <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WHITE">white</a> flowers—with <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> flowers—with purple flowers—with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RED">red</a> flowers—with white and yellow flowers—white and purple flowers—purple and yellow flowers—red and yellow flowers. Several other varieties often rise from seed; and it is remarkable, that although several of the above colours and variegations are sometimes common to the same plant, yet it is rare that a plant of this species produces flowers of one of those colours alone; sometimes, however, the same plant <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a> exhibit only white and purple flowers separate, and sometimes both colours in the same flowers, intermixed with the plain ones; the same is also observable in the red and yellow; others have plain flowers of several different colours, and sometimes variegated flowers also on the same plants. This species has a large tap root, which, when cut across, is not unlike that of the true jalap; but, when dried, is white, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, and springy. 2. The longiflora, or long-flowered mirabilis, hath a large, thick, fleshy root; a thick stalk, dividing low into many declinated spreading branches, extending two or three feet every way; large, heart-formed, hairy, viscid leaves, in opposite pairs; and all the branches and shoots terminated by white flowers in clusters, having very long tubes, nodding downward. 3. The dichotoma, dichotomous, or forked mirabilis, has a thick fleshy root; an upright, thick, swollen, jointed stem, branching forkedly two or three feet high; oblong opposite leaves; and smallish red flowers at the axillas, singly and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CLOSE">close</a>-fitting. All these plants flower in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>, continuing in plentiful succession until October, very conspicuous and elegant. They have the singularity of being shut all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, and expanding towards the evening when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> declines; hence the inhabitants of the Indies, where they grow naturally, called them four o'clock flowers: their <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> of opening here, however, depends on the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>; for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> cloudy, or that the sun is not very vehement, they often open <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> of the day. They are naturally perennial in root; but in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> considered as annuals: for they rise from seed in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, and the same year produce flowers and perfect seed; and if left to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> in the open <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>, totally perish in winter, at the first attack of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FROST">frost</a> or excessive wet. If in autumn, however, when the stalks begin to assume a state of decay, the roots are taken up, and preserved in sand in a dry room all winter, and planted again in spring, they shoot out fresh stronger than at first, and sometimes obtain four or five feet stature, with very spreading heads; or if plants growing in pots, having the stems cut <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DOWN">down</a> in autumn, and the pots placed in a <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-GREEN_HOUSE">green-<a cl</a>ass="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, or garden-frames under glasses, the roots may also be preserved <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOUND">sound</a>, and will shoot out again in spring as above. The roots of all these plants are purgative; but require to be given in a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> to operate equal to the true jalap, which is a species of convolvulus. See Convolvulus.

MIRACLE

Pages 181-186

in its original <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, is a word of the same import with wonder; but in its usual and more appropriate signification, it denotes "an effect contrary to the established <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> and course of things, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> a sensible deviation from the known laws of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>." That the visible world is governed by stated general rules, or that there is an order of causes and effects established in every <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> of the system of nature which falls under our observation, is a fact which cannot be controverted. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the Supreme Being, as some have supposed, be the only real <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGENT">agent</a> in the universe, we have the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>, that, in the particular system to which we belong, he acts by stated rules. If he employs inferior agents to conduct the various motions from which the phenomena result, we have the same evidence that he has subjected those agents to certain fixed laws, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called the laws of nature. On either <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a>, effects which are produced by the regular operation of these laws, or which are conformable to the established course of events, are properly called <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a>; and every <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a> to this constitution of the natural system, and the correspondent course of events in it, is called a miracle. If this <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a> of a miracle be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a>, no event can be deemed miraculous merely because it is strange, or even to us unaccountable; since it may be nothing more than a regular effect of some unknown <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAW">law</a> of nature. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> earthquakes are rare; and for monstrous births perhaps no particular and satisfactory account can be given: yet an earthquake is as regular an effect of the established laws of nature as any of those with which we are most intimately acquainted; and under circumstances in which there would always be the same kind of production, the monster is nature's genuine issue. It is therefore necessary, before we can pronounce any effect to be a true miracle, that the circumstances under which it is produced be known, and that the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMON">common</a> course of nature be in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> understood; for in all those <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CASES">cases</a> in which we are totally ignorant of nature, it is impossible to determine what is, or what is not, a deviation from its course. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">Miracles</a>, therefore, are not, as some have represented them, appeals to our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a>. They suppose some antecedent knowledge of the course of nature, without which no proper judgment can be formed concerning them; though with it their reality may be so apparent as to prevent all possibility of a dispute. Thus were a physician to cure a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLIND">blind</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAN">man</a> of a cataract, by anointing his eyes with a chemical <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> which we had never before seen, and to the nature and effects of which we are <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> strangers, the cure would undoubtedly be wonderful; but we could not pronounce it miraculous, because, for any thing known to us, it might be the natural effect of the operation of the unguent on the eye. But were he to recover his patient merely by commanding him to see, or by anointing his eyes with spittle, we should with the utmost confidence pronounce the cure to be a miracle; because we know perfectly that neither the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> nor human spittle have, by the established constitution of things, any such power over the difficulties of the eye. No one is now ignorant, that persons apparently dead are often restored to their families and friends, by being treated in the manner recommended by the Humane <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>. To the vulgar, and sometimes even to men of science, these effects appear very wonderful; but as they are known to be produced by physical agency, they can never be considered as miraculous deviations from the laws of nature. On the other <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, no one could doubt of his having witnessed a real miracle who had seen a person that had been four days dead come alive out of his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a> at the call of another, or who had even beheld a person exhibiting all the symptoms of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEATH">death</a> instantly resuscitated merely by being desired to live. Thus easy is it, in all cases in which the course of nature is understood, to determine whether any particular event be really a miracle; whilst in circumstances where we know nothing of nature and its course, even a true miracle, were it performed, could not be admitted as such, or carry any conviction to the mind of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>. If miracles be effects contrary to the established constitution of things, we are certain that they <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a> never be performed on trivial occasions. The constitution of things was established by the Creator and Governor of the universe, and is undoubtedly the offspring of infinite <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> pursuing a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> for the best of purposes. From this plan no deviation can be made but by God himself, or by some powerful being acting with his permission. The plans devised by wisdom are steady in proportion to their perfection, and the plans of infinite wisdom must be absolutely perfect. From this consideration, some men have ventured to conclude, that no miracle was ever wrought, or can rationally be expected; but mature reflection must soon satisfy us that all such conclusions are hasty. Man is unquestionably the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> creature in this world, and apparently the only one in it who is capable of being made acquainted with the relation in which he stands to his Creator. We cannot, therefore, doubt, but that such of the laws of nature as extend not their operation beyond the limits of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> were established chiefly, if not solely, for the good of mankind; and if, in any particular circumstances, that good can be more effectually promoted by an occasional deviation from those laws, such a deviation may be reasonably expected. Were man, in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of his mental and corporeal powers, subjected to the laws of physical <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a>, the circumstances supposed would indeed never occur, and of course no miracle could be admitted. But such is not the nature of man. Without repeating what has been said elsewhere (See <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-METAPHYSICS">Metaphysics</a>, Part III. chap. v.) of necessity and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, we shall here take it for granted, that the relation between motives and actions is different from that between cause and effect in physics; and that mankind have such command over themselves, as that by their voluntary conduct, they can make themselves in a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> degree either happy or miserable. We know likewise from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, that, by some means or other, almost all mankind were once sunk into the grossest ignorance of the most important truths; that they knew not the Being by whom they were created and supported; that they paid divine <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADORATION">adoration</a> to stocks, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, and the vilest reptiles; and that they were slaves to the most impious, cruel, and degrading superstitions. From this depraved state it was surely not unworthy of the common "Father of all" to rescue his helpless creatures, to enlighten their understandings that they might perceive what is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, and to present them motives of sufficient force to engage them in the practice of it. But the understandings of ignorant barbarians cannot be enlightened by arguments; because of the force of such arguments as regard moral science they are not qualified to judge. The philosophers of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a> and Rome inculcated, indeed, many excellent moral precepts, and they sometimes ventured to expose the absurdities of the reigning <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>; but their lectures had no influence upon the multitude; and they had themselves imbibed such erroneous notions respecting the attributes of the Supreme Being, and the nature of the human <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>, and converted those notions into first principles, of which they would not permit an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a>, that even among them a thorough reformation was not to be expected from the powers of reasoning. It is likewise to be observed, that there are many truths of the utmost importance to mankind, which unsifted reason could never have discovered. Amongst these we may confidently reckon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMMORTALITY">immortality</a> of the soul, the terms upon which God will be reconciled to sinners, and the manner in which that all-perfect Being may be acceptably worshipped; about all of which philosophers were in such uncertainty, that, according to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a>, "Whatever is set right, and as it should be, in the present evil state of the world, can be so only by the particular interposition of God (A)." An immediate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REVELATION">revelation</a> from Heaven, therefore, was the only method by which infinite wisdom and perfect goodness could <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-REFORM">reform</a> a bewildered and vicious <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-RACE">race</a>. But this revelation, at whatever <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> we suppose it given, must have been made directly either to some chosen individuals commissioned to instruct others, or to every man and woman for whose benefit it was ultimately intended. Were every person instructed in in the knowledge of his duty by immediate <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-INSPIRATION">inspiration</a>, and were the motives to practise it brought home to his mind by God himself, human nature would be wholly changed: men would not be masters of their own actions; they would not be moral agents, nor by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> be capable either of reward or of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>. It remains, therefore, that if God has been graciously pleased to enlighten and reform mankind, without destroying that moral nature which is essential to virtue, he can have done it only by revealing his truths to certain chosen instruments, who were the immediate instructors of their contemporaries, and through them have been the instructors of succeeding ages. Let us suppose this to have been actually the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CASE">case</a>, and consider how those inspired teachers could communicate to others every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> which had been revealed to themselves. They might easily, if it was part of their duty, deliver a sublime system of natural and moral science, and establish it upon the common basis of experiment and demonstration; but what foundation could they lay for those truths which unassisted reason cannot discover, and which, when they are revealed, appear to have no necessary relation to anything previously known? To a bare <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFFIRMATION">affirmation</a> that they had been immediately received from God, no rational being could be expected to assent. The teachers might be men of known veracity, whose simple assertion would be admitted as sufficient evidence for any fact, in conformity with the laws of nature; but as every man has the evidence of his own consciousness and experience that revelations from heaven are deviations from these laws, an assertion so apparently extravagant would be rejected as false, unless supported by some better <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> than the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> affirmation of the teacher. In this state of things, we can conceive no evidence sufficient to make such doctrines be received as the truths of God, but the power of working miracles committed to him who taught them. This would, indeed, be fully adequate to the purpose. For if there were nothing in the doctrines themselves impious, immoral, or contrary to truths already known, the only thing which could render the teacher's assertion incredible, would be its implying such an intimate <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a> with God as is contrary to the established course of things, by which men are left to acquire all their knowledge by the exercise of their own faculties. Let us now suppose some of those inspired teachers to tell his countrymen, that he did not declare them, on his ipse dixit, to believe that he had any preternatural communion with the Deity, but that for the truth of his assertion he would give them the evidence of their own senses; and after this <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a> let us suppose him immediately to raise a person from the dead in their presence, merely by calling upon him to come out of his grave. Would not the only possible objection to the man's veracity be removed by this miracle? and his assertion that he had received such and such doctrines from God be as fully credited, as if it related to the most common occurrence? Undoubtedly it would; for when so much preternatural power was visibly communicated to this person, no one could have reason to question his having received an equal portion of preternatural knowledge. A palpable deviation from the known laws of nature, in one instance, is a sensible proof that such a deviation is possible in another; and in such a case as this it is the witness of God to the truth of a man. Miracles, then, under which we include prophecy, are the only <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> evidence which can be given of divine inspiration. When a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, or any <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> truth, is to be revealed from heaven, they appear to be absolutely necessary to enforce its reception among men; and this is the only case in which we can suppose them necessary, or believe for a moment that they ever have been or will be performed. The history of almost every religion abounds with relations of prodigies and wonders, and of the intercourse of men with the gods; but we know of no religious system, those of the Jews and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> excepted, which appealed to miracles as the sole evidence of its truth and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>. The pretended miracles mentioned by Pagan historians and poets are not said to have been publicly wrought to enforce the truth of a new religion contrary to the reigning idolatry. Many of them may be clearly shown to have been mere natural events; (see <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAGIC">Magic</a>). Others of them are represented as having been performed in secret on the most trivial occasions, and in obscure and fabulous ages <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> to the era of the writers by whom they are recorded. And such of them as at first view appear to be best attested, are evidently tricks contrived for interested purposes; to flatter power, or to promote the prevailing superstitions. For these reasons, as well as on account of the immoral character of the divinities by whom they are said to have been wrought, they are altogether unworthy of examination, and carry in the very nature of them the complete proofs of falsehood and imposture. But the miracles recorded of Moses and of Christ bear a very different character. None of them is represented as wrought on trivial occasions. The writers who mention them were eye-witnesses of the facts; which they affirm to have been performed publicly, in attestation of the truth of their respective systems. They are indeed incorporated with these systems, that the miracles cannot be separated from the doctrines; and if the miracles were not really performed, the doctrines cannot possibly be true. Besides all this, they were wrought in support of revelations which opposed all the religious systems, superstitions, and prejudices, of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> in which they were given: a circumstance which of itself sets them, in point of authority, infinitely above the Pagan prodigies, as well as the lying wonders of the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. It is indeed, we believe, universally admitted, that the miracles mentioned in the book of Exodus and in the four Gospels, might, to those who <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAW">saw</a> them performed, be sufficient evidence of the divine inspiration of Moses and of Christ; but to us it may be thought that they are no evidence whatever, as we must believe in the miracles themselves, if we believe in them at all, upon the bare authority of human testimony. Why, it has been sometimes asked, are not miracles wrought in all ages and countries? If the religion of Christ was to be of perpetual <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>, every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a> of men ought to have complete evidence of its truth and divinity. To the performance of miracles in every age and in every country, perhaps the same objections <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> as to the immediate inspiration of every individual. Were those miracles universally received as such, men would be so overwhelmed with the nature rather than with the force of their authority, as hardly to remain masters of their own conduct; and in that case the very end of all miracles would be defeated by their frequency. The truth, however, seems to be, that miracles so frequently repeated would not be received as such, and of course would have no authority; because it would be difficult, and in many cases impossible, to distinguish them from natural events. If they recurred regularly at certain intervals, we could not prove them to be deviations from the known laws of nature, because we should have the same experience for the one <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of events as for the other; for the regular succession of preternatural effects, as for the established constitution and course of things. Be this, however, as it may, we shall take the liberty to affirm, that for the reality of the Gospel miracles we have evidence as convincing to the reflecting mind, though not so striking to vulgar <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APPREHENSION">apprehension</a>, as those who were <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> with Christ and his apostles, and actually saw the mighty works which he performed. To the admirers of Mr Hume's <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> this assertion will appear an extravagant <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PARADOX">paradox</a>; but we hope to demonstrate its truth from principles which, consistently with himself, that author could not have denied. He has indeed endeavoured to prove *, that "no testimony is sufficient to establish a miracle;" and the reasoning employed for this purpose is, that "a miracle being a violation of the laws of nature, which a firm and unalterable experience has established, the proof against a miracle, from the very nature of the fact, is as entire as any argument from experience can be; whereas our experience of human veracity, which (according to him) is the sole foundation of the evidence of testimony, is far from being uniform, and can therefore never preponderate against that experience which admits of no exception." This boasted and plausible argument has been equal candour and acuteness been examined by Dr Campbell †; who justly observes, that so far is experience from being the sole foundation of the evidence of testimony, that, on the contrary, testimony is the sole foundation of by far the greater part of what Mr Hume calls firm and unalterable experience; and that if in certain circumstances we did not give an implicit <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> to testimony, our knowledge of events would be confined to those which had fallen under the immediate observation of our own senses. For a short view of this celebrated controversy, in which the Christian so completely vanquishes the philosopher, see the word ABRIDGEMENT. But though Dr Campbell has exposed the sophistry of his opponent's reasonings, and overturned the principles from which he reasons, we are persuaded that he might safely have joined issue with him upon those very principles. To us, at least, it appears that the testimony upon which we receive the Gospel miracles is precisely of that kind which Mr Hume has acknowledged sufficient to establish even a miracle. "No testimony (says he) is sufficient to establish a miracle, unless the testimony be of such a kind that its falsehood would be more miraculous than the fact which it endeavours to establish. When one tells me that he saw a dead man restored to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, I immediately consider with myself whether it be more probable that this person should either deceive or be deceived, or that the fact which he relates should really have happened. I weigh the one miracle against the other; and according to the superiority which I discover I pronounce my decision, and always reject the greater miracle." In this passage every reader may remark what did not escape the perspicacious eye of Dr Campbell, a strange confusion of terms: but as all miracles are equally easy to the Almighty; and as Mr Hume has elsewhere observed, that "the raising of a feather, when the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> wants ever so little of a force requisite for that purpose, is as real a miracle as the raising of a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> or a ship into the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>;" candour obliges us to suppose, that by talking of greater and less miracles, and of always rejecting the greater, he meant nothing more but that of two deviations from the known laws of nature he always rejects that which in itself is least probable. If, then, we can show that the testimony given by the apostles and other first preachers of Christianity to the miracles of their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MASTER">Master</a> would, upon the supposition that those miracles were not really performed, have been as great a deviation from the known laws of nature as the miracles themselves, the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a> must be considered as evenly poised by opposite miracles; and whilst it continues so, the judgment must remain in a state of suspense. But if it shall appear, that in this case the false testimony would have been a deviation from the laws of nature less probable in itself than the miracles recorded in the Gospels, the balance will be instantly destroyed; and by Mr Hume's maxim we shall be obliged to reject the supposition of falsehood in the testimony of the apostles, and admit the miracles of Christ to have been really performed. In this argument we need not waste time in proving that those miracles, as they are represented in the writings of the New <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, were of such a nature, and performed before so many witnesses, that no imposition could possibly be practised on the senses of those who affirm that they were present. From every page of the Gospels this is so evident, that the philosophical adversaries of the Christian faith never suppose the apostles to have been themselves deceived, but boldly accuse them of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> false witness. But if this <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACCUSATION">accusation</a> be well founded, their testimony itself is as great a miracle as any which they record of themselves or of their Master. It has been shown elsewhere (see Metaphysics, no. 138.), that by the law of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSOCIATION">association</a>, which is one of the laws of nature, mankind, in the very <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of learning to speak, necessarily learn to speak the truth; that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> and relations are in the mind of every man so closely associated with the words by which they are expressed in his native tongue, and in every other <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of which he is master, that the one cannot be entirely separated from the other; that therefore no man can on any occasion speak falsehood without some effort; that by no effort can a man give consistency to an unpremeditated detail of falsehood, if it be of any length, and include a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of particulars; and that it is still less possible for several men to agree in such a detail, when at a distance from each other, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>-questioned by their enemies. This being the case, it follows, if the testimony of the apostles to their own and their Master's miracles be false, either that they must have concerted a consistent scheme of falsehood, and agreed to publish it at every hazard; or that God, or some powerful agent appointed by him, must have dissolved all the affections formed in their minds between ideas of sense and the words of language, and arbitrarily formed new associations, all in exact conformity to each other, but all in direct contradiction to truth. One or other of these events must have taken <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a>; because, upon the supposition of falsehood, there is no other alternative. But such a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> and formation of associations as the latter implies, must, to every man who shall attentively consider it, appear to be as real a miracle, and to require as great an exertion of power, as the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RESURRECTION">resurrection</a> of the dead. Nor is the supposed voluntary agreement of the apostles in a scheme of falsehood an event less miraculous. When they sat <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to fabricate their pretended revelation, and to contrive a series of miracles to which they were unanimously to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a> for its truth, it is plain, since they proved successful in their daring enterprise, that they must have foreseen every possible circumstance in which they could be placed, and have prepared consistent answers to every question that could be put to them by their most inveterate and most enlightened enemies; by the statesman, the lawyer, the philosopher, and the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>. That such foreknowledge as this would have been miraculous, will not surely be denied; since it forms the very <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> which we find it most difficult to allow even to God himself. It is not, however, the only miracle which this supposition would compel us to swallow. The very <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> of the apostles to propagate the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> of false miracles in support of such a religion as that which is taught in the New Testament, is as great a miracle as human imagination can easily conceive. When they formed this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, either they must have hoped to succeed, or they must have foreseen that they should fail in their undertaking; and in either case, they chose evil for its own sake. They could not, if they foresaw that they should fail, look for anything but that contempt, disgrace, and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a>, which were then the inevitable consequences of an unsuccessful endeavour to overthrow the established religion. Nor could their prospects be brighter upon the supposition of their success. As they knew themselves to be false witnesses and impious deceivers, they could have no hopes beyond the grave; and by determining to oppose all the religious systems, superstitions, and prejudices of the age in which they lived, they wilfully exposed themselves to inevitable misery in the present life, to insult and imprisonment, to stripes and death. Nor can it be said that they might look forward to power and influence when they should, through sufferings, have converted their countrymen; for so desirous were they of obtaining nothing but misery as the end of their mission, that they made their own perfection a test of the truth of their doctrines. They introduced the Master from whom they pretended to have received these doctrines as telling them, that "they were sent forth as sheep in the midst of wolves; that they should be delivered up to councils, and scourged in synagogues; that they should be hated of all men for his name's sake; that the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> should deliver up the brother to death, and the father the child; and that he who took not up his cross and followed after him was not worthy of him." The very system of religion, therefore, which they invented and resolved to impose upon mankind, was so contrived, that the worldly prosperity of its first preachers, and even their exemption from persecution, was incompatible with its success. Had these clear predictions of the Author of that religion, under whom the apostles acted only as ministers, not been verified, all mankind must have instantly perceived that their pretence to inspiration was false, and that Christianity was a scandalous and impudent imposture. All this the apostles could not but foresee when they formed their plan for deluding the world. Whence it follows, that when they resolved to support their pretended revelation by an appeal to forged miracles, they wilfully, and with their eyes open, exposed themselves to inevitable misery, whether they should succeed or fail in their enterprise; and that they concerted their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> so as not to admit of a possibility of recompense to themselves, either in this life or in that which is to come. But if there be a law of nature, for the reality of which we have better evidence than we have for others, it is, that "no man can choose misery for its own sake," or make the acquisition of it the ultimate end of his pursuit. The existence of other laws of nature we know by testimony and our own observation of the regularity of their effects. The existence of this law is made known to us not only by these means, but also by the still clearer and more conclusive evidence of our own consciousness. Thus, then, do miracles force themselves upon our assent in every possible view which we can take of this interesting subject. If the testimony of the first preachers of Christianity was true, the miracles recorded in the Gospel were certainly performed, and the doctrines of our religion are derived from heaven. On the other hand, if that testimony was false, either God must have miraculously effaced from the minds of those by whom it was given all the associations formed between their sensible ideas and the words of language, or he must have endowed those men with the gift of prescience, and have impelled them to fabricate a pretended revelation for the purpose of deceiving the world, and involving themselves in certain and foreseen destruction. The power necessary to perform the one series of these miracles may, for any thing known to us, be as great as that which would be requisite for the performance of the other; and considered merely as exertions of preternatural power, they may seem to balance each other, and to hold the mind in a state of suspense. But when we take into consideration the different purposes for which these opposite and contending miracles were wrought, the balance is instantly destroyed. The miracles recorded in the Gospels, if real, were wrought in support of a revelation which, in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of all by whom it is received, has brought to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> many important truths which could not otherwise have been made known to men; and which, by the confession of its adversaries, contains the purest moral precepts by which the conduct of mankind was ever directed. The opposite series of miracles, if real, was performed to enable, and even to compel, a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of Jews, of the lowest <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RANK">rank</a> and of the narrowest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, to fabricate, with the view of inevitable destruction to themselves, a consistent scheme of falsehood, and by an appeal to forged miracles to impose it upon the world as a revelation from heaven. The object of the former miracles is worthy of a God of infinite wisdom, goodness, and power. The object of the latter is absolutely inconsistent with wisdom and goodness, which are demonstrably attributes of that Being by whom alone miracles can be performed. Whence it follows, that the supposition of the apostles bearing false testimony to the miracles of their Master, implies a series of deviations from the laws of nature infinitely less probable in themselves than those miracles; and therefore, by Mr Hume's maxim, we must necessarily reject the supposition of falsehood in the testimony, and admit the reality of the miracles. So true is it, that for the reality of the Gospel-miracles we have evidence as convincing to the reflecting mind, as those who had who were contemporary with Christ and his apostles, and were actual witnesses to their mighty works.

MIRANDA-DE-EBRO

Pages 186-186

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> in Old Castile, with a strong castle; seated in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> that produces excellent wine. The town is divided into two parts by the river, over which there is a handsome <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3.10. N. Lat. 42.52.

MIRANDE

Pages 186-186

a town of Gascony in France, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Astarac; seated on a mountain near the river Baute. E. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 0.21. N. Lat. 42.53.

MIRANDO-DE-DOURO

Pages 186-186
or Duero, a strong town of Portugal, and capital of the province of Tra-los-Montes, with a bishop's see. It is well fortified, and seated on a rock near the confluence of the river Douro and Freina. W. Long. 5.40. N. Lat. 41.30.

MIRANDOLA

Pages 186-186

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of the same name, situated between the duchies of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MANTUA">Mantua</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MODENA">Modena</a>. It is a pretty <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, well fortified, and has also a strong citadel and fort. It has been several times taken and retaken; the last <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-SARDINIA">Sardinia</a> in 1742. E. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 11.5. N. Lat. 44.52. MIRANDULA. See Picus.

MIREVELT

Pages 186-186

son of Michael, was born at Delft in 1596, and died in 1632. In his manner of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, in his style of colouring, and in the delicacy of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a>, he exactly resembled his father; and by the best judges of that <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> he was accounted to be in no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> inferior to him.

MIRIAM

Pages 186-186

sister of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AARON">Aaron</a> and Moses, makes two <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> three remarkable appearances in scripture. It was owing to her that her mother was employed by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PHARAOH">Pharaoh</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> as nurse to Moses. She put herself at the head of the women of Israel after their passage through the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RED_SEA"><a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RED">Red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>, in order to sing the song which the men had sung before. She joined with her <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Aaron in murmuring against Moses, and was severely chastised for that <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a>; for she became leprous, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> separate from the rest without the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAMP">camp</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> days. She died before her brothers, though in the same year with them, and was buried at the public expense.

MIRROR

Pages 186-186

a name for a looking glass, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> any polished body, whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> is to form the images of distant objects, by reflection of the rays of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>. See Reflection. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRRORS">Mirrors</a> are either plain, convex, or concave.
