The first reflect the rays of light in a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> exactly similar to that in which they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> upon them, and therefore represent bodies of their <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> magnitude. The convex ones make the rays diverge much more than before reflection, and therefore greatly diminish the images of those objects which they show; while the concave ones, by collecting the rays into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FOCUS">focus</a>, not only magnify the objects they show, but <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a> burn very fiercely when exposed to the rays of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>; and hence they are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> known by the name of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> mirrors. See Burning Mirrors. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> times the mirrors were made of some kind of metal; and from a passage in the Mosaic writings we learn that the mirrors used by the Jewish women were made of bras. The Jews certainly had been taught to use that kind of mirrors by the Egyptians; from whence it is probable that brazen mirrors were the first kind used in the world. Any kind of metal, indeed, when well polished, will reflect very powerfully; but of all others silver reflects the most, tho' it has been in all countries too expensive a material for <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMON">common</a> use. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GOLD">Gold</a> also is very powerful; and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, or even wood, gilded and polished, will <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> very powerfully as burning mirrors. Even polished <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a>, or straw nicely plaited together, will form mirrors capable of burning, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> on a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-SCALE">scale</a>. Since the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of glass, and the application of quicksilver to it, became generally known, it hath been universally employed for those plain mirrors used as ornaments to houses; but in making reflecting telescopes, they have been found much inferior to metallic ones. It doth not appear that the same superiority belongs to the metallic burning mirrors, considered merely as burning glasses; since the mirror with which Mr Macquer melted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLATINA">platina</a>, though only 22 inches diameter, and which was made of quicksilvered glass, produced much greater effects than M. Vilette's metallic speculum, which considerably exceeded it in size. It is very probable, however, that this mirror of M. Vilette's was by no means so well polished as it ought to have been; as the art of preparing the metal for taking the finest polish has but lately been discovered and published in the Philosophical Transac-

MISADVENTURE

Pages 187-187

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAW">law</a>, has an especial signification for the killing a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAN">man</a> partly by negligence, and partly by chance. See <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOMICIDE">HOMICIDE</a>. MISANTHROPY (formed μισος, hatred, and ανθρωπος, a man); a general dislike <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> aversion to man, and mankind. In which <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> it stands opposed to philanthropy, or the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of mankind. MISCARRIAGE. See <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABORTION">ABORTION</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MIDWIFERY">MIDWIFERY</a>.

MISDEMEANOUR

Pages 187-187

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAW">law</a>, signifies a crime. Every crime is a misdemeanor; yet the law has made a distinction between crimes of a higher and a lower <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>; the latter being denominated misdemeanours, the former felonies, &c. For the understanding of which distinction, we shall give the following <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a> from Blackstone's Commentaries, vol. iv. 5. "A crime, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> misdemeanor, is an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> committed or omitted, in violation of a public law, either forbidding or commanding it. This general definition comprehends both crimes and misdemeanours; which, properly speaking, are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SYNONYMOUS">synonymous</a> terms; though, in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMON">common</a> usage, the word crime is made to denote such offences as are of a deeper and more atrocious dye; while smaller faults, and omissions of less <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>, are comprised under the gentler name of misdemeanours only."

MISE

Pages 187-187

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAW">law</a>-books, is used in various senses; thus it sometimes signifies costs <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> expenses; in which <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> it is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> used in entering of judgments in actions personal. It is also used for the issue to be tried on the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> assize; in which <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CASE">case</a>, joining of the mise upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, is putting in issue between the tenant and defendant, Who has the best or clearest right.

MISE ALSO

Pages 187-187

e also signifies a tax <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> tallage, &c. An honorary gift, or customary present from the people of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WALES">Wales</a> to every new <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">king</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of Wales, anciently given in cattle, wine, and corn, but now in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, being 500l. or more, is denominated a mise; so was the usual tribute or fine of 300 merks paid by the inhabitants of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> palatine of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHESTER">Chester</a> at the change of every owner of the said earldoms, for enjoying their liberties. And at Chester they have a mise-book, wherein every town and village in the county is rated what to pay towards the mise. The 27 Hen. VIII. c. 26. ordains that lords shall have all such mises and profits of their lands as they had in times past, &c. Mise, is sometimes also corruptly used for meafe, in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAW">law</a> French mees, "a meffuage;" as a mise <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, in some manors, is such a meffuage or tenement as answers the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LORD">lord</a> a heriot at the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of its owner. 2 Inst. 528.

MISENUM

Pages 187-188
or Misenum, (anc. geog.); a promontory, port, and town in Campania, situated to the south-west of Baiae, in the Sinus Putolanus, on the north side. Here Augustus had a fleet, called Caius Milenustris, for guarding the Mare Inferum; as he had another at Ravenna for the Superum. On this peninsula a villa was built by Caius Marius, with a degree of elegance that gave great offence to the more austere among the Romans, who thought Miser. it ill suited to the character of so rough a soldier. Upon the same foundation Lucullus, the plunderer of the eastern world, erected an edifice, in comparison of which the former house was a cottage; but even his magnificence was eclipsed by the splendour of the palace which the emperors raised upon the same spot. To these proud abodes of heroes and monarchs, which have long been levelled to the ground, a few fishing huts, as Mr Swinburn informs us, and a lonely public house, have succeeded; hither boatmen resort to tipple, perhaps on the identical site where the voluptuous masters of the world quaffed Chian and Falernian wines.

MISER

Pages 188-191

a parsimonious person who is at the same <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> rich; <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> a wretch covetous to extremity, whom avarice has divested of all the charities of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, and made even an enemy to himself. Of this most unaccountable of all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, many instances occur; some of them so extraordinary as almost to surpass <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a>. The following are here selected, as being of recent <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DATE">date</a>, perfectly authentic, and the last of them in particular exhibiting an assemblage of qualities the most singular perhaps that ever centered in the same person. Too little dignified to merit a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in regular biography, yet too curious a variety of human character to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> unnoticed in this <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WORK">Work</a>, the present seemed the only <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TITLE">title</a> under which it could with propriety be introduced. 1. In <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1792, died at <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, literally of want, Mr Ottervald, a well-known banker. This <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAN">man</a>, originally of Neuchatel, felt the violence of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> of avarice (for surely it is rather a disease than a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> of the mind) so strongly, that, within a few days of his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, no opportunities could induce him to buy a few pounds of meat for the purpose of making a little soup for him. "Tis true (said he), I should not dislike the soup, but I have no appetite for the meat; what then is to become of that?" At the time that he refused this nourishment, for fear of being obliged to give away two or three pounds of meat, there was tied round his neck a silken bag, which contained 800 assignats of 1000 livres each. At his outset in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, he drank a pint of beer, which served him for <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SUPPER">supper</a>, every night at a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> much frequented, from which he carried home all the bottle-corks he could come at. Of these, in the course of eight years, he had collected as many as sold for 12 <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LOUIS">louis</a> d'or, a sum that laid the foundation of his future fortune, the superstructure of which was rapidly raised by his uncommon success in stock jobbing. He died possessed of three millions of livres (£1,250,000 <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>). 2. The late John Elwes, Esq., was member for <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BERKSHIRE">Berkshire</a> in three successive parliaments. His family name was Meggot; and his father was a brewer of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> eminence, and distinguished by no peculiarity of character; but his mother, though she was left nearly £100,000 by her husband, starved herself to death! At an early <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of life he was sent to Westminster school, where he remained for 10 or 12 years. During that time he certainly had not misapplied his talents; for he was a good classical scholar to the last; and it is a circumstance not a little remarkable, though well authenticated, that he never read afterwards, nor had he ever any knowledge in accounts; to which may in some <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> be attributed the total <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> he was always in as to his affairs. From Westminster school Mr Meggot removed to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-GENEVA">Geneva</a>, where he soon entered upon pursuits more agreeable to him than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a>. The riding-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the academy there had then to boast perhaps of three of the best riders in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, Mr Worsley, Mr Elwes, and Sir <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-SYDNEY">Sydney</a> Meadows. Of the three, Elwes was reckoned the most desperate; the young horses were always put into his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, and he was the rough-rider to the other two. On his return to England, after an absence of two or three years, he was to be introduced to his uncle the late Sir Harvey Elwes, who was then living at Stoke in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SUFFOLK">Suffolk</a>, perhaps the most perfect <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> of human penury that ever existed. The attempts at saving <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> were in him so extraordinary, that Mr Elwes perhaps never quite reached them, even at the last period of his life.—Of what <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPERANCE">temperance</a> can do, Sir Harvey was an instance. At an early period of life he was given over for a consumption, and he lived till betwixt 80 and 90 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. On his death, his fortune, which was at least £1,250,000, fell to his nephew Mr Meggot, who by <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a> was ordered to assume the name and arms of Elwes. To this uncle, and this <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, Mr Elwes succeeded when he had advanced beyond the 40th year of his age. And for 15 years previous to this period, it was that he was known in the more fashionable circles of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. He had always a turn for play; and it was only late in life, and from paying always and not always being paid, that he conceived disgust at it. The <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> which he professed, "that it was impossible to ask a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> for money," he perfectly confirmed by the practice; and he never violated this feeling to the latest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> of his life. The manners of Mr Elwes were such—so gentle, so attentive, so gentlemanly, and so engaging—that rudeness could not ruffle them, nor strong ingratitude <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> their observance. He retained this peculiar feature of the old <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COURT">court</a> to the last; but he had a praise beyond this; he had the most gallant disregard of his own person, and all care about himself, that can be imagined. The instances in younger life, in the most imminent personal hazard, are innumerable; but when age had despoiled him of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a>, and might have rendered care and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> about himself <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a>, he knew not what they were: He wished no one to afflict him: "He was as young as ever; he could walk; he could ride, and he could dance; and he hoped he should not give trouble even when he was old:" He was at that time 75. It is curious to remark how he contrived to mingle small attempts at saving with objects of the most unbounded dilapidation. After sitting up a whole night at play for thousands with the most fashionable and profligate men of the time, amidst splendid rooms, gilt sofas, wax lights, and waiters attendant on his call, he would walk out about four in the morning, not towards home, but into Smithfield, to meet his own cattle, which were coming to market from Thaydonhall, a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FARM">farm</a> of his in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a>! There would this same man, forgetful of the scenes he had <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> left, stand in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLD">cold</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> bartering with a carcass-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BUTCHER">butcher</a> for a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SHILLING">shilling</a>! Sometimes, when the cattle did not arrive at the hour he expected, he would walk on in the mire to meet them; and more than once has gone on foot the whole whole way to his farm without stopping, which was 17 miles from London, after sitting up the whole night. Had every man been of the mind of Mr Elwes, the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-RACE">race</a> of innkeepers must have perished, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a>-chaises have been returned back to those who made them; for it was the business of his life to avoid both. He always travelled on horseback. To see him setting out on a journey, was a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> truly curious; his first care was to put two or three eggs, boiled hard, into his great-coat pocket, or any scraps of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> which he found; baggage he never took; then mounting one of his hunters, his next attention was to get out of London into that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ROAD">road</a> where turnpikes were the fewest; then, stopping under any hedge where grass presented itself for his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, and a little <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WATER">water</a> for himself, he would sit <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DOWN">down</a> and refresh himself and his horse together. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> residence of Mr Elwes at this period of his life was in Berkshire, at his own seat at Marcham. Here it was he had two natural sons born, who inherit the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> of his property by a will made about the year 1735. The keeping fox-hounds was the only instance in the whole life of Mr Elwes of his ever sacrificing money to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>; and may be selected as the only period when he forgot the cares, the perplexities, and the regret, which his wealth occasioned. But even here everything was done in the most frugal manner. Scrub, in the Beaux Stratagem, when compared with Mr Elwes's huntman, had an idle life of it. This famous huntman might have fixed an epoch in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of servants: for in a morning, getting up at four o'clock, he milked the cows; he then prepared breakfast for Mr Elwes or any friends he might have with him; then slipping on a green coat, he hurried into the stable, fiddled the horses, got the hounds out of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KENNEL">kennel</a>, and away they went into the field. After the fatigues of hunting, he refreshed himself by rubbing down two or three horses as quickly as he could; then running into the house to lay the cloth, and wait at dinner; then hurrying again into the stable to feed the horses—diversified with an interlude of the cows again to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MILK">milk</a>, the dogs to feed, and eight hunters to litter down for the night. In the penury of Mr Elwes there was something that seemed like a judgment from heaven. All earthly comforts he voluntarily denied himself; he would walk home in the rain in London rather than pay a shilling for a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COACH">coach</a>; he would fit in wet cloaths sooner than have a fire to dry them; he would eat his <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> in the last stage of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PUTREFACTION">putrefaction</a> sooner than have a fresh <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> from the butchers; and he wore a wig for above a fortnight, which his biographer <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAW">saw</a> him pick up out of a rut in a lane where they were from whose riding. This was the last extremity of laudable economy; for to all appearance it was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a>-off wig of some beggar! Mr Elwes had now resided about 13 years in Suffolk, when the contest for Berkshire presented itself on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>; and when, to preserve the peace of that <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>, he was nominated by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Craven. Mr Elwes, though he had retired from public business for some years, had still left about him some of the seeds of more <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> life, and he agreed to the proposal. It came farther enhanced to him, by the agreement, that he was to be brought in by the freeholders for nothing. All he did on the occasion was dining at the ordinary at <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-READING">Reading</a>; and he got into parliament for 18 pence! Though a new man, Mr Elwes could not be called a young member; for he was at this time nearly 60 years old when he thus entered on public life. But he was in possession of all his activity; and, preparatory to his appearance on the boards of St Stephen's Chapel, he used to attend constantly during the races and other public meetings all the great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> where his voters resided. At the different assemblies, he would dance amongst the youngest to the last, after riding over on horseback, and frequently in the rain, to the place of meeting. A gentleman who was one night standing by, observed on the extraordinary agility of so old a man.—“O! that is nothing (repined another); for Mr Elwes, to do this, rode 20 miles in the rain, with his shoes stuck into his boots and his bag-wig in his pocket.” The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of parliament made no <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> in the dress of Mr Elwes: on the contrary, it seemed at this time to have attained additional neatness; and nearly to have reached that happy climax of poverty, which has more than once drawn on him the compassion of those who passed by him in the street. For the speaker's dinners, however, he had one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUIT">suit</a>, with which the speaker in the course of the sessions became very familiar. The minister likewise was well acquainted with it; and at any dinner of opposition till was his apparel the same. The wits of the minority used to say, “that they had full as much reason as the minister to be satisfied with Mr Elwes, as he had the same <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> with everybody.” At this period of his life Mr Elwes wore a wig. Much about the time when his parliamentary life ceased, that wig was worn out; so then, being older and wiser as to expense, he wore his own <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, which like his expenses was very small. All this time the income of Mr Elwes was increasing hourly, and his present expenditure was next to nothing; for the little pleasures he had once engaged in he had now given up. He kept no house, and only one old <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> and a couple of horses: he resided with his nephew; his two sons he had stationed in Suffolk and Berkshire, to look after his respective estates: and his dress certainly was no expense to him; for had not other people been more careful than himself, he would not have had it even mended. When he left London, he went on horseback to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>-seats with his couple of hard eggs, and without once stopping upon the road at any house. He always took the most unfrequented road, and used every shift to avoid turnpikes. Marcham was the seat he now chiefly visited; which had some reason to be flattered with the preference, as his journey into Suffolk cost him only two-pence halfpenny, while that into Berkshire amounted to four-pence! As Mr Elwes came into parliament without expense, he performed his duty as a member would have done in the pure days of our <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>. What he had not bought, he never attempted to sell; and he went forward in that straight and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> path, which can alone satisfy a reflecting mind. Amongst the smaller memorials of the parliamentary life of Mr Elwes may be noted, that he did not follow the cu- When he quitted parliament, he was, in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMON">common</a> phrase, "a fish out of water!" The style of Mr Elwes's life had left him no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> scenes to which he could retire—his home was dreary and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POOR">poor</a>—his rooms received no cheerfulness from fire; and while the outside had all the appearance of a "House to be Let," the inside was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a>; but he had his penury alone to thank for this, and for the want of all the little consolations which should attend old age, and smooth the passage of declining life. At the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> of 1785, he wished again to visit, which he had not done for some years, his seat at Stoke. But then the journey was a most serious object to him. The famous old servant was dead, all the horses that remained with him were a couple of worn-out broodmares; and he himself was not in that vigour of body in which he could ride 60 or 70 miles on the sustenance of two boiled eggs. The mention of a post-chaise would have been a crime—"He afford a post-chaise, indeed! where was he to get the money?" would have been his exclamation. At length he was carried into the country as he was carried into parliament, free of expense, by a gentleman who was certainly not quite so rich as Mr Elwes. When he reached Stoke—the seat of more active scenes, of somewhat resembling hospitality, and where his fox-hounds had spread somewhat like vivacity around—he remarked, "he had expended a great <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of money once very foolishly; but that a man grew wiser by time." The rooms at this seat, which were now much out of repair, and would have all fallen in but for his son John Elwes, Esq.; who had resided there, he thought too expensively furnished, as worse things might have served. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> a window was broken, there was to be no repair but that of a little <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, or that of piecing in a bit of broken glass; which had at length been done so frequently, and in so many shapes, that it would have puzzled a mathematician to say "what <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> they described." To <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-SAVE">save</a> fire, he would walk about the remains of an old greenhouse, or sit with a servant in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KITCHEN">kitchen</a>. During the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a> he would amuse himself with going into the fields to glean the corn on the grounds of his own tenants; and they used to leave a little more than common to please the old gentleman, who was as eager after it as any pauper in the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>. In the advance of the season, his morning employment was to pick up any stray chips, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BONES">bones</a>, or other things, to carry to the fire, in his pocket—and he was one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> surprised by a neighbouring gentleman in the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of pulling down, with some difficulty, a crow's nest for this purpose. On the gentleman wondering why he gave himself this trouble—"Oh, Sir, (replied old Elwes), it is really a shame that these creatures should do so. Do but see what waste they make! They <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DON">don</a>'t care how extravagant they are!" As no gleam of favourite passion, or any ray of amusement, broke through this gloom of penury, his insatiable desire of saving was now become uniform Miser, and systematic. He used still to ride about the country on one of these mares—but then he rode her very economically, on the soft turf, adjoining the road, without putting himself to the expense of shoes, as he observed, "The turf was so pleasant to a horse's foot!" And when any gentleman called to pay him a visit, and the boy who attended in the stables was profuse enough to put a little hay before his horse, old Elwes would flit back into the stable, and take the hay very carefully away. That very strong appetite which Mr Elwes had in some measure restrained during the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a> sitting of parliament, he now indulged most voraciously, and on everything he could find. To save, as he thought, the expense of going to a butcher, he would have a whole sheep killed, and to eat mutton to the end of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a>. When he occasionally had his river drawn, though sometimes horse-loads of small fish were taken, not one would he suffer to be thrown in again; for he observed, "He should never see them again!" <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAME">Game</a> in the last state of putrefaction, and meat that walked about his plate, would he continue to eat, rather than have new things killed before the old provision was finished. With this diet—the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHARNEL">charnel</a>-house of sustenance—his dress kept pace—equally in the last stage of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> dissolution. Sometimes he would walk about in a tattered brown-coloured hat, and sometimes in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RED">red</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WHITE">white</a> woolen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>, like a prisoner confined for debt. His shoes he never would suffer to be cleaned, lest they should be worn out the sooner. But still, with all this self-denial—that penury of life to which the inhabitant of an almshouse is not doomed—still did he think he was profuse, and frequently say, "He must be a little more careful of his property." His disquietude on the subject of money was now continual. When he went to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a>, he would put five or ten guineas into a bureau; and then, full of his money, after he had retired to rest, and sometimes in the middle of the night, he would come down to see if it was there. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of mortification at which Mr Elwes was now arrived was all but a denial of the common necessaries of life: and indeed it might have admitted a doubt, whether or not, if his manors, his fishponds, and some grounds in his own hands, had not furnished a subsistence, where he had not anything actually to buy, he would not, rather than have bought anything have starved. Strange as this may appear, it is not exaggerated.—He one day, during this period, dined upon the remaining part of a moorhen, which had been brought out of the river by a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RAT">rat</a>! and at another eat an undigested part of a pike which a larger one had swallowed, but had not finished, and which were taken in this state in a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NET">net</a>. At the time this last circumstance happened, he discovered a strange kind of satisfaction; for he said to a friend, "Aye! this was killing two birds with one <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-STONE">stone</a>!" In the room of all comment—of all moral—it let be remarked, that at this time Mr Elwes was perhaps worth nearly eight hundred thousand pounds! and, at this period, he had not made his will, of course was not favoring from any sentiment of affection for any person. The <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> of 1788 Mr Elwes passed at his house in Welbeck-street, London; and he passed that summer without any other <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> than that of two maid servants; servants; for he had now given up the expense of keeping any <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MALE">male</a> domestick. His chief employment used to be that of getting up early in a morning to visit some of his houses in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>-le-Bone, which during the summer were repairing. As he was there generally at four o'clock in a morning, he was of course on the spot before the workmen; and he used contentedly to sit down on the steps before the door, to scold them when they did come. The neighbours who used to see him appear thus regular every morning, and who concluded, from his apparel, he was one of the workmen, observed, "there never was so punctual a man as the old carpenter." During the whole morning he would continue to run up and down stairs to see the men were not idle for an instant, with the same anxiety as if his whole <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> in life had been centered in the finishing this house, regardless of the greater property he had at stake in various places, and for ever employed in the minutiae only of affairs. Indeed such was his anxiety about this house, the rent of which was not above L. 50 a-year, that it brought on a fever which nearly cost him his life; but the fate which dragged him on thus strangely to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BURY">bury</a> him under the load of his own wealth, seemed as restless as it was unaccountable. In the muscular and unencumbered frame of Mr Elwes there was everything that promised <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> length of life; and he lived to above 70 years of age without any natural disorder attacking him; but, as Lord <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BACON">Bacon</a> has well observed, "the minds of some men are a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAMP">lamp</a> that is continually <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BURNING">burning</a>;" and such was the mind of Mr Elwes. Removed from those occasional public avocations which had once engaged his attention, money was now his only thought. He rove upon money—upon money he lay down to rest; and as his capacity sunk away from him by degrees, he dwindled from the real cares of his property into the puerile concealment of a few guineas. This little store he would carefully wrap up in various papers, and depositing them in different corners, would amuse himself with running from one to the other, to see whether they were all safe. Then forgetting, perhaps, where he had concealed some of them, he would become as seriously afflicted as a man might be who had lost all his property. Nor was the day alone thus spent—he would frequently rise in the middle of the night, and be heard walking about different parts of the house, looking after what he had thus hidden and forgotten. During the winter of 1789, the last winter Mr Elwes was fated to see, his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> visibly weakened every day; and from the unceasing wish to save money he now began to fear he should die in want of it. Mr Gilson had been appointed his builder in the room of Mr Adams; and one day, when this gentleman waited upon him, he said with apparent concern, "Sir, pray consider in what a wretched state I am; you see in what a good house I am living; and here are five guineas, which is all I have at present; and how I shall go on with such a sum of money puzzles me to death. I dare say you thought I was rich; now you see how it is!" Mr George Elwes having now settled at his seat at Marcham in Berkshire, he was naturally desirous that, in the affections of his wife, his father might at length find a comfortable home. In London he was certainly most uncomfortable: but still, with these temptations before and behind him, a journey with any expense annexed to it was insurmountable. This, however, was luckily obviated by an offer from Mr Partis, a gentleman of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAW">law</a>, to take him to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> seat in Berkshire with his purse perfectly whole. But there was one circumstance still very distressing—the old gentleman had now nearly worn out his last coat, and he would not buy a new one; his son, therefore, with a pious fraud, contrived to get Mr Partis to buy him a coat and make him a present of it. Thus, formerly having had a good coat, then a bad one, and at last no coat at all, he was kind enough to accept one from a neighbour. Mr Elwes carried with him into Berkshire five guineas and a half, and half a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>. Left the mention of this sum may appear singular, it should be said, that previous to his journey he had carefully wrapped it up in various folds of paper, that no part of it might be lost. On the arrival of the old gentleman, Mr George Elwes and his wife did every thing they could to make the country a scene of quiet to him. But "he had that within" which baffled every effort of this kind. Of his heart it might be said, "there was no peace in Israel." His mind, cast away upon the vast and troubled ocean of his property extending beyond the bounds of his calculation, returned to amuse itself with fetching and carrying about a few guineas, which in that ocean was indeed a drop. But nature had now carried on life nearly as far as she was able, and the sand was almost run out. The first symptoms of more immediate decay was his inability to enjoy his rest at night. Frequently would he be heard at midnight as if struggling with some one in his chamber, and crying out, "I will keep my money, I will; nobody shall rob me of my property." On any one of the family going into his room, he would start from this fever of anxiety, and, as if waking from a troubled dream, again hurry into bed, and seem unconscious of what had happened. At length, on the 26th November 1789, expired this miserably rich man, whose property, nearly reaching to a million, extended itself almost through every county in England.

MISERICORDIA

Pages 191-191

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAW">law</a>, is an arbitrary fine imposed on any person for an offence; this is called misericordia, because the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERCEMENT">amercement</a> ought to be but small, and less than that required by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGNA_CHARTA">magna <a cla</a>ss="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARTA">charta</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> a person be outrageously amerced in a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COURT">court</a> that is not of record, the writ called moderata misericordia lies for moderating the amercement according to the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the fault. MISFORTUNE. An unlucky accident.

MISFORTUNE

Pages 191-192
or chance, in law, a deficiency of the will; or committing of an unlawful act by misfortune or chance, and not by design. In such case, the will observes a total neutrality, and does not cooperate with the deed: which therefore wants one main ingredient of a crime. See CRIME. Of this, when it affects the life of another, we have spoken under the article HOMICIDE; and in this place have only occasion to observe, that if any accidental mischief happens to follow from the performance of a lawful act, the party stands excused from all guilt: but if a man be doing any thing unlawful, and a consequence ensues which he did not foresee or intend, as the death of a man or the like, his want of foresight shall be no excuse; for, being guilty of one offence, in doing antecedently what is in itself unlawful, he is criminally guilty of whatever consequence may follow the first misbehaviour.

MISHNA

Pages 187-187
or Misna, (from נון, iteravit), a part of the Jewish Talmud. The Mishna contains the text; and the Gemara, which is the second part of the Talmud, contains the commentaries: so that the Gemara is, as it were, a glossary on the Mishna. The Mishna consists of various traditions of the Jews, and of explanations of several passages of scripture; these traditions serving as an explication of the written law, and supplement to it, are said to have been delivered to Moses during the time of his abode on the Mount; which he afterwards communicated to Aaron, Eleazar, and his servant Joshua. By these they were transmitted to the 70 elders, by them to the prophets, who communicated them to the men of the great sanhedrim, from whom the wise men of Jerusalem and Babylon received them. According to Prideaux's account, they passed from Jeremiah to Baruch, from him to Ezra, and from Ezra to the men of the great synagogue, the last of whom was Simon the Just; who delivered them to Antigonus of Socho; and from him they came down in regular succession to Simeon, who took our Saviour in his arms; to Gamaliel, at whose feet Paul was educated; and last of all to Rabbi Judah the Holy, who committed them to writing in the Mishna. But Dr Prideaux, rejecting this Jewish fiction, observes, that after the death of Simeon the Just, about 299 years before Christ, the Mishnaical doctors arose, who, by their comments and conclusions, added to the number of those traditions which had been received and allowed by Ezra and the men of the great synagogue; so that towards the middle of the second century after Christ, under the empire of Antoninus Pius, it was found necessary to commit these traditions to writing; more especially, as their country had considerably suffered under Adrian, and many of their schools had been dissolved, and their learned men cut off; and therefore the usual method of preserving their traditions had failed. Rabbi Judah on this occasion being rector of the school at Tiberias, and president of the sanhedrim in that place, undertook the work, and compiled it in six books, each consisting of several tracts, which altogether make up the number of 63. Prud. Consec. vol. ii. p. 468, &c. ed. 9. This learned author computes, that the Mishna was composed about the 150th year of our Lord; but Dr Lightfoot says, that Rabbi Judah compiled the Mishna about the year of Christ 190, in the latter end of the reign of Commodus; or, as some compute, in the year of Christ 220. Dr Lardner is of opinion, that this work could not have been finished before the year 190, or later. Collect. of Jewish and Heathen Testimonies, &c. vol. i. p. 178. Thus the book called the Mishna was formed; a book which the Jews have generally received with the greatest veneration. The original has been published with a Latin translation by Surenhusius, with notes of his own, and others from the learned Maimonides, &c. in 6 vols. fol. Amsterd. A.D. 1608—1703. (See TALMUD). It is written in a much purer style, and is not near so full of dreams and visions as the Gemara.

MISNOMER

Pages 192-192

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAW">law</a>, a misnaming <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> mistaking a person's name. The Christian name of a person should always be perfect; but the law is not so strict in regard to surnames, a small mistake in which <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a> be dispensed with to make good a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a>, and support the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of the party. See <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PLEA">Plea</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDICTMENT">Indictment</a>.

MISPRISIONS

Pages 192-192

(a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TERM">term</a> derived from the old French, misprit, a neglect <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> contempt), are, in the acceptation of our <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAW">law</a>, generally understood to be all such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> offences as are under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, but nearly bordering thereon: and it is said, that a misprision is contained in every <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TREASON">treason</a> and felony whatsoever; and that, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">king</a> so pleases, the offender may be proceeded against for the misprision only. And upon the same principle, while the jurisdiction of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STAR_CHAMBER"><a class="xr</a>ef" href="vol17.html#article-STAR">star</a>-chamber subsisted, it was held that the king might remit a prosecution for treason, and cause the delinquent to be censured in that <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COURT">court</a>, merely for a high misdemeanor: as happened in the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CASE">case</a> of Roger <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Rutland, in 43 Eliz. who was concerned in the earl of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a>'s rebellion. Misprisions are generally divided into two sorts; <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEGATIVE">negative</a>, which consist in the concealment of something which ought to be revealed; and positive, which consist in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> of something which ought not to be done. 1. Of the first, or negative kind, is what is called misprision of treason; consisting in the bare knowledge and concealment of treason, without any degree of assent thereto: for any assent makes the party a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> traitor; as indeed the concealment, which was construed aiding and abetting, did at the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMON">common</a> law; in like manner as the knowledge of a plot against the state, and not revealing it, was a capital crime at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>, and other states of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. But it is now enacted by the statute 1 & 2 Ph. & Mar. c. 1c. that a bare concealment of treason shall be only held a misprison. This concealment becomes criminal, if the party apprised of the treason does not, as soon as conveniently may be, reveal it to some judge of assize or <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> of the peace. But if there be any probable circumstances of assent, as if one goes to a treasonable meeting, knowing beforehand that a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSPIRACY">conspiracy</a> is intended against the king; or, being in such <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> once by accident, and having heard such treasonable conspiracy, meets the same company again, and hears more of it, but conceals it; this is an implied assent in law, and makes the concealer guilty of actual high-treason. Misprision of felony is also the concealment of a felony which a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAN">man</a> knows, but never assented to; for, if he assented, this makes him either principal or <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACCESSORY">accessory</a>. And the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> of this, in a public officer, by the statute Welfm. r. 3 Edw. I. c. 9, is imprisonment for a year and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>; in a common person, imprisonment for a less discretionary <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a>; and, in both, fine and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RANSOM">ransom</a> at the king's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>; which misprision-pleasure of the king must be observed, once for all, not to signify any extrajudicial <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a> of the sovereign, but such as is declared by his representatives, the judges in his courts of justice; voluntas regis in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CURIA">curia</a>, non in camera. 2. Misprisions, which are merely positive, are generally denominated contempt or high misdemeanor; of which the principal is the mal-administration of such high officers as are in public trust and employment. This is usually punished by the method of parliamentary impeachment; wherein such penalties, short of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, are inflicted, as to the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEERS">peers</a> shall seem proper; confining usually of banishment, imprisonment, fines, or perpetual disfability. Hither also may be referred the offence of embezzling the public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, called among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> peculatus; which the Julian law punished with death in a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a>, and with deportation, or banishment, in a private person. With us it is not a capital crime, but subjects the committer of it to a discretionary fine and imprisonment.—Other misprisions are, in general, such contempts of the executive magistrate as demonstrate themselves by some arrogant and undutiful behaviour towards the king and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>: for a detail of which, vide Blackstone's Comment. iv. 22.

MISSAL

Pages 192-192

the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MASS">mass</a>-book, containing the several masses to be said on particular days. It is derived from the Latin word missa, which, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Christian <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, signified every <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> of divine <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>.

MISSIO

Pages 192-192

among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, was a full discharge given to a soldiery after 20 years <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, and differed from the exauditorio, which was a discharge from duty after 17 years service. Every soldiery had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to claim his missio at the end of 20 years.

MISSION

Pages 192-193

in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>, denotes a power <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> to preach the gospel. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ gave his disciples their mission in these words, Go and teach all nations, &c. The Romanists reproach the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>, that their ministers have no mission, as not being authorized in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of their ministry, either by an uninterrupted succession from the apostles, or by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a>, or by any extraordinary <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of a vocation. Many among us deny any other mission necessary for the ministry than the talents necessary to discharge it. Mission is also used for an establishment of people zealous for the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> of God and the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-SALVATION">salvation</a> of souls; who go and preach the gospel in remote countries and among infidels. There are missions in the East as well as in the West Indies. Among the Romanists, the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> orders of St Dominic, St Francis, St Augustine, and the Jesuits, have missions in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEVANT">Levant</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, &c. The Jesuits have also missions in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, and all other parts of the globe where they have been able to penetrate. There have been also several Protestant missions for diffusing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> of Christianity through the benighted regions of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> and America. Of this kind has been the Danish mission planned by Frederic IV. in 1706. And the liberality of private benefactors in our own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> has been also extended to the support of missionaries among the Indians in America, &c.

MISSIONARY

Pages 193-193

an ecclesiastic who devotes himself and his labours to some mission, either for the instruction of the orthodox, the conviction of heretics, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> the conversion of infidels. See Jesuits.

MISSISSIPPI

Pages 193-193

also called the river of St <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, is one of the largest in the world. Its source is unknown. It passes south through <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LOUISIANA">Louisiana</a>, and runs above 2000 miles, till it falls into the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLORIDA">Florida</a>. Like the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NILE">Nile</a>, it has periodical inundations, by the melting of snow in the north, so that in May it overflows the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> on each side, from 60 to 90 miles, and the inundation continues till near the end of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>. In the lowest parts of the country there are marshes, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a>, along the banks, which are generally covered with trees, and in some places the course of the river is confined between <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> precipices. Its inundations always leave a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of mud upon the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAND">land</a>, and sometimes carry <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DOWN">down</a> trees to the river's mouth, where they form new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, and render the entrance difficult.

MISSON

Pages 193-193

whose pleadings before the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in favour of the reformers bear genuine marks of eloquence and ability, retired into England after the revocation of the edict of Nantes, and became a strenuous assertor of the Protestant <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. In the years 1687 and 1688 he travelled to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> as governor to an English nobleman; in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of which he published at the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAGUE">Hague</a>, "A new voyage to Italy," 3 vols 12mo; which has been translated into English with many additions. He published also the "Sacred <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-THEATRE">Theatre</a> at Cevennes, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> an account of Prophecies and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">Miracles</a> performed in that <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LANGUEDOC">Languedoc</a>," <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONDON">London</a> 1707. "Observations and Remarks of a Traveller," 12mo, Hague. He died at London in 1721.

MISSUS

Pages 193-193

in the Circenian games, were the matches in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> chariot races. The usual <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of matches in one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> was 24; though the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Domitian presented the people with 100. The last <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MATCH">match</a> was generally made at the expense of the people, who made a collection for the purpose; hence it was called missus aerarius, a subscription plate.

MISTAKE

Pages 193-193

any wrong <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> committed, not thro' an evil <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, but through an <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-ERROR">error</a> of judgement.

MISUSER

Pages 193-193

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAW">law</a>, is an abuse of any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> benefit; as "He shall make fine for his misuser." Old Nat. Br. 149. By misuser a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> of a corporation may be forfeited; so also an office, &c.

MISY

Pages 193-193

in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of the chalcantha, a fossil very <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in the Turkish dominions, and sometimes found in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of Cremonitz in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>. It is a considerably firm substance, of an <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> texture, not <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a>; much resembling some of our more gaudy marcasites, but wanting in their <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HARDNESS">hardness</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>. It is of no determinate shape <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> size; but is often found in small detached masses, which are usually <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, flat, and very rugged at the edges. As to its medical virtues, they are no other than those of the green vitriol.

MITCHELSOWN

Pages 193-193

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a>-town of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Cork and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MUNSTER">Munster</a> in Ireland, 102 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>. Here is a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> for the support of 12 decayed gentlemen and 12 decayed gentlewomen, who have L. 40 yearly, and handsome apartments, and a chaplain at L. 100 a-year, with a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>; divine <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> is daily performed in a neat chapel belonging to the college: the whole was founded by the late <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Kingdon. Here is also a most magnificent seat of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Kingsborough.—<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAIRS">Fairs</a> are held at this town 30th <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> and 12th November.

MITELLA

Pages 193-193
BASTARD AMERICAN SANICLE: A genus of the digynia order, belonging to the decandra clas of plants; and in the natural method ranking under the 13th order, Succulenta. The calyx is quinquefid; the corolla pentapetalous, and inserted into the calyx; the petals pinnatifid; the capsule unicellular and bivalved, with the valves equal. There are two species, both natives of North America, rising with annual herbaceous stalks from five or six to eight or nine inches in height, and producing spikes of small whitish flowers, whose petals are fringed on their edges. They are easily propagated by parting their roots; and should be planted in a shady situation, and in a soft loamy soil.

MITHRA

Pages 193-193

feasts of, in antiquity, were feasts celebrated among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MITHRAS">Mithras</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>. The most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> instance of this Mithras among the Romans occurs in an inscription dated in the third consulate of Trajan, or about the year of Christ 101. This is the dedication of an altar to the sun under the above name, thus <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a>, Dio Soli Mithrae. But the worship of Mithras was not known in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-ORIGEN">Origen</a>, who died about the year of Christ 263; though it was <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMON">common</a> at Rome for more than a century before this time. The worship of Mithras was proscribed at Rome in the year 378, by order of Gracchus, prefect of the praetorium. According to M. Freer, the feasts of Mithras were derived from Chaldea, where they had been instituted for celebrating the entrance of the sun into the sign Taurus.

MITHRAS

Pages 628-643
or, according to the Persian, Mithr, was one of the great gods of the Assyrians. His worship was for many ages confined to Persia. Afterwards, however, it was propagated to far and wide, that some have imagined they had discovered vestiges of it even in Gaul. Mithr, according to Dr Hyde, signifies *Relig. vet. love, and likewise the Sun. If we might presume to differ from so respectable an authority, we should conjecture that it is a cognate of the Hebrew word Muthir, "excellence, pretantia." That there was an analogy between the Hebrew and old Persian, is generally admitted by the learned. Be that as it may, Mithras was the sun (p) among the Persians; and in honour of (k) Persons who had descended into Trophonius's vault were said to have been so terrified with shocking sights, that they never laughed during the remainder of their lives. (l) These were itrolling poets like our minstrels, who frequented the houses of the great men of Greece, and entertained the company upon public occasions with singing and tales of other times. (m) Bishop Warburton has, with much ingenuity, and a vast profusion of reading, endeavoured to prove that Virgil borrowed the whole scenery of the sixth Æneid from the sources mentioned in the text. (n) Isis was the moon, and the original Juno was the same planet. (o) Bacchus was the Osiris of the Egyptians, and Ceres was the Isis of the same people. (p) Mofheim, in his notes on Cudworth's Intellectual System, page 330, has taken much pains to prove that Mithras was a deified mortal; but we cannot agree with that learned man in this point. of that luminary this institution was established. Mithras, according to Plutarch (q.), was the middle god between Oramaz and Ariman, the two supreme divinities of Persia. But the fact is, the solar planet was the visible emblem of Oramaz, the good genius of the Persian tribes, and the same with the Osiris of the Egyptians. From these people, some have imagined that Zoroaster (r), or Zerdusht, borrowed his mysteries of Mithras. To this opinion we cannot give our assent, because the probationary trials to be undergone by the candidates among the former were much more savage and sanguinary than among the latter. Both, however, were instituted in honour of the same deity; and probably the scenes exhibited, and the information communicated in both, were analogous; a circumstance which perhaps gave birth to the opinion above-mentioned. The grand festival of Mithras was celebrated six days, in the middle of the month Mihr (s). Upon these days, it was lawful for the kings of Persia to get drunk and dance. On this festival, we imagine, the candidates for initiation, having duly proved their vocation, were solemnly admitted to the participation of the mysteries. Zoroaster (t) worshipped Mithras, or the Sun, in a certain natural cave, which he formed into a temple, and filled up in a manner exactly mathematical. There Mithras was represented as presiding over the lower world with all the pomp of royal magnificence. In it too were seen the symbols of Mithras and of the world, philosophically and mathematically exhibited, to be contemplated and worshipped. This deity was sometimes represented as mounted on a bull, which he is breaking, and which he kills with a sword. On some bas reliefs still existing, he appears as a young man with his tiara turned upward, after the manner of the Persian kings. He is clothed with a short tunic and breeches, after the Persian fashion. Sometimes he wears a small cloke. By his sides are seen other human figures, with tiaras of the same fashion on their heads, but without clokes. One of these figures commonly holds in his one hand a torch lifted up; in the other one turned downward. Sometimes over the cave is seen the chariots of the sun and moon, and divers constellations, such as cancer, scorpion, &c. In one of those caves the ceremonies of initiation were performed; but before the candidate could be admitted, he was forced to undergo a course of probationary exercises, so numerous and so rigorous, that very few had courage and fortitude enough to go through them. He was obliged to live a life of virtue and abstinence for a space of seven years previous to the period of his initiation. Some months before it, he was obliged to submit to a long and austere fast, which continued fifty days. He was to retire several days to a deep and dark dungeon, where he was successively exposed to all the extremes of heat and cold. Meanwhile he frequently underwent the bastinado, which the priests applied without mercy. Some say this flogging continued two whole days, and was repeated no less than fifteen times. In the course of these probationary exercises, the candidate was generally reduced to a skeleton; and we are told, that there have been several instances of persons who have perished in the attempt. Upon the eve of the initiation, the aspirant was obliged to brace on his armour, in order to encounter giants and savage monsters. In those spacious subterranean mansions a mock hunting was exhibited. The priests and all the subordinate officers of the temple, transformed into lions, tygers, leopards, boars, wolves, and other savage creatures, affrighted him with loud howlings, roaring, and yelling, and every instance of ferine fury. In those mock combats, the hero was often in danger of being really worried, and always came off with bruises and wounds. Lampridius informs us, that when the emperor Commodus was initiated, he actually carried the joke too far, and butchered one of the priests who attacked him in the figure of a wild beast. The Persians worshipped Mithras or the Sun by a perpetual fire; hence the votary was obliged to undergo a fiery trial; that is, to pass seven times through the sacred fire, and each time to plunge himself into cold water. Some have made these probationary penances amount to eighty; others have thought that they were in all only eight. As we find no good authority for either of these numbers, we think ourselves at liberty to hazard the following conjecture: The number seven was deemed sacred over all the earth. The Mythric penances we imagine were either seven, or if they exceeded it, were regulated by seven repetitions of that number. The candidate having undergone all these torturing trials with becoming patience and fortitude, was declared a proper subject for initiation. But before his admission he was obliged to bind himself by the most solemn oath, with horrible imprecations annexed, never to divulge any single article of all that should be communicated to him in the course of his initiation. What ineffable secrets were imparted to revelations the initiated, it is impossible at this distance of time to discover with any tolerable degree of certainty. We may, however, rest assured, that the most authentic tradition concerning the origin of the universe; the nature, attributes, perfections, and operations, of Ormazd; the baleful influences of Ariman; and the benign --- (q.) Isis and Osiris, page 369 l. 20, from the bottom. This philosopher makes Zoroaster, according to some, 5000 years prior to the Trojan war. This date is certainly extravagant. We cannot, however, agree with some moderns, who make him contemporary with Darius Hystaspes, the immediate successor of Cambyses, because it contradicts all antiquity. (r.) M. Silohwette, Differ. V. page 17, asserts that Zoroaster was initiated among the Egyptians. (s.) The month Mihr began September 30, and ended October 30. (t.) See Dr Hyde de Rel vet. Perf. page 16, 17. Mr Bryant's Anal. vol. i. page 232. Porphyre de antro Nymph, page 254. This philosopher often mentions the cave of Mithras, and always attributes the institution of his rites to Zoroaster. nign effects of the government of Mithras, were unfolded and inculcated. The secret phenomena of nature, as far as they had been discovered by the magi, were likewise exhibited; and the application of their effects, to astonish and delude the vulgar, were taught both in theory and practice. The exercise of public and private virtues was warmly recommended; and vice represented in the most odious and frightful colours. Both these injunctions were, we may suppose, enforced by a display of the pleasures of Elysium and the pains of Tartarus, as has been observed above in describing the mysteries of the Egyptians. Those initiations are mentioned by Lampridius in the life of Commodus, and likewise by Justin Tryphon, and Tertullian, who both flourished in the second century. The last of these two speaks of a kind of baptism, which washed from the souls of the initiated all the stains which they had contracted during the course of their lives prior to their initiation. He at the same time mentions a particular mark which was imprinted upon them (v), of an offering of bread, and an emblem of the resurrection; which particulars, however, he does not describe in detail. In that offering, which was accompanied with a certain form of prayer, a vessel of water was offered up with the bread. The same father elsewhere informs us, that there was presented to the initiated a crown suspended on the point of a sword; but that they were taught to say, Mithras is my crown. By this answer was intimated, that they looked upon the service of that deity as their chief honour and ornament. After that the Telete (x) were finished, the pupil was brought out of the cave or temple, and with great solemnity proclaimed a lion of Mithras (y); a title which imported strength and intrepid courage in the service of the deity. They were now consecrated to the god, and were supposed to be under his immediate protection; an idea which of course animated them to the most daring and dangerous enterprises. The worship of Mithras was introduced into the Roman empire towards the end of the republic, where it made very rapid progress. When Christianity began to make a figure in the empire, the champions for paganism thought of proposing to men the worship of this power of benevolence, in order to counterbalance or annihilate that worship which the Christians paid to Jesus Christ the true Sun of righteousness. But this mode was soon abolished, together with the other rites of paganism. The Persian grandness often affected names compounded with Mithras; hence Mithridates, Mithrobarzanes, &c.: Hence, too, the precious stone called Mithridat*, which by the reflexion of the sun sparkled with a variety of colours. There is likewise a certain pearl of many different colours, which they call Mithras. It is found among the mountains near the s="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RED">Red Sea; and when exposed to the sun, it sparkles with a variety of dyes. We find likewise a king of Egypt of that name who reigned at Heliopolis; who being commanded in a dream to erect an obelisk to the solar deity, reared a most prodigious one in the neighbourhood of that city. The votaries of Mithras pretended that he was sprung from a rock, and that therefore the place where the mysterious ceremonies were communicated to the initiated was always a cave. Many different reasons have been assigned for the origin of this rock-born deity, most of which appear to us unsatisfactory. If our readers will be obliging enough to accept of a simple and obvious conjecture, they may take the following: A rock is the symbol of strength and stability; from a rock, the dominion of Mithras, in the opinion of his votaries, was firm as a rock, and stable as the everlasting hills. If our readers should not admit the probability of this conjecture, we would beg leave to remit them to the learned Mr Bryant's Analysis of Mythology, where they will find this point discussed with deep research and wonderful ingenuity. Whatever may have been the origin of this opinion with relation to the birth of Mithras, it is certain that some reverence to rocks and caves was kept up a long time even after the establishment of Christianity. Hence the prohibition given to some of the profane to that religion, that they should no more presume to offer up their prayers ad petras at the rocks (a). We shall conclude our account of the mysteries of Mithras with a passage from Mr Anquetil, to whom we are so much indebted for what knowledge we have of the Persian theology, and in which the functions of that deity are briefly and comprehensively delineated. "The peculiar functions of Mithras are to fight continually against Abriman and the impure army of evil genii, whose constant employment is to scatter terror and devastation over the universe; to protect the frame of nature from the demons and their productions. For this purpose he is furnished with a thousand ears and a thousand eyes, and traverses the space between heaven and earth, --- (v) In allusion to this practice of imprinting a sacred mark, probably on the forehead of the initiated, we find the injunction to the angel, Ezek. chap. ix. ver. 4, and the Revelation paffim. (x) The mysteries were called Telete, which imports, "the rites which confer perfection." (y) Tertull. adv. marc. p. 55. The priests of Mithras were called the lions of Mithras, and his priestesses lionesses; some say hyenas. The other inferior ministers were called eagles, hawks, ravens, &c. and on their festivals they wore marks corresponding to their titles, after the Egyptian manner, where the priests appeared at the ceremonies with masks resembling the heads of lions, apes, dogs, &c. a circumstance which furnishes a presumption that the mysteries of Mithras were of Egyptian original. (z) Our Saviour probably alludes to this emblem, when he talks of building his church on a rock; and adds, that the gates of hell should not prevail against it. (a) The Caledonian druids seem to have regarded certain stones with a superstitious veneration, in which the Catholics imitated them. There are in several places of Scotland large stones, which the vulgar call lecre stones, i.e. we imagine, lecture. earth, his hands armed with a club or mace. Mithras gives to the earth light and sun; he traces a course for the waters; he gives to men corn, pastures, and children; to the world virtuous kings and warriors; maintains harmony upon earth, watches over the law, &c." As the history of Mithras, and the nature of his mysteries, are not generally known, we imagined it would be agreeable to many of our readers to have the most important articles relating to that subject laid before them as it were in detail. We now proceed to the orgia, or mysteries of Bacchus, which we shall introduce with a brief history of that deity. The original Dionysus or Bacchus was the Osiris of the Egyptians, which last was the Sun (b). Whether there was an Egyptian monarch of that name, as Diodorus Siculus affirms (c), has no manner of connection with the present disquisition. The Greek name of that deity is plainly oriental, being compounded of di, "bright;" and napha or nafa, in the Æolic dialect nua, "a prince." This name was imported from the East by Orpheus, Cadmus, or by whoever else communicated the worship of Osiris to the Greeks. That the Dionysus of the Greeks was the same with the Osiris of the Egyptians, is universally allowed. Herodotus tells us expressly*, that Osiris is Dionysus in the Greek language: Martianus Capellus, quoted above, expresses the very same idea.
