Mithridates, on his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a>, sent to Rome Gordius the governor of his son; who solemnly declared before the Roman people, that the youth who sat on the throne of Cappadocia was the third son and lawful heir of Ariarathes, and that he was supported as such by Mithridates. This intricate affair displeased the Roman senate; and finally to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> the dispute they took away the kingdom of Cappadocia from Mithridates, and Paphlagonia from Nicomedes. These two kingdoms being thus separated from their original possessors, were presented with their freedom and independence; but the Cappadocians refused it, and received Ariobarzanes for king. Such were the first seeds of enmity between Rome and the king of Pontus. Mithridates never lost an opportunity by which he might lessen the influence of his adversaries; and the more effectually to destroy their power in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, he ordered all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> that were in his dominions to be massacred. This was done in one night, and no less than 150,000, according to Plutarch, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> 80,000 Romans, as Appian mentions, were made the victims of his cruelty. This called aloud for vengeance. Aquilius, and soon after Sylla, marched against Mithridates with a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>. The former was made prisoner; but Sylla obtained a victory over the king's generals; and another decisive engagement rendered him <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of all <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACEDONIA">Macedonia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-IONIA">Ionia</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASIA_MINOR">Asia <a cl</a>ass="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a>. This ill fortune was aggravated by the loss of about 200,000 men, who were killed in the several engagements that had been fought; and Mithridates, weakened by repeated ill success by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SEA">sea</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAND">land</a>, sued for peace from the conqueror, which he obtained on condition of defraying the expenses which the Romans had incurred by the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WAR">war</a>, and of remaining satisfied with the possessions which he had received from his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>. While these negotiations of peace were carried on, Mithridates was not unmindful of his real <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>. His poverty, and not his inclinations, obliged him to wish for peace. He immediately took the field with an army of 140,000 infantry and 16,000 horses, which consisted of his own forces and those of his son-in-<a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAW">law</a> Tigranes king of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMENIA">Armenia</a>. With such a numerous army, he soon made himself master of the Roman provinces in Asia; none dared to oppose his conquests; and the Romans, relying on his fidelity, had withdrawn the greatest part of their armies from the country. The news of his warlike preparations was no sooner heard, than Lucullus the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a> marched into Asia; and without delay he blocked up the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAMP">camp</a> of Mithridates, who was then besieging Cyzicus. The Asiatic monarch escaped from him, and fled into the heart of his kingdom. Lucullus pursued him with the utmost celerity; and would have taken him prisoner after a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, had not the avidity of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> preferred the plundering of a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MULE">mule</a> loaded with <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> to the taking of a monarch who had exercised such cruelties against their countrymen, and shown himself so faithless to the most solemn engagements. After this escape Mithridates was more careful about the safety of his person; and he even ordered his wives and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SISTERS">sisters</a> to destroy themselves, fearful of their falling into the enemy's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. The appointment of Gabrio to the command of the Roman forces, instead of Lucullus, was favourable to Mithridates, who recovered the greatest part of his dominions. The sudden arrival of Pompey, however, soon put an end to his victories. A battle in the night was fought near the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EUPHRATES">Euphrates</a>, in which the troops of Pontus laboured under every disadvantage. The engagement was by <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MOON">moon</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, and as the moon then shone in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FACE">face</a> of the enemy, the lengthened shadows of the arms of the Romans having induced Mithridates to believe that the two armies were <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> together, the arrows of his soldiers were darted from a great distance, and their efforts rendered ineffectual. An universal overthrow ensued, and Mithridates, bold in his misfortunes, rushed through the thick ranks of the enemy at the head of 800 horsemen, 500 of whom perished in the attempt to follow him. He fled to Tigranes; but that monarch refused an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASYLUM">asylum</a> to his father-in-law, whom he had before supported with all the collected forces of his kingdom. Mithridates found a safe retreat among the Scythians; and though destitute of power, friends, and resources, yet he meditated the overthrow of the Roman empire, by penetrating into the heart of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> by land. These wild projects were rejected by his followers, and he sued for peace. It was denied to his ambassadors; and the victorious Pompey declared, that, to obtain it, Mithridates must ask it in person. He scorned to trust himself in the hands of his enemy, and resolved to conquer or to die. His subjects refused to follow him any longer; and revolting from him, made his son Pharnaces king. The son showed himself ungrateful to his father; and even, according to some writers, he ordered him to be put to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. This unnatural treatment broke the heart of Mithridates; he obliged his wife to poison herself, and attempted to do the same himself: It was in vain: the frequent antidotes he had taken in the early part of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, strengthened his constitution against the poison; and when this was unavailing, he attempted to stab himself. The blow was not mortal; and a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a> who was then present, at his own request gave him the fatal stroke, about 64 years before the Christian era. Such were the misfortunes, abilities, and miserable end, of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAN">man</a>, who supported himself so <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a> against the power of Rome, and who, according to the declarations of the Roman authors, proved a more powerful and indefatigable adversary to the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Italy than the great Annibal, Pyrrhus, Perseus, or Antiochus. Mithridates has been commended for his eminent virtues, and censured for his vices. As a commander, he deserves the most unbounded applause; and it may create admiration to see him waging war, with such success, during so many years, against the most powerful people on earth, led to the field by a Sylla, a Lucullus, and a Pompey. He was the greatest monarch that ever sat on a throne, according to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of Cicero; and indeed no greater <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> character can be brought, than the mention of the great rejoicings which happened in the Roman armies and in the capital at the news of his death. No less than 12 weeks were appointed for public thanksgivings to the immortal gods; and Pompey, who had sent the first intelligence of his death to Rome, and who had partly hastened his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>, was rewarded with the most uncommon honours. It is said that Mithridates conquered 24 nations, whose different languages he knew, and spoke with the same ease and fluency as his own. As a man of letters he also deserves <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>. He was acquainted with the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, and even wrote in that dialect a treatise on <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>. His skill in physic is well known; and even now there is a celebrated antidote which bears his name, and is called mithridate. <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SUPERSTITION">Superstition</a> as well as <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> had united to render him great; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we rely upon the authority of Justin, his birth was accompanied by the appearance of two large <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMETS">comets</a>, which were seen for 70 days successively, and whose splendor eclipsed the mid-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, and covered the fourth part of the heavens.

MITRA

Pages 195-195

was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> covering for the head, worn by the Roman ladies, and sometimes by the men; but it was looked upon as a mark of effeminacy in the last, especially when it was tied upon their heads.

MITRE

Pages 195-195

a sacerdotal ornament worn on the head, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> and certain abbots on solemn occasions; being a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>, pointed and cleft at top. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> among the Jews wore a mitre <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BONNET">bonnet</a> on his head. The inferior priests of the same <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATION">nation</a> had likewise their mitres; but in what respect they differed from that of the high-priest, is uncertain. Some contend that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> bishops wore mitres; but this is by no means certain. **Mitre**, in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, is the workmen's <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TERM">term</a> for an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> that is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> 45 degrees, or half a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> one. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the angle be a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of a right angle, they call it a half-mitre. To describe such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a>, they have an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> called the *mitre-<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>*; with this they strike mitre-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> on their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> or battens; and for dispatch, they have a *mitre-box*, as they call it, which is made of two pieces of wood, each about an inch thick, one nailed upright on the edge of the other; the upper piece hath the mitre-lines struck upon it on both sides, and a kerf to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAW">saw</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> the mitre-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a> readily, by only applying the piece into this box. **Mitre** is used by the writers of the Irish <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> for a sort of base <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, which was very <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMON">common</a> there about the year 1270, and for 30 years before and as many after. There were beside the mitre several other pieces called according to the figures impressed upon them, rofaries, lionades, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-EAGLES">eagles</a>, and by the like names. They were imported from France and other countries, and were so much below the proper currency of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, that they were not worth so much as a halfpenny each. They were at length decreed in the year 1300, and good coins struck in their <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. These were the first Irish coins in which the sceptre was left out. They were struck in the reign of Edward, the son of our Henry III, and are still found among the other antiquities of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. They have the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">king</a>'s head in a triangle full-faced. The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PENNY">penny</a>, when well preserved, weighs 22 grains; the halfpenny 10½ grains.

MITRIDATICUM BELLUM

Pages 195-195

the *Mithridatic <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WAR">War</a>*, one of the longest and most celebrated wars ever carried on by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> against a foreign power. See Pontus.

MITTAU

Pages 195-195

the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COURLAND">Courland</a>. It is strongly fortified; but was taken by the Swedes in 1701, and by the Muscovites in 1706. E. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">Long</a>, 23. §1. N. Lat. 56° 44'.

MITTIMUS

Pages 195-195

as generally used, hath two significations. 1. It signifies a writ for removing <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> transferring of records from one <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COURT">court</a> to another. 2. It signifies a precept, or command in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, under the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAND">hand</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEAL">seal</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> of the peace, directed to the gaoler or keeper of some prison, for the receiving and safe keeping of an offender <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with any crime, until he be delivered by due course of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAW">law</a>.

MITYLENE

Pages 195-195
or **Mytelen** (anc. geog.), a celebrated, powerful, and affluent city, capital of the island of Lefbos. It receives its name from Mitylene, the daughter of Macareus, a king of the country. It is greatly commended by the ancients for the flateliness of its buildings and the fruitfulness of its soil, but more particularly for the great men it produced: Pitacus, Alcæus, Sappho, Terpander, Theophanes, Helianicus, &c. were all natives of Mitylene. It was long a seat of learning; and with Rhodes and Athens, it had the honour of having educated many of the great men of Rome and Greece. In the Peloponnesian war, the Mitylenians suffered greatly for their revolt from the power of Athens; and in the Mithridatic wars, they had the boldness to resist the Romans, and disdain the treaties which had been made between Mithridates and Sylla. See Metelin.

MIXTURE

Pages 195-196

a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> assemblage of several different bodies in the same <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MASS">mass</a>. Simple mixture, consists only in the simple <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APPOSITION">apposition</a> of parts of different bodies to each other. Thus, when powders of different kinds are rubbed together, the mixture is only simple, and each of the powders retains its particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>. In like manner, when <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OIL">oil</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WATER">water</a> are mixed together, though the parts of both are confounded, so that the liquor may appear to be homogeneous, we cannot say that there is any more than a simple simple apposition of the parts, as the oil and water may very easily be again separated from each other. But the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CASE">case</a> is very different when bodies are chemically mixed; for then one or both bodies assume new properties, and can by no means be discovered in their proper form without a particular chemical <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> adapted to this purpose. Hence chemical mixture is attended with many phenomena which are never observed in simple mixtures; such as <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, effervescence, &c. To chemical mixture belongs the union of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ACIDS">acids</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ALKALIES">alkalies</a>, the amalgamation of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, solution of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GUMS">gums</a>, &c., and upon it depend many of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> operations of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>. See that article paffim. Mixture, in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PHARMACY">pharmacy</a>, a medicine which differs from a julep in this respect, that it receives into its <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> not only salts, extracts, and other substances dissoluble in water; but also earths, powders, and such substances as cannot be dissolved.

MIZEN

Pages 196-196

in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, is a particular mast <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> sail. The mizen-mast stands in the sternmost <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> of the ship. In some <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> ships there are two of these; when that next the main-mast is called the main-mizen, and that next the poop the bonaventure mizen.

MIZRAIM

Pages 196-196
or Misraim, the dual name of Egypt, used in scripture to denote the Higher and Lower Egypt, which see. It sometimes occurs singular, Mazor: 2 Kings xix. Isaiah xix. Micah vii.

MNEMOSYNE

Pages 196-196

a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Cælus and Terra. She married <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, by whom she had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NINE">nine</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MUSES">muses</a>. The word mnemosyne signifies "<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>;" and therefore the poets have rightly called Memory the mother of the muses, because it is to that mental endowment that mankind are indebted for their progress in science.

MOAB

Pages 196-196

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a> Petraea; so called from Moab the son of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">Lot</a>, to whose posterity this country was allotted by divine appointment, Deut. xi. 9. It was originally occupied by the Emim, a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-RACE">race</a> of giants exterminated by the Moabites, ibid. Moab anciently lay to the south of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMMON">Ammon</a>, before Sihon the Amorite stripped both nations of a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> of their territory, afterwards occupied by the Israelites, Numb. xxii.; and then Moab was bounded by the river Arnon to the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, the Lacus Aphalites to the west, the brook Zared to the south, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> Abarim to the east.

MOAT

Pages 196-196
or Ditch, in fortification, a deep trench dug round the rampart of a fortified place, to prevent surprises. The brink of the moat, next the rampart, is called the scarpe; and the opposite one, the counter-scarpe. A dry moat round a large place, with a strong garison, is preferable to one full of water; because the passage may be disputed inch by inch, and the besiegers, when lodged in it, are continually exposed to the bombs, grenades, and other fire-works, which are thrown incessantly from the rampart into their works. In the middle of dry moats, there is sometimes another small one, called cuvette; which is generally dug so deep till they find water to fill it. The deepest and broadest moats are accounted the best; but a deep one is preferable to a broad one: the ordinary breadth is about 20 fathoms, and the depth about 16. To drain a moat that is full of water, they dig a trench deeper than the level of the water, to let it run off; and then throw hurdles upon the mud and slime, covering them with earth or bundles of rushes, to make a sure and firm passage.

MOATAZALITES

Pages 196-196
or Separatists, a religious sect among the Turks, who deny all forms and qualities in the Divine Being; or who divest God of his attributes. There are two opinions among the Turkish divines concerning God. The first admits metaphysical forms or attributes; as, that God has wisdom, by which he is wise; power, by which he is powerful; eternity, by which he is eternal, &c. The second allows God to be wise, powerful, eternal; but will not allow any form or quality in God, for fear of admitting a multiplicity. Those who follow this latter opinion are called Moatazalites; they who follow the former, Sephatites. The Moatazalites also believed that the word of God was created in subjecto, as the schoolmen term it, and to consist of letters and found; copies thereof being written in books to express or imitate the original; they denied absolute predetermination, and affirmed that man is a free agent. This sect is said to have first invented the scholastic divinity, and is subdivided into no less than 20 inferior sects, which mutually brand one another with infidelity.

MOBILE

Pages 196-197

moveable, any thing susceptible of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> that is disposed to be moved either by itself or by some other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> mobile or mover. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRIMUM_MOBILE">Primum Mobile</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>, was a ninth heaven or sphere, imagined above those of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a> and fixed stars. This was supposed to be the fifth Mobile, first mover, and to carry all the lower spheres round Mocho along with it; by its rapidity communicating to them a motion whereby they revolved in 24 hours. But the diurnal revolution of the planets is now accounted for without the affluence of any such primum mobile. Perpetuum Mobile. See Perpetual Motion.

MOCHO

Pages 197-197

Moco, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> Mokha; by some supposed to be the Muta or Muza of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>, is a port and town on the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RED_SEA"><a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RED">Red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>, of considerable trade; contains about 10,000 inhabitants, Jews, Armenians, and Mohammedans; is surrounded with walls after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> manner; and has four gates and four towers, the last mounted with cannon; but there is no ditch. It gives name to a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> extending along the most southern <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>; of which that <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> which lies next the sea is a dry barren <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a>, in some places 10 or 12 leagues over; but bounded by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, which being well watered, enjoy an almost perpetual <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>; and besides coffee, the peculiar produce of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, yields corn, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MYRRH">myrrh</a>, frankincense, cassia, balm, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GUMS">gums</a> of several sorts, mangos, dates, pomegranates, &c. The <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> here is so hot and sultry in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, especially when the south <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> blows, that it would be insupportable, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it was not mitigated by the cool breezes that generally blow from the mountains on the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, or the Red and Arabic Seas on the west and east. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> in winter is equal to that of our warmest summers; and it is very seldom that either <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> are seen. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Mocho is now the emporium for the trade of all <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a> to the Red Sea. The trade was removed hither from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADEN">Aden</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the prophecy of a sheik, much revered by the people, who foretold that it would soon become a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of extensive <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> notwithstanding its disadvantageous situation. It stands <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to the sea, in a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, dry, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> plain, that affords no good <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WATER">water</a> within 20 miles of the city; what they drink comes from Mofa, and costs as dear as small-beer in England. The water near the town, as it is thought, produces a worm, which the naturalists call the dracunculus, which is about two feet and a half <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a>, very slender, and breeds in the fleshy parts of the body: in extracting it <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> care must be used, the consequence being dangerous if any part of it remains in the body. The buildings here are lofty, and tolerably regular, having a pleasant aspect from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MECCA">Mecca</a>. The steeples of several mosques are very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, presenting themselves to view at a great distance. Their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a> are well stored with beef, mutton, lamb, kid, camels, and antelope <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMON">common</a> fowls, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a> hens, partridges, and pigeons. The sea affords plenty of fish, but not savoury; which some think proceeds from the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> saltness of the water and the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of their aliment. The markets are also stocked with fruit, such as grapes, peaches, apricots, quinces, and nectarines; although neither shrub nor tree is to be seen near the town, except a few <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DATE">date</a>-trees. Frequently no rain falls here in two or three years, and seldom more than a shower or two in a year; but in the mountains, at the distance of about 20 miles from Mokha, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> is watered with a gentle shower every morning, which makes the valleys fertile in corn and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>. The Arab inhabitants, though remarkably <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a> and superstitious, are said to be extremely covetous and hypocritical; robbing, thieving, and committing <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PIRACY">piracy</a>, without the least scruple or remorse. The English and Dutch companies have handsome houses here, and carry on a great trade in coffee, olibanum, myrrh, aloes, liquid orrax, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WHITE">white</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> arsenic, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GUM">gum</a>-arabic, mummy, balm of Gilead, and other drugs. One inconvenience, however, they sustain from the violence and exactions of the Arabian princes; but the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">king</a>'s customs are easy, being fixed at three per cent. to Europeans. Of the coins at Mocha, the most current is the camafice, which rises and falls in value at the banker's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a>: they are from 50 to 80 for a current dollar, which is but an imaginary <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> being always reckoned one and a half per cent. lower than Spanish dollars. As to their weights, they are almost infinite, according to the nature of the thing to be weighed: they have the banian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, the magnet, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AMBERGRIS">ambergris</a>, the agala, the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver weights, &c.

MODE

Pages 197-199

which is a word of the same general import with manner, is used as a technical <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TERM">term</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-METAPHYSICS">metaphysics</a>, and music. For its import in Grammar, see that article, n° 80. Mode, in metaphysics, seems properly to denote the manner of a thing's existence: but Locke, whose <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> in that science is generally adopted, uses the word in a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> somewhat different from its ordinary and proper signification. "Such complex <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a>, which, however compounded, contain not in them the supposition of subsisting by themselves, but are considered as dependencies on, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> affections of, substances," he calls mode. Of these modes, there are, according to him, two sorts, which deserve distinct consideration. Firstly, there are some "which are only variations, or different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBINATIONS">combinations</a> of the same simple idea, without the mixture of any other, as a dozen or a score; which are nothing but the ideas of so many distinct units added together;" and these he calls simple modes. Secondly, "there are others compounded of simple ideas of several kinds put together to make one complex one; v.g. <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, consisting of a certain <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, causing delight in the beholder; theft, which being the concealed change of the possession of anything without the consent of the proprietor, contains, as is visible, a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a> of several ideas of several kinds;" and these he calls mixed modes. For the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> distinction between ideas and notions, as well as between ideas and the qualities of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> objects, which in this account of modes are all confounded together, see Metaphysics. Mode, in music; a regular disposition of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> and accompaniments relative to certain <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> sounds upon which a piece of music is formed, and which are called the essential sounds of the mode. There is this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between the mode and the tone, that the latter only determines the principal <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOUND">sound</a>, and indicates the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a> which is most proper to be occupied by that system which ought to constitute the basis of the air; whereas the former regulates the thirds, and modifies the whole <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-SCALE">scale</a> agreeably to its <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FUNDAMENTAL">fundamental</a> sounds. Our modes are not, like those of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, characterized Mode. racterized by any sentiment which they tend to excite, but result from our system of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> alone. The sounds essential to the mode are in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> three, and form together one perfect chord. 1. The tonic or <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KEY">key</a>, which is the fundamental <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> both of the tone and of the mode; (See Tone and Tonic). 2. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DOMINANT">dominant</a>, which is a fifth from the tonic; (See Dominant). 3. The mediant, which properly constitutes the mode, and which is a third from the same tonic. As this third may be of two kinds, there are of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> two different modes. When the mediant forms a greater third with the tonic, the mode is <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAJOR">major</a>; when the third is lesser, it is <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MINOR">minor</a>. The major mode is immediately <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENERATED">generated</a> by the resonance of sounding bodies, which exhibit the third major of the fundamental sound; but the minor mode is not the product of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>; it is only found by <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANALOGY">analogy</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-INVERSION">inversion</a>. This is equally true upon the system of Sig. Tartini as upon that of M. Rameau. This last author, in his various and successive publications, has explained the origin of this minor mode in different ways, of which his interpreter M. d'Alembert was satisfied with none. It is for this reason that he has founded this origin on a different principle, which cannot be better explained than in the words of that eminent geometrician. See Music, Art. 28, 29, 30, and 31. When the mode is once determined, every note in the scale assumes a name expressive of its relation to the fundamental sound, and peculiar to the place which it occupies in that particular mode. We subjoin the names of all the notes significant of their relative values and places in each particular mode, taking the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OCTAVE">octave</a> of ut as an example of the major mode, and of la as an example of the minor. Major, ut re mi fa sol la si ut, Minor, la si ut re mi fa sol la. It is necessary to remark, that when the seventh note is only a semitone distant from the highest in the octave, that is to say, when it forms a third major with the dominant, as si <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> in the major mode, or sol sharp in the minor, that seventh sound is then called a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SENSIBLE_NOTE">sensible note</a>, because it discovers the tonic and renders the tone appreciable. Nor does each gradation only assume that name which is suitable to it; but the nature of each <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> is determined according to its relation to the mode. The rules established for this are as follow: 1. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SECOND">second</a> note must form a second major above the tonic, the fourth note and the dominant should form a fourth and fifth exactly true; and this equally in both modes. 2. In the major mode, the mediant or third, the sixth and the seventh from the tonic, should always be major; for by this the mode is characterized. For the same reason these three intervals ought always to be minor in the minor mode; nevertheless, as it is necessary that the sensible note should likewise there be perceived, which cannot be effectuated without a false relation whilst the sixth note still remains minor; this occasions exceptions, of which in the course of the air or harmony care must be taken. But it is always necessary that the clef, with its transpositions, should preserve all the intervals, as determined with relation to the tonic, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of the mode. For this a general rule <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a> be found at the word Clef, in Rousseau's Musical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DICTIONARY">Dictionary</a>. As all the natural chords in the octave of ut give, with relation to that tonic, all the intervals prescribed for the major mode, and as the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CASE">case</a> is the same with the octave of la for the minor mode, the preceding example, which was only given that we might have an opportunity of naming the notes, may likewise serve as a formula for the rule of the intervals in each mode. This rule is not, as one might imagine, established upon principles that are merely arbitrary: it has its source in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a> of harmony, at least in a certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> you give a perfect major chord to the tonic, to the dominant, and the sub-dominant, you will have all the sounds of the diatonic scale for the major mode: to obtain that of the minor, leaving still its third major to the dominant, give a third minor to the two other chords. Such is the analogy of the mode. As this mixture of major and minor chords introduces into the minor mode a false relation between the sixth and the sensible note, to avoid this false relation, they sometimes give the third major to the fourth note in ascent, or the third minor to the dominant in descending, chiefly by inverting the chords; but these in this case are licences. There are properly no more than two modes, as we have seen: but there are twelve different sounds in the octave which may be made fundamental sounds, and of consequence form as many keys or tones; and as each of these tones are susceptible of the major or minor mode, music may be composed in twenty-four modes or manners. Nay, in the manner of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> music, there are even thirty-four passable modes; but in practice ten are excluded; which when thoroughly examined are nothing else but a repetition of the other ten, under relations much more difficult, in which all the chords must change their names, and where it must cost any one some trouble to know what he is about. Such is the major mode upon a note raised above its natural pitch by a semitone, and the minor mode upon a note depressed by a semitone. Thus, instead of composing upon sol sharp with a third major, it is much more eligible to operate upon la flat, which will give you an opportunity to employ the same tones; and instead of composing upon re flat with a third minor, you will find it more convenient to choose ut sharp for the same reason; viz. on one <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAND">hand</a> to avoid a fa with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> sharp, which would be <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> to a sol natural; and on the other hand a si with a double flat, which would become a la natural. The composer does not always continue in the same mode, nor in the same key, in which he has begun an air; but, whether to alter the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> or introduce variety, modes and keys are frequently changed, according to the analogy of harmony; yet always returning to those which have been first heard; this is called <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MODULATION">modulation</a>. From thence arises a new <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of modes into such as are principal and such as are relative; the principal is that in which the piece begins and ends; the relative modes are such as the composer interweaves with the principal in the flow of the harmony. (See Modulation). Others have proposed a third species, which they call a mixed mode, because it participates the modulation of both the others, or rather because it is composed of them; a mixture which they did not reckon an inconvenience, but rather an advantage, as it increases the variety, and gives the composer a greater latitude both in air and harmony. This new mode, not being found by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALYSIS">analysis</a> of the three chords like the two former, is not determined, like them, by harmonies essential to the mode, but by an entire scale which is peculiar to itself, as well in rising as descending; so that in the two modes above-mentioned the scale is investigated by the chords, and in this mixed mode the chords are investigated by the scale. The following notes exhibit the form of this scale in succession, as well rising as descending: mi fa sol la si ut re mi. Of which the essential difference is, as to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-MELODY">melody</a>, in the position of the two semitones; of which the first is found between the first and the second note, and the last between the fifth and sixth; and, with respect to the harmony, the difference consists in this, that upon its tonic it carries a third minor in the beginning, and major in ending, in the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACCOMPANIMENT">accompaniment</a> of this scale, as well in rising as descending, such as it has been given by those who proposed it, and executed at a spiritual <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONCERT">concert</a>, May 30, 1751. They object to its inventor, That his mode has neither chords nor harmony essential to itself, nor cadences which are peculiar to it, and which sufficiently distinguish it from the major or minor mode. He answers to this, That the distinction of his mode is less in harmony than in melody, and less even in the mode itself than in the modulation; that in its beginning it is distinguished from the major mode by its third minor, and in its end from the minor mode by its plagal cadence. To which his opponents reply, That a modulation which is not exclusive cannot be sufficient to establish a mode; and that his must inevitably occur in the two other modes, and above all in the minor; and, as to his plagal cadence, that it necessarily takes place in the minor mode as often as transition is made from the chord of the tonic to that of the dominant, as has <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a> been the case in practice, even upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FINAL">final</a> notes, in plagal modes, and in the tone proper to the fourth. From whence it is concluded, that his mixed mode is not so much a particular species, as a new denomination for the manner of interweaving and combining the major and minor modes, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> as harmony, practised at all periods; and this appears to be so true, that, even when he begins his scale, its author will neither venture to give the fifth nor the sixth to his tonic, for fear lest by the first the tonic should be determined in the minor mode, or the mediant in the major mode by the second. He leaves the harmony equivocal by not filling up his chord. But whatever objections may be made against the mixed mode, whose name is rather rejected than its practice, this will not prevent the author from appearing as a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAN">man</a> of genius, and a musician profoundly learned in the principles of his art, by the manner in which he treats it, and the arguments which he uses to establish it. Mode Major. See Interval. Mode Minor.

MODEL

Pages 199-202

in a general <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, an original pattern, proposed for any one to copy <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> imitate. This word is particularly used, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, for an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> pattern made in wood, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a>, or other kinds of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, with all its parts and proportions, in order for the better conducting and executing some <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>, and to give an idea of the effect it <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a> have in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a>. In all great buildings, it is much the surest way to make a model in relievo, and not to trust to a bare <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> or draught. There are also models for the building of ships, &c. and for extraordinary staircases, &c. They also <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> models in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a>; whence, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACADEMIES">academies</a>, they give the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TERM">term</a> model to a naked <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAN">man</a> or woman, disposed in several postures, to afford an opportunity to the scholars to design him in various views and attitudes. Models in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of any <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> or artificial substance, are most usually made by means of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOULDS">moulds</a> composed of plaster of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. For the purpose of making these moulds, this kind of plaster is much more fit than any other substance, on account of the power it has of absorbing <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and soon condensing into an hard substance, even after it has been rendered so thin as to be of the consistence of cream. This happens in a shorter or longer <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> as the plaster is of a better or worse <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>; and its good or bad properties depend very much upon its <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, to which, therefore, particular regard ought to be had. It is sold in the shops at very different prices; the finest being made use of for casts, and the middling sort for moulds. It may be very easily coloured by means of almost any kind of powder excepting what contains an alkaline <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-SALT">salt</a>; for this would chemically decompose the substance of it, and render it unfit for use. A very considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of chalk would also render it soft and useless, but lime hardens it to a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>. The addition of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMON">common</a> size will likewise render it much harder than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> water is made use of. In making either moulds or models, however, we must be careful not to make the mixture too thick at first; for if this is done, and more water added to thin it, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> must always prove brittle and of a bad quality. The particular manner of making models (or casts, as they are also called) depends on the form of the subject to be taken. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> is easy, where the parts are elevated only in a slight degree, or where they form only a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> or obtuse <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> surface from which they project; but where the parts project in smaller <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a>, or form curves inclined towards the principal surface, the work is more difficult. This observation, however, holds good only with regard to hard and inflexible bodies; for such as are soft may often be freed from the mould, even though they have the shape last mentioned. But though this be the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CASE">case</a> with the soft original substance, it is not so with the inflexible model when once it is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a>. The moulds are to be made of various degrees of thickness, according to the size of the model to be cast; and may be from half an inch to an inch, or, if very large, an inch and an half. Where a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of models are to be taken from one mould, it will likewise be necessary to have it of a stronger contexture than where only a few are required, for very obvious reasons. It is much more easy to make a mould for any soft substance than a rigid one, as in any of the viscera of the animal body: for the fluidity of the mixture makes it easily accommodate itself to the projecting parts of the substance; and as it is necessary to inflate these substances, they may be very readily extracted again by letting out the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> which distended them. When a model is to be taken, the surface of the original is first to be greased, in order to prevent the plaster from sticking to it; but if the substance itself is slippery, as is the case with the internal parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> body, this need not be done: when necessary, it may be laid over with linseed <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OIL">oil</a> by means of a painter's <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BRUSH">brush</a>. The original is then to be laid on a smooth <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, previously greased or covered with a cloth, to prevent the plaster sticking to it; then surround the original with a frame or ridge of glazier's putty, at such a distance from it, as will admit the plaster to rest upon the table on all sides of the subject for about an inch, or as much as is sufficient to give the proper degree of strength to the mould. A sufficient quantity of plaster is then to be poured as uniformly as possible over the whole substance, until it be everywhere covered to such a thickness as to give a proper substance to the mould, which may vary in proportion to the size. The whole must then be suffered to remain in this condition till the plaster has attained its <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HARDNESS">hardness</a>; when the frame is taken away, the mould may be <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-INVERTED">inverted</a>, and the subject removed from it; and when the plaster is thoroughly dry let it be well seasoned. Having formed and seasoned the moulds, they must next be prepared for the casts by greasing the inside of them with a mixture of olive oil and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARD">lard</a> in equal parts, and then filled with fine fluid plaster, and the plain of the mould formed by its resting on the surface of the table covered to a sufficient thickness with coarse plaster, to form a strong basis or support for the cast where this support is requisite, as is particularly the case where the thin and membranous parts of the body are to be represented. After the plaster is poured into the mould, it must be suffered to stand until it has acquired the greatest degree of hardness it will receive; after which the mould must be removed: but this will be attended with some difficulty when the shape of the subject is unfavourable; and in some <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CASES">cases</a> the mould must be separated by means of a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MALLET">mallet</a> and chisel. If by these instruments any parts of the model should be broken off, they may be cemented by making the two surfaces to be applied to each other quite wet; then interposing between them a little liquid plaster; and lastly, the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> smoothed after being thoroughly dry. Any small holes that may be made in the mould can be filled up with liquid plaster, after the sides of them have been thoroughly wetted, and smoothed over with the edge of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a>. In many cases it is altogether impracticable to prepare a mould of one piece for a whole subject; and therefore it must be considered how this can be done in such a manner as to divide the mould into the fewest pieces. This may be effected by making every piece cover as much of the pattern as possible, without surrounding such projecting parts, or running into such hollows as would not admit a separation of the mould. It is impossible, however, to give any particular directions in this matter which can hold good in every instance, the number of pieces of which the mould is to consist being always determined from the shape of the pattern. Thus the mould of the human <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CALCULUS">calculus</a> will require no more than three pieces, but that of an os femoris could scarce have fewer than ten or twelve.—Where any internal pieces are required, they are first to be made, and then the outer pieces after the former have become hard. To make a mould upon an hard and dry substance, we must, in the first <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, rub the surface of it smoothly over with the mixture of oil and lard above-mentioned. Such hollows as require internal pieces are then to be filled up with fluid plaster; and while it continues in this state, a wire loop must be introduced into it, by which, when hardened, it can be pulled off. The plaster should be somewhat raised in a pyramidal form around this wire, and afterwards cut smooth with a knife while yet in its soft state; preserving two or three angular ridges from the loop to the outer edge, that it may fix the more steadily in the outer piece of the mould to be afterwards made upon it. Let the outer piece then be well greased, to prevent the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SECOND">second</a> piece from adhering; the loop being inclosed with some glazier's putty, both to prevent the second piece from adhering and to preserve an hollow place for the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CORD">cord</a>. To form the second or outside piece, mix a quantity of plaster proportioned to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of surface it is to cover and the intended thickness of the mould: when it is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> beginning to thicken, or assumes such a confidence as not to run off very easily, spread it over the internal piece or pieces as well as the pattern, taking care at the same time not to go too far lest it should not deliver safely; and as the plaster becomes more tenacious, add more upon the pattern until it has become sufficiently thick, keeping the edges <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> and smooth like the edge of a board. The plaster should be spread equally upon all parts, which is best done by a painter's pallet-knife or apothecary's bolus-knife: but for this the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> should be somewhat less pliable than it is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> made. When the outside piece is hardened, the edges are to be pared smooth, and nearly made square with a small pointed knife. Little holes of a conical shape are to be made with the point of a knife about an inch distant from one another, according to the size of the piece. These are designed to receive the fluid plaster in forming the adjacent parts of the mould, and occasion <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POINTS">points</a> corresponding to the hollows; and are intended to preserve the edges of the different pieces readily in their proper relative situations. The third piece is then to be formed in a manner similar to the second; second; greasing the edges of the former plentifully with <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOG">hog</a>'s lard and oil, to prevent the pieces from adhering to each other. Thus the pattern is to be wholly inclosed, only leaving a proper orifice for pouring in the platter to form the model; small holes being also bored in the mould opposite to the wire-loops fixed in the inside pieces, through which a cord is to be conveyed from the loop to confine such pieces during the time of casting. In some cases, however, it is not necessary that the mould should totally inclose the pattern; for instance, where a model is to be made of a pedestal, or a butt of any <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> of the human body. The bottom of such moulds being left open, there is accordingly ample room for pouring in the platter. After the mould is completely formed, it is next to be dried either naturally or by a gentle artificial <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, and then seasoned in the following manner: Having been made thoroughly dry, which, if the mould is large, will require two or three weeks, it is to be brushed over plentifully with linseed oil boiled with <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, finely levigated <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LITHARGE">litharge</a>, or oil of vitriol. The inside and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a> of the mould should be particularly well supplied with it. If the mould be large, it is needless to attend to the outside; but when the moulds are small, it will not be improper to boil them in the oil; by which means their pores are more exactly filled than could otherwise be done. After the moulds have undergone this operation, they are again set by to dry, when, being greased with olive-oil and hog's lard, they are fit for use. If linseed oil be used for greasing the moulds, it will in a short time impart a disagreeable <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> to the casts. The mould being properly prepared and seasoned, nothing more is requisite to form the model than to pour the finest liquid plaster of Paris into it. After a layer of this, about half an inch in thickness, has been formed all round the mould, we may use the coarser kind to fill it up entirely, or to give to the model what thickness we please. Besides the models which are taken from inanimate bodies, it has been frequently attempted to take the exact resemblance of people while living, by using their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FACE">face</a> as the original of a model, from whence to take a mould; and the operation, however disagreeable, has been submitted to by persons of the highest ranks in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. A considerable difficulty occurs in this, however, by reason of the person's being apt to shrink and distort his features when the liquid is poured upon him; neither is he altogether without danger of suffocation, unless the operator well understands his business. To avoid the former inconvenience, it will be proper to mix the plaster with warm instead of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLD">cold</a> water, by which means the person will be under no temptation to shrink; and to prevent any danger of a fatal accident, the following method is to be practised: Having laid the person horizontally on his back, the head must first be raised by means of a pillow to the exact position in which it is naturally carried when the body is erect; then the parts to be represented must be very thinly covered over with fine oil of almonds by means of a painter's brush: the face is then to be first covered with fine fluid plaster, begin- ning at the upper part of the forehead, and spreading it over the eyes, which are to be kept <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CLOSE">close</a>, that the plaster may not come in contact with the globe; yet not closed so strongly as to cause any unnatural wrinkles. Cover then the nose and ears, plugging first up the meatus auditorii with cotton, and the nostrils with a small quantity of tow rolled up, of a proper size, to exclude the plaster. During the time that the nose is thus stopped, the person is to breathe through the mouth; in this state the fluid plaster is to be brought <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DOWN">down</a> low enough to cover the upper lip, observing to leave the rolls of tow projecting out of the plaster. When the operation is thus far carried on, the plaster must be suffered to harden; after which the tow may be withdrawn, and the nostrils left free and open for breathing. The mouth is then to be closed in its natural position, and the plaster brought down to the extremity of the chin. Begin then to cover that part of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a> which is to be represented, and spread the plaster to the outsides of the arms and upwards, in such a manner as to meet and join that which is previously laid on the face; when the whole of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MASS">mass</a> has acquired its due hardness, it is to be cautiously lifted, without breaking or giving pain to the person. After the mould is constructed, it must be seasoned in the manner already directed; and when the mould is cast, it is to be separated from the model by means of a small mallet and chisel. The eyes, which are necessarily shown closed, are to be carved, so that the eye-lids may be represented in an elevated posture; the nostrils hollowed out, and the back part of the head, from which, on account of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, no mould can be taken, must be finished according to the skill of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a>. The edges of the model are then to be neatly smoothed off, and the butt fixed on its pedestal. The method of making models in the plaster of Paris is undoubtedly the most easy way of obtaining phical models. When models, however, are made of such large objects that the model itself must be of considerable size, it is vain to attempt making it in the way above described. Such models must be constructed by the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAND">hand</a> with some soft substance, as wax, clay, putty, &c., and it being necessary to keep all the proportions with mathematical exactness, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of a single model of this kind must be a work of great labour and expense as well as of time. Of all those which have been undertaken by human industry, however, perhaps the most remarkable is that constructed by General Pfister, to represent the mountainous parts of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>. It is composed of 142 compartments, of different sizes and forms, respectively numbered, and so artfully put together, that they can be separated and replaced with the greatest ease. The model itself is 20½ feet <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a> and 12 <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, and formed on a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-SCALE">scale</a> which represents two English miles and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> by an English foot; comprehending part of the cantons of Zug, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ZURICH">Zurich</a>, Schwyz, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNTERWALDEN">Unterwalden</a>, Lucerne, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BERNE">Berne</a>, and a small part of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of Glarus; in all, an extent of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of 18½ leagues in length and 12 in breadth. The highest point of the model, from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of the centre (which is the lake of Lucerne), is about ten inches; and as the most elevated mountain represented therein rises 1475 MOD toises or 9440 feet above the lake of Lucerne, at a gros calculation, the height of an inch in the model is about 900 feet. The whole is painted of different colours, in such a manner as to represent objects as they exist in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>; and so exactly is this done, that not only the woods of oak, beech, pine, and other trees, are distinguished, but even the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-STRATA">strata</a> of the several rocks are marked, each being shaped upon the spot, and formed of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GRANITE">granite</a>, gravel, or such other sub- stances as compose the natural mountain. So minute also is the accuracy of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>, that it comprises not only all the mountains, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, villages, and forests, but every cottage, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TORRENT">torrent</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ROAD">road</a>, and even every path is distinctly marked. The principal material employed in the construc- tion of this extraordinary model, is a mixture of char- coal, lime, clay, a little pitch, with a thin coat of wax; and is so hard that it may be trodden upon without any damage. It was begun in the year 1756, at which time the general was about 50 years of age, and it employed him till the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of August 1783; during which long space of time he was employ- ed in the most laborious and even dangerous tasks.— He raised the plans with his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> on the spot, took the elevation of mountains, and laid them down in their several proportions. In the prosecution of this laborious employment he was twice arrested for a spy; and in the popular cantons was frequently forced to work by <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MOON">moon</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, in order to avoid the jealousy of the peasants, who imagined that their li- berty would be endangered should a plan of their country be taken with such minute exactness. Be- ing obliged frequently to remain on the tops of some of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a>, where no <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> could be procured, he took along with him a few <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MILK">milk</a>-goats, who sup- plied him with nourishment. When any part was finished, he sent for the people residing near the spot, and desired them to examine each mountain with ac- curacy, whether it corresponded, as far as the smallness of the scale would admit, with its natural appearance; and then, by frequently retouching, corrected the de- ficiencies. Even after the model was finished, he <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> his Alpine expeditions with the same ar- dour as ever, and with a degree of vigour that would fatigue a much younger person. All his elevations were taken from the level of the lake of Lucerne; which, according to M. Saussure, is 1408 feet above the level of the Mediterranean.

MODENA

Pages 202-202

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CITY">city</a>, in Latin Mutina, which gives name to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and is its <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>. It stands 28 miles east of Parma, 44 almost south of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MANTUA">Mantua</a>, and 20 west of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOLOGNA">Bologna</a>; and is a pretty <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and populous, but not a handsome city. It is much celebrated by Roman authors for its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a> and opulence; but was a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> sufferer by the siege it underwent during the troubles of the triumvirate. It hath <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a> been the usual residence of the dukes; and is also the see of a bishop, who is suffragan to the archbishop of Bologna. Mr Keyser says, that when Decius Brutus was besieged here by Mark Antony, Hirtius the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a> made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CARRIER">carrier</a>-pigeons; and that, even at this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, pigeons are trained up at Mo- dena to carry letters and bring back answers. This city hath given birth to several celebrated persons, particularly Tasso the poet, Correggio the great painter, Sigonius the civilian and historian, da Vig- nola the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECT">architect</a>, and Montecuculi the imperial gen- eral. The tutelary saint of it is named Geminianus. The ducal <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> is a very noble edifice, in which, among the other fine pictures, the birth of Christ by Correggio, called la Notte Felice, is much celebrated. The only manufacture for which this city is noted, is that of minks, of which great numbers are exported. The churches of the Jesuits, of the Theatines, and of St Dominic, are well worth viewing. In the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of St Carlo Boromeo between 70 and 80 young <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a>- men are continually maintained, and instructed both in the sciences and genteel exercises. St Beatrix, who was of the family of <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol9.html#article-ESTE">Este</a>, is said to knock always at the gate of the palace three days before any of the family dies. Before most of the houses are covered walks <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> porticos, as at Bologna. The city is fortifi- ed, and on its south side stands the citadel.

MODERATION

Pages 202-202

in ethics, is a virtue consist- ing in the proper <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of our appetites, pas- sions, and pursuits, with respect to honours, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RICHES">riches</a>, and pleasures; and in this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> it is <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SYNONYMOUS">synonymous</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPERANCE">temperance</a>: it is also often used to denote can- dour.

MODERATOR

Pages 202-202

in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, the person who presides at a dispute, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> in a public <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>: thus the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> of the annual assembly of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Scot- <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAND">land</a> is styled moderator.

MODERN

Pages 202-202

something new, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> of our <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a>; in opposition to what is antique or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>. MODERN Authors, according to Naude, are all those who have wrote since <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOETHIUS">Boethius</a>. The modern philo- sophy commences with Galileo; the modern <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a> with Copernicus.

MODESTY

Pages 202-203

in ethics, is sometimes used to de- <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> humility; and sometimes to express chastity, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> purity of sentiments and manners.—Modesty, in this last <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, and as particularly applied to women, is de- fined by the authors of the Encyclopédie Méthodique, as a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a>, chary, and honest shame; a secret fear; a feeling Modesty, feeling on account of what may be accompanied with disgrace. Women who possess only the remains of a suspicious modesty, make but feeble efforts to resist; those who have obliterated every trace of modesty from their countenance, soon extinguish it completely in their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>, and throw aside forever the veil of decency. She, on the contrary, who truly possesses modesty, passes over in silence attempts against her <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, and forbears speaking of those from whom she has received an outrage, when in doing so she must reveal actions and expressions that might give alarm to virtue. The idea of modesty is not a chimera, a popular <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a>, or an illusion arising from laws and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURE">Nature</a>, which speaks the same <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> to all men, has, with the unanimous consent of nations, annexed contempt to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> incontinence. To resist and to attack are laws of her appointment; and while she bellows defies on both parties, they are in the one accompanied with boldness, in the other with shame. To individuals she has allotted <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a> spaces of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> for the purposes of self-preservation, and but moments for the propagation of their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>. What arms more gentle than Modesty could she have put into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SEX">sex</a> which she designed to make resistance! <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> it were the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> for both sexes to make and receive advances indiscriminately, vain importunity would not be prevented: the fire of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> would never be stilled up, but languish in tedious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>; the most amiable of all feelings would scarcely warm the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>; its object would with difficulty be attained. That obstacle which seems to remove this object at a distance, in fact brings it nearer. The veil of shame only makes the desires more attractive. Modesty kindles that <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FLAME">flame</a> which it endeavours to suppress: its fears, its evasions, its caution, its timid avowals, its pleasing and affecting niceties, speak more plainly what it wishes to conceal, than passion can do without it: it is Modesty, in short, which enhances the value of a favour, and mitigates the pain of a refusal. Since modesty is the secret fear of ignominy; and since all nations, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MODERN">modern</a>, have confessed the obligation of its laws; it must be absurd to violate them in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> of crimes, which should always have for its object the re-establishment of order.
