Was it the intention of those oriental nations, who exposed women to elephants, trained for an abominable species of punishment, to violate one <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAW">law</a> by the observance of another? By an ancient practice among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, a girl could not be put to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEATH">death</a> before she was marriageable. Tiberius found means to evade this law by ordering them to be violated by the executioner previous to the infliction of punishment; the refinement of a cruel <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a>, who sacrificed the morals to the customs of his people! When the legislature of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JAPAN">Japan</a> caused women to be exposed naked in the market-places, and obliged them to walk on all fours like <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-BRUTES">brutes</a>, modesty was shocked: but when it wanted to force a mother—when it wanted to compel a son—nature received an outrage. Such is the influence of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> in other countries, that the physical <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LOVE">love</a> possesses an almost irresistible force. The resistance is feeble; the attack is accompanied with a certainty of success. This is the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CASE">case</a> at Patana, at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BANTAM">Bantam</a>, and in the small kingdoms on the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a>. When the women in these countries (says Mr Smith) meet with a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAN">man</a>, they lay hold of him, and threaten to inform their husbands if he despises their favours. But here the sexes seem to have abolished the laws peculiar to each. It is fortunate to live in a temperate climate like ours, where that sex which possesses the most powerful charms exerts them to embellish <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>; and where modest women, while they reserve themselves for the pleasures of one, contribute to the amusement of all.

MODIFICATION

Pages 203-203

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, that which modifies a thing, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> gives it this or that manner of being. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">Quantity</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> are accidents which modify all bodies. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">Degree</a> of Modification, in Scots <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAW">law</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DECREE">decree</a> ascertaining the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of a minister's stipend, without proportioning it among the persons liable in payment.

MODILLIONS

Pages 203-203

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, ornaments in the cornice of the Ionic, Corinthian, and Composite columns.

MODIUS

Pages 203-203

a Roman dry <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> for all sorts of grain, containing 32 heminae, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> 16 sextarii, or one-third of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMPHORA">amphora</a>, amounting to an English peck. See Measure.

MODREVIUS

Pages 203-203

secretary to Sigismund Augustus <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, acquired considerable reputation by his learning and works. He broke off from the Romish <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, favoured the Lutherans and Anti-trinitarians, and took <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> pains in order to unite all Christian <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a> under the same <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a>. Grotius has placed him in the class of the reconcilers of the different schemes of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. His <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> is intitled, De republica emendanda.

MODULATION

Pages 203-205

in music, derived from the Latin modulari. This word in our <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> is susceptible of several different significations. It frequently means no more than an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of musical sounds properly connected and arranged. Thus it answers to what Mr Malcolm understands by the word tune, when he does not expressly treat concerning the tuning of instruments. Thus likewise it expresses the French word chant; for which reason, in the article Music, we have frequently expressed the one word by the other. But the precise and technical acceptation to which it ought to be confined, is the art of composing <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-MELODY">melody</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> agreeably to the laws prescribed by any particular <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KEY">key</a>, that of changing the key, or of regularly and legitimately passing from one key to another. In what remains to be said upon the subject we follow Rousseau. Modulation (says he) is properly the manner of ascertaining and managing the modes; but at this <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> the word most frequently signifies the art of conducting the harmony, and the air successively through several modes, in a manner agreeable to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-EAR">ear</a> and conformed to rules. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the different modes be produced by harmony, from thence likewise must <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> the laws of modulation. These laws are simple in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONCEPTION">conception</a>, but difficult in practice. We proceed therefore to show in what they consist. To modulate properly in the same tone, it is necessary, 1. To run through all the sounds of it in an agreeable air, frequently repeating the sounds which are most essential to it, and dwelling upon these sounds with the most remarkable emphasis; that is to say, that the chord containing the sensible notes, and that of the tonic, should frequently be heard in it, but under different appearances, and obtained by different procedures to prevent <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MONOTONY">monotony</a>. 2. That repose or cadences should only be established upon these two chords: the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, however, which ought to be taken with the rule is, that a cadence or repose may be established on the chord of the sub-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DOMINANT">dominant</a>. 3. In short, that none of the sounds of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MODE">mode</a> ought ever to be altered; for without quitting it we cannot introduce a sharp or a flat which does not belong to it, nor <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSTRACT">abstract</a> any one which in reality does belong to it. But passing from one mode to another, we must consult <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANALOGY">analogy</a>, we must consider the relations which a key bears to the other notes in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a>, and to the number of sounds <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to both the modes, that from whence we <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a>, and that into which we enter. If we pass from a mode <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAJOR">major</a>, whether we consider the fifth from the key as having the most simple relation with it except that of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OCTAVE">octave</a>, or whether we consider it as the first <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> which enters into the harmonics of the same key, we shall always find, that this fifth, which is the dominant of the mode, is the chord upon which we may establish the modulation most analogous to that of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> key. This dominant, which constituted one of the harmonics of the first key, makes also one of its own peculiar key, of which it is the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FUNDAMENTAL">fundamental</a> sound. There is then a connection between these two chords. Besides, that same dominant carrying, as well as the tonic, a perfect chord major upon the principle of resonance, these two chords are only different one from the other by the dissonance, which passing from the key to the dominant is the sixth superadded, and when ascending from the dominant to the key is the seventh. Now these two chords, thus distinguished by the dissonance which is suitable to each, by the sounds which compose them when ranged in order, form precisely the octave, or the diatonic <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-SCALE">scale</a>, which we call a gamut, which determines the mode. This same series of the key, altered only by a sharp, forms the scale belonging to the mode of the dominant; which shows how striking the analogy is between these two tones, and gives the easiest opportunity of passing from one to the other by means of one single <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> alone. The mode then of the dominant is the first which presents itself after that of the key in the order of modulations. The same simplicity of relations which we find between a tonic and its dominant, is likewise found between the same tonic and its sub-dominant: for that fifth, in ascending, which is formed by the dominant with the tonic, is likewise formed by the sub-dominant in descending; but that sub-dominant does not form a fifth with the tonic, except by <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-INVERSION">inversion</a>; it is directly a fourth, if we take that tonic below, as it ought to be, and which fixes the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of their relations: for in this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> the fourth, whose ratio is as 3 to 4, immediately follows the fifth, whose ratio is as 2 to 3. So that, if that sub-dominant does not enter into the chord of the tonic, in return the tonic enters into its perfect chord. For let ut mi sol be the chord of the tonic, that of the sub-dominant shall be fa la ut: thus it is the ut which here forms the connection, and the two other sounds of this new chord, are exactly the two dissonances of the preceding. Besides, we need not alter more sounds for this new mode than for that of the dominant; they are both in the one and the other quite the same chords of the principal mode, except one. Add a flat to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SENSIBLE_NOTE">sensible <a c</a>lass="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> fa or B, and all the notes in the mode of ut or C <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a> serve for that of fa or F. The mode of the sub-dominant then is scarcely less analogous to the principal mode than that of the dominant. It ought likewise to be remarked, that after having made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the first modulation in order to pass from a principal mode ut or C, to that of the dominant sol or G, we are obliged to make use of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SECOND">second</a> to return to the principal mode: for if sol or G be the dominant in the mode of ut or C, ut is the sub-dominant in the mode of sol: thus one of these modulations is no less necessary than the other. The third sound which enters into the chord of the tonic is that of third formed by its mediant; and, after the preceding, it is likewise the most simple of relations. Here then is a new modulation which presents itself, and which is so much the more analogous, because two of the sounds of the principal tonic enter likewise into the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MINOR">minor</a> chord of its mediant: for the former chord being ut mi sol, the latter must be mi sol fa, where it may be perceived that mi and sol are common. But what renders this modulation a little more remote, is the number of sounds which are necessary to be altered, even for the minor mode, which is most suitable to this mi. In the article Music (234.) will be found a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TABLE">table</a> for all the modes; and Rouffeau, in his Musical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DICTIONARY">Dictionary</a>, has given the formula of a scale both for the major and minor: now, by applying this formula to the minor mode, we find nothing in reality, but the fourth sound fa heightened by a sharp in ascending; but in rising, we find two others which are altered, viz. the principal tonic ut, and its second re, which here becomes a sensible note: it is certain that the alteration of so many sounds, and particularly of the tonic, must remove the mode and weaken the analogy. If we should invert the third as we have <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-INVERTED">inverted</a> the fifth, and take that third below the tonic on the fifth note la, which ought here to be called a sub-mediant, or the mediant below, we shall form upon this note la a modulation more analogous to the principal mode than that of mi; for as the perfect chord of this sub-mediant is la ut mi, there once more we find, as in that of the mediant, two of the sounds which enter into the chord of the tonic, viz. ut and mi: moreover, since the scale of this new key is composed, at least in descending, of the same sounds with that of the principal key; and since it has only two sounds altered in ascending, that is to say, one fewer than the series of the mediant; it follows that the modulation of this fifth note is preferable to that of the mediant; and by so much the more, that there the principal tonic forms one of the sounds essential to the mode; which is more proper for approximating the idea of the modulation. The mi may afterwards follow. Here then are four sounds, *mi fa sol la*, upon each of which we may modulate in passing from the major mode of *ut*. *Re* and *fa* remain, which are the two harmonics of the dominant. This last, as being a sensible note, cannot become a tonic by any proper modulation, at least it cannot immediately become one; this would be an abrupt application of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> too much opposed to the same sounds, and would likewise be to give it a harmony too remote from the principal sound. As to the second note *re*, we may likewise, by favour of a consonant procedure in the fundamental base, modulate upon it in a third minor; but this must be only <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> for an instant, that the audience may not have time to forget the modulation of *ut*, which is itself altered in that <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a>; otherwise, instead of returning immediately to *ut*, we must pass through intermediate modes, where we must run <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> hazard of deviation. By following the same analogies, we may modulate in the following order, to make our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXIT">exit</a> from a minor mode; first upon the mediant, afterwards the dominant, next the sub-dominant, then the sub-mediant, or fifth note. The mode of each of these <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACCESSORY">accessory</a> keys is determined by its mediant taken from the principal sound. For instance, issuing from the major mode of *ut*, to modulate upon its mediant, we render the mode of that mediant minor; because *sol*, the dominant of the principal sound, forms a third minor with that mediant, which is *mi*. On the contrary, in our egress from the minor mode of *la*, we modulate upon its mediant *ut* in the major mode; because *mi*, the dominant of the tone from whence we issue, forms a third major with the key of that into which we enter, &c. These rules, comprehended in one general formula, import, that the modes of the dominant and of the sub-dominant are like that of the tonic, and that the mediant and the fifth note require a mode opposed. We must, however, remark, that, by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> which we have of passing from the major to the minor, and vice versa, upon the same key, we may likewise change the order of modes from one key to another; but whilst we thus remove ourselves from the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> modulation, we must presently think of our return: for it is a general rule, that every piece of music ought to terminate in that key with which it began. In his Musical Dictionary, plate B, fig. 6. and 7. Rousseau has collected in two examples, which are very short, all the modes to which we may immediately pass; the first, in passing from the major mode; and the second, from the minor. Each note indicates a particular modulation; and the value of the notes in each example likewise shows the relative <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DURATION">duration</a> suitable to each of these modes, according to its relation with the principal mode. These immediate transitions from one mode to another, furnish us with the means of passing by the same rules to modes still more remote, and from thence to return to the principal mode, of which we never should lose sight. But it is not sufficient to know what course we ought to pursue; we must likewise be acquainted with the method of entering into it. A summary therefore of the precepts which are given in this department shall immediately follow. In melody, in order to discover and introduce the modulation which we have chosen, nothing is necessary but to render perceptible the alterations which it causes in the sounds of that mode from whence we issue, to make them proper for the mode into which we enter. Are we now in the major mode of *ut*? there needs no more than to sound the note *fa* sharp, that we may discover the mode of the dominant; or a *fa* flat, that we may show the mode of the sub-dominant. Afterwards you may run over the sounds essential to the mode in which you enter; if it is well chosen, your modulation will always be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> and regular. In harmony, the difficulty is a little increased: for it is necessary that the change of modes should be made at the same time through all the parts, care must be taken of the harmony, and of the air, that we may avoid pursuing different modulations at the same time. Huygens has happily remarked, that the prohibition of two fifths in immediate succession proceeds upon this rule as its principle: in reality, between two parts it is scarcely possible to form a number of just fifths in uninterrupted succession without operating in two different modes. To introduce a mode, a great many pretend that it is sufficient to form the perfect chord of its principal sound, and this is indispensible in order to produce the mode. But it is certain, that the mode cannot be exactly determined but by the chord containing the sensible note, or the dominant: we must then cause this chord to be heard when we enter into a new modulation. The most eligible rule would be, That in it the seventh, or minor dissonance, should always be prepared, at least the first time in which it is heard: but this method is not practicable in every admissible modulation; and provided that the fundamental basis proceeds by consonant intervals, that the connection of harmony be observed, the analogy of the mode pursued, and false relations avoided, the modulation will always be approved. Composers prescribe as another rule, That a mode should not be changed except after a perfect cadence: but this <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-INTERDICT">interdict</a> is useless, and no person observes it. All the possible methods of passing from one mode to another, are reducible to five with respect to the major mode, and to four with respect to the minor, which, in the Musical Dictionary, plate B, fig. 8. will be found implied in a fundamental basis intended for each modulation. If there be any other modulation which cannot be resolved into some one of these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NINE">nine</a>, unless that modulation be enharmonic, it must infallibly be illegitimate. See Enharmonic.

MODULE

Pages 205-205

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, a certain <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> bigness, taken at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, for regulating the proportions of columns, and the symmetry or disposition of the whole <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>. Architects generally choose the semidiameter of the bottom of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLUMN">column</a> for their module, and this they subdivide into parts or minutes.

MOEBIUS

Pages 205-206

professor of physic at Iena, MOG Moenius was born at Lauch in Thuringia in 1611. He became first physician to Frederic William <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BRANDENBURG">Brandenburg</a>, to Augustus <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>, and to William duke of Saxe-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WEIMAR">Weimar</a>. He wrote several medical works, which are esteemed; and died at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HALLE">Halle</a>, in Saxony, in 1664.

MOENIUS

Pages 206-206

a celebrated Roman <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a>, conqueror of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Latins, 338 B.C. He was the first who hung up the prows, &c. of the galleys he had taken at the naval engagement of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIUM">Actium</a>, upon the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where the tribunes harangued the people; from whence it was called the rostra. MÆONIA, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> Mæonia. See Mæonia and Lydia. MŒSIA, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MYSIA">Mysia</a>, (anc. geog.) a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, extending from the confluence of the Savus and the Danube to the shores of the Euxine. It was divided into Upper and Lower Mœsia. Lower Mœsia was on the borders of the Euxine, and comprehended that tract of country which received the name of Pontus from its vicinity to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. Upper Mœsia lay beyond the other, in the inland country.

MOFFAT

Pages 206-206

a village of Scotland, in the shire of Annandale, 50 miles south-west of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>; famous for its sulphurous well, which has been in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> estimation for near 150 years as a remedy in all cutaneous and scrophulous complaints; and for its chalybeate <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, perhaps the strongest in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, which was discovered about 45 years ago, and is of a very bracing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>.—The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is chiefly supported by the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> who <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> thither for the benefit of its waters and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>; but it has also a manufacture of coarse woollen stuffs. It is a well-built clean village; and contains many good and even elegant lodgings, a tolerable <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>-room, a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOWLING">bowling</a>-green and walks, and one of the best inns between <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONDON">London</a> and Edinburgh. MOFFETTA. See Ampsancti.

MOGODORE

Pages 206-206
or Mogadore, a large, uniform, and well-built town in the kingdom of Morocco, situated about 350 miles from Tangier on the Atlantic ocean, and surrounded on the land-side by deep and heavy sands. The European factory here consists of about a dozen mercantile houses of different nations, whose owners, from the protection granted them by the emperor, live in full security from the Moors, whom indeed they keep at a rigid distance. They export, to America, mules; to Europe, Morocco leather, hides, gum arabic, gum sandarac, ostrich feathers, copper, wax, wool, elephant's teeth, fine mats, beautiful carpeting, dates, figs, raisins, olives, almonds, oil, &c. In return, they import timber, artillery of all kinds, gunpowder, woollen clothes, linens, lead, iron in bars, all kinds of hardware and trinkets, such as looking-glasses, snuff-boxes, watches, small knives, &c. tea, sugar, spices, and most of the useful articles which are not otherwise to be procured in this empire. The town is regularly fortified on the sea-side; and on the land, batteries are so placed as to prevent any incursion from the southern Arabs, who are of a turbulent disposition, and who, from the great wealth which is known to be always in Mogodore, would gladly avail themselves of any opportunity that offered to pillage the town. The entrance, both by sea and land, consists of elegant stone arch-ways, with double gates. The market-place is handsomely built, with piazzas of the same materials; and at the water-port there is a customhouse and powder magazine, both of which are neat stone buildings. Besides these public edifices, the emperor has a small but handsome palace for his occasional residence. The streets of the town, though very narrow, are all in straight lines; and the houses, contrary to what we meet with in the other towns of the empire, are lofty and regular. The bay, which is little better than a road, and is very much exposed when the wind is at north-west, is formed by a curve in the land, and a small island about a quarter of a mile from the shore.—Its entrance is defended by a fort well furnished with guns.

MOGULS

Pages 206-212

a celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATION">nation</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, whose conquests formerly were the most rapid and extensive of any people recorded in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. They themselves deduce their origin from Japhet, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a>, as they call him, Japhir, the son of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NOAH">Noah</a>. His son Turk, Moguls they say, was the first <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">king</a>, or khan, of those nations who are now known by the separate names of Turks, Tartars, and Moguls; and the Tartars especially, assert that their proper designation is Turks. To this <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> is attributed many of those inventions which barbarous nations <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> ascribe to their first sovereigns. He was succeeded by Taunak; in whose reign the whole posterity of Turk were divided into four <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> tribes, denominated the orda's of Erlat, Gialair, Kaugin, Berlas or Perlas; of which last came the famous Timur Beg, or <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TAMERLANE">Tamerlane</a>.—From this <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> to that of Alanza Khan, we meet with nothing remarkable. In his reign the Turks being immersed in all kinds of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a>, universally apostatized into idolatry. Having two sons, Tartar and Mogul, he divided his dominions among them, and thus gave rise to the two empires of the Tartars and Moguls. The two nations had not <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a> existed before they began to make <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WAR">war</a> upon each other; and after long contention, the event at last was, that II Khan, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> of the Moguls, was totally overthrown by Siuatz Khan, emperor of the Tartars; ar i fo <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> was the defeat, that the Mogul nation seems to have been almost exterminated. Only two of II Khan's family survived this disaster. These were Kajan his youngest son, and Nagos his nephew, who were both of an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, and had both been married the same year. These two princes, with their wives, had been taken prisoners by Siuatz Khan, but found means to make their escape to their own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. Here they seized upon all the cattle which had not been carried off by the Tartars; which was easily done, as having none to dispute the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> with them; then stripping some of the slain, they took their clothes, and retired into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>. They passed several mountains without much difficulty; but at last advanced to the foot of one exceedingly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, which had no way over it but a very small path made by certain animals, called in the Tartar <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> arebaha. This path they found themselves obliged to make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of, though it was so frail, that only one could <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> at a time, and he was in the most imminent danger of breaking his neck at the least false step. Having Having ascended the mountain on one side by this path, they descended by the same on the other side; and were agreeably surprised to find themselves in a most delightful track, interspersed with rivulets and charming meadows, abounding with a vast variety of delicious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, and inclosed on all sides by inaccessible mountains, in such a manner as to shelter them from all future pursuits of the Tartars. Here they lived some time, and gave this beautiful country the name of Ir-gana-kon, in allusion to its situation; Irgana signifying, in the old language of the Moguls, a "valley," and Kon a "steep height." In <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of time these two families very much increased. Kajan, whose posterity was the most numerous, called his descendants Kajat; but the people springing from Nagos were divided into two tribes; one of which received the appellation of Naggyler, and the other that of Durlagan. These two Mogul princes and their descendants lived in this <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a> for more than 400 years; but the latter then finding it too narrow for them, meditated a return to the country from which their forefathers had been driven. For some time, however, they found this impracticable, as the path that conducted their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> had been long since destroyed. At last they discovered, that one <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> of the high mountain above-mentioned was not very thick in a certain place; and also, that it consisted entirely of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-IRON">iron</a>-ore. To this, having before set fire to a layer of wood, and another of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHARCOAL">charcoal</a>, laid along the foot of the mountain, they applied 70 large bellows, and at last melted the mountain in such a manner, that an opening was made large enough for a loaded camel to pass; and through this passage they all marched out with great joy. The Moguls having thus issued as it were from a new world, overthrew the Tartars in their turn; and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to be a very considerable nation till the time of their great <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HERO">hero</a> Temujin, afterwards called Jenghiz Khan, whom they extol in the most extravagant manner. It is difficult, however, to say, at the time Temujin made his appearance, how far the dominions of the Moguls extended, or in what estimation they were held by their neighbours. It seems to be pretty certain, that great part of the vast region now known by the name of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TARTARY">Tartary</a>, was then in a state of considerable civilization, and likewise extremely populous, as we find mention made of many cities which the Moguls destroyed; and the incredible multitudes whom they slaughtered, abundantly show the populousness of the country. On the east, the country of the Moguls and Tartars had the great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> which divides Tartary from <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHINA">China</a>; on the west, it had the empire of Karazm, founded by Mahmud Gazni; and on the south, were the countries now known by the name of Indofrom, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SIAM">Siam</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PEGU">Pegu</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TONQUIN">Tonquin</a>, and Cochinchina. Thus it comprehended the eastern part of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> Tartary, and all <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SIBERIA">Siberia</a>. This whole region was divided among a great <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of Aymacks, or tribes; who had each one or more khans, according as it was more or less numerous, or divided into branches. Among these, that of the Karaits was the most powerful; their prince assumed the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GRAND">Grand</a> Khan, and among the rest the Moguls were tributary to him; but, according to the Chinese historians, both the one and the other were tributary to the emperor of Kitay or Katay. China was divided into two parts; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NINE">nine</a> southern provinces were in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the Chinese emperors of the Song dynasty, who kept their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COURT">court</a> at Hang-chew, the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Chekyang; the five northern provinces, excepting part of Shenli, were policed by the Kin, a people of Eastern Tartary, from whom are descended the Manchew Tartars, at present masters of China. This vast dominion was named Kitay or Katay, and was divided into two parts: that which belonged to China, was properly called Kitay; and the part which belonged to Tartary was called Karakitay, in which some even include the territories of the Moguls, Karaitis, and other tribes, which are the subject of the present history. The western part of the empire of Kitay was policed by a Turkish prince, who had lately founded a new <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> there, called Hya; whose capital <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CITY">city</a> was Hya-chew, now Ninghya in Shenli, from whence the kingdom took its name. To the west of Hya lay Tangut; a country of great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, and formerly very powerful; but at that time reduced to a low state, and divided among many princes; some of whom were subject to the emperor of Hya, and others to the emperor of China. All Tartary to the westward, as far as the Caspian <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, with the greater part of Little Buchkaria, which then passed under the general name of Turkistan, was subject to Ghurkhan, Khurkhan, or Kavar Khan; to whom even the Gazni monarchs are said to have been tributary. This Ghurkhan had been prince of the Western Kitan or Lyaou; who, driven out of Kitay by the king, settled in Little Buchkaria, and the country to the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, where they founded a powerful state about the year 1124. Thus the Moguls, properly so called, had but a very small extent of empire which could be called their own, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> indeed they had any, when Temujin made his appearance. This hero is said by the Tartars to have been of divine origin, since his family could be traced no farther back than ten generations, the mother of whom was got with child by a spirit. The names and transactions of his predecessors are equally uncertain and unimportant; he himself, however, was born in the year 1163, and is said to have come into the world with congealed blood in his hands; from whence it was prognosticated that he would be a great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WARRIOR">warrior</a>, and obtain the victory over all his enemies. This prediction, if any such there was, Temujin most literally fulfilled. At the time of his father's <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, his subjects amounted to between 30,000 and 40,000 families; but of these two thirds quickly deserted, and Temujin was left almost without subjects. When only 13 years of age, he fought a bloody <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> against these revolters; but either was defeated, or gained an indecisive victory; so that he remained in obscurity for 27 years longer. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a> at last owed to the friendship of Wang Khan, who ruled over a great number of Tartar tribes to the north of Kitay, and has been heard of under the name of Prefect John among the Europeans. This prince took Temujin under his protection; and a rebellion being afterwards raised against himself, Temujin was made his general, and the khan was kept in possession of his throne; soon after which, Temujin subdued the tribes which had revolted from himself, treating them at the same time with the utmost barbarity. This happened in the year 1203; but Vang Khan, instead of continuing the friend of Temujin, now became jealous, and resolved to destroy him by treachery. With this view he proposed a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> between Temujin's son Juiji and his own <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>, and another between Temujin's daughter and his own son. Temujin was invited to the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAMP">camp</a> of Vang Khan, in order to celebrate this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> marriage; but, receiving intelligence of some evil intention against him, he excused himself to Vang Khan's messengers, and desired that the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> might be put off to some other time. A few days after the departure of these messengers, Badu and Kishlik, two brothers, who kept the horses of one of Vang Khan's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> domestics, came and informed Temujin, that the grand Khan finding he had missed his aim, was resolved to set out instantly, and surprise him next morning, before he could suspect any danger. Temujin, alarmed at this intelligence, quitted his camp in the night-time, and retired with all his people to some distance. He was scarce gone when Vang Khan's troops arrived, and discharged an incredible number of arrows among the empty tents; but finding nobody there, they pursued Temujin in such haste that they fell into great disorder. In this condition they were suddenly attacked and routed by Temujin; after which an open war with Vang Khan took place. By this quarrel almost all the princes of Tartary were put in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, some siding with Temujin, and others with Vang Khan. But at last fortune declared in favour of the former: Vang Khan was overthrown in a battle, where he lost 40,000 men; and obliged to fly for refuge to a prince named Tayyan Khan, who was Temujin's father-in-<a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAW">law</a>, and his own enemy, and by whom he was ungenerously put to death. Temujin immediately began to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> on his dominions, great part of which voluntarily submitted; but a confederacy was formed against him by a number of Vang Khan's tributaries, at the head of whom was Jamuka, a prince who had already distinguished himself by his enmity to Temujin; and even Tayyan Khan himself was drawn into the plot, through jealousy of his son-in-law's good fortune. But Temujin was well prepared; and in the year 1204 attacked Tayyan Khan, entirely routed his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, killed himself, and took Jemuka prisoner, whose head he caused instantly to be struck off; after which he marched against the other tribes who had conspired against him. Them he quickly reduced; took a city called Kaibin, where he put all to the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> who had borne arms against him; and reduced all the Mogul tribes in 1205. Temujin now, having none to oppose him, called a general diet, which he appointed to be held on the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> 1206; that is, on the day in which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> entered Aries. To this diet were summoned all the great lords both Moguls and Tartars; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time, to establish good order in the army, he divided his soldiery into bodies of 10,000, 1,000, 100, and 10 men, with their respective officers, all subordinate to the generals, or those who commanded the bodies of 10,000; and these were to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> under his own sons. On the day of holding the diet, the princes of the blood and great lords appeared dressed in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WHITE">white</a>. Temujin, dressed in the same manner, with his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> on his head, sat <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DOWN">down</a> on his throne, and was complimented by the whole <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>, who wished him the continuance of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> and prosperity. After this they confirmed the Mogul empire to him and his successors, adding all those kingdoms which he had subdued, the descendants of whose vanquished kings were deprived of all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> or title to them; and after this he was proclaimed emperor with much ceremony. During this inauguration, a pretended prophet declared that he came from God to tell the assembly, that from thenceforth Temujin should assume the name of Jenghiz Khan, or the Most Great Khan of khans; professing also, that all his posterity should be khans the title of from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a> to generation. This prophecy, which Jenghiz was no doubt owing to Temujin himself, had a surprising effect on his subjects, who from that time concluded that all the world belonged of right to them, and even thought it a crime against heaven for any body to pretend to resist them. Jenghiz Khan having now reduced under his subjection all the wandering tribes of Moguls and Tartars, began to think of reducing those countries to the south and south-west of his own, where the inhabitants were much more civilized than his own subjects; and the countries being full of fortified cities, he must of course expect to meet with more resistance. He began with the emperor of Hya, whose dominions he invaded in 1205, who at last submitted to become his tributary. But in the meantime Jenghiz Khan himself was supposed to be tributary to the emperor of Kitay; who, in 1210, sent him an officer, demanding the customary tribute. This was refused with the utmost indignation, and a war commenced, which ended not but with the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> of the empire of Kitay, as mentioned under the article China. In the year 1216, Jenghiz Khan resolved to carry his arms westward, and therefore left his general Mochuli to pursue his conquests in Kitay. In his journey westward he overthrew an army of 300,000 Tartars who had revolted against him; and, in 1218, sent ambassadors desiring an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> with Mohammed Karazm Shah, emperor of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-GAZNA">Gazna</a>. His <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> was haughtily treated; however, the alliance was concluded; but soon after broken, through the treachery, as it is said, of the Karazmian monarch's subjects. This brought on a war attended with the most dreadful devastations, and which ended with the entire destruction of the empire of Karazm or Gazna, as related under the article Gazna. After the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REDUCTION">reduction</a> of Karazm, part of the Moguls broke into Iran or <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, where also they made large conquests, while others of their armies invaded <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GEORGIA">Georgia</a> and the countries to the west; all this time committing such enormities, that the Chinese historians say both men and spirits burst with indignation. In 1225, Jenghiz Khan returned to Hya, where he made war on the emperor for having sheltered some of his enemies. The event was, that the emperor was slain, and his kingdom conquered, or rather destroyed; which, however, was the last exploit of this most cruel conqueror, who died in 1227, as he marched to complete the destruction of the Chinese. The Mogul empire, at the death of Jenghiz Khan, vast extent extended over a prodigious tract of country; being of his command more than 1800 leagues in length from east to west, and upwards of 1000 in breadth from north to south. Its princes, however, were still insatiable, and pushed on their conquests on all sides. Oktay was acknowledged emperor after Jenghiz Khan; and had under his immediate <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> Mogulestan (the country of the Moguls properly so called), Kitay, and the countries eastward to the Tartarian sea. Jagaty his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> governed under him a great part of the western conquests. The country of the Kinjacks, and others to the east and north-east, north and north-west, were governed by Batu or Patu the son of Juji, who had been killed in the wars; while Tuli or Toley, another son of Jenghiz Khan, had Khorassan, Persia, and what part of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a> was conquered. On the east side the Mogul arms were still attended with success; not only the empire of Kitay, but the southern part of China, was conquered, as already related under that article, n° 24—42. On the west side matters continued much in the same way till the year 1254, when Magu, or Menkho, the fourth khan of the Moguls, (the fame who was afterwards killed at a siege in China*), raised a great army, which he gave to his brother Hulaku, or Hulagu, to extend his dominions westward. In 1255 he entered Iran, where he suppressed the Assassins or Alaffins, of whom an account is given under the article Assassins; and two years afterwards he advanced to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAGDAD">Bagdad</a>, which he took, and cruelly put the khalif to death, treating the city with no more lenity than the Moguls usually treated those which fell into their hands. Every thing was put to fire and sword; and in the city and its neighbourhood the number of slain, it is said, amounted to 1,600,000. The next year he invaded <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>; the city of Damascus was delivered up, and, as it made no resistance, the inhabitants were spared; but <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEPPO">Aleppo</a> being taken by storm, a greater slaughter ensued there than had taken place at Bagdad, not even the children in their cradles being spared. Some cities of this country revolted the next year, or the year after; but falling again into the hands of the Moguls, they were plundered, and the inhabitants butchered without mercy, or carried into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a>. Hulaku died in 1264, and at his death we may fix the greatest extent of the Mogul empire. It now comprehended the whole of the continent of Asia, excepting part of Indostan, Siam, Pegu, Cochinchina, and a few of the countries of Lesser Asia, which had not been attacked by them; and during all these vast conquests no Mogul army had ever been conquered, except one by Jalaloddin, as mentioned under the article Gazna.—From this <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, however, the empire began to decline. The ambition of the khans having prompted them to invade the kingdoms of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JAPAN">Japan</a> and Cochinchina, they were miserably disappointed in their attempts, and lost a great number of men. The same bad success attended them in Indostan; and in a short time this mighty empire broke into several smaller ones. The governors of Persia being of the family of Jenghiz Khan, owned no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">allegiance</a> to any superior; those of Tartary did the same. The Chinese threw off the yoke; and thus the continent of Asia wore much the same <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FACE">face</a> that it had done before Jenghiz Khan began his conquests. The successors of Hulaku reigned in Persia till the year 1335; but that year Abu Said Khan, the eighth from Hulaku, dying, the affairs of that country fell into confusion for want of a prince of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-RACE">race</a> of Jenghiz Khan to succeed to the throne. The empire, therefore, was divided among a great number of petty princes, who fought against each other almost without intermission, till, in the year 1369, Timur Bek, or Tamerlane, one of these princes, having conquered a number of others, was crowned at Balkh, with the pompous title of Salab Karan; that is, "the emperor of the age, and conqueror of the world." As he had <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> before taken that city, and destroyed one of his most formidable rivals who had shut himself up in it, the new emperor began his reign with beheading some of the inhabitants, imprisoning others, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> their houses, and selling the women and children for slaves. In 1370 he crossed the Silun, made war on the Getes, and attacked Karazm. Next year he granted a peace to his enemies; but two years after, he again invaded the country of the Getes, and by the year 1379 had fully conquered that country as well as Korazan; and from that time he continued to extend his conquests in much the same manner as Jenghiz Khan had done, though with less cruelty.—In 1387 he had reduced <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMENIA">Armenia</a>, Georgia, and all Persia; the conquest of which last was completed by the reduction of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ISPAHAN">Ispahan</a>, 70,000 of the inhabitants of which were slaughtered on account of a sedition raised by some rash or evil disposed persons. After the reduction of Persia, Timur turned his arms northward and westward, subduing all the countries to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EUPHRATES">Euphrates</a>. He took the city of Bagdad; subdued Syria; and having ravaged great part of Russia, returned to Persia in 1396, where he splendidly feasted his whole army. In 1398 he invaded Indostan; crossed the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-INDUS">Indus</a> on the 17th of September, reconquered several fortresses, and made a vast number of captives. However, as he was afraid that, in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CASE">case</a> of any emergency, these prisoners might take part with the enemy, he gave orders to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> to put all their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> slaves to death; and, in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of this inhuman order, more than 100,000 of these <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POOR">poor</a> wretches were slaughtered in less than an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>. In the beginning of the year 1399, Timur was met by the Indian army; whom, after a desperate battle, he defeated with great slaughter, and soon after took the city of Dehli, the capital of the country. Here he seated himself on the throne of the Indian emperors, and here the sharifs, kadis, and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> inhabitants of the city, came to make their submission, and begged for mercy. The tame elephants and rhinoceroses likewise were brought to kneel before him as they had been accustomed to do to the Indian emperors, and made a great cry as if they implored his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CLEMENCY">clemency</a>. These war-elephants, 120 in number, were, at his return, sent to Samarcan, and to the province where his sons resided. After this, at the request of the lords of the court, Timur made a great feast; at which he distributed presents to the princes and principal officers. Dehli at this time consisted of three cities, called The city of Seyri, Old Dehli, and Jehan Penah. Seyri was sur-Dehli de-rounded with a wall in form of a circle. Old Dehli stood, was the same, but much larger, lying south-west of the inhabitants other. These two parts were joined on each side by slaughter- a wall; and the third, lying between them, was called ed. Jehan Penah, which was larger than Old Dehli. Pe-nah nah had ten gates; Seyri had <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a>, three of which looked towards Jehan Penah; this last had thirteen gates, six to the north-west, and seven to the south-east. Everything seemed to be in a quiet posture; when, on the 12th of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1399, the soldiers of Timur being assembled at one of the gates of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DELHI">Delhi</a>, insulted the inhabitants of the suburbs. The great emirs were ordered to put a stop to these disorders; but their endeavours were not effectual. The folktas having a curiosity to see the rarities of Delhi, and particularly a famous <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> adorned with 1000 pillars, built by an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> king of India, went in with all the court; and the gate being on that occasion left open for everybody, above 15,000 soldiers got in unperceived. But there was a far greater number of troops in a large place between Delhi, Seyri, and Jehan Penah, who committed great disorders in the two last cities. This made the inhabitants in despair <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> on them; and many, setting fire to their houses, burnt their wives and children. The soldiers seeing this confusion, did nothing but pillage the houses; while the disorder was increased by the admission of more troops, who seized the inhabitants of the neighbouring places who had fled thither for shelter. The emirs, to put a stop to this mischief, caused the gates to be shut; but they were quickly opened by the soldiers within, who rose in arms against their officers; so that by the morning of the 15th the whole army was entered, and this great city was totally destroyed. Some soldiers carried out 150 slaves, men, women, and children; nay, some of their boys had 20 slaves apiece to their share. The other spoils, in jewels, plate, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>, were immense; for the Indian women and girls were adorned with precious <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, and had bracelets and rings on their hands, feet, and even toes, so that the soldiers were loaded with them. On the 15th, in Old Delhi, the Indians retired into the great mosque to defend themselves; but being attacked by the Tartars, they were all slaughtered, and towers erected with their heads. A dreadful carnage now ensued throughout the whole city, and several days were employed before the inhabitants could be made to quit it entirely; and as they went, the emirs took a number of them for their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. The artisans were also distributed among the princes and commanders; all but the masons, who were reserved for the emperor, in order to build him a spacious <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-STONE">stone</a> mosque at Samarqand. After this terrible devastation, Timur marched into the different provinces of Indofan, everywhere defeating the Indians who opposed him, and slaughtering the Ghebrs or worshippers of fire. On the 25th of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MARCH">March</a> he set out on his return, and on the 9th of May arrived at Samarqand. In a few months after his arrival, he was obliged to undertake an expedition into Persia, where affairs were in the utmost disorder on account of the misconduct of his son, whom he had appointed sovereign of that empire. Here Timur soon settled matters; after which he again set out on an expedition westward, reduced many places in Georgia which had not submitted before, and invaded and conquered Syria. At the same time he quarrelled with Bajazet the Turkish <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SULTAN">sultan</a>, then buried in an enterprise against Constantinople, in which he would probably have succeeded had not Timur interposed. The cause of this quarrel at first was, that Bajazet had demanded tribute from a prince who was under Timur's protection, and is said to have returned an insulting answer to the Tartar ambassadors who were sent to him on that account. Timur, however, who was an enthusiast in the cause of Mahometanism, and considered Bajazet as engaged in the cause of heaven when besieging a Christian city, was very unwilling to disturb him in so pious a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>; and therefore undertook several expeditions against the princes of Syria and Georgia, in order to give the Turkish <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a> time to cool and return to reason. Among other places, he again invested the city of Bagdad, which had <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> off its allegiance to him; and having taken it by storm, made such a dreadful massacre of the inhabitants, that 120 towers were erected with the heads of the slain. In the meantime Bajazet continued to give fresh provocation, by protecting one Kara Yufef a robber, who had even insulted the caravan of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MECCA">Mecca</a>; so that Timur at length resolved to make war upon him. The sultan, however, foreseeing the danger of bringing such a formidable enemy against himself, thought proper to ask <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a>, by a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LETTER">letter</a>, for what was past, and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> obedience to Timur's <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a> for the future. This embassy was graciously received; and Timur returned for answer, that he would forbear hostilities, provided Bajazet would either put Kara Yufef to death, send him to the Tartar camp, or expel him out of his dominions. Along with the Turkish ambassadors he sent one of his own; telling Bajazet that he would march into the confines of Anatolia, and there wait his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FINAL">final</a> answer. Though Bajazet had seemed at first willing to come to an agreement with Timur, and to dread his superior power; yet he now behaved in such an unsatisfactory manner, that the Tartar monarch desired him to prepare for war; upon which he raised the siege of Constantinople, and having met Timur with an army greatly inferior to the Tartars, was utterly defeated and taken prisoner. According to some accounts, he was treated with great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>; while others inform us, that he was shut up in an iron cage, against which he dashed out his brains the following year. At any rate, it is certain that he was not restored to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, but died in confinement. This victory was followed by the submission of many places of the Lesser Asia to Timur; the Greek emperor owned himself his tributary, as did also the sultan of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>. After this, Timur once more returned to Georgia, which he cruelly ravaged; after which he marched to Samarqand, where he arrived in the year 1405. Here, being now an old <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAN">man</a>, this mighty conqueror began to look forward to that state which at one time or other is the dread of all living creatures; and Timur, in order to quiet the remorse of his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a>, came to the following curious <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a>, which he communicated to his intimate friends; namely, that "as the vast conquests he had made were not obtained without some violence, which had occasioned the destruction of a great number of God's creatures, he was resolved, by way of atonement for his past crimes, to perform some good <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a>; namely, to make war on the infidels, and exterminate the idolaters of China." This atonement, however, he did not live to accomplish; for he died the same year. year of a burning fever, in the 71st year of his age and 36th of his reign. On the death of Timur, his empire fell immediately into great disorder, and the civil wars continued for five or six years; but at last peace was restored, by the settlement of Shah Rukh, Timur's son, on the throne. He did not, however, enjoy the empire in its full extent, or indeed much above one half of it; having only Karazm, Khorassan, Kandahar, Perlia, and part of Indostan. Neither was he able, though a brave and warlike prince, to extend his dominions, though he transmitted them to his son Ulug Beg. He proved a wise and learned monarch; and is famous for the astronomical tables which he caused to be composed, and which are well known at this day. He was killed in 1448 by his son Abdolatif, who six months after was put to death by his own soldiers. After the death of Abdolatif, Abdollah, a grandson of Shah Rukh, seized the throne; but, after reigning one year, was expelled by Abu saif Mirza, the grandson of Miran Shah the son of Timur. His reign was one continued <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of wars and tumults; till at last he was defeated and taken prisoner by one Haflan Beg, who put him to death in 1468. From this time we may look upon the empire of Timur as entirely dissolved, though his descendants still reigned in Persia and Indostan, the latter of which is still known by the name of the Mogul empire. On the death of the above mentioned monarch, his son Babr or Babor succeeded him, but was soon driven out by the Uzbek Tartars; after which he resided some time in Gazna, whence he made incursions into Hindostan, and at length became <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the whole empire, excepting the kingdoms of Dekan, Guzerat, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENGAL">Bengal</a>.—For the transactions subsequent to this period, see the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> HINDOSTAN and INDIA. What remains to be supplied here is an account of the revolution that has lately happened at Delhi the capital of the Mogul empire. Gholam Khadur, author of the revolution, was the son of Zabda Khan. His father disinherited him, and drove him from his presence on account of his vices and his crimes. Shah Allum, the king of Delhi, took him under his protection, treated him as his own son, and conferred on him the first title in the kingdom, Amere ul Omraow. He lived with the king, and raised a body of about 8000 troops of his own countrymen the Moguls, which he commanded. Gholam Khadur was of a passionate temper, haughty, cruel, ungrateful, and debauched. In the latter end of the year 1788, the king had formed suspicions that some of the neighbouring rajahs (princes) would make an attempt to plunder and destroy his territories. These suspicions were verified by the approach of a considerable army towards his capital, commanded by Hmael Beg Khan, and assisted by Scindia. Gholam Khadur told the king on this, that he had nothing to fear; for that he had an army sufficiently strong to oppose the enemy; that all the king had to do was to march out with his troops, give them a supply of cash, and he would lay his head on the enemy's being overcome. The king on this replied, that he had no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> to carry on a contest. Gholam Khadur said, that this objection would soon be obviated, as he (Gholam Khadur) would advance the necessary supply of cash, and that all his majesty had to do was to head the army. "This (said he) will animate them and give them confidence; the presence of a monarch is above half the battle." The king agreed in appearance, and requested Gholam Khadur to assemble the army, pay their arrears, and inform them of his intentions. Gholam Khadur retired contentedly; but great was his astonishment, when he intercepted the next day a letter from the king to Scindia, deferring him to make as much haste as possible, and destroy Gholam Khadur; for, says he, Khadur wishes me to act contrary to my wishes, and oppose you. On this discovery, Gholam Khadur marched out with his Moguls, crossed the Jumna, and encamped on the other side opposite the fort of Delhi. He sent to the king the intercepted letter, and asked him if his conduct did not deserve to be punished by the loss of his throne?—He began to besiege the fort, and carried it in a few days. He entered the palace in arms; flew to the king's chamber; insulted the old man in the most barbarous manner; knocked him down; and, kneeling on his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>, with his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a> took out one of his eyes, and he ordered a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> of the king's to take out the other. After this he gave up the palace to pillage, and went to the king's zazana (the residence of his women); where he insulted the ladies, and tore their jewels from their noses and ears and off their arms and legs. As he had lived with the king, he was well acquainted with the different places where the king's treasures were hid; he dug up the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a> of the king's own <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a>-room, and found there two chests, containing in specie 120,000 <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> mohurs, or L. 1,020,000 <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>; this he took, and vast sums more. To get at the hidden jewels of the women, he practised one of the most villainous schemes that ever was thought of. The third day after these horrid cruelties, he ordered that all the king's ladies and daughters should come and pay their respects to him, and promised to set those free who could please him by their appearance and drefs. The innocent, unthinking women, brought out their jewels, and adorned themselves in their richest attires to please this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a>. Gholam Khadur commanded them to be conveyed into a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, where he had prepared <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMON">common</a> dresses for them; these dresses he made them put on by the affluence of cunuchs; and taking possession of their rich dresses and jewels, sent the women home to the palace to lament their loss and curse his treachery. Gholam Khadur did not even stop here; but insulted the princes, by making them dance and sing. The most beautiful of the king's daughters, Mobaruck ul Mouk, was brought to this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a> to gratify his lust; but she refused, and is said to have stabbed herself in order to avoid force. Scindia soon after this came to the assistance of the king, rather to make him his prey. Gholam Khadur fled and took refuge in the fort of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRA">Agra</a>, a large city about 150 miles from Delhi. Scindia's troops besieged him there. Perceiving at last that he must be taken if he continued in the fort, he took the advantage of a dark night, stuffed his saddle with a large stock of precious stones, took a few followers, and fled from the fort towards Persia. Unluckily for him, he fell off his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SECOND">second</a> night after his flight; by MOI Mohair. This means a party of horse which had been sent in pursuit of him came up with him, and took him prisoner. He was brought to Scindia; who, after <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EXPOSING">exposing</a> him for some time in irons, and some time in a cage, ordered his ears, his nose, his hands, and his feet, to be cut off, and his eyes taken out; in which state he was allowed to expire. Scindia has rewarded himself by seizing upon the kingdom which he came to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GUARD">guard</a>: And all that now belongs to Shah Allum, the nominal emperor, is the city of Delhi, with a small district around it, where, even deprived of sight, he remains an empty shadow of royalty; an instance of the instability of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> greatness, and of the precarious state of despotic governments.

MOHAIR

Pages 212-212

in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> of a kind of goat frequent about Angria in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a>; the inhabitants of which <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CITY">city</a> are all employed in the manufacture of camlets made of this hair. Some give the name mohair to the camlets <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> stuffs made of this hair: of these there are two kinds; the one smooth and plain, the other watered like tabbies; the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between the two only consists in this, that the latter is calendered, the other not. There are also mohairs both plain and watered, whose woof is of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, cotton, or thread. MOHAIR-Shell, in <a class="xref" href="../1815/vol6.html#article-CONCHOLOGY">conchology</a>, a name given to a peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of voluta, which seems of a closely and finely reticulated texture, and resembles on the surface a piece of mohair or a very <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SILK">silk</a>-worm's web. MOHAWKS. See Muck. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MOHAWK">MOHAWK</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">Country</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, inhabited by one of the five nations of the Iroquois, situated between the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEW_YORK">New <a c</a>lass="xref" href="vol0.html#article-YORK">York</a> and the lake <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-ONTARIO">Ontario</a> or Frontignac.

MOHILOF

Pages 212-212

a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and strong <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Lithuania, and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PALATINATE">palatinate</a> of Mecislau. It is well built, populous, and has a considerable trade. Near this <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a> the Swedes obtained a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> victory over the Russians in 1707.

MOHLA

Pages 212-212
or Moelia, one of the Comoros islands in the Indian sea, between the north end of the island of Madagascar and the continent of Africa. The inland parts are mountainous and woody; but the lands adjoining to the sea are watered by several fine streams which descend from the mountains; and the grass is green all the year, so that it affords a most delightful habitation. There are plenty of provisions of all kinds; and the East India ships of different nations sometimes touch here for refreshment.

MOINE

Pages 212-212

an excellent French painter, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1688, and trained up under Galloche professor of the academy of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>; which office he himself afterwards filled. Le Moine painted the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SALOON">saloon</a> which is at the entrance into the apartments of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VERSAILLES">Versailles</a>, and which represents the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOTHEOSIS">apotheosis</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>. He was four years about it; and the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">king</a>, to show how well pleased he was with it, made him his first painter in 1736, and gave him a pension of 4000 livres. A fit of lunacy seized this painter the year after; during which he run himself through with his <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, and died, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 4, 1737, aged 49.

MOIRA

Pages 212-213

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, situated in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DOWN">Down</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Ulster, 69 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>; noted for its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> manufacture, and a monthly market for vending the same. It gives <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-EARL">earl</a> to the family of Rawdon. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Moira has here a very beautiful seat; and here is a handsome <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> school, and two dissenting meeting-houses. MOISTURE. See Humidity. The moisture of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> has considerable effects on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> body. For the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of the food, and the proportion of the meat to the drink, being given, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of a human body is less, and consequently its discharges greater in dry <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> than in wet weather; which may be thus accounted for: the moisture of the air moistens the fibres of the skin and lessens perspiration by lessening their vibratory <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>. When perspiration is thus lessened by the moisture of the air, urine indeed is by degrees increased. increased, but not equally. Hence, according to Dr Bryan Robinson, we learn, that to keep a body of the same weight in wet weather as in dry, either the quantity of food must be lessened, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> the proportion of the meat to the drink increased; and both these may be done by lessening the drink without making any change in the meat. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> used for determining the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of moisture in the air, is called an hygrometer. See Hygrometer.

MOIVRE

Pages 213-213

was born at Vitri in Champagne, A.D. 1667. His father was a surgeon. At the revocation of the edict of Nantes, he determined to fly into England rather than abandon the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> of his fathers. Before he left France, he had begun the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MATHEMATICS">Mathematics</a>; and having perfected himself in that science in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, he was obliged, by the means of his circumstances, to teach it. Newton's Principia, which accidentally fell into his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, showed him how little progress he had made in a science of which he thought himself <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MASTER">master</a>.
