From this <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> he acquired a knowledge of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a> of infinites with as <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> facility as he had learned the elementary geometry; and in a short <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> he was fit to be ranked with the most celebrated mathematicians. His success in these studies procured him a seat in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> of London and in the Academy of Sciences at <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. His merit was so well understood in the former, that he was thought capable of deciding in the famous dispute between Leibnitz and Newton concerning the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DIFFERENTIAL">differential</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CALCULUS">calculus</a>. —He published a Treatise on Chances in 1738, and another on <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ANNUITIES">annuities</a> in 1752; both extremely accurate. The Philosophical Transactions contain many interesting <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-MEMOIRS">memoirs</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>.—Some of them treat of the method of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FLUXIONS">fluxions</a>; others are on the lunula of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIPPOCRATES">Hippocrates</a>; others on physical <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>, in which he resolved many important problems; and others, in short, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALYSIS">analysis</a> of the games of chance, in which he followed a different course from that of Montmort. Towards the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> he lost his sight and hearing; and the demand for <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> became so great that he required 20 hours of it in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>. He died at London, 1754, aged 87. His knowledge was not confined to mathematics; but he retained to the last a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for polite literature. He was intimately acquainted with the best authors of antiquity; and he was frequently consulted about difficult <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> in their works. Rabelais and Molière were his favourite French authors; he had them by heart; and he one day observed to one of his acquaintance, "that he would rather have been Molière than Newton." He recited whole scenes of the Misanthrope with that delicacy and force with which he remembered to have heard them recited at Paris 70 years before, by Molière's own <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>. The character indeed was somewhat similar to his own. He judged severely of mankind; and could never conceal his disgust at the conversation of a fool, nor his aversion to cunning and dissimulation. He was free from the affectation of science; and no one could know him to be a mathematician but from the accuracy of his thoughts. His conversation was general and instructive. Whatever he said was well digested and clearly expressed. His style possessed more strength and solidity than ornament and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANIMATION">animation</a>; but he was always correct, and he bestowed as much pains on his sentences as on his calculations. He could never endure any bold affections <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> indecent witticisms against religion. "I show you that I am a Christian (said he one day to a person who thought to pay him a compliment by observing that mathematicians were attached to no religion), by forgiving the speech you have now made." The practice of giving vails to servants was not laid aside in his time; and, on this account, when a nobleman asked him why he did not dine oftener with him? "You must excuse me, my <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LORD">lord</a> (replied he), I cannot afford it."

MOJQUALIS

Pages 434-435

a small <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATION">nation</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, inhabiting to the east of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of the Dauses, in the valley which separates their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> from those of Damascus; of which the following account is given by Mr Volney in his Travels, vol. ii. p. 84. The characteristic distinction between them and the other inhabitants of Syria (says our author) is, that they, like the Persians, are of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALI">Ali</a>, while all the Turks follow that of Omar <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> Moaouia. This distinction, occasioned by the schism which in the 6th year of the Hijra arose among the Arabs, respecting the successors of Mahomet, is the cause of an irreconcilable hatred between the two parties. The sectaries of Omar, who consider themselves as the only orthodox, assume the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Sonnites, which has that signification, and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TERM">term</a> their adversaries Shiites, that is "sectaries of Ali." The word Motouali has the same meaning in the dialect of Syria. The followers of Ali, dissatisfied with this name, substitute that of Akia, which means "afforters of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>," literally "Justiciaries;" a denomination which they have assumed in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of a doctrinal point they advance in opposition to the Sonnite <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FINAL">final</a> Arabic treatise, entitled Theological Fragments concerning the Sects and Religions of the World, has the following passage: "Those sectaries who pretend that God acts only on principles of justice, conformable to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> reason, are called Akia or Justiciaries. God cannot (say they) command an impracticable worship, nor ordain impossible actions, nor enjoin men to perform what is beyond their ability; but wherever he requires obedience, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a> bestow the power to obey. He removes the cause of evil, he allows us to reason, and imposes only what is easy, not what is difficult; he makes no <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAN">man</a> responsible for the actions of another, nor punishes him for that in which he has no <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a>; he imputes not as a crime what himself has created in man; nor does he require him to avoid what <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESTINY">destiny</a> has decreed. This would be injustice and tyranny, of which God is incapable from the perfection of his being." To this doctrine, which diametrically opposes the system of the Sonnites, the Motouali add certain ceremonies which increase their mutual aversion. They curse Omar and Moaouia as rebels and usurpers; and celebrate Ali and Hosain as saints and martyrs. They begin their ablutions at the elbow, instead of the end of the finger, as is customary with the Turks; they think themselves defiled by the touch of strangers; Motouali, and contrary to the general practice of the East, neither eat nor drink out of a vessel which has been used by a person not of their sect, nor will they even sit with such at the same <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TABLE">table</a>. These doctrines and customs, by separating the Motouali from their neighbours, have rendered them a distinct <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>. It is said they have <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a> existed as a nation in this country, though their name has never been mentioned by any European writer before the present century; it is not even to be found in the maps of Donville: La Roque, who left their country not a hundred years ago, gives them the name of Amadens. Be this as it may, in later times their wars, robberies, successes, and various changes of fortune, have rendered them of consequence in Syria. Till about the middle of this century, they only possessed Balbek, their <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, and a few places in the valley, and Anti-Lebanon, which seems to have been their original country. At that <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> we find them under a like <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> with the Druzes, that is to say, under a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of Shaiks, with one <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of the family of Harfoush. After the year 1750 they established themselves among the heights of Bekaa, and got footing in Lebanon, where they obtained lands belonging to the Maronites, almost as far as Becharrai. They even incommode them so much by their ravages, as to oblige the Emir Yousef to attack them with open force and expel them; but on the other side, they advanced along the river even to the neighbourhood of Sour (<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TYRE">Tyre</a>). In this situation, Shaik Daher had the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a>, in 1760, to attach them to his party. The pachas of Saide and Damascus claimed tributes, which they had neglected paying, and complained of several robberies committed on their subjects by the Motouali; they were desirous of chastising them; but this vengeance was neither certain nor easy. Daher interposed; and by becoming security for the tribute; and promising to prevent any depredations, acquired allies who were able, as it is said, to arm 10,000 horsemen, all resolute and formidable troops. Shortly after they took possession of Sour, and made this village their principal <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port. In 1771 they were of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to Ali Bey and Daher against the Ottomans. But Emir Yousef having in their absence armed the Druzes, ravaged their country. He was besieging the castle of Djezin, when the Motouali, returning from Damascus, received intelligence of this invasion. At the relation of the barbarities committed by the Druzes, an advanced corps, of only 500 men, were so enraged, that they immediately rushed forward against the enemy, determined to perish in taking vengeance. But the surprise and confusion they occasioned, and the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DISCORD">discord</a> which reigned between the two factions of Mansour and Yousef so much favoured this desperate attack, that the whole <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, consisting of 25,000 men, was completely overthrown. In the following year, the affairs of Daher taking a favourable turn, the zeal of the Motouali cooled towards him, and they finally abandoned him in the catastrophe in which he lost his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. But they have suffered for their imprudence under the administration of the pacha who succeeded him. Since the year 1777, Djezzar, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACRE">Acre</a> and Saide, has ince- Motteux faintly laboured to destroy them. His <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a> forced them in 1784 to a reconciliation with the Druzes, and to enter into an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> with the Emir Yousef. Though reduced to less than 700 armed men, they did more in that <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAMPAIGN">campaign</a> than 15,000 or 20,000 Druzes and Maronites assembled at Dair-el-Kamar. They alone took the strong fortress of Mar-Djebaa, and put to the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> 50 or 60 Epirots who defended it. But the misunderstanding which prevailed among the chiefs of the Druzes having rendered abortive all their operations, the pasha has obtained possession of the whole valley, and the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Balbek itself. At this period not more than 500 families of the Motoualis remained, who took refuge in Anti-Lebanon, and the Lebanon of the Maronites; and, driven as they now are from their native <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, it is probable they will be totally annihilated, and even their very name become extinct.

MOLA

Pages 213-213

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> town of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, and in the Terra di Lavoro, where they pretend to show the ruins of Cicero's <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. It is situated on the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 17° 50'. N. Lat. 41° 5'. Mola Salfa, (<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-SALT">Salt</a> Cake), in antiquity, was barley parched, and afterwards ground to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MEAL">meal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> flour, then mixed with salt and frankincense, with the addition of a little <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WATER">water</a>. Thus prepared, it was sprinkled between the horns of the victim before it was killed in sacrifice. This <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> was called immolatio, and was <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to the Greeks as well as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>; with this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>, that the mola of the Romans was of wheat. The Greeks called it ἀναγκή or ἀναγκήν.

MOLARES

Pages 213-213
or Dentes molares, in anatomy, the large teeth, called in English the grinders. See Anatomy, p. 27.

MOLDAVIA

Pages 213-213

a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east by the river Nisec, which divides it from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>; on the east, by Bessarabia; on the south by the Danube, which parts it from Bulgaria; and on the west, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALACHIA">Walachia</a> and Transylvania; it being 240 miles in length and 150 in breadth. It lies in a good <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> and fruitful <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, producing corn, wine, rich pastures, a good breed of horses, oxen, sheep, plenty of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAME">game</a>, fish, fowl, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, wax, and all European <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>. Its <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> are the Danube, Nisec, Pruth, Bardalach, and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CERET">Ceret</a>. The inhabitants are <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> of the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JASSY">Jassy</a> is the principal town. It has been tributary to the Turks ever since the year 1574; who appoint a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> who is a native of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, but have no regard to his being of the principal families. They pay a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> yearly tribute; besides which, they are obliged to raise a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> body of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> at their own expense.

MOLE

Pages 214-214

(mole,) among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, was also used for a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAUSOLEUM">mausoleum</a>, built in manner of a round tower on a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> base, insulated, encompassed with columns, and covered with a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DOME">dome</a>.—The mole of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Adrian, now the castle of St Angelo, was the greatest and most stately of all the moles. It was crowned with a brazen pineapple, wherein was a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> urn containing the ashes of the emperor. MOLE Cricket, in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ZOOLOGY">zoology</a>. See Gryllotalpa. MOLE-HILLS. These little hillocks of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> are a very <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a> to the pasture lands, not only in wasting so much of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAND">land</a> as they cover, but in hindering the scythe in mowing. In the west of England they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> a peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> for the breaking up of these; it is a flat board, very thick, and of about eight inches in diameter, into which there is fastened a perpendicular handle of three <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> four feet <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a>. It has four <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> and sharp <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-IRON">iron</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> at the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FRONT">front</a>, which readily cut through the hill, and spread the earth it consists of; and behind there is a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> knob proper for breaking the clods with, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> there are any. Some use a spade, or other <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMON">common</a> instrument, in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of this, but not so well. There is, however, a much better instrument even than this, for destroying these hills, where they are in very great numbers. This is a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>-machine; it has a sharp iron about three feet over, and with a strong back.—It is about four or five inches broad, and has two long handles for a horse to be harnessed to, and a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAR">bar</a> of iron to strengthen it at the bottom of the handles, reaching from the one handle to the other. The middle of this cross-bar is furnished with one, two, or more sharp pieces of iron like small ploughshares, to cut the mole-hills into two, three or more parts. The iron behind is of a semicircular <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>. A single horse is harnessed to this machine, and a boy must be employed to drive it, and a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAN">man</a> to hold and guide it; the sharp irons or shares are the first things that meet the hills, they run through it, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> its texture, and cut it into several parts; and the circular iron following immediately behind them, cuts up the whole by the roots, and leaves the land <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LEVEL">level</a>. This instrument <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a> destroy as many mole-hills in one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> as a common labourer can in eight, and would be of very great advantage to the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> if brought into general use. It is to be observed, that this leaving a naked space in the place of every hill, it will be necessary to go over the land, and sow them with hay seed, otherwise the spots will want the produce of grass the first years. The farmers in some parts of England are not willing to destroy the mole-hills, but let them stand from year to year, supposing that they get some ground by them, but the advantage by this means is so little, that it does not <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a> the unrighteousness and damage to the mowing.

MOLESWORTH

Pages 214-214

Viscount Moleworth, an eminent statesman and polite writer, born at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a> in 1656, where his father was a merchant. He was attainted by <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">King</a> James for his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a>'s invasion; but the latter, when he was settled on the throne, called up Mr Moleworth into the privy-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, and sent him envoy-extraordinary to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>. Here he resided above three years, and then returned upon some disquiet, without an audience of leave. Upon his return, he drew up his Account of Denmark, a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> well known, in which he represented that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> as arbitrary; and hence gave <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> offence to George prince of Denmark. The Danish envoy presented a memorial to King William concerning it; and then furnished materials for an answer, which was executed by Dr William King. Mr Moleworth was member of the houses of commons in both kingdoms; King George I. made him a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSIONER">commissioner</a> of trade and plantations, and advanced him to the peerage of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, by the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Baron Philipstown, and Viscount Moleworth of Swords.

MOLIERE

Pages 214-215

a famous French comedian, whose true name was Poquelin, which for some reason <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> other he took for that of Molière. He was the son of a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-VALET">valet</a> de chambre, and was born at <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> about the year 1620. He went through the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the classics under the Jesuits in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of Clermont, and was designed for the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAR">bar</a>; but at his quitting the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAW">law</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, he made choice of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTOR">actor</a>'s profession. From the prodigious fondness he had for the drama, his whole study and application being directed to the stage, he <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> till his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEATH">death</a> to exhibit plays, which were greatly applauded. It is said the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> of his going upon the stage was to enjoy the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of an actress for whom he had contracted a violent fondness. His comedies are highly esteemed. And it is no wonder he so justly represented <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> feuds, and the torments of jealous husbands, or of those who have reason to be so, it being asserted that no <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAN">man</a> ever experienced all this more than Molière, who was very unhappy in his wife. His last <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a> was La Malade imaginaire, which was brought on the stage in 1673; and Molière died on the fourth night of its representation; some say acting the very <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> of the pretended dead man, which gave some <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> for the wits of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a>; but according to others he died in his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a> that night, from the bursting of a vein in his lungs by coughing. The <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">king</a>, as a last mark of his favour, prevailed with the archbishop of Paris to suffer him to be buried in consecrated ground; though he had irritated the clergy by his Tartuffe. The most esteemed editions of his works are that of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a>, 5 vols 12mo, 1699; and that of Paris, 6 vols 4to, 1734.

MOLINA

Pages 215-215

a Spanish lawyer, who was employed by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> II., <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> in the councils of the Indies and of Castile. He is the author of a learned treatise concerning the entails of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> estates of the Spanish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, entitled, De Hispanorum Primogenitorum Origine et Natura, published in 1603, in folio. This book is likewise applicable to several provinces in France. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> Molina must not be confounded with John Molina, a Spanish historian, author of Cronica antiqua d'<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARAGON">Aragon</a>, published in 1524, in folio; and also of De las Cajas memorables d'Espagne, in folio. The first <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> appeared at <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-VALENCIA">Valencia</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SECOND">second</a> at Alcala. MOLINÆUS. See Moulin.

MOLINISTS

Pages 215-215

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> in the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, who follow the doctrine and sentiments of the Jesuit Molina, relating to sufficient and efficacious <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>. He taught that the operations of divine grace were entirely consistent with the freedom of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a>; and he introduced a new kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a> to remove the difficulties attending the doctrines of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PREDESTINATION">predestination</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, and to reconcile the jarring opinions of Augustines, Thomists, Semi-Pelagians, and other contentious divines. He affirmed, that the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DECREE">decree</a> of predestination to eternal <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> was founded upon a previous knowledge and consideration of the merits of the elect; that the grace, from whose operation these merits are derived, is not efficacious by its own intrinsic power only, but also by the consent of our own will, and because it is administered in those circumstances, in which the Deity, by that branch of his knowledge which is called scientia media, foresees that it will be efficacious. The kind of prescience, denominated in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> scientia media, is that foreknowledge of future contingents that arises from an acquaintance with the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and faculties of rational beings, of the circumstances in which they shall be placed, of the objects that shall be presented to them, and of the influence which their circumstances and objects must have on their actions.

MOLINOS

Pages 215-215

a Spanish <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>, who endeavoured to spread new doctrines in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. He was born in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of Saragossa in 1627; and entered into priest's orders, though he never held any <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> benefice. He was a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAN">man</a> of good <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> and learning, and his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> was exemplary; though, instead of practising austerities, he gave himself up to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONTEMPLATION">contemplation</a> and mystical <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>. He wrote a book intitled, Il Guida Spirituale, containing his peculiar notions, which was greedily read both in Italy and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>. His followers are called Quietists; because his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> principle was, that men ought to annihilate themselves in order to be united to God, and afterwards remain in quietness of mind, without being troubled for what shall happen to the body. He was taken up in 1687; and his 68 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPOSITIONS">propositions</a> were examined by the pope and inquisitors, who decreed that his doctrine was false and pernicious, and that his books should be burned. He was forced to recant his errors publicly in the Dominican <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, and was condemned to perpetual imprisonment. He was 60 years old when he was taken, and had been spreading his doctrine 22 years before. He died in prison in 1692.

MOLINOSISTS

Pages 215-215

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> among the Romanists, who adhere to the doctrine of Molinos. These are the same with what are otherwise called Quietists.

MOLLOY

Pages 215-216

descended from a good family in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, was born in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>, and received <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> at Trinity <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> there, of which he afterwards became a fellow. At his first coming to England he entered himself of the Middle Temple, and was supposed to have had a very considerable <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAND">hand</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> of a periodical <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> called "Fog's Journal;" as also since that <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> to have been almost the sole author of another well-known paper, intitled "<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMON">Common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SENSE">Sense</a>." All these papers give testimony of strong abilities, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> depth of understanding, and clearness of reasoning. Dr <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">King</a> was a considerable writer in the latter, as were lords Chesterfield and Lyttleton. Our author had <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> offers made him to write in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of Sir Richard Walpole, but these he rejected notwithstanding which, at the great change in the ministry in 1742, he was entirely neglected, as well as his fellow-labourer Amherit, who conducted "The Craftsman." Mr Molloy, however, having married a lady of fortune, was in circumstances which enabled him to treat the ingratitude of his patriotic friends with the contempt it deserved. He lived many years after this <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, dying so lately as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 16, 1767. He also wrote three dramatic pieces, viz. The perplexed Couple; The Coquet; and, The Half-pay Officers; none of which met with much success.

MOLLUGO

Pages 216-216

AFRICAN CHICKWEED: A genus of the trigynia order, belonging to the triandra class of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 22d order, Caryophyllae. The calyx is pentaphylous; there is no corolla; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPSULE">capsule</a> is trilocular, and trivalved. Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> are these: The emplacement of the flower is composed of five <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> small leaves, coloured on their insides, and permanent; the flower has five oval petals shorter than the emplacement; and three bristly stamens, which stand near the style, terminated by single summits; it has an oval germen, having three furrows, supporting three very short styles: the germen becomes an oval capsule with three cells, filled with small kidney-shaped seeds. There are several <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, few of which are admitted into gardens. Miller reckons two and Linnæus five species. This plant is said to have an aperitive virtue.

MOLOCH

Pages 216-216

a false god of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMMONITES">Ammonites</a>, who dedicated their children to him, by making them "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through the fire," as the scriptures express it. There are various opinions concerning this method of consecration. Some think, the children leaped over a fire sacred to Moloch; others, that they passed between two fires; and others, that they were really burnt in the fire, by way of sacrifice to this god. There is foundation for each of these opinions. For, first, it was usual among the pagans to illustrate <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> purify with fire; and, in the next <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, it is expressly said, that the inhabitants of Sepharvaim burnt their children in the fire to Anamellech and Adramelech; much such deities as Moloch of the Ammonites. Moses, in several places, forbids the Israelites to dedicate their children to this god as the Ammonites did, and threatens <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEATH">death</a> and utter extirpation to such persons as were guilty of this abominable idolatry. And there is <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> that the Hebrews were much addicted to the worship of this deity; since <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMOS">Amos</a>, and after him St Stephen, reproaches them with having carried along with them into the wilderness the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TABERNACLE">tabernacle</a> of their god Moloch. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a> built a temple to Moloch upon the mount of Olives; and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MANASSEH">Manasseh</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> after, imitated his impiety, by making his son pass through the fire in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of Moloch. It was chiefly in the valley of Tophet and Hinnom, to the east of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, that the Israelites paid their idolatrous worship to this false god of the Ammonites. There are various sentiments concerning the relation which Moloch had to the other pagan divinities. Some believe he was the same with <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-SATURN">Saturn</a>, to whom it is well known that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> sacrifices were offered. Others suppose him to be <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a>; others, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MARS">Mars</a>; others, Mitras; and others, Venus. Lastly, others take Moloch to be the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, or the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">king</a> of heaven. Moloch was likewise called Milcom; as appears from what is said of Solomon, that he went after Aholithroth the abomination of the Zidonians, and Milcom the abomination of the Ammonites.

MOLOSSES

Pages 216-217

MOLASSES, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> Melasses, that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> fluid <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> remaining of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a> after refining, and which no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a> bring to a consistence more <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> than that of syrup; hence also called syrup of sugar. Properly, molasses are only the sediment of one kind of sugar called chypre, or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> sugar, which is the refuse of other sugars not to be whitened or reduced into loaves. Molasses are much used in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>, and also among <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POOR">poor</a> people instead of sugar. There is a kind of brandy or spirit made of molasses; but by some held exceedingly unwholesome. See below. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">Artificial</a> Molasses. There has been found a method of making molasses from apples without the addition of sugar. The apple that succeeds best in this operation is a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> sweeting of a middle size, pleasant to the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, and so full of juice that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> bushels will yield a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARREL">barrel</a> of cider. The manner of making it is this: the apples are to be ground and pressed, then the juice is to be boiled in a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, till three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of it be evaporated: this will be done with a moderate fire in about six hours, with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of juice above mentioned; by this <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> it will be of the consistence and taste as well as of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of molasses. This new molasses serves to all the purposes of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMON">common</a> kind, and is of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in preserving cider. Two quarts of it, put into a barrel of racked cider, will preserve it, and give it an agreeable colour. The <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of this kind of molasses was owing to Mr Chandler of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WOODSTOCK">Woodstock</a> in New England, who living at a distance from the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and where the common molasses was very dear and scarce, provided this for the supply of his own family, and soon made the practice among people of the neighbourhood. It is to be observed, that this sort of apple, the sweeting, is of great use in making cider, one of the very best kinds we know being made of it. The people in New England also feed their hogs with the fallings of their orchards of these apples; and the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of this is, that their pork is the finest in the world. Molasses Spirit; a very clean and pure spirit, much used in England, and made from molasses or common treacle dissolved in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and fermented in the same manner as malt or the common malt spirit. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISTILLATION">Distillation</a>, No. 10. Molasses spirit coming dearer than that of malt, it is frequently met with basely adulterated with a mixture of that spirit, and indeed seldom is to be bought without some dash of it. Many have a way of mixing malt in the fermenting liquor; by this the yield of the whole is greatly increased, and the maker may assure the buyer that the spirit is pure as it ran from the worm. In most of the nice cafes in our <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> distillery, Molosses spirit supplies the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of a pure and clean spirit. Our <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CINNAMON">cinnamon</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITRON">citron</a>, and other fine cordial waters, are made with it; for the malt spirit would impart to these a very disagreeable flavour. Molosses spirit gives a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> stain to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> or other substances dipped into it; and may therefore be of use in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DYEING">dyeing</a>. It is possible also that the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a>-makers may find use for it in their way; but the most advantageous of all its uses is to the distiller himself; a quantity of it added to new treacle intended for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FERMENTATION">fermentation</a> will be of great use in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROCESS">process</a>, and increase very considerably the quantity of spirit; but the proportion in regard to the new matter must not be too great.

MOLOSSI

Pages 217-217

a people of Epirus, who inhabited that <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> which was called Molosia <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> Molossia, from <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">king</a> Molossus, a son of Pyrrhus and Andromache. This country had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of Ambracia on the south, and the country of the Perhaeanians on the east. The dogs of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a> were famous, and received the name of Molossi among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DODONA">Dodona</a> was the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the country, according to some writers. Others, however, reckon it as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Thephrotia.

MOLOSSUS

Pages 217-217

in the Greek and Latin <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, a foot consisting of three <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a> syllables. As audiri, cantabant, virtutem. It takes its name either from a dance in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> among the people called Molossi <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> Epireote; or from the temple of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> Molossus, where odes were sung, in which this foot had a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> share; or else because the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MARCH">march</a> of the Molossi, when they went to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a>, was composed of these feet, or had the cadence thereof. The same foot was also called among the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, Vertumnus, extensipes, hippius, &c. canius.

MOLSA

Pages 217-217

an eminent poet of the 16th century, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MODENA">Modena</a>. He gained so prodigious a reputation by his Latin and Italian <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, that, as Paul Jovius tells us, "for 30 years together the patrons of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WIT">wit</a> at Rome strove to promote him." <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> he had behaved with the least <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a>, he might easily have raised himself to considerable preferments and fortunes in the world; but he managed so ill that it was not possible to serve him.—He was entirely debauched, and at the same <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> devoid of all prudence and decency in the management of his pleasures. Hence he destroyed his reputation, and put an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> stop to the progress of his fortunes. He died, in 1544, of the French <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>. Molsa was a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> orator as well as a great poet. He met once with a favourable opportunity of displaying his <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> this way; for having seen the people of Rome highly incensed against Lorenzo de Medici, who had struck off the heads of a great <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a>, he accused him of that <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, and (according to Paul Jovius) made so lively an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORATION">oration</a> upon it, that he perfectly overwhelmed him with confusion and despair; and it was generally believed that Lorenzo de Medici was so confounded at the infamy with which he was branded in that oration, that, in order to efface it, he resolved to restore the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a> to its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, by afflaming Alexander de Medici his near relation, which he did in 1537. Molsa (Tarquinia), <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Camillo Molsa, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a> of the order of St James of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, and granddaughter of Francis <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MARIA">Maria</a> Molsa, was one of the most accomplished ladies that ever appeared in the world; wit, learning, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, and virtue, all uniting in her in a most extraordinary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>. Her father observing, while she was yet very young, the goodness and excellence of her genius, procured her the best masters in every branch of literature and science. Lazaro Labadini, a celebrated grammarian of those times, taught her polite literature; and her Latin compositions in prose and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> show that she attained the art of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> well, and composing correctly. She became learned in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a> under Camillo Corcapani; Anthony Guarini the mathematician taught her the doctrine of the sphere; the learned poetry under Francis Patricius the famous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>; and logic and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> under P. Latoni, who also instructed her thoroughly in the Greek tongue. The rabbi <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABRAHAM">Abraham</a> taught her the principles of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>; and John Marier Barbier formed her in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POLITENESS">politeness</a> of the Tuscan tongue; in which she has not only written a great number of easy and elegant verses, but likewise several letters and other pieces which are in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> esteem with the polite and learned in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. Besides her original works, she has translated several things from Greek and Latin in a manner which shows her to have understood those languages as well as her own. Afterwards she learned music, as a relaxation and diversion from her more serious studies; and in this art she attained the highest degree of perfection. She used to play upon the violin as well as upon the lute, and sing to it at the same time in so exquisite a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> as charmed every hearer; and she instituted at length a choir of ladies, over which she herself used to preside. This lady was in high reputation at the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COURT">court</a> of Alphonso II., <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FERRARA">Ferrara</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of great judgment, and a passionate lover of every thing that was elegant; and we are told, that he stood ravished with admiration upon finding so many more accomplishments than he had been taught to expect in her. But the most authentic testimony and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a> of her high merit and character, was that which she received from the city of Rome; which, by a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DECREE">decree</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>, in which all her excellences and qualifications are set forth, honoured her with the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Singular, and bestowed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> of a Roman citizen upon her and the whole family of Molsa. Molsa was married; but losing her husband without having any children, would never consent to be married again, although she was very young. She gave such lively tokens of her grief, that Patricius compares her to another <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTEMISIA">Artemisia</a>.

MOLUCCA ISLANDS

Pages 217-218
lie in the East Indian sea under the line; of which there are five principal, namely, Ternate, Tydor, Machian, Motyr, and Bachian. The largest of them is hardly 30 miles in circumference. They produce neither corn, rice, nor cattle, except. except goats: but they have oranges, lemons, and other fruits; and are most remarkable for spices, especially cloves. They have large snakes, which are not venomous, and very dangerous land crocodiles. At present they have three kings; and the Dutch, who are very strong there, keep out all other European nations, being jealous of their spice trade. The religion is idolatry; but there are many Mahometans. They were discovered by the Portuguese in 1511, who settled upon the coast; but the Dutch drove them away, and are now masters of all these islands.

MOLUCILLA

Pages 217-217

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>: A genus of the gymnoperma order, belonging to the didynamia class of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 42d order, Verticillate. The calyx is campanulated, gradually widening larger than the corolla, and spinous.

MOLUSCA

Pages 216-216

in the Linnæan system, is the denomination of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SECOND">second</a> genus of vermes <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-WORMS">worms</a>. These are simple naked animals, not included in a shell, but furnished with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a>, and comprehend eighteen subordinate genera, and one hundred and ten <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>.

MOLWITZ

Pages 218-218

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SILESIA">Silesia</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Grottkau, remarkable for a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> gained by the Prussians over the Austrians in 1741. E. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 16° 45'. N. Lat. 50° 26'. MOLY. The name of this plant is rendered famous by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>; and hence has been much inquired into, as to its true <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, by the botanists of almost all times. The old interpreters of Homer explain this word by the "wild rue;" and the only reason for this is, that at some <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a>, probably long after the days of Homer, the people of Cappadocia called the wild rue moly. But this plant is wholly different from the moly of Homer, which <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-THEOPHRASTUS">Theophrastus</a> affirms grew in his time in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCADIA">Arcadia</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> plenty, and had a round bulbous root like an onion, and long and grassy leaves like the squill. On the whole, the moly of Homer seems to have been a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of allium <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> garlic.

MOLYBDENA

Pages 218-218

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a>, a mineral often confounded with plumbago <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, but possessed of different properties. It is composed of scaly laminae of various magnitudes, scarcely adhering to each other; somewhat greasy to the touch, foiling the fingers, and leaving traces on <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> of a blackish grey <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. In powder it is of a bluish colour. "Perfect molybdena (says Mr Fourcroy) slightly detonates with nitre; the residue contains molybdene, tartar, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CALX">calx</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-IRON">iron</a>. From the experiments of Mr Scheele, molybdene appears to consist of a peculiar combustible <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> and iron. The <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the combustible matter is not yet perfectly known. Mr Hielm, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of the celebrated Bergman, appears to have succeeded in converting it into a regulus. Mr Pelletier affirms, that he has had the same success; but the properties of this new metal have not yet been examined. The molybdenic acid appears to be a metallic one. Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, its flinty and astringent <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, its dry and pulverulent form, its fusibility, insolubility, the colour it assumes by <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FLAME">flame</a> and combustible matters, its precipitation by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NUT">nut</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALLS">galls</a> and the acid of Prussian blue, show that it is somewhat similar to the arsenical acid. This substance is so rare in France, that no chemist except M. Pelletier has had an opportunity of making a regular <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of experiments upon it. It is greatly to be wished that they should be <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a>, especially with a view of deciding whether the molybdenic acid be truly different from all others; for I cannot avoid thinking, notwithstanding its peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, that a substance which does not become acid but by the assistance of 30 parts of weak nitrous acid, and is with so much difficulty brought to assume the saline state, ought not to be considered as an acid truly peculiar." See Chemistry-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>; and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MINERALOGY">Mineralogy</a>, p. 134. Molybdene is found sometimes along with tin-ores and iron-ores, that are attracted by the magnet, among copperiferous pyrites; and also with wolfram, in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ICELAND">Iceland</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, France, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, &c.

MOLYBDIA

Pages 218-218

in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, the name of a genus of crystals of a cubic form, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> composed of six sides, at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a>, like a dye.

MOLYN

Pages 218-218

called Tempesta and Pietro <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MULIER">Mulier</a>, an eminent painter, was born at Haerlem in 1637. According to some authors, he was the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Snyder, whose manner of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> he at first imitated. But his genius led him to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of dismal subjects; and he so far excelled in painting tempests, storms at <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and shipwrecks, that he was called by way of distinction Tempesta. His pictures are very rare, and held in the greatest estimation. The name of Pietro Mulier, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> de Mulieribus, was given him on account of having caused his wife to be assassinated, in order to marry a young lady of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-GENOA">Genoa</a> with whom he was in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LOVE">love</a>. But this villainous transaction being discovered, he was seized, imprisoned, and capitally condemned. However, the greatness of his merit as an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a> occasioned a mitigation of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a>; but he was still detained in prison, where he diligently followed his profession, and would have <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> there in all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, had he not met with an opportunity of escaping to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACENTIA">Placentia</a>, at the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIV. bombarded the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Genoa, after he had been in confinement 16 years. To this artist are attributed several very neat <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTS">prints</a>, executed with the graver only, in a style greatly resembling that of John Vander Velde. They consist chiefly of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CANDLE">candle</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> pieces and dark subjects. M. Heineken mentions <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> Molyn the elder, who was a native of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, and a painter; but not so eminent as Tempesta. Some suppose the prints above mentioned ought to be ascribed to the latter; as, though very neatly executed, they are laboured heavy performances, and not equal in any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> to what one might expect from the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAND">hand</a> of an artist of so much repute as Tempesta.

MOLYNEUX

Pages 218-219

son of the former, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHESTER">Chester</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1684; and educated with <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> care by his father, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> laid <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DOWN">down</a> by Locke upon that subject. When his father died, he fell under the management of his uncle, Dr Thomas Molyneux, an excellent scholar and physician at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>, and also an intimate friend of Mr Locke; who executed his trust so well, that Mr Molyneux became afterwards a most polite and accomplished <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>, and was made secretary to his late majesty when he was <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a> being his favourite <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a>, as it had been his father's, he projected many schemes for the advancement of it, and was particularly employed in the years 1723, 1724, and 1725, in perfecting the method of making telescopes; one of which, of his own making, he had presented to John V., <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>. In the midst of these thoughts, being appointed a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSIONER">commissioner</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADMIRALTY">admiralty</a>, he became so engaged in public affairs, that he had not leisure to pursue these enquiries any farther; and gave his papers to Dr Robert Smith, professor of astronomy at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, whom he invited to make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a> of instruments, in order to finish what he had left imperfect. Mr Molyneux dying soon after, Dr Smith lost the opportunity; yet, supplying what was wanting from Mr Huygens and others, he published the whole in his "Complete Treatise of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OPTICS">Optics</a>."

MOMBASA

Pages 219-219

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a> in Zanguebar, subject to the Portuguese, from whence they export slaves, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>, and other <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, with which they supply the settlements in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRAZIL">Brazil</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">king</a> of this country being a Christian, had a quarrel with the Portuguese governor, took the castle by assault, turned Mahometan, and murdered all the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, in 1631; but in 1729 they became masters of the territory again.

MOMENT

Pages 219-219

in the doctrine of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a>, an instant, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> the most minute and indivisible <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>.

MOMENTUM

Pages 219-219

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a>, signifies the same with impetus, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> in a moving body; which is always equal to the quantity of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> multiplied into the velocity; or, which is the same thing, it may be considered as a rectangle under the quantity of matter and velocity. See Mechanics.

MOMORDICA

Pages 219-220
MALE BALSAM APPLE: A genus of the syngeaeceae order, belonging to the monoecia class of plants; and in the natural method ranking under the 34th order, Cucurbitaceae. The male calyx is quinquefid; the corolla septapartite; the filaments are three in number. The female calyx is trifid; the corolla quinquepartite; the style trifid; the fruit is an apple parting afunder with a spring. The most remarkable species are, 1. The balsamina, or male balsam apple. This is a native of Asia; and has a trailing stalk like those of the cucumber or melon, with smooth leaves, cut into several segments, and spread open like a hand. The fruit is oval, ending in acute points, having several deep angles, with sharp tubercles placed on their edges. It changes to a red or purplish colour when ripe, opening with an elasticity, and throwing out its seeds. 2. The elaterium, wild or spurting cucumber, has a large fleshy root, somewhat like briony, from whence come forth every spring several thick, rough, trailing stalks, dividing into many branches, and extending every way two or three feet; these are garnished with thick, rough, almost heart-shaped leaves, of a grey colour. colour, standing upon long foot-stalks. The flowers come out from the wings of the stalks; these are male and female, growing at different places on the same plant like those of the common cucumber: but they are much less, of a pale yellow colour, with a greenish bottom; the male flowers stand upon thick, short, foot-stalks, but the female flowers sit upon the young fruit; which, after the flower is faded, grows of an oval form, an inch and a half long, swelling like a cucumber, of a grey colour like the leaves, and covered over with short prickles. This species has one of its names from the property of casting out its seeds, together with the viscid juice in which the seeds are lodged, with a violent force, it touched while ripe. Uses. The first species is famous in Syria for curing wounds. The natives cut open the unripe fruit, and infuse it in sweet oil, which they expose to the sun for some days, until it becomes red; and then present it for use. Dropped on cotton, and applied to a fresh wound, the Syrians reckon this oil the best vulnerary next to balsam of Mecca, having found by experience that it often cures large wounds in three days. The leaves and stems of this plant are used for arbores or bowers. The elaterium of the shops is the fruit, or rather the inspissated fecula, of the juice of the unripe fruit of the wild cucumber. It is usually sent us from Spain and the southern parts of France, where the plant is common. We receive it in small, flat, whitish lumps, or cakes, that are dry, and break easily between the fingers. It is of an acrid, nauseous, bitter taste, and has a strong offensive smell when newly made; but these, as well as its other properties, it loses after being kept for some time. It is a very violent purge and vomit, and is now but seldom used. From the property which the plant has of throwing out its seeds, it has sometimes been called Noli me tangere.

MOMUS

Pages 220-220

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, the god of raillery, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> the jester of the celestial <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>, and who ridiculed both gods and men. Being chosen by Vulcan, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol7.html#article-NEPTUNE">Neptune</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a>, to give his judgment concerning their works, he blamed them all: Neptune for not making his bull with horns before his eyes, in order that he might give a surer blow; Minerva for <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> that could not be removed in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CASE">case</a> of bad neighbours; and Vulcan, for making a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAN">man</a> without a window in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>, that his treacheries might be seen. For his free reflections upon the gods, Momus was driven from heaven. He is generally represented raising a mask from his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FACE">face</a>, and holding a small <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> in his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAND">hand</a>.

MONA

Pages 220-220

two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> of this name in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SEA">sea</a> lying between <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>. The one described by Cæsar, as situated in the mid-passage between both islands, and stretching out in length from south to <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NORTH">north</a>. Called Monaëda (<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>); Monapia, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> Monabia (Pliny). Supposed to be the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAN">Man</a>.—Another Mona, (Tacitus); an <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> more to the south, and of greater breadth; situated on the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of the Ordovices, from which it is separated by a narrow strait. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> seat of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DRUIDS">Druids</a>. Now called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLESEY">Anglesey</a>, the island of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">Angles</a> or English.

MONACO

Pages 220-220

a small but handsome and strong town of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the territory of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-GENOA">Genoa</a>, with a castle, citadel, and a good harbour. It is seated on a craggy rock, and has its own <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, under the protection of France. E. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 9° 33'. N. Lat. 43° 48'.

MONAD

Pages 220-220

see Leibnitzian <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">Philosophy</a>.

MONADELPHIA

Pages 220-220

(from μονάς alone, and ἀδελφία a brotherhood;) a "single brotherhood;" The name of the 16th class in Linnæus's sexual system, consisting of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> with hermaphrodite <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>; in which all the stamens, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MALE">male</a> organs of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a>, are united below into one body or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CYLINDER">cylinder</a>, through which passes the pointal or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> organ. See <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, p. 437.

MONAGHAN

Pages 220-220

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a>, fair, and market town, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of that name, is distant 62 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>; it is a borough, and returns two members to <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Clermont. It gives <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of baron to the family of Blayney, and has six <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a>. It was anciently called Muinechban. An <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> was founded here in a very early <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, of which Mocholius the son of Aodh was <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a>. In 1462, a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> for conventual Franciscans was erected on the site of this abbey, which was granted on the general suppression of monasteries to Edward Withe, and a castle has been since erected on the site by Edward Lord Blayney.

MONAMY

Pages 220-220

a good painter of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-pieces, was born in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JERSEY">Jersey</a>; and certainly (says Mr Walpole), from his circumstances <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> the views of his family he had little reason to expect the fame he afterwards acquired, having received his first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> from a sign and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> painter on <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONDON">London</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>. But when <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> gives real talents they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> forth in the home-taught school. The shallow waves that rolled under his window taught young Monamy what his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MASTER">master</a> could not teach him, and fitted him to imitate the turbulence of the ocean. In painter's <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HALL">hall</a> is a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> piece by him, painted in 1726. He died at his house in Westminster the beginning of 1749.

MONANDRIA

Pages 220-220

(from μονάς alone, and ἀδελφός a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAN">man</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> husband;) The name of the first class in Linnæus's sexual system; consisting of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> with hermaphrodite <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, which have only one stamen or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MALE">male</a> organ.

MONARCHY

Pages 220-221

a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> state governed by one; <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> a state where the supreme power is lodged in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of a single person. The word comes from the Greek μονάρχης, "one who governs alone;" formed of μόνος, solo, and ἄρχω imperium, "<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>." Of the three forms of government, viz. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEMOCRACY">democracy</a>, aristocracy, and monarchy, the last is the most powerful, all the fineness of government being knit together, and united in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAND">hand</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>; but then there is imminent Monarchy, imminent danger of his employing that strength to imprudent or oppressive purposes. As a democracy is the best calculated to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> the end of a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAW">law</a>, and an aristocracy to invent the means by which that end shall be obtained, a monarchy is most fit for carrying those means into execution. The most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> monarchy was that of the Assyrians, which was founded soon after the deluge. We usually reckon four <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> or universal monarchies; the Assyrian, Persian, Grecian, and Roman; though St Augustine makes them but two, viz. those of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BABYLON">Babylon</a> and Rome. Belus is placed at the head of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of Assyrian kings who reigned at Babylon, and is by profane authors esteemed the founder of it, and by some the same whom the scriptures call Nimrod.
