They allowed of two wills in Christ, considered with regard to the two natures; but reduced them to one, by reason of the union of the two natures; thinking it absurd there should be two free wills in one and the same person. They were condemned by the sixth general <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> in 680, as being supposed to destroy the perfection of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> of Jesus Christ, depriving it of will and operation. Their sentiments were afterwards embraced by the Maronites.

MONOTONY

Pages 254-254

an uniformity of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOUND">sound</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> a fault in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRONUNCIATION">pronunciation</a>, when a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of words are delivered in one unvaried tone. See <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-READING">Reading</a>.

MONOTROPA

Pages 254-254
Bird's-nest: A genus of the monogynia order, belonging to the monandra clas of plants; and in the natural method ranking with those of which the order is doubtful. There is no calyx, but 10 petals; and of these the five exterior have a melliferous hollow at the base. The capsule is quinquivalved. In some of the flowers a fifth part of the number is excluded as in the M. hippocastanum. There are two species; of which the only remarkable one is the hippocastanum, a native of Britain and some of the more northerly kingdoms of Europe. It is about five inches high, having no other leaves than oval scales, and terminated with a nodding spike of flowers, which in the feeding state becomes erect: the whole plant is of a pale yellow colour, smelling like the primrose, or like beans in blossom. The country people in Sweden give the dried plant to cattle that have a cough. MONREAL. See Montreal.

MONRO

Pages 254-256

a most eminent physician and anatomist, was descended by his father from the family of Monro of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MILTON">Milton</a>, which had <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> possessions in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Roxburgh; and by his mother, from that of Forbes of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CULLODEN">Culloden</a>. His father John, youngest son of Sir Alexander Monro of Bearcroft, was bred to physic and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SURGERY">surgery</a>, Monro, and served for some years as a surgeon in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> under <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">King</a> William in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>; but, for several successive years, obtaining leave of absence from the army in the winter, he during that season resided with his wife in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, where his son Alexander was born in the 1697. About three years thereafter, he quitted the army, and went to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> as a surgeon at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>; where his knowledge in his profession, and engaging manners, soon introduced him into an extensive practice. The son showed an early inclination to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of physic; and the father, after giving him the best <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> that Edinburgh then afforded, sent him successively to London, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>, to improve himself further in his profession. At London, he attended the lectures of Messrs Hawksbee and Whiston on <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-EXPERIMENTAL_PHILOSOPHY">experimental <a class="</a>xref" href="vol14.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, and the anatomical demonstrations of Mr Cheselden. At Paris, he attended the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a>, and the lectures which were read on the different branches of physic and surgery at that <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a>. Towards the end of autumn 1718, he went to Leyden, and studied under the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> Boerhaave; by whom he was particularly esteemed. On his return to Edinburgh in autumn 1719, Messrs Drummond and Macgill, who were then conjunct nominal professors and demonstrators of anatomy to the surgeons <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, having resigned in his favour, his father prevailed on him to read some public lectures on anatomy, and to illustrate them by showing the curious anatomical preparations which he had made and sent home when abroad. He at the same time persuaded Dr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTON">Alton</a>, then a young <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAN">man</a>, to give some public lectures on <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>. Accordingly, in the beginning of the winter 1720, these two young professors began to give regular courses of lectures, the one on the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">materia medica</a> and botany, the other on anatomy and surgery; which were the first regular courses of lectures on any of the branches of medicine that had ever been read at Edinburgh, and may be looked upon as the opening of that medical school which has since acquired such great reputation all over <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. In <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> 1721 and 1722, Dr Monro, by the persuasion of his father, read some lectures on chirurgical subjects; particularly on wounds and tumors, which he never would publish, having wrote them in a hurry and before he had much <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>; but inserted from time to time the improvements he thought might be made in surgery, in the volumes of Medical Essays and Observations to be hereafter mentioned. About the year 1720, his father communicated to the physicians and surgeons at Edinburgh, a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>, which he had <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a> formed in his own mind, of having the different branches of physic and surgery regularly taught at Edinburgh; which was highly approved of by them, and by their <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> regular professorships of anatomy and medicine were instituted in the university. His son, Dr Monro, was first made university-professor of anatomy; and two <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> three years afterwards, Drs Sinclair, Rutherford, Innes, and Plummer, were made professors of medicine; the professorship of materia medica and botany, which Dr Alton then held, having been added to the university many years before. Immediately after these gentlemen were elected professors, they began to deliver regular courses of lectures on the different branches of medicine, and they and their successors have uniformly <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> so to do every winter. The plan for a medical education at Edinburgh was still incomplete without a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>, where students could see the practice of physic and surgery, as well as hear the lectures of the professors. A scheme was therefore proposed by Dr Monro's father, and others, particularly the members of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of physicians and board of surgeons, for raising by subscription a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FUND">fund</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> and supporting an hospital for the reception of diseased <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POOR">poor</a>; and our author published a pamphlet setting forth the advantages that would attend such an <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a>. In a short time a considerable sum of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> was raised, a small <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> was fitted up, and patients were admitted into it, and regularly attended by many of the physicians and surgeons in town. The fund for this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> increasing very considerably, in a great <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> and influence of that very worthy citizen and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a> George Drummond, Esq; the foundation was laid of the present large, commodious, and useful hospital, the Royal Infirmary; in the planning of which Dr Monro suggested many useful hints, and in particular the elegant room for chirurgical operations was designed and executed under his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>. Provost Drummond and he were nominated the building committee; and the fabric was entirely completed in a short space of time. It has since been so largely endowed, as to be capable of receiving a great <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of diseased poor, whose <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CASES">cases</a> the students of physic and surgery have an opportunity of seeing daily treated with the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> and care by physicians and surgeons eminent in their profession; and a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-REGISTER">register</a> of the particulars of all the cases which have been received into the house since its first opening has been kept, in books appropriated for that purpose, for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the students. In order to make the hospital of still further use to the students, Dr Monro frequently, while he continued professor of anatomy, gave lectures on the chirurgical cases; and the late judicious physician, Dr Rutherford professor of the practice of physic, began, in the year 1743, to deliver clinical lectures, to be continued every winter, on the most remarkable cases in the hospital. <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DOCTOR">Doctor</a> Monro, though he was elected professor of anatomy in the year 1721, was not received into the university till the year 1725, when he was inducted along with that great mathematician the late Mr Colin MacLaurin, with whom he ever lived in the strictest friendship. From this time he regularly every winter gave a course of lectures on anatomy and surgery, from October to May, upon a most judicious and comprehensive plan: A task in which he persevered with the greatest assiduity, and without the least interruption, for near 40 years; and so great was the reputation he had acquired, that students flocked to him from the most distant corners of his majesty's dominions. In 1759, our professor entirely relinquished the benefits of the anatomical <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a> to his son Dr Alexander, who had returned from abroad, and had assisted him in the course of lectures the preceding year. But after this resignation, he still endeavoured to render his labours labours useful to mankind, by <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-READING">reading</a> clinical lectures at the hospital for the improvement of the students; of which Dr. Duncan, who was one of his pupils, has given the following account. "There I had myself the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> of being a pupil, who profited by the judicious conduct of his practice, and was improved by the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> and acuteness of his remarks. I have indeed to regret that I attended only the last course of lectures in which he had ever a share, and at a time when he was subjected to a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> which proved at length fatal. Still, however, from what I <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAW">saw</a> and from what I heard, I can venture to assert, that it is hardly possible to conceive a physician more attentive to practice, or a preceptor more anxious to communicate instructions. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>, in the former of these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, led him to bestow the most anxious care on his patients while they were alive; and his zeal in the latter induced him to make them the subject of useful <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LESSONS">lessons</a> when they happened to die.—In the different stations of physician, of lecturer, and of manager in the hospital, he took every measure for inquiring into the causes of diseases by dissection—He personally attended the opening of every body; and he not only dictated to the students an accurate report of the dissection, but with nice discrimination contrasted the diseased and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> state of every organ. Thus, in his own person, he afforded to the students a conspicuous example of the advantages of early anatomical pursuits, as the happiest foundation for a medical superstructure. His being at once engaged in two departments, the anatomical theatre and clinical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a>, furnished him with opportunities both on the dead and living body, and placed him in the most favourable situation for the improvement of medicine; and from these opportunities he derived every possible advantage which they could afford." His father, old Mr. Monro, lived to an advanced <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>; and enjoyed the unspeakable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> of beholding a son, esteemed and regarded by mankind, the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTOR">actor</a> in the execution of his favourite plan, the great object of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, the founding a seminary of medical education in his native <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>: The son, who survived him near 30 years, had the satisfaction to behold this seminary of medical education frequented yearly by 300 or 400 students, many of whom came from the most distant corners of his majesty's dominions, and to see it arrive to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of reputation far beyond his most sanguine hopes, being equalled by few, and inferior to none, in Europe. Few men were members of more <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a> than Dr. Monro; still fewer equally assiduous in their attendance of those which in any way tended to promote public utility. He was a manager of many public charities; and not only a member of different medical societies, but likewise of several others instituted for promoting literature, arts, sciences, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>, in Scotland, and was one of their most useful members.—While he was held in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> estimation at home, he was equally esteemed and respected abroad, and was elected member of the Royal <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> of London, and an honorary member of the Royal Academy of Surgery at Paris. He was not only very <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> in the line of his own profession, but as a citizen and general member of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a>; for, after he had resigned the anatomical chair to his son, he executed with the strictest punctuality the duties of several engagements both of a civil and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>: He was a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DIRECTOR">director</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BANK">Bank</a> of Scotland, a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JUSTICE">Justice</a> of the Peace, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSIONER">Commissioner</a> of High <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">Roads</a>, &c. At length, after a life spent in the most active industry, he became afflicted with a tedious and painful disease, which he bore with equal courage and resignation till his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, which happened on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 10th 1767, in the 70th year of his age. Of his works, the first in order is his Osteology, which was written for the use of students, but is capable also of affording instruction to the oldest and most experienced practitioner; as, besides a minute <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of the parts copied from nature, it everywhere abounds with new and important observations immediately applicable to practice. It has been translated into many different languages; has passed through numerous editions; and has been reprinted in foreign countries in the most superb manner, accompanied with elegant and masterly engravings. His description of the Lacteal Sac and Thoracic Duct contains the most accurate account of that important <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> of the body which has been yet published; and his Anatomy of the Nerves <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a> transmit to posterity an excellent example of accurate dissection, faithful description, and ingenious reasoning. The five volumes of Medical Essays and Observations, published by a society in Edinburgh, are universally known and esteemed. To that society he was appointed secretary; but, after the publication of the first volume, to which he had largely contributed, the members growing remiss in their attendance, he became the sole collector and publisher of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>: To him we are therefore in a great measure indebted for those numerous and important discoveries with which this publication has enriched every department of medical knowledge. In the two first volumes of the Physical and Literary Essays, published by the physical society of Edinburgh, in which he had the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of one of the presidents, we find several papers written by him, which are not the least ornaments of that collection. His account of the Successes of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-INOCULATION">Inoculation</a> in Scotland may be considered as his last publication: It demonstrates his extensive correspondence and indefatigable industry, and has had great influence in promoting that salutary practice. Besides these, he was also the author of several other elegant and masterly productions, which were either never published, or were published without his knowledge and from incorrect copies. A collection of all his works, properly arranged, corrected, and illustrated with copperplates, has been published by Dr. Alexander Monro, his son and successor in the anatomical chair, in a splendid quarto volume, printed for Elliot, Edinburgh, 1781; to which is prefixed a life of the author, by another of his sons, Dr. Donald, physician in London. The observation of an excellent judge, the illustrious Haller, concerning our author's Medical Essays and Observations, which now form a part of this collection, may with no less justice be applied to the whole: It is a "book which ought to be in the possession of every medical practitioner."

MONS

Pages 256-257

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, handsome, rich, and very strong <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the Austrian <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, in Hainault. There is a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> consisting of 30 ladies of distinction, who have the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of leaving the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a> when they intend to marry. They have several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>, and a good trade. It was taken by the allies in 1709, and by the French in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1746; but rendered back by the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIX">Aix</a>-la-Chapelle, after the fortifications were demolished. It stands partly on a hill, and partly on a plain in a marshy foil, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Haine and Trouilli, by which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> about it may be overflowed at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>. It has been lately taken by the armies of the French Republic. E. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3° 39'. N. Lat. 50° 25'. Mons Sacer, (anc. geog.), a mountain of the Sabines beyond the Anio, to the east of Rome; whither the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMON">common</a> people retired once and again to avoid the tyranny of the patricians. From this secession, and the altar of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> Terribilis erected there, the mountain took its name.

MONSIEUR

Pages 257-257

in the plural Messeigneurs, a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TERM">term</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of civility, used by the French in speaking to their equals, or those a little below them, answering to Mr or Sir among the English. Monsieur, absolutely used, was a title or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> appropriated to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SECOND">second</a> son of France, or the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>. The king was also called Monsieur, but that only by the children of France.

MONSON

Pages 257-257

a brave English <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a>, third son of Sir John Monson of South Carlton in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINCOLNSHIRE">Lincolnshire</a>, was born in 1569. He was employed in many expeditions against the Spaniards in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a>, and was highly honoured; the queen knighted him for his services in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a>'s expedition to <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CADIZ">Cadiz</a>, where he assisted much by his wife and moderate counsel to the earl. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MILITARY">Military</a> men were no favourites with James I. therefore, on the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of the queen, he received no recompense <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> pay beyond the ordinary <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> in which he was engaged; nevertheless, as admiral of the narrow seas, he supported the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the British <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLAG">flag</a> against the infant influence of the Dutch states, of which he frequently complains in his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NAVY">Navy</a> Tracts; and protected our trade against the encroachments of France. He had the misfortune to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> into disgrace by his vigilance, and was imprisoned in the Tower through the resentment of some powerful courtiers; yet he was discharged, and wrote a vindication of his own conduct, intituled, "Concerning the insolencies of the Dutch, and a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JUSTIFICATION">justification</a> of Sir William Monson." He spent his latter days in peace and privacy, which he employed in digesting his Navy Tracts, and died in 1643.—<a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">Part</a> of these tracts were printed in 1682; and they were afterwards all included in Churchill's Collection of Voyages.

MONSONIA

Pages 257-257

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>: A genus of the dodecandra order, belonging to the polyadelphia clas of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. The calyx is pentaphyllous; the corolla pentapetalous and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a>; the stamina are 15 in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, and coalesced into five filaments; the style bifid; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPSULE">capsule</a> pentacocca.

MONSOON

Pages 257-264

a regular <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> periodical <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, in the East Indies, blowing constantly the same way, during six months of the year, and the contrary way the remaining six. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> ocean, the winds are partly general, and blow all the year round the same way, as in the Ethiopic ocean; and partly periodical, i.e., half the year blow one way, and the other half near on the opposite <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POINTS">points</a>: and those points and times of shifting differ in different parts of this ocean. These latter are what we call monsoons. The shifting of these monsoons is not all at once; and in some places the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the change is attended with calms, in others with variable winds, and particularly those of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, at ceasing to be westerly, are very subject to be tempestuous; and such is their violence, that they seem to be of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the West <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a> hurricanes, and render the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a> of those seas very unsafe at that time of the year. These tempests the seamen call the breaking up of the monsoons. Monsoons, then, are a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of what we otherwise call trade-winds. They take the denomination monsoon from an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> pilot, who first crossed the Indian <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SEA">sea</a> by means hereof. Though others derive the name from a Portuguese word, signifying <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> or change of wind, and sea. Lucretius and Apollonius make mention of annual winds which arise every year, stesia flabriae, which seem to be the same with what in the East Indies we now call monsoons. For the physical cause of these winds, see Wind. MONSTER; a birth or production of a living being, degenerating from the proper and usual disposition of parts in the species to which it belongs: As, when there are too many members, or too few; or some of them are extravagantly out of proportion, either on the side of defect or excess. The word comes from the Latin monstrum, of monstrando, "showing." Whence also the box wherein relics were anciently kept to be shown, was called monstrum. Dugdale mentions an inventory of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-YORK">York</a> with this article, Item unum monstrum cum aliibus sancti Petri in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BERYL">Beryl</a>, & crucifixo in summitate. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a> defines a monster to be a defect of nature, when, acting towards some end, it cannot attend to it, from some of its principles being corrupted. Monsters do not propagate their kind; for which reason some <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RANK">rank</a> mules among the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of monsters, as also hermaphrodites. Females which bring forth twins, are found most liable to produce monsters. The reason, probably, is owing to this; that though the twins are covered with one <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMON">common</a> chorion, yet they have each their separate amnios, which by their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONTIGUITY">contiguity</a> may chance to grow together, and so occasion a confusion or blending of the parts. Hence so many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> creatures. F. Malebranche accounts for the production of monsters in the animal world in the following manner. "The Creator has established such a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> between the several parts of his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CREATION">creation</a>, that we are not only naturally led to imitate one another, i.e., have a disposition to do the same things and assume the same manners with those with whom we <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONVERSE">converse</a>; but also have certain <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> dispositions which incline us to compassion as well as <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a>. These things most men feel, and are sensible of; and therefore need not be proved. The animal spirits, then, are not only naturally carried into the respective parts of the body to perform the same actions and the same motions which we see others do, but also to receive in some manner their wounds, and take <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> in their sufferings. "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">Experience</a> tells us, that when we look attentively on any person severely beaten, or that hath a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> wound, ulcer, or the like, the spirits immediately flow into those parts of our body which answer to those we see suffer in the other; unless their course be stopped from some other principle. This <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FLUX">flux</a> of spirits is very sensible in persons of a delicate <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, who frequently shudder, and find a kind of trembling in the body on these occasions; and this sympathy in bodies produces compassion in the mind. "Now it must be observed, that the view of a wound, &c., wounds the person who views it the more strongly and sensibly, as the person is more weak and delicate; the spirits making a stronger <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> on the fibres of a delicate body than in those of a robust one. Thus strong, vigorous men, &c., see an execution without much concern, while women, &c., are struck with pity and horror. As to children still in their mother's womb, the fibres of their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> being incomparably finer than those in women, the course of the animal spirits must necessarily produce much greater alterations. "These things being laid <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, monsters are easily accounted for. Suppose, e.g., a child born a fool, and with all its legs and arms broke in the same manner as those of criminals in some countries are; which <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CASE">case</a> we choose to instance in, because we are told from <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> that such a monster was actually born there, and lived in one of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a> 20 years; the cause of this accident, according to the principles laid down, was, that the mother seeing a criminal executed, every stroke given to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POOR">poor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAN">man</a>, struck forcibly the imagination of the woman; and, by a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COUNTER">counter</a>-stroke, the tender and delicate brain of the child. "Now, though the fibres of the woman's brain were strangely shaken by the violent flux of animal-spirits on this occasion, yet they had strength and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSTANCY">constancy</a> enough to prevent an entire disorder; whereas the fibres of the child's brain being unable to bear the shock of those spirits, were quite ruined, and the ravage was <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> enough to deprive him of reason all his lifetime. "Again, the view of the execution frightening the woman, the violent course of the animal spirits was directed forcibly from the brain to all those parts of the body corresponding to the suffering parts of the criminal; and the same thing must happen in the child. But in regard the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BONES">bones</a> of the mother were strong enough to resist the impulse of those spirits, they were not damaged; and yet the rapid course of these spirits could easily overpower and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> the tender and delicate fibres of the bones of the child; the bones being the last parts of the body that are formed, and having a very slender confidence while the child is yet in the womb." To which it may be here added, that had the mother determined the course of these spirits towards some other part of her body, by tickling or scratching herself vehemently, the child would not in all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> have had its bones broken; but the part answering that to which the motion of the spirits was determined, would have been the sufferer. Hence appears the reason why women in the time of gestation, feeling persons, &c., marked in such a manner in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FACE">face</a>, impress the same mark on the same parts of the child: and why, upon rubbing some hidden part of the body when startled at the sight of anything or agitated with any extraordinary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>, the mark or impression is fixed on that hidden part rather than on the face of the child. From the principles here laid down, may most, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not all, the phenomena of monsters be easily accounted for. Various other theories have been formed by different philosophers and physiologists. But after all, it must be confessed, that we seem as yet to be very little acquainted with Nature in her sports and errors. For each organized being there appears to exist a primitive germ or <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MODEL">model</a> of the different species drawn by the Creator, determined by forms and sexes, and realized in the individuals of both sexes, which must unite in order to their <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-REPRODUCTION">reproduction</a>. From this model nature never departs, unless when compelled by circumstances which derange the primitive organization common to the species, and produce what we call monsters. With respect to structure, we have already remarked, that monsters are of various kinds. Some have an excess or defect in certain parts; such as those which are called <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACEPHALOUS">acephalous</a>, or who want the head; those which have two heads, two arms, two legs, and one body, or which have two bodies and one head, or which have three legs; and those which want the arms or the legs. Others err through an extraordinary and deformed conformation, through an unnatural union of certain parts or vice versa, through a great derangement in one or more of their members, and through the extraordinary <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a> which these often occupy in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of this derangement or transposition. The monster described by Dr. Eller of the academy of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BERLIN">Berlin</a> was of this kind. It was a fetus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NINE">nine</a> months, 28 inches <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a>, with an enormous head and frightful countenance; and in the middle of a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> and vast forehead it had a reddish eye, without either eyebrows or eyelids, and sunk deep into a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> hole. Immediately below this eye was an excrescence which strongly resembled a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENIS">penis</a> with a glans, a prepuce, and an <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-URETHRA">urethra</a>: the part covered with <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> was likewise below the nape of the neck. In other monsters we meet with the unnatural union of some parts, which, from their destination and functions, ought always to be separate; and the separation of other parts, which, for the same reasons, ought constantly to be united. The reader may see the different ways in which the formation of monsters takes place in four <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-MEMOIRS">memoirs</a> by M. Lemery, inserted in L'Histoire de l'Academie des Sciences 1738 and 1739. M. du Verney has likewise published a Memoir on the same subject. In the volume published by the Academy of Sciences in 1724, mention is made by M. Geoffroy of a monster born in Barrois 1722. This monstrous production consisted of two children without the inferior extremities, joined together by a common navel; each of them had a nurse, sucked, and eat pap; and the one sucked while the other slept. The reader may likewise consult the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SECOND">second</a> part of Winiford's Memoirs on Monsters, inserted in the volume published by the Academy of Sciences in 1734, where he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a> find the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of two very extraordinary twin monsters, who evidenced during their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> a great <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> in their moral and physical qualities. We are obliged simply to refer to those Memoirs, as they are too long for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABRIDGMENT">abridgment</a>. It is observed by Haller, that in some monsters the natural structure is changed by some shock or passion; in others the structure, independent of any accident, is originally monstrous; such as when all the members are reversed from left to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, when the person has six fingers, and in many other instances. M. de Maupeutre mentions, that there is at Berlin a family who have had six fingers on each <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAND">hand</a> for several generations. M. de Rivière <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAW">saw</a> an instance of this at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MALTA">Malta</a>, of which he has given a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>. M. Renou, surgeon at Pommeraye in Anjou, has published an account of some families with six fingers, which are to be found in several parishes of the Lower Anjou, and which have existed there from time immemorial. This <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEFORMITY">deformity</a> is perpetuated in these families even when they intermarry with persons who are free from it. Whether the propagation of these supernumerary organs, which are not only useless but inconvenient and even disagreeable, be owing to the father or mother, their children of both sexes are subject to it indiscriminately. A father or mother with six fingers frequently have a part, and sometimes the whole, of their children, free from this deformity; but it again makes its appearance, and in a very great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, in the third <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a>. From this it appears, that this fault in the conformation is <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a>. M. Reaumur has likewise published the history of a family in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Malta, the children of which are born with six fingers and six toes. But it deserves to be inquired, whether these supernumerary fingers are real fingers? The reader may here consult the Journal de Physique for November 1774, p. 372. This variety of sexidiglary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> and feet is not comprehended in the Recherches sur quelques conformations monstrueuses des doigts dans l'homme, which is inserted in the Memoirs of the Academy of Sciences for 1771. In the Journal de Physique for August 1776, we find a description of a double uterus and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VAGINA">vagina</a> observed in a woman who died in childbirth, by Dr Purcell of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>: and in that for <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1788, we have an account of a man with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> fingers on each hand, by Baron Dietrich. Several monstrous productions are to be seen in the cabinet at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHANTILLY">Chantilly</a>. 1. Two calves joined together in the body, with each a separate head and neck, and four legs in whole. 2. Two calves united only by the pelvis, with only one anus and one tail: the whole is supported by six legs, four before and two behind. 3. A lamb with six legs, four of which are behind. 4. The skeleton of a ram, which has likewise six legs. 5. A hermaphrodite deer. 6. The head of a foal, which has only one eye in the middle of the forehead. 7. Some leverets with six and eight legs. 8. A puppy, the lips of which are divided fourfold. 9. Some statuettes of a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOG">hog</a> which have a kind of tube upon their forehead one or two inches long; and another, the hinder part of which is double in every thing. 10. Two double <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> statuettes joined by the belly, with four arms and three legs. 11. A young chicken with two bodies and one head. 12. A pigeon and a duck, each with two bills. 13. A duck with two heads. 14. A pigeon with four feet. 15. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPON">capon</a> with three feet; the third being fixed to the anus. 16. Two heads of a calf joined together, each of them with two ears: these two heads were both fixed to one neck. 17. In the Menagerie at Chantilly there was formerly to be seen a cow with five feet, the fifth of which was connected with the dug. 18. A rabbit without ears. 19. Two cats, each having two heads. 20. Two leverets newly brought forth, well shaped in the body and legs, but connected together by means of only one head. 21. Several eggs, in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of which there occur some monstrous appearances and extraordinary deformities, sufficient to show that they are contrary to the established form of nature. Everhard Hume, Esq; F. R. S. some time ago presented to John Hunter, Esq; F. R. S. the double skull of a child, born at <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CALCUTTA">Calcutta</a> in May 1783 of poor parents aged 30 and 35, and which lived to be nearly two years old. The body of this child was naturally formed; but the head had the phenomenon of appearing double; another head of the same size, and almost equally perfect, being attached to its upper part. In this extraordinary and preternatural head no pulsation could be felt in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTERIES">arteries</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>, but the superficial veins were very evident; one of the eyes had been hurt by the fire, upon which the midwife, in her first alarm, threw the child: the other moved readily; but the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-IRIS">iris</a> was not affected by the approach of anything to it. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> ears of this head were very imperfect; the tongue adhered to the lower jaw, except for about half an inch at the lip, which was loose; the jaw was capable of motion, but there were no <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>. The child was shown about the streets of Calcutta for a curiosity; but was rendered unhealthy by confinement, and died at last of a bite of the cobra de capello. It was dug up by the East India <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMPANY">Company</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGENT">agent</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-SALT">salt</a> at Tumlock, and the skull is now in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MUSEUM">museum</a> of Mr Hunter. Among the monstrous productions of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ANIMAL_KINGDOM">animal <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, we may rank those individuals which ought only to possess one <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SEX">sex</a>, but in which we observe the union or the appearance of two. See the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANDROGYNES">ANDROGYNES</a> and HERMAPHRODITE. M. Fabri arranges mutilations of the members, distortions, gibbosities, tumors, divisions of the lips or of the palate, compressions of the cranium, and many other deformities of this kind, in the class of morbid monstrosities. In that which he calls connaturation (connaturelle) monstrosities, are placed the plurality, transposition, and inflection of the parts. To explain these facts, a great many writers have had recourse to the effect of the imagination of pregnant women.—The causes of the first class of monstrosities are discussed by M. Fabri, who observes, that some of them are internal with regard to the mother, and others external. By an internal cause, he here means all those deprivations or morbid principles which can affect the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a>, and which vitiate the form and structure of the solids; in particular the uterus, in which such deprivations have often been found to occur. To these he adds violent affections of the mind, spasmodic contractions, hysterical convulsions, and the many inconveniences of this kind to which women are extremely subject. External causes comprehend every thing which can <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> externally upon the fetus contained in the uterus, such as the pressure of the clothes; and in short every thing which prevents the free <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DILATATION">dilatation</a> of the belly in women who are pregnant, violent motions, falls, blows, and all accidents of this kind. These external causes, and especially the first, compress the fetus in the womb, and oblige it to remain in a very confined situation. This, according to the observation of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIPPOCRATES">Hippocrates</a>, produces those embryos which are born with some entire part wounded. M. Fabri maintains, that all deformities of the fetus proceed from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> and accidental causes. The name of monsters is likewise given to animals enormous for bulk; such as the elephant among terrestrial <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-QUADRUPEDS">quadrupeds</a>, and the shark and the whale among sea animals; to other animals remarkable for fierceness and cruelty; and to animals of an extraordinary species, which, we are told, arises from the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COPULATION">copulation</a> of one animal with another of a different genus. According to the report of travellers, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a> abounds with monsters of this kind; and accounts of the East are full of descriptions of sea monsters, which, however, are seldom to be seen, such as sea men, mermaids, &c. Monsters are more common and more extraordinary in the vegetable than in the animal kingdom, because the different juices are more easily deranged and confused together. Leaves are often seen, from the internal part of which other leaves <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> forth; and it is not uncommon to see <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> of the ranunculus, from the middle of which issues a stalk <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> another flower. M. <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BONNET">Bonnet</a> informs us, that in certain warm and rainy years he has frequently met with monsters of this kind in rose-trees. This observer saw a rose, from the centre of which issued a square stalk of a whitish <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, tender, and without prickles, which at its top bore two flower-buds opposite to each other, and totally destitute of a calyx; a little above the buds issued a petal of a very <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> shape. Upon the prickly stalk which supported the rose, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a> was observed which had the shape of trefoil, together with a broad flat pedicle. In the Memoirs of the Academy of Sciences for 1707, p. 448, mention is made of a rose, from the centre of the leaves of which issued a rose-branch two or three inches long, and furnished with leaves. See the same Memoirs for 1749, p. 44, and for 1724, p. 20. In the Memoirs for 1755, a very singular instance is mentioned of a monstrosity observed by M. Duhamel, in an apple-tree grafted with clay. At the point of the insertion, there appeared a bud which produced a stalk and some leaves; the stalk and the pedicle of the leaves were of a pulpy substance, and had the most perfect resemblance both in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> and smell to the pulp of a green apple. An extraordinary chamomile is mentioned in the Ada Helvetica. M. Bonnet, in his Recherches sur l'usage des feuilles, mentions likewise some monstrous productions which have been found in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> with kernels, analogous in their nature to those which occur in the flowers of the ranunculus and of the rose-tree. He has seen a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEAR">pear</a>, from the eye of which issued a tuft of 13 or 14 leaves, very well shaped, and many of them of the natural size. He has seen another pear which gave rise to a ligneous and knotty stalk, on which grew another pear somewhat larger than the first. The stalk had probably flourished, and the fruit had formed. The lilium <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBUM">album</a> polyanthos, observed some years ago at Brellaw, which bore on its top a bundle of flowers, consisting of 102 lilies, all of the common shape, is well known. M. Reynier has mentioned some individuals monstrous with respect to the flower, in the Journal de Physique et d'Histoire Naturelle, for November 1785. He has likewise mentioned a monstrous tulip which is seen in the gardens of some amateurs; juniper berries with horns; a halfamine with three spurs, &c. These vegetable productions, which are so extraordinary, and so contrary to the common course of things, do nevertheless present deviations subject to particular laws, and reducible to certain principles, by distinguishing such as are perpetuated either by seed or by transplanting, from those which are only accidental and passing. Monstruities which are perpetuated exist in the original organization of the seed of the plant, such as marked or curled leaves, &c. The word monster is more properly applied to those irregularities in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> which arise from frequent transplantation, and from a particular culture, such as double flowers, &c.; but those monstruities which are not perpetuated, and which arise from accidental and transient causes deranging the primitive organization of the plant, when it comes to be unfolded, as is the effect of diseases, of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, of a superfluity or scarcity of juices, of a deprivation of the vessels contributing to <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUTRITION">nutrition</a>, of the sting of insects, of contusions and natural grafts, retain also the name of monsters. Of this kind are knobs or swellings, stunting, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-GALL">gall</a>-nuts, certain streaks, and other similar defects. All the parts of plants are subject to some of these monstruities, which vary with respect to their situation, figure, proportion, and number. Some trees are naturally of so great a size, that they may be considered as a kind of whale species in the vegetable kingdom: of this kind are the baobab and the ceiba. Others, as the oak, the yew, the willow, the lime, and many others, sometimes, though rarely, attain to extraordinary a bulk that they are likewise monsters among the vegetables. It is conjectured, in short, that monsters are more common in the vegetable than in the animal kingdom, because in the latter the methods of propagation are not so numerous. Plants are seldom monstrous in all their parts; some are monstrous only through excess in the calyx and corolla; others are so through defect only in the leaves, stamina, and fruit. Now, a monstruosity, says M. Adanson, has never changed the name or affected the immutability of a species. Every skilful succeeding botanist has arranged these monstruities in plants among accidental circumstances, which, in whatever manner they are are propagated, have always a tendency to revert to the order and regularity of their original species when they are multiplied by means of seed; which method of reproduction is the most natural and the most certain for determining the species. One species may be compared with another; but a monster can only be put in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> with an individual of the species from which it comes. The reader may consult the Observations Botaniques of M. Schletterbeec, of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a>, concerning monsters in plants, wherein he pretends to demonstrate, that in their production nature follows the same course in the vegetable as in the animal kingdom. Mont-alban, a strong town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in the kingdom of Arragon, with a strong citadel; seated on the river Riomartin, 44 miles south of Saragossa, and 92 <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by west of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-VALENCIA">Valencia</a>. W. Long. o. 30. N. Lat. 41. 9. Mont-Didier, an ancient town of France in Picardy, where the kings of France formerly had a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> and kept their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COURT">court</a>. It is seated on a mountain, 17 miles from Amiens and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMPEIGNE">Compeigne</a>, and 58 north of Paris. W. Long. 2. 34. N. Lat. 49. 39. Mont-Lheri, a town of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of France, 15 miles from Paris. Here are the remains of a tower, which may be seen at a great distance. E. Long. 2. 0. N. Lat. 48. 38. Mont-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a>, a small but strong town of France, in the Pyrenees, with a strong citadel; seated on an eminence, 430 miles south of Paris. E. Long. 2. 5. N. Lat. 42. 30. Mont-Luel, a town of France in Bretagne, and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the territory of Valbonne; seated in a fertile pleasant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> on the river Seraine, eight miles from Lyons, and 205 south-east of Paris. E. Long. 5. 8. N. Lat. 45. 49. Mont-Luzon, a town of France in Bourbonnois; seated on the river Cher, 35 miles south-west of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MOULINS">Moulins</a>, and 150 south of Paris. E. Long. 2. 45. N. Lat. 46. 22. Mont-Blanc. See Mont-Blanc. Montabour, a small fortified town of Germany, in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-ELECTORATE">electorate</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TREVES">Treves</a>, between <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COBLENZ">Coblenz</a> and Limpurg. E. Lon. 7. 50. N. Lat. 50. 30. Montagniac, a considerable town of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-NATOLIA">Natolia</a>, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Bec-Sangel, on the sea of Marmora. It carries on a great trade, especially in fruits, and is seated on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of the same name, 12 miles from Bursa, and 60 south-east of Constantinople. E. Long. 29. 40. N. Lat. 40. 20. Montague (Edward), <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-SANDWICH">Sandwich</a>, an illustrious Englishman, who shone from the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 19, and united the qualifications of general, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a>, and statesman; yet there were strange incongruities in his character. He acted early against <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I; he persuaded Cromwell, whom it is said he admired, to take the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>; and he was zealous for the restoration of Charles II. All this is imputed to a fond and unaccountable passion which he had for royalty. Upon general Monk's coming into England, he failed with the fleet to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, and soon after he had the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to convey his majesty to England. For this he was created <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-GARTER">garter</a>; and on the 12th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1660 he was created baron Montague of St Neot's in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Huntingdon, Viscount Hinchinbrooke in the same county, and earl of Sand- Montague, which in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>, sworn one of his majesty's most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> privy-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, made <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">king</a>'s wardrobe, admiral of the Narrow Seas, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a>-admiral to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of York, as <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> admiral of England. When the Dutch <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WAR">war</a> broke out in 1694, and the duke of York took upon himself the command of a fleet as high-admiral, his lordship commanded the blue squadron, and by his industry and care abundance of the enemies ships were taken; and in the great <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> fought on the third of June 1665, in which the Dutch lost admiral Opdam, and had 18 men of war taken and 14 destroyed, a large share of the honour of the victory was justly given to the conduct of the earl of Sandwich. On the return of the English <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>, the command of the whole fleet was given to the earl of Sandwich, which he was ordered to put as speedily as possible in a condition to return to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Holland. Accordingly the earl sailed on the 5th of July with 60 men of war to the Dutch coast; when finding that their East India and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SMYRNA">Smyrna</a> fleets were to return home north about, he steered for the coast of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a>, and found they had taken shelter in the port of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BERGEN">Bergen</a>, where the fleet were attacked: but leaving them there, and failing back towards the coast of Holland, he met with four Dutch East Indiamen, with several other merchant ships, under a good convoy, and took eight men of war, two of their East India ships, and 20 sail of merchant men; and a few days after, a part of the fleet falling in with 18 of the Hollanders, the greatest part of them were also taken, with four Dutch men of war, and above 1000 prisoners. On his return he was received by the king with distinguished marks of favour; and soon after, he was sent <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> extraordinary to the court of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MADRID">Madrid</a>, to mediate a peace between the crowns of Spain and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>; when he had the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> to conclude a peace between the two nations to their mutual satisfaction. On the breaking out of the last Dutch war, his lordship went to sea with the duke of York, and commanded the blue squadron; the French admiral, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COUNT">count</a> d'Estrees, commanding the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WHITE">white</a>. The fleet was at sea in the beginning of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of May; and coming to an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a> in Southwold-bay in order to take in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WATER">water</a>, we are told, that on the 27th many officers and seamen were permitted to go on shore, and were at Southwold, Dunwich, and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALDBOROUGH">Aldborough</a>; when, the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> being hazy, the earl gave it as his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that, the wind standing as it did, the fleet rode in danger of being surprised by the Dutch; and indeed, between two and three the next morning, they were informed of their approach, upon which his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> highness made the signal for weighing anchor. The blue squadron was out first, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RED">red</a> next, and the white was much after. The earl of Sandwich in the Royal James, which carried 100 guns, began the fight, and fell furiously on the squadron of Van Ghent in order to give the rest of his fleet time to form; when <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BRAKEL">Brakel</a>, in the Great Holland, attacked the Royal James; but was soon disabled, as were several other men of war, and three fire-ships sunk. By this time most of his men were killed; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HULL">hull</a> of the Royal James was so pierced with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a>, that it was impossible to carry her off. In this distress he might have Montague been relieved by his vice-admiral Sir <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> Jordan, had not that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> been more solicitous about afflicting the duke. When therefore he saw him fail by, heedless of the condition in which he lay, he said to those who were about him, "There is nothing left for us now, but to defend the ship to the last man." Being at length grappled by a fourth fire-ship, he begged his captain Sir Richard Haddock, and all his servants, to get into the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOAT">boat</a> and leave themselves, which they did; yet some of the sailors refused to quit the admiral, and staying endeavoured to extinguish the fire, but in vain; the ship blew up about noon. His lordship's body was found about a fortnight after, and was interred with great state in Henry VII.'s chapel.—We have of his lordship's <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, 1. The Art of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-METALS">Metals</a>, in which is declared the manner of their generation, translated from the Spanish of Albaro Alonso Barba, 8vo. 2. Several letters during his embassy to Spain, published with Arlington's letters. 3. A <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to secretary Thurloe. 4. Original letters and negotiations of Sir Richard Fanshaw, the earl of Sandwich, the earl of Sunderland, and Sir William Godolphin, wherein <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> matters between the three crowns of England, Spain, and Portugal, from the year 1663 to 1678, are set in a clear <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, 2 vols 8vo. Montague (Charles), earl of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HALIFAX">Halifax</a>, fourth son of George Montague of Harton in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTHAMPTONSHIRE">Northamptonshire</a>, Esq; son of Henry the first earl of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MANCHESTER">Manchester</a>, was born in 1661. He was educated at Westminster-school and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, showed very early a most pregnant genius, and quickly made great progress in learning. In 1684, he wrote a poem on the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of King Charles II., in which he displayed his genius to such advantage, that he was invited to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONDON">London</a> by the earl of Dorset; and upon his coming thither he soon increased his fame, particularly by a piece which he wrote in conjunction with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIOR">Prior</a>, published at London in 1687, under the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of, "The Hind and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PANTHER">Panther</a> transferred to the Story of the Country-mouse and the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CITY">City</a>-mouse." Upon the abdication of King James II., he was chosen one of the members of the convention, and recommended by the earl of Dorset to King William, who immediately allowed him a pension of £500 per annum. Having given proofs of his great abilities in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of commons, he was made one of the commissioners of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a>, and soon after <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> of the exchequer: in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> he brought about that great <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> of recoining all the current <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATION">nation</a>. In 1698, he was appointed first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSIONER">commissioner</a> of the treasury; and in 1699 was created a peer of England, by the title of Baron Halifax in the county of York. In 1701, the house of commons impeached him of six articles, which were dismissed by the house of Lords. He was attacked again by the house of commons in 1702, but without success. In 1705, he wrote, An Answer to Mr Bromley's Speech in relation to the occasional Conformity-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BILL">bill</a>. In 1706, he was one of the commissioners for the Union with Scotland; and upon passing the bill for the naturalization of the illustrious house of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HANOVER">Hanover</a>, and for the better security of the succession of the crown in the Protestant line, he was made choice of to carry that act to Hanover. Upon the death of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>, when the king had taken possession of his throne, his lordship was appointed first Montague, commissioner of the treasury, and created earl of Halifax and knight of the garter. He died in 1715. His lordship wrote several other pieces besides those above-mentioned; all which, with some of his speeches, were published together in 1716 in an octavo volume. Montague (Lady <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> Wortley) accompanied her husband who was sent on an embassy to Constantinople in the beginning of this century. On her return she introduced the practice of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-INOCULATION">inoculation</a> into England, and thence acquired great celebrity. She cultivated the belles lettres; and at one <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of her life she was the friend of Pope, and at another his enemy. While they were at enmity with each other, Lady Mary Montague embraced every opportunity of defaming the poet, who well knew how to take <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a>. Both of them carried their animosity to so great a height, that they became the subject of public conversation. After a long life, full of singular and romantic adventures, she died about the year 1760. From her we have Letters, written during her travels from the year 1716 to the year 1718. They have been translated into French, and published at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROTTERDAM">Rotterdam</a> 1764, and at Paris 1783, one vol. 12mo. They are composed in a lively, interesting, and agreeable style, and contain many curious facts relating to the manners and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of the Turks, which are nowhere else to be found. The Baron de Tott, who lived many years at Constantinople, attacked them with great severity; but they have been defended with equal zeal by M. Guis de Marfeilles, who has published a valuable work on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a>. It need not appear extraordinary, that persons who have visited the same country should not see things in the same light. How few travellers agree in their accounts of the same objects, which they nevertheless pretend to have seen and to have examined with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>. Montague (Edward Wortley), son of the former, passed through such variegated scenes, that a bare recital of them would favour of the marvellous. From Westminster-school, where he was placed for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, he ran away three several times. He exchanged clothes with a chimney-sweeper, and he followed for some time that footy occupation. He next joined himself to a fisherman, and cried flounders in Rotherhithe. He then sailed as a cabin-boy to Spain; where he had no sooner arrived, than he ran away from the vessel, and hired himself to a driver of mules. After thus vagabondising it for some time, he was discovered by the confus, who returned him to his friends in England. They received him with a joy equal to that of the father of the prodigal son in the gospel. A private <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a> was employed to recover those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of learning which a life of dissipation, of blackguardism, and of vulgarity, might have obliterated. Wortley was sent to the West Indies, where he remained some time; then returned to England, acted according to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of his birth, was chosen a member, and served in two successive parliaments. His expenses exceeding his income, he became involved in debt, quitted his native country, and commenced that wandering traveller he <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to the time of his death. Having visited most of the eastern countries, he contracted a partiality for their manners. He drank little wine; a great <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of coffee; wore a long <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARD">beard</a>; smoked much; and, Montague and, even whilst at <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, he was habited in the elegant style. He sat <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>-legged in the Turkish fashion through choice. With the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a>, the Arabic, the Chaldaic, and the Persian languages, he was as well acquainted as with his native tongue. He published several pieces. One on the "Rise and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">Fall</a> of the Roman Empire." Another an exploration of "The Causes of Earthquakes." As this gentleman was remarkable for the uncommon incidents which attended his life, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of that life was no less marked with singularity. He had been early married to a woman who aspired to no higher a character than that of an industrious washerwoman. As the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> was solemnized in a frolic, Wortley never deemed her sufficiently the wife of his bosom to cohabit with her. She was allowed a maintenance. She lived contented, and was too submissive to be troublesome on account of the conjugal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a>. Mr Montague, on the other hand, was a perfect <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PATRIARCH">patriarch</a> in his manners. He had wives of almost every nation. When he was with <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALI">Ali</a> Bey in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, he had his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a> of Egyptian females, each striving who should be the happy she who could <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> the greatest ascendancy over this Anglo-Eastern <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASHAW">bashaw</a>. At Constantinople, the Grecian women had charms to captivate this unsettled wanderer. In Spain a Spanish brunette, in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> the olive-complexioned <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> were solicited to partake the honours of the bridal-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a>. It may be asked what became of this <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GROUP">group</a> of wives? Mr Montague was continually shifting the place, and consequently varying the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-SCENE">scene</a>. Did he travel with his wives as the patriarchs did with their flocks and herds? No such thing. Wortley, considering his wives as bad travelling companions, generally left them behind him. It happened, however, that news reached his ears of the death of the original Mrs Montague the washerwoman. Wortley had no issue by her; and without issue <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MALE">male</a>, a very large estate would revert to the second son of lord Bute. Wortley, owing the family no obligations, was determined, if possible, to defeat their expectations. He resolved to return to England and marry. He acquainted a friend with his intentions; and he commissioned that friend to advertise for any young decent woman who might be in a pregnant state. Several ladies answered it. One out of the number was selected, as being the most eligible object. She waited with eagerness for the arrival of her expected bridegroom; but, behold, whilst he was on his journey, death very impertinently arrested him in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAREER">career</a>. Montague-Island, one of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HEBRIDES">Hebrides</a>, in the South Sea, near Sandwich Island. E. Long. 168. 37. S. Lat. 17. 26. Montaigne (Michel de), a French gentleman, was born in Perigord in 1533. His father educated him with great care, and made him learn Latin as other children learn their mother-tongue. His tutors were Nicholas Gronchi, who wrote De Comitibus Romanorum; William Guerenti, who wrote on Aristotle; George Buchanan; and M. Anthony <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol15.html#article-MURET">Muret</a>. He was also taught Greek by way of recreation; and because some think that starting children out of their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> spoils their understanding, he was awakened every morning with the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> of music. He was counsellor for a while in the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> of Bordeaux; afterwards made mayor of Bordeaux. He published his Essays, so much known in the world, in 1580. Montaigne had a great deal of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WIT">wit</a> and subtlety, but no small share of conceit and vanity. The learned and ingenious are much divided in their opinion about his works. He died in 1592. Montalcino, a small populous town of Italy, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a>, and in the territory of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SIENNA">Sienna</a>, with a bishop's see. It is seated on a mountain, 17 miles southeast of Sienna, and 44 southeast of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>. E. Long. 11. 30. N. Lat. 43. 7. Montalto, an episcopal town of Italy, in the Marche of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCONA">Ancona</a>; seated on the river Monacio, 10 miles north of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASCOLI">Ascoli</a>, and 45 south of Ancona. E. Long. 13. 20. N. Lat. 42. 54. Montanini (Pietro), called Petruccio Perugino, an eminent landscape painter, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PERUGIA">Perugia</a> in 1619.
