physician and professor of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, was born at Aberdeen in 1620, bred at the university there, and taught <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> for some <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> in it; but having a strong inclination to botany, made <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> progress in it. The civil wars obliged him to leave his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; which, however, he did not do till he had first signalized his zeal for the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">king</a>, and his courage, in a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> fought between the inhabitants of Aberdeen and the Presbyterian troops on the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> of Aberdeen, in which he received a dangerous wound on the head. As soon as he was cured of it, he went into France; and fixing at <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, he applied assiduously to botany and anatomy. He was introduced to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-ORLEANS">Orleans</a>, who gave him the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> gardens at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLOIS">Blois</a>. He exercised the office till the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, and afterwards went over to England in 1660. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II., to whom the duke of Orleans had presented him at Blois, sent for him to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, and gave him the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of his physician, and that of professor royal of botany, with a pension of 200l. per annum. The Preludium Botanicum, which he published in 1669, procured him so much reputation, that the university of Oxford invited him to the professorship of botany in 1669; which which he accepted, and acquitted himself in it with great ability. He died at London in 1633, aged 63. He published a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SECOND">second</a> and third <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">Plants</a>, in 2 vols, folio; with this title, *Plantarum Historia Oxoniensis Universalis*. The first part of this excellent <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> has not been printed; and it is not known what has become of it.

MORISONIA

Pages 342-342

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>: A genus of the polyandria order, belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MONADELPHIA">monadelphia</a> class of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 25th order, *Putaminae*. The calyx is single and bifid; the corolla tetrapetalous; there is one <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PISTIL">pistil</a>; the berry has a hard bark, is unilocular, polypermous, and pedicellated.

MORLACHIA

Pages 346-347

both the cause and effect of their shameful neglect of Morley, their persons. When a Morlack husband mentions his wife, he always promises, by your leave, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> begging your <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a>. And when the husband has a bedflead, the wife must <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a> near it. Our author often lodged in Morlack houses, and observed that the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SEX">sex</a> is universally treated with contempt; it is true, that the women are by no means amiable in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; they even deform and spoil the gifts of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. The pregnancy and births of those women would be thought very extraordinary among us, where the ladies suffer so much, notwithstanding all the care and circumspection used before and after labour. On the contrary, a Morlack woman neither changes her food nor interrupts her daily fatigue on account of her pregnancy; and is frequently delivered in the fields, or on the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ROAD">road</a>, by herself; and takes the infant, washes it in the first <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WATER">water</a> she finds, carries it home, and returns the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> after to her usual labour, or to feed her flock. The little creatures, thus carelessly treated in their tenderest moments, are afterwards wrapped in miserable rags, where they remain three or four months, under the same ungentle management; and when that <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TERM">term</a> is elapsed, they are set at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, and left to crawl about the cottage and before the door, till they learn to walk upright by themselves; and at the same <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> acquire that singular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of strength and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> with which the Morlacchi are endowed, and are able, without the least inconvenience, to expose their naked breasts to the severest frosts and snow. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INFANTS">infants</a> are allowed to suck their mother's <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MILK">milk</a> while she has any, or till she is with child again; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> that should not happen for three, four, or six years, they continue all that time to receive nourishment from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>. The prodigious length of the breasts of the Morlacchian women is somewhat extraordinary; for it is very certain, that they can give the teat to their children over their shoulders, or under their arms. They let the boys run about, without breeches, in a shirt that reaches only to the knee, till the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 13 or 14, following the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of Bosnia, subject to the Porte, where no haraz or capitation-tax is paid for the boys till they wear breeches, they being considered before that time as children, not capable of labouring, or of earning their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>. On the occasion of births, and especially of the first, all the relations and friends send presents of eatables to the woman in childbirth, or rather to the woman delivered; and the family makes a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SUPPER">supper</a> of all those presents together. The women do not enter the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> till 40 days after child-birth. The Morlacchi <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> their youth in the woods, attending their flocks and herds; and in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of quiet and leisure they often become dexterous in carving with a simple <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a>; they make wooden cups, and whistles adorned with fanciful bas-reliefs, which are not void of merit, and at least show the genius of the people.

MORLEY

Pages 347-347

bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WINCHESTER">Winchester</a>, was the son of Francis Morley, Esq.; and was born at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONDON">London</a> in 1597. He was educated at Christ-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, of which he had the canonry in 1641, and the next year was made <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>. He had also several church-preferments, of which he was deprived by the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> visitors in the beginning of the year 1648. After this, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">king</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I. sent for him to assist at the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> of Wight. After the king's <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEATH">death</a> he attended the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LORD">lord</a> Capel at his execution, and then retired to Charles II. at the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAGUE">Hague</a>, on whom he constantly waited till his majesty went to Scotland, when he retired to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTWERP">Antwerp</a>, where he read the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the church of England, as he afterwards did at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BREDA">Breda</a>. At the Restoration he was first made <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEAN">dean</a> of Christ church, and in 1660 was consecrated bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WORCESTER">Worcester</a>, and soon after was made dean of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> chapel. In 1662 he was translated to the bishopric of Winchester, when he bestowed considerable sums on that see, in repairing <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FARNHAM">Farnham</a>-castle and his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> at Westminster, and in purchasing Winchester <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> at Chelsea. He died at Farnham-castle in 1684. He was a Calvinist, and before the wars was thought a friend to the Puritans; but after his promotion he took care to free himself from all suspicions of that kind. He was a pious and charitable <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAN">man</a>, of a very exemplary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, but extremely passionate. He published, 1. Epistolae apologicae et pararheticae <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AD">ad</a> theologum quendam Belgam scripta, in 4to. 2. The sum of a short conference between Father Darcey a Jesuit and Dr Morley at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BRUSSELS">Brussels</a>. 3. An argument drawn from the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> and certainty of feme against the doctrine of Traufulibation. 4. A <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a> duchess of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-YORK">York</a>. 5. Several sermons, and other pieces.

MORNAY

Pages 347-348

seigneur du Plessis-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MARLY">Marly</a>, was born at Biuh <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> Bihiuy in Upper Normandy, November 9th, 1549, and educated at <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. What was then thought a prodigy in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>, he made a rapid progress in the belles lettres, in the learned languages, and in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>. He was at first destined for the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>; but the principles of Calvinism, which he had imbibed from his mother, effectively excluded him from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> preferments to which he was entitled by his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>, abilities, and birth. After the horrible massacre of St Bartholomew, Philippe de Mornay made the tour of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, Germany, England, and the Low Countries; and he was equally improved and delighted by his travels. Mornay afterwards joined the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">king</a> of Navarre, at that <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> leader of the Protestant party, and so well known since by the name of Henry IV. This <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> sent Mornay, who employed his whole abilities, both as a soldier and a writer, in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of the Protestant cause, to conduct a negociation with <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of England; and left him wholly to his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a> in the management of that business. He was successful in almost every negociation, because he conducted them like an able politician, and not with a spirit of intrigue. He tenderly loved Henry IV. and spoke to him on all occasions as to a friend. When he was wounded at Aumale, he wrote to him in these words: "Sire, you have <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a> enough acted the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> of Alexander, it is now time you should <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> that of Caesar. It is our duty to die for your majesty, &c. It is glorious for you, Sire, and I dare venture to tell you it is your duty, to live for us." This faithful subject did every thing in his power to raise Henry to the throne. But when he deserted the Protestant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, he reproached him in the bitterest manner, and retired. Mornay retired from <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COURT">court</a>. Henry still loved him; and was extremely affected with an insult which he received in 1597 from one Saint-Phal, who <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> him with a cudgel, and left him for dead. Mornay demanded <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> from the king; who gave him the following answer, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> as well of his spirit as of his goodness of heart. "Monsieur Duplessis, I am exceedingly offended at the insult you have received; and I sympathize with you both as your sovereign and your friend. In the former capacity, I shall do justice to you and to myself; and had I sustained only the character of your friend, there are few perhaps who would have drawn their <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> or sacrificed their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> more cheerfully in your cause. Be satisfied, then, that I <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a> act the part of a King, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, and a friend, &c." Mornay's knowledge, probity, and valour, made him the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> of the Protestant party, and procured him the contemptuous appellation of the Pope of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HUGUENOTS">Huguenots</a>. He defended their doctrines both by speech and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>. One of his books on the Iniquity of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MASS">Mass</a>, having stirred up all the Catholic divines, he refused to make any reply to their censures and criticisms except in a public conference. This was accordingly appointed to be held A.D. 1600, at Fontainebleau, where the court then was. The two champions were, du Perron bishop of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EVREUX">Evreux</a>, and Mornay. After a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> many arguments and replies on both sides, the victory was adjudged to du Perron. He had boasted that he would point out to the satisfaction of every one five hundred errors in his adversary's book, and he partly kept his word. The Calvinists did not fail to claim the victory on this occasion, and they still continue to do so. This conference, instead of putting an end to the differences, was productive of new quarrels among the controversialists, and of much profane <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WIT">wit</a> among the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIBERTINES">libertines</a>. A Huguenot minister, who was present at the conference, observed with great concern to a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> of the same party.—"The bishop of Evreux has already driven Mornay from several strong holds." "No <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> (replied the folder), provided he does not drive him from <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-SAUMUR">Saumur</a>." This was an important <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a> on the river <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LOIRE">Loire</a>, of which Duplessis was governor. Hither he retired, his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> being constantly occupied in defending the Huguenots, and in making himself formidable to the Catholics. When <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIII. was making preparations against the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>, Duplessis wrote him a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LETTER">letter</a>, dissuading him against such a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>. After employing the most plausible arguments, he concludes in the following manner: "To make <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WAR">war</a> on the subject, is an indication of weakness in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. Authority consists in the quiet submission of the people, and is established by the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a> and justice of the governor. Force of arms ought never to be employed except in repelling a foreign enemy. The late king would have sent the new ministers of state to learn the first elements of politics, who like unskilful surgeons would apply violent remedies to every <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>, and advise a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAN">man</a> to cut off an arm when his finger aches." These remonstrances produced no other effect than the loss of the government of Saumur, of which he was deprived by Louis XIII. in 1621. He died two years after, November 11th, 1623, aged 74, in his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARONY">Barony</a> de la Forêt-sur-Sèvre in Poitou. The Prote- Cet enfant des courtisans, mais à la cour aimé ; Fier ennemi de Rome, et de Rome éliminé.

MORNE-GAROU

Pages 348-351

a very remarkable volcanic mountain on the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of St Vincent's in the West Indies. It was visited by Mr James Anderson surgeon in the year 1784, who is the only person that ever ascended to the top of it, and from whose account, in the Philosophical Transactions, Vol. LXXV. the following is taken. The mountain in question is situated on the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> of the island, and is the highest in it. It is constantly reported to have emitted volcanic eruptions; and the ravins at the bottom seem to corroborate the traditions of the inhabitants in this respect. The structure of it, when viewed at a distance, appears different from that of any other mountain in the island, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> that Mr Anderson had seen in the West Indies. He could perceive it divided into many different ridges, separated by deep chasms, and its summit appeared quite destitute of every vegetable production. Several ravins, that run from the bottom a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> way up the mountain, were found quite destitute of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and pieces of pumice-<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHARCOAL">charcoal</a>, and several earths and minerals of a particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, found in them, plainly indicated some very great singularity in this mountain. Some very old men also informed our author, that they had heard it related by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> of a ship, that between this island and St Lucia he <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAW">saw</a> flames and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> rising from the top of the mountain, and next morning his decks were covered with ashes and small <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-STONES">stones</a>. Mr Anderson's curiosity was so much excited by these circumstances, that he formed a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> of going up to the top; but was informed that this was impossible, nor could he find either <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAN">man</a>, Caribbee, or negro, who would undertake to show him the way. Having observed the basis as well as he could, with a view to discover the most proper <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a> for attempting an ascent, he found several dry ravins that seemingly ran a great way up, though he could not be certain that they were not intersected by rocks or precipices lying across. Having examined the mountain with a good glass, he thought he perceived two ridges by which there was a possibility of getting up; and though they appeared to be covered for a great way with wood, he hoped by a little <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> to open a way through it. On the 26th of February 1784 our author began his journey, having been furnished by Mr Maloune, who lives within a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MILE">mile</a> of the foot of the mountain, with two stout <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a>, and having another boy who waited on himself. They arrived at the bottom of the mountain a little before <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> in the morning, having each a good cutlass to cut through the woods, or to defend themselves in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CASE">case</a> of an attack from the Caribbees or runaway negroes. Before they could get at either of the ridges, however, they had a rock to climb upwards of 40 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>. Having scrambled up this with great difficulty, they found themselves in the bottom of a deep and narrow ravine, which having ascended a little way, they arrived at the habitation of Mr Gasco a Frenchman. Mr Anderson expresses his surprise, that a young and healthy man, and a good mechanic, should seclude himself from the world among woods and precipices, where he was besides in continual danger of being swept away with his whole habitation by the torrents occasioned by the rains. He found him, however, an intelligent man, and was hospitably entertained by him. "The difficulty (says Mr Anderson) in going through woods in the West Indies, where there are no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a> or paths, is far beyond anything an European can conceive. Besides tall trees and thick underwood, there are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">hundreds</a> of different climbing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> twisted together like <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a>, and running together in all directions to a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, and even to the tops of the highest trees. They cannot be broken by pushing on; and many of them are not to be cut without difficulty. Besides these, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of grass, the *Lithophyllum*, with ferrated leaves, cuts and tears the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FACE">face</a> terribly." By reason of these obstructions, it was upwards of two hours before they got upon the ridge; but here they found their passage more difficult than before. They were now surrounded by a thick forest, rendered more impracticable by the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> piles of trees blown <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DOWN">down</a> by the hurricanes; which obliged them in many places to creep on their hands and feet to get below them, while in others it was necessary to climb to a considerable height to get over them; at the same <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> that by the trunks being frequently rotten, they often tumbled headlong from a great height, and could not extricate themselves without great difficulty. The fatigue of cutting their way through the woods soon became intolerable to the negroes; so that about four in the afternoon he could not prevail on them to go any farther. Mr Anderson therefore perceiving it was impossible to get to the summit that night, and his water being totally expended, returned to Mr Gasco's, where he spent the night, determining to try another route next morning. The hospitable Frenchman entertained him in the best manner he could; but though he parted with his own hammock to him, and slept on a board himself, Mr Anderson found it impossible to shut his eyes the whole night by reason of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLD">cold</a>. "His hut (says he) was built of *rofaux* or large reeds, between each two of which a dog might creep through, and the top was covered with dry grass. It is situated in the bottom of a deep gully, where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> does not shine till <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NINE">nine</a> in the morning nor after four in the afternoon. It is surrounded by thick wood; and during the night the whole of the mountain is covered with thick <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a>, from which it frequently rains, and which makes the night-<a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> exceedingly cold." Early next morning Mr Anderson set out in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> with the negro boy, who <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> very faithful to him during the whole of the journey. He now determined to take his course up the ravine, and proceeded for about a mile and a half without any considerable obstruction. It now, however, began to narrow fast; there were numbers of rocks and precipices to climb over, with many bushes and vines which could scarcely be got through. At last the ravine terminated at the bottom of a very high precipice. It was impossible to know the extent of this, as the top was covered with thick wood; but from the bottom upward, as far as he could see, was loose sand with ferns and tufts of grass, which as soon as he took hold of them came up by the roots. Though the ascent was plainly at the risk of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, Mr Anderson resolved to attempt it; and therefore telling the boy to keep at some distance behind, lest he should tumble and drive him down, he began to ascend, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DIGGING">digging</a> holes with his cutlass to put his feet in, and taking hold of the tufts of grass as lightly as possible. Notwithstanding all his care, however, he frequently slipped down a considerable way; but as it was only loose sand, he could easily push his cutlass into it up to the handle, and thus by taking hold of it recover himself again. At last he got up to some wild plantains, which continued all the way to the place where the trees began to grow. Here he rested for some time, waiting for the boy, who got up with much less difficulty than he had done. On getting up to the top of the precipice, he found himself on a very narrow ridge, covered with wood, and bounded by two ravines, the bottoms of which he could not see, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> to them appearing to be nearly perpendicular, though all the way covered with thick wood. Proceeding onwards, they found the ridge exceedingly narrow, in many places not six feet <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>; with a tremendous <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> on each side, into which they were every moment in danger of falling; so that Mr Anderson was obliged to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> down on his belly with great caution, in order to see through the bushes how the ridge tended. Here a fulphurous smell, or rather one like <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUNPOWDER">gunpowder</a>, began to be perceived; which, Mr Anderson knew, must proceed from the top of the mountain, as the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> then blew that way; and as it plainly grew stronger as he advanced, he was in hopes that the top could not be very far distant. Perceiving a rising before him, he imagined, that, by getting upon it, he might have a view of the top of the mountain; but when this was done, he could only see a peak on the north-west side of the mountain, to which, by appearance, he judged himself very little nearer than when at the bottom. The woods now became very difficult, great quantities of fallen trees lying buried among the grass; and being rotten, he was frequently buried very deep among them when he thought himself walking upon firm ground. About noon he was alarmed with a rustling among the bushes, and something like a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> behind him; but as he was preparing to defend himself against Caribbees or run-away negroes, he was agreeably surprised with the sight of those who had formerly left him, with three others, sent by Mr Maloune with plenty of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>. Encouraged by this affixture, after refreshing themselves, they renewed their labours with fresh vigour, and Mr Anderson thought himself sure of reaching the top before night. In a little time he had a fair view of the ravine on the left, which was of prodigious depth, and ran from near the top of the mountain to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. Its bottom seemed to be a rock nearly resembling <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAVA">lava</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, and it seemed as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> there had been vast torrents of sulphurous <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> running upon it for some time.—He now regretted much that he knew not of this ravine before he commenced his excursion, as, by passing a headland in a canoe, and getting into it, he might have gained the summit without all those delays and difficulties he had encountered. About four in the afternoon he had no prospect of the top of the mountain, but imagined that if he could get into the ravine before night, he might easily reach it next morning. After cutting through wild plantains for a great way, however, he found himself at sunset on the brink of a precipice, over which he prevented himself from falling by catching hold of some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">shrubs</a>. They were now about half way down, but all the rest of the way seemed a perpendicular precipice, which it was impossible to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a>; the top of the mountain was yet a great way off, and there was no other resource than to attempt the ridge they had left. The evening was now so far advanced, that they were obliged to take up their residence where they were; and there was only time to place two or three sticks against the stump of a tree, and slightly to cover them with plantain leaves for a night's habitation.—Their situation, however, was extremely uncomfortable: it began to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> and blow violently, which prevented them from getting a fire made, so that they were almost chilled with cold. As soon as they could see, they renewed their <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> with great alacrity, and in a short time had the satisfaction to perceive that the woods became thin. About eleven o'clock they obtained a full view of the top, about a mile distant. It seemed to be composed of six or seven ridges, very much broken in the sides, as if they had suffered great convulsions; and they were divided by excessively deep ravines without any water in them. Mr Anderson directed his course towards a high peak that overlooked a large excavation where the ridges met, and which he supposed to be the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CRATER">crater</a> of the volcano. In his way, he found the last wood composed of a most beautiful species of trees. After that he entered into a thick <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a> grass intermixed with fern, which branched and ran in every <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>. Thro' this they were obliged to cut their way with almost as much difficulty as they had done through the woods, and it seemed to continue very near to the top of the mountain. The fatigue of this work soon reduced them to such a situation, that they were scarce able to stand; and they were obliged to quench their thirst, which was excessive, by chewing the leaves of the begonia obliqua, there being no water to be had in the place. Two of the negroes returned, and the rest refused to proceed any farther; so that Mr Anderson himself was obliged to abandon the enterprise, and they all began to descend about half an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> after twelve; and as there was now a clear path all the way down, they arrived at Mr Gafco's by sun-set; and notwithstanding his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> weariness, Mr Anderson continued his journey to Mr Maloune's, where he arrived between six and seven at night. Our traveller having refreshed himself to the 4th of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MARCH">March</a>, in order to sustain the fatigues of his journey the better, set out about four that morning in company with a Mr Fraser, who had resolved to accompany him. They met with little difficulty till they came to the place whence they had formerly returned. Here, however, they were obliged for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of a mile to cut their way through the grass and ferns already mentioned; which being done, they met with no further obstruction. When they came within a quarter of a mile of the top, they found the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> suddenly altered, the air very cold, and the vegetable productions changed, the whole summit of the mountain being barren. On the confines of the grassy and barren regions, however, he found some beautiful plants; and he observes, that this is the only place in the West Indies where he ever found moss; but here it grows in such plenty, that he frequently sunk in it up to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNEES">knees</a>. About noon they reached the summit, and were instantly surprised with the sight of a most extraordinary cavity. It is situated in the very centre of the mountain, at the place where all the ridges meet. Its diameter is something more than a mile, and its circumference to appearance a perfect circle. Its depth from the surrounding margin is above a quarter of a mile, and it narrows a little, but very regularly, to the bottom. Its sides are very smooth, and for the most part covered with short moss, except towards the south, where there are a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of small holes and rents. This is the only place where it is possible to go down to the bottom; and the descent is very dangerous on account of the numberless small chasms. On the west side is a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SECTION">section</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RED">red</a> rock like <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GRANITE">granite</a>, cut very smooth, and having the same declivity with the other parts. All the rest of the surrounding sides seem to be composed of sand, which has undergone the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of an intense fire. It has a crust quite smooth, and about an inch thick, almost as hard as rock; on breaking thro' which we meet with nothing but loose sand. In the centre stands a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> mountain about a mile in circumference, of a conic form, "but quite <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LEVEL">level</a>." Out of the middle of the summit rises a small eminence eight or ten feet high, and perfectly conical; from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APEX">apex</a> of which a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLUMN">column</a> of smoke constantly issues. It is composed of large masses of red granite-like rock, of various shapes and sizes, which appear to have been split into their present form by some terrible convulsion of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>; and are piled up very regular. Great quantities of smoke issue from most parts of the mountain, especially on the north side, which appears to be burning from top to bottom; and the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> is so intense, that it is impossible to ascend it. It is even very dangerous to go round the base, as large masses of rock are constantly splitting with the heat and tumbling down. At the bottom, on the north side, is a very large rock split in two. Each of these halves, which are rent in all directions, are separated to a considerable distance from each other, and the crevices have gloomy efflorescences tasting like vitriol. There are also beautiful crystallizations of sulphur; and on all parts of the mountain are great quantities of sulphur, also <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a>, vitriol, &c. From the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> appearance of this mountain, Mr Anderson conjectures that it had but lately begun to burn; as on several parts of it he saw small shrubs and grass, which looked as if they had been but lately scorched and burnt. There were also several holes on the south from which smoke issued, that appeared to have broken out but lately, the adjacent bushes being but lately burnt. On two opposite sides, the east and west, of the burning mountain, are two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> of water, about a stone's throw in breadth. They appear to be deep in the middle, and have a bottom of a kind of clay. The water is a chalybeate, and has a pleasant <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>. These lakes probably derive their existence in a great <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, if not totally, from the rain-water running down the sides of the crater. On the north side Mr Anderson observed the traces of great torrents, that to appearance had conveyed vast quantities of water to these lakes; and by the stones at the bottom he could perceive that <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSORPTION">absorption</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EVAPORATION">evaporation</a>, or both, went on very fast. The greater part of the bottom of the crater is very level; and on the south side are some shrubs and small trees. Some pieces of pumice-stone were met with, and many stones about the size of a man's fist, rough, and blue upon one side, are scattered all over the mountain. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the clouds on the top of this mountain was very singular. Though there were several parts higher than the crater, yet the clouds seemed always to be attracted by the latter. After entering on its east or <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WINDWARD">windward</a> side, they sunk a considerable way into it; then mounting the opposite side, and whirling round the north-west corner of the mountain, they ran along a ridge which tended nearly north-east, and afterwards sunk into a deep ravine dividing this ridge from another on the north-west corner of the mountain, and the highest on it, lying in a direction nearly north and south. They keep in this ridge to the south end, and then whirl off in their <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> direction. From the situation of these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> to one another, and to the continent of South <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, Mr Anderson conjectures, that there are submarine communications between the volcanoes in each of them, and from them to those in the high <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of South America. He observes, that the crater in this island lies nearly in a line with Soufriere in St Lucia and Morne Pelee in Martinique; and probably from thence to a place of the same kind in Dominique, and from thence to the other islands; there being something of the kind in each, Barbadoes and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TOBAGO">Tobago</a> excepted.

MORNING

Pages 351-352

the beginning of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>-rising. The astronomers reckon morning, mane, from the time of midnight to that of midday. Thus an eclipse is said to begin at 11 o'clock in the morning, &c. Morning <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-STAR">star</a>, is the planet Venus, when a little to the westward of the sun; that is, when she rises a little before. In this situation she is called by the Greeks Phosphorus; by the Latins Lucifer, &c.

MOROC

Pages 351-351
or MOROC, a beautiful bird of Abyssinia described by Mr Bruce, who thinks its name is derived from mar "honey," though he says that he never heard it was further concerned in the honey than destroying bees. It seems to pursue those insects out of enmity or diversion as well as for food, leaving great numbers dead on the ground, besides those which it devours for food." In consequence of this property, the moroc is never found anywhere but in those parts where the honey is very plentiful, tho' the Abyssinians never take any notice of the ravages they commit among their stocks of bees. The moroc resembles the cuckoo in size and shape, but differs in other respects. Its mouth is very wide, the opening reaching almost to his eyes; the inside of the mouth and throat yellow, the tongue sharp-pointed, and capable of being drawn almost half its length out of the mouth beyond the point of its beak, and is very flexible. The head and neck are brown, without any mixture of other colours: there are likewise a number of very small and scarcely visible hairs at the root of the beak. The eyebrows are black; the beak pointed, and very little crooked; the pupil of the eye black, and surrounded with an iris of a dull and dusky red: The fore-part of the neck is light yellow, darker on each side than in the middle, where it is partly white: the yellow on each side reaches near the shoulder, or round part of the wing; and from this the whole breast and belly is of a dirty white to the under part of the tail; and from this the feathers begin to be tipped with white, as are all those that cover the outside of the wing. The wing has eight feathers of the largest size and six of the second: the tail consists of twelve feathers, the longest three being in the middle: they are placed closely together; and the tail is of an equal breadth from top to bottom, the feathers being also tipped with white. The thighs are covered with feathers of the same colour as those of the belly, reaching more than half way down the legs, which are black, as well as the feet, and marked distinctly with scales. There are two toes before and behind, each of which has a sharp and crooked claw. It makes a sharp snapping noise when it catches the bees, evidently from closing its beak; but Mr Bruce never could discover that it had any song. This seems to be the creature mentioned by Dr Sparman under the name of cuculus indicator, which (he says) has the singular property of discovering the nests of wild bees, and leading travellers by a certain cry to the place where the treasure is deposited. According to Sparman's account, it makes known these discoveries by the same cry to foxes as well as to the human species; but Jerome Lobo, who mentions the Abyssinian bird, does not take notice of the foxes, though he mentions its singing melodiously when it arrives at the place where the honey is deposited. Both these accounts are feverly criticised by Mr Bruce. "I cannot (says he), for my own part, conceive, in a country where there are so many thousand hives, that there was any use for giving to a bird a peculiar instinct or faculty of discovering honey, when, at the same time, nature had deprived him of the power of availing himself of any advantage from the discovery; for man seems in this case to be made for the service of the moroc, which is very different from the common and ordinary course of things; man certainly needs him not, for on every tree, and on every hillock, he may see plenty of honey at his own deliberate disposal. I cannot then but think, with all submission to these natural philosophers, that the whole of this is an improbable fiction; nor did I ever hear a single person in Abyssinia suggest, that either this or any other bird had such a property. Sparman says it was not known to any inhabitant of the Cape, any more than that of the moroc was in Abyssinia; it was a secret of nature, hid from all but these two great men; and I most willingly leave it among the catalogue of their particular discoveries."

MOROCCO

Pages 352-370

an empire of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, comprehending a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAURITANIA">Mauritania</a>, is bounded on the west by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATLANTIC_OCEAN">Atlantic Ocean</a>; on the east by the river Muluya, which separates it from Algiers; on the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the Mediterranean; and on the south by mount <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATLAS">Atlas</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> rather by the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUS">Sus</a>, which divides it from the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Tafilet. Its greatest length is from the north-east to the south-west, amounting to above 590 miles; its breadth is not above 260 where broadest, and in the most narrow places is not above half that breadth. The ancient <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of Morocco has been already given under the article MAURITANIA. It <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> under the dominion of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> upwards of 400 years. On the decline of that empire it fell under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOTHS">Goths</a>, who held it till about the year 600, when the Goths were driven out by the Vandals, the Vandals by the Greeks, and they in their turn by the Saracens, who conquered not only this empire, but we may say the whole continent of Africa; at least their <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, one way or other, is to be found in all parts of it. The Saracen empire did not continue <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a> united under one head, and many princes set up for themselves in Africa as well as elsewhere, through whose divisions the Almoravides were at length raised to the sovereignty, as related under the article ALGIERS, no. 2. Yulef, or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SECOND">second</a> monarch of that line, built the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Morocco, conquered the kingdom of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FEZ">Fez</a>, and the Moorish dominions in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>; all which were lost by his grandson Abbu Hali, who was defeated and killed by the Spaniards. On this <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEATH">death</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> passed to the Mokedans, or Almohedes, with whom it had not continued above three generations, when Mohammed the son of Al Manfur lost the famous <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Sierra Morena, in which 200,000 Moors were slain, and in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of which Alphonso X. retook a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> many of the Moorish conquests immediately after. Mohammed died soon after this disgrace, and left several sons, between whom a civil <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WAR">war</a> ensued, during which the viceroys of Fez, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TUNIS">Tunis</a>, and Tremelen, found means to establish themselves as independent princes. At length one of the princes of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> blood of Tremelen having defeated the Almohedes, made himself <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the kingdoms of Morocco and Fez, and entailed them on his own family. In a short <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a>, however, this family was expelled by the Merini, the Merini by the Oatazes, and these by the Sharifs of Hascen, who have kept the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> ever since. This happened about the year 1516; and since that time, what we have under the name of history is little else than a catalogue of the enormous vices and excesses of the emperors. They have been in general a set of bloody tyrants; though they have had among them some able princes, particularly Muley Moluc, who defeated and killed <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DON">Don</a> Sebastian <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>. See the article PORTUGAL, no. 26. They have lived in almost a continual state of warfare with the kings of Spain and other Christian princes ever since; nor does the crown of Great <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> sometimes disdain, as in the year 1769, to purchase their friendship with presents. Nothing can be conceived more unjust and despotic than the government of Morocco, and nothing more degenerate than the character of the people. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> is allowed to have not only an uncontrollable power over the lives and fortunes of his subjects, but in a great <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> over their consciences, such as they are; in as much as he is the only person who, as the successor of the prophet, has a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to interpret the Koran; and appoints all the judges under him, of whom those of Morocco and Fez are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>, whose business it is to explain and dispense all matters relating to their religion; and who, being his creatures and dependents, dare not steer otherwise than as he directs. Whenever therefore the laws are enacted by him, and proclaimed by his governors in all the provinces, as is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> done, that none may plead <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a>, they are everywhere received with an implicit and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> submission. On the other <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, the subjects are bred up with a notion, that those who die in the execution of his command are entitled to an immediate admittance into paradise, and those who have the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to die by his hand to a still greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> in it. After this we need not wonder at finding so much cruelty, oppression, and tyranny on the one side, and so much submission, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PATIENCE">patience</a>, and misery on the other. This latter, however, extends no farther than the Moors: for as to the mountaineers, the subjection and tribute they pay to those tyrants was always involuntary, and altogether forced; and as for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a>, their zeal and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> is owing merely to the great sway and power which they have gained in the government, on various accounts. They were first introduced, or rather their importation increased, by the policy of Muley Ishmael, a late emperor, at a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> when there was a great decrease of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> in the empire, occasioned in some degree by the enormous cruelties exercised by its former sovereigns, who have been known not unfrequently, through a slight difficulty, to abandon a whole town or <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>. In the character of Muley Ishmael were found the most singular inconsistencies; for it is certain, that although a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a> of the same class, yet in other respects, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> to repair the mischief which he committed, he left nothing undone for the encouragement of population.—He introduced, as above-mentioned, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> colonies of negroes from <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a>; built <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> for them, many of which are still remaining; assigned them portions of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAND">land</a>, and encouraged their increase by every possible means. He soon initiated them in the Mahometan <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>; and had his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> been followed, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> by this time would have been populous, and probably flourishing. As the negroes are of a more lively, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a>, and enterprising disposition than the Moors, they might soon have been taught the arts of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>; and their singular ingenuity might have been directed to other useful purposes. It is true, Muley Ishmael, when he adopted this plan, had more objects in view than that of merely peopling his dominions. He <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAW">saw</a> plainly that his own subjects were of too capricious a disposition to form <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> calculated for his tyrannical purposes. They had uniformly manifested an inclination to change their sovereigns, though more from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of variety than to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-REFORM">reform</a> the government, or restrain the abuses of tyranny. In short, whatever revolutions... revolutions took <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the country, consisted merely in a change of one tyrant for another. Muley Ishmael had discernment enough to see, therefore, that by forming an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of slaves, whose sole dependence should rest upon their master, he could easily train them in such a manner as to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> in the strictest conformity to his wishes. He soon learnt that the great object with the negroes was plenty of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of plunder; in these he liberally indulged them, and the plan fully answered his expectations. Though, however, Muley Ishmael had no great merit in introducing subjects for the purposes of tyranny, yet the good effects of this new colonization were very generally experienced. By intermarrying among themselves, and intermixing among the Moors (for the Moors <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a> keep negro women as concubines, though they seldom marry them), a new <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-RACE">race</a> of people started up, who became as useful subjects as the native inhabitants, and brought the empire into a much more flourishing state than it had ever been since their great revolution. Sidi Mahomet, his grandson and successor, had different views, and was actuated by different motives. From his inordinate avarice, he ceased to act towards his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> troops in the generous manner which had distinguished his predecessor Muley Ishmael; and they soon showed themselves discontented with his conduct. They frequently threatened to revolt, and support those of his sons who were in opposition, and who promised them the most liberal rewards. They offered to place his eldest son Muley <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALI">Ali</a>, who is since dead, on the throne; but this prince, not unmindful of the duty which he owed his father and sovereign, declined their offer. They next applied to Muley Yazid, the late emperor, who at first accepted of the assistance they tendered, but in a short time relinquished the plan. Sidi Mahomet, disgusted with this conduct of the negroes, determined to curb their growing power, by disbanding a considerable part of these troops, and banishing them to distant parts of the empire. This important <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of population has therefore been of late years neglected, while no better system has been substituted in its room; for though the late emperor indulged in cruelty much less frequently than his predecessors, yet population has, perhaps, been more completely impeded by the general poverty which he has introduced into the country by his severe exactions, than if he had made a liberal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the sword or of the bow-string. A most flagrant <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of despotism, which renders the emperors still more formidable to their subjects, is their making themselves their sole heirs, and, in virtue of that, seizing upon all their effects, and making only such provision for their families as they think proper; and often, on some frivolous pretence, leaving them destitute of any, according to the liking or dislike they bear to the deceased; so that, upon the whole, they are the only makers, judges, and interpreters, and in many instances likewise the executioners, of their own laws, which have no other limits than their own arbitrary will. To preserve, however, some show or shadow of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, they allow their mufti a kind of superiority in spirituals, and a sort of liberty to the meanest subject to summon them before his tribunal. But the danger which such an attempt would bring upon a plaintiff, perhaps no less than death and destruction, is of itself sufficient to deter any <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAN">man</a> from it; especially considering the little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> there is that the judges of it would run the risk of declaring themselves against a monarch whose creatures they are, and on whom their lives and fortunes so absolutely depend. The titles which the emperors of Morocco assume, are those of Most glorious, mighty, and noble emperor of Africa, king of Fez and Morocco, Taphilet, Suz, Darba, and all the Algarbe, and its territories in Africa; <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> Sharif (or, as others write it, Xarif, that is, "successor, or vicegerent,") of the great prophet Mohammed, &c. The judges or magistrates that act immediately under the emperor are either spiritual or temporal, or rather <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MILITARY">military</a>. The mufti and the kadi are judges of all religious and civil affairs; and the bashaws, governors, alcaldes, and other military officers, of those that concern the state or the army: all of them the most obsequious creatures and slaves of their prince, and no less the rapacious tyrants of his subjects, and from whom neither justice nor favour can be obtained but by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> dint of money and extortionate bribery, from the highest to the lowest. Neither can it indeed be otherwise in such an arbitrary government, where the highest posts must not only be bought of the prince at a most extravagant price, and kept only by as exorbitant a tribute, which is yearly paid to him, but where no one is sure to continue longer than he can bribe some of the courtiers to infatuate to the monarch that he pays to the utmost of his power, and much beyond what was expected from him. Add to this, that those bashaws, governors, &c. are obliged to keep their agents and spies in constant pay at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COURT">court</a>, to prevent their being supplanted by higher bidders, slanderers, or other undermers. In short, power and weakness, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RANK">rank</a> and meanness, opulence and indigence, are here equally dependent, equally uncertain. There are instances of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SULTAN">Sultan</a> elevating at once a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMON">common</a> folder to the rank of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASHAW">bashaw</a>, or making him a confidential friend; the following <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> he would perhaps imprison him, or reduce him again to the station of a private folder. It is surprising that men under these circumstances should be ambitious of rank, or deaf to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> and power. Yet such is the disposition of these people, that they have an unbounded thirst for rank and power with all their uncertainties; and what is more extraordinary, when they have obtained a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> station, they seldom fail to afford their sovereign a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PLEA">plea</a> for ill treating them, by abusing in some way or other their trust. From what has been said, it may be reasonably concluded that the revenue arising to the emperors, from the last mentioned source, that of bribery, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTORTION">extortion</a>, and confiscation, must be very considerable, though there is no possibility to make any other conjecture of its real amount than that it must be an immense one. Another considerable branch is the piratical trade, which brings the greater income into his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a>, as he is not at any expense either for fitting of corsair vessels out, or maintaining their men; and yet has the tenth of all the cargo and of all the captives; besides which, he appropriates to himself all the rest of them, by paying the captors 50 crowns per head, by which means he engrosses all the slaves to his own <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> and advantage. This article is indeed a Morocco, very considerable addition to his revenue, not only as he sells their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RANSOM">ransom</a> at a very high rate, but likewise as he has the profit of all their labour, without allowing them any other maintenance than a little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, or any other assistance when sick than what medicines a Spanish convent, which he tolerates there, gives them gratis; and which, nevertheless, is forced to pay him an annual present for that toleration, besides furnishing the court with medicines, and the slaves with lodging and diet when they are not able to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>. Another branch of his revenue consists in the tenth part of all cattle, corn, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, wax, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIDES">hides</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, and other products of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, which is exacted of the Arabs and Berbers, as well as of the natives; and these are levied, or rather farmed, by the bailiffs, governors, alcaldes, &c., with all possible levity. The Jews and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> likewise pay an income or capitation, the former of five crowns per head on all males from fifteen years and upwards, besides other arbitrary imposts, fines, &c. That on the Christians, for the liberty of trading in his dominions, rises and falls according to their <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> they drive; but which, whatever it may bring yearly into his coffers, is yet detrimental to trade in general, seeing it discourages great numbers from settling there, notwithstanding the artful invitations which the emperors and their ministers make use of to invite them to it; for, besides those arbitrary exactions, there is still another great hardship attending them, viz., that they cannot leave the country without forfeiting all their debts and effects to the crown. The duties on all imports and exports is another branch of his income, the amount of which, communibus annis, no author has yet given us any account of; only confid <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HATFIELD">Hatfield</a> has computed the whole yearly revenue, including ordinaries and extraordinaries, to amount to 500 quintals of silver, each quintal, or 100 lb. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, valued at somewhat above 330l. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-STERLING">Sterling</a>: so that the whole amounts to no more, according to him, than 165,000l.; a small revenue indeed for so large an empire, if the calculation may be depended upon. But St Olan, though he does not pretend so much as to guess at the yearly amount of it, in general represents it as so considerable, that Muley Ishmael was reckoned to have amassed out of it a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver of about 50 effective millions; but whether of crowns or livres he does not tell us, nor how he came by his knowledge of it; because that politic prince, even by his own confession, not only caused all his riches to be buried in sundry places under-ground, his gold and silver to be melted into great lumps, and laid in the same privacy underground, but likewise all those whom he entrusted with the secret to be as privately murdered. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> of the empire of Morocco is in general sufficiently temperate, healthy, and not so hot as its situation might <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> us to suppose. The chain of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> which form Atlas, on the eastern side, defends it from the east winds, that would scourch up the earth were they frequent. The summit of these mountains is always covered with snow; and their abundant descending streams spread verdure through the neighbourhood, make the winter more <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, and temper the heats of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SEA">sea</a> on the west side, which extends along the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COAST">coast</a> from north to south, also refreshes the land with regular breezes, that seldom vary according to their seasons. At a distance from the sea, within land, the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> is so great, that the rivulets become dry in summer; but as in hot countries dews are plentiful, the nights are always cool. The rains are tolerably regular in winter; and are even abundant, though the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a> is not loaded with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a> as in northern latitudes. Those rains which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> by intervals are favourable to the earth, and increase its fecundity. In <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> the country is covered with verdure, and enamelled with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>. Barley is cut in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MARCH">March</a>, but the wheat <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a> is in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JUNE">June</a>. All fruits are early in this climate; and in forward years the vintage is over in the beginning of September. Though in general there is more uniformity and less <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a> in hot than in northern climates, the first are nevertheless exposed to the intemperance of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>: too heavy rains often impede the harvest; and drought has still greater inconveniences, for it ensues the propagation of locusts. These fatal insects, which have so often laid desolate hot countries, sometimes commit the most dreadful ravages in the empire of Morocco. They come from the south, spread themselves over the lands, and increase to infinity when the rains of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> are not sufficiently heavy to destroy the eggs they deposit on the earth. The large locusts, which are near three inches long, are not the most destructive: as they fly, they yield to the current of <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, which hurries them into the sea, or into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> deserts, where they perish with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUNGER">hunger</a> or fatigue. The young locusts, that cannot fly, are the most ruinous; they creep over the country in such multitudes, that they leave not a blade of grass behind; and the noise of their feeding announces their approach at some distance. The devastations of locusts increase the price of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, and often occasion famines: but the Moors find a kind of compensation in making food of these insects; prodigious quantities of which are brought to market salted and dried like <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RED">red</a> herrings. They have an oily and rank <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, which <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> only can render agreeable: they are eaten here, however, with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>. The winters in Morocco are not severe, nor is there an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> need of fire. In the coldest weather the thermometer seldom sinks to more than five degrees below the freezing point. The longest days in Morocco are not more than 14 hours, and the shortest consequently not less than ten. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> of Morocco is exceedingly fertile. It is soil, and moist in the inland provinces. On the western coast it is in general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> and stony, and is better adapted to the vine and olive than the culture of wheat. They annually burn, before the September rains, the stubble, which is left rather long; and this and the dung of cattle, every day turned to pasture, form the sole manure the land receives. The soil requires but little labour, and the ploughing is so light that the furrows are scarcely six inches deep; for which reason, in some provinces, wooden ploughshares are used for cheapness. The empire of Morocco might supply itself with all necessaries, as well from the abundance and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of its products, as from the few <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> wants of the Moors occasioned by climate or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>. Its wealth consists in the fruitfulness of its soil: its corn, fruits, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GUMS">gums</a>, and wax, would not only supply its necessities, but yield a superflux, which might become become an object of immense trade and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BARTER">barter</a> with other nations. Such numerous exports might return an inexhaustible treasure, were its government fixed and secure, and did subjects enjoy the fruits of their labour and their <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> in safety. The increase of corn in Morocco is often as sixty to one, and thirty is held to be but an indifferent harvest. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a> of this corn is burdened by the laws, and by the prejudices of an intolerant religion, which permits them not to sell their superabundance to infidels. The property of land is besides entirely precarious; so that each individual grows little more than sufficient for his own wants. Hence it happens, when the harvest fails from the ravages of locusts or the intemperance of seasons, these people are exposed to misery, such as Europeans have no <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONCEPTION">conception</a> of, who enjoy a stable administration, which obviates and provides for all their wants. The Moors, naturally indolent, take little care of the culture of their fruits. Oranges, lemons, and thick-skinned fruits, the trees of which require little nurture, grow in the open fields; and there are very large plantations of them found, which they take the trouble to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WATER">water</a> in order to increase their produce. Their vines, which yield excellent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a>, are planted as far as the 33rd degree, as in the southern provinces of France, and are equally vigorous. But at Morocco, where they yield a large and delicious grape, they are supported by vine-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a> five and six feet above ground; and as they are obliged to be watered, the little wine made there is seldom preserved. Figs are very good in some parts of the empire, but toward the south they are scarcely ripe before they are full of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-WORMS">worms</a>; the heats and night dews may, perhaps, contribute to this speedy decay. Melons, for the same reason, are rarely eatable; they have but a moment of maturity; which passes so rapidly that it is with difficulty feasted. Water-melons are everywhere reared, and in some provinces are excellent. Apricots, apples, and pears, are in tolerable plenty in the neighbourhood of Fez and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-MEQUINEZ">Mequinez</a>, where water is less scarce and the climate more temperate. But in the plains, which extend along the western coast, these delicate fruits are very indifferent, have less juice or taste, and the peaches there do not <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RIPEN">ripen</a>. The tree called the prickly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEAR">pear</a>, or the Barbary fig, is plentifully found in the empire of Morocco; and is planted round vineyards and gardens, because its thick and thorny leaves, which are wonderfully prolific, form impenetrable hedges. From these leaves a fruit is produced, covered with a thorny skin, that must be taken off with care. This fruit is mild, and full of very hard, small, kernels. The olive is everywhere found along the coast, but particularly to the south. The trees are planted in rows, which form alleys the more agreeable because the trees are large, round, and high in proportion. They take care to water them, the better to preserve the fruit. Oil of olives might here be plentifully extracted, were <a class="xref" href="../1823/vol6.html#article-TAXATION">taxation</a> fixed and moderate; but such has been the variation it has undergone, that the culture of olives is so neglected as scarcely to produce oil sufficient for internal consumption. In 1758 and 1769 there were near 40,000 quintals of oil exported from Mogador and Santa-Cruz to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MARSEILLES">Marseilles</a>, and ten years after it cost 15 d. per <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POUND">pound</a>. Thus do the vices of government expose nations to dearth and famine who live in the very bosom of abundance.
