In these and other beautiful birds, nature supplied them with all the colours which art can produce, and also some which art cannot imitate. At the undertaking of every Mosaic-work several artists assembled: After having agreed upon a design, and taken their measures and proportions, each artist charged himself with the execution of a certain part of the image, and exerted himself so diligently in it with such patience and application, that he frequently spent a whole day in adjusting a feather; first trying one, then another, viewing it sometimes one way, then another.

MOSAIC LAW

Pages 387-391
or the Law of Moses, is the most ancient that we know of in the world, and is of three kinds; the moral law, the ceremonial law, and the judicial law. The different manner in which each of these was delivered, may perhaps suggest to us a right idea of their different natures. The moral law, or ten commandments, for instance, was delivered on the top of the mountain, in the face of the whole world, as being of universal influence, and obligatory on all mankind. The ceremonial was received by Moses in private in the tabernacle, as being of peculiar concern, belonging to the Jews only, and destined to cease when the tabernacle was down, and the veil of the temple rent. As to the judicial law, it was neither so publicly nor so audibly given as the moral law, nor yet so privately as the ceremonial; this kind of law being of an indifferent nature, to be observed or not observed, as its rites suit with the place and government under which we live. The five books of Moses called the Pentateuch, are frequently styled, by way of emphasis, the Law. This was held by the Jews in such veneration, that they would not allow it to be laid upon the bed of any sick person, lest it should be polluted by touching the dead. MOSAMBICQUE

Pages 392-395

a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, lying south of Quiloa, and taking its name from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> town, which is situated on an <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, at the mouth of a river of the same name, in 15 deg. S. Lat. The island is 30 miles in circumference, and very populous, though the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> is said to be very hot, and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> in general dry, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a>, and barren; yet they have most of the tropical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> cattle, hogs, and sheep. There is a kind of fowl here, both the feathers and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> of which are black, inasmuch that, when they are boiled, the broth looks like <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-INK">ink</a>; and yet their flesh is very delicate and good food. The town of Mosambique is regularly fortified, and has a good harbour, defended by a citadel, with several churches and monasteries. The Portuguese shipping to and from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a> touch here for refreshments. As the island abounds in cattle, the Portuguese slaughter and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-SALT">salt</a> up a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of beef, which they afterwards send to the Brazils, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> sell to the European shipping. They also <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BARTER">barter</a> European goods with the natives for <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, elephants <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>, and slaves. There is another town called Mongole, situated also on an island, and garrisoned by the Portuguese, being their chief <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAGAZINE">magazine</a> for European goods. The gold they receive from the natives is found near the surface of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, or in the sands of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>; no gold <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>, or at least very few, being at present wrought in Africa.

MOSCHION

Pages 395-395

a name <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to four different writers, whose compositions, character, and native <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, are unknown. Some fragments of their writings remain, some few verses, and a treatise De mulierum affectibus.

MOSCHUS

Pages 395-396

in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ZOOLOGY">zoology</a>; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-QUADRUPEDS">quadrupeds</a> of the order of pecora, having no horns. There are eight small <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> in the lower jaw; in the upper, no cutting <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> fore teeth; but two <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a> tusks, one on each side, projecting out of the mouth. 1. The moschiferus, or Thibet <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MUSK">musk</a>, has a bag or tumour on the belly near the navel, and a very short tail almost hid in the fur. The length of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MALE">male</a> is about three feet three inches from the nose to the origin of the tail, and about two feet three inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> at the shoulder; the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> is less than the male, has a sharper nose, has no tusks nor musk-bag, and is provided with two teats. The head resembles that of the roe: the fur is coarse like that of the animals of the deer kind; but softer, very smooth, erect, plentiful, thick, and long: the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> varies according to the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of the animal and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the year; but is chiefly blackish <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> on the upper, and hoary, seldom <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, on the under parts of the body; the hoofs are long, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, and much divided, and the spurious hoofs of the fore feet are very long: the scrotum is of a bright <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RED">red</a> colour, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENIS">penis</a> very small. It inhabits the Asiatic <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a>, especially the highest <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROCKY_MOUNTAINS">rocky <a class=</a>"xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> from the Altai chain to that which divides Thibet from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a>; likewise in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHINA">China</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TONQUIN">Tonquin</a>, and in eastern <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SIBERIA">Siberia</a> about lake <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAIKAL">Baikal</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Jenicha and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARGUN">Argun</a>. It avoids mankind, dwelling solitarily in the most precipitous places of the mountains, among rocks in the small narrow valleys surrounded by the snowy hills, and the pine forests which grow in their interstices. It is a very gentle and timid animal, except in rutting time, when the males fight violently with their tusks for the females; it is exceedingly <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LEAPING">leaping</a>, running, climbing, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWIMMING">swimming</a>, and is very difficultly tamed; the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> is eatable, and that of the younger animals is reckoned delicate. chace of them is a trade equally difficult and hazardous; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> pursued, they seek the highest tops of the snowy peaks, inaccessible to men or dogs. They take amazing leaps over the tremendous chains of their alps, or from rock to rock; treading so lightly on the snow with their true and false hoofs extended, as scarcely to leave a mark; while the dogs which pursue them sink in, and are forced to desist from the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHASE">chase</a>. They are so fond of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> as never to be kept alive in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a>. They are mostly taken in snares, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> by crossbows placed in their tracks, with a string from the trigger for them to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREAD">tread</a> on, and discharge. The Tungus shoot them with bows and arrows. The skins are used for bonnets and winter dresses. The Russian often scrape off the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, and have a way of preparing them for <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> clothing, so as to become as soft and shining as <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SILK">silk</a>. The noted drug the musk is produced from the male. The bag or follicle that contains it is situated near the prepuce; and is of a somewhat oval <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, flat on one side and rounded on the other, having a small open orifice. In young animals this bag is empty; but in adults it is filled with a clotted, oily, friable <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, of a dark brown colour: this is the true musk, of which each bag contains from a dram and a half to two drams. The best comes from Thibet; that which is produced in Siberia having somewhat of the flavour of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CASTOR">castor</a>. 2. The Americanus, or Brazilian musk, of a reddish brown colour, with a black muzzle and white throat, is scarcely so <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> as a roe-buck. The fur is soft and short; the colour of the head and upper <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> of the neck is dark brown; the lower part of the neck and throat are white; the body and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a> are reddish brown; the hind legs are longer than the fore. This animal, which inhabits <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GUIANA">Guiana</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRAZIL">Brazil</a>, is exceedingly timid, active, and swift. Numbers are frequently seen swimming the rivers, and at that time are easily taken. The Indians hunt them, and their flesh is esteemed very delicate. The French of Guiana call them biches or does, because, notwithstanding their likenesses to deer, both sexes are without horns. Gmelin supposes this animal may only be a tawn of the American roe. 3. The Indicus, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> musk, has short hair of a tawny colour on the upper and whitish on the under parts of the body; the tail is short, and the feet have spurious hoofs. It inhabits India, and is much of the same size with the moschiferus, but the tail is longer and more perceptible; the legs are very slender; and the head resembles that of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, with erect <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> ears. 4. The pigmæus, or pigmy musk, is marked as to colour like the former, but has no spurious hoofs.—The body and head <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> only <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NINE">nine</a> inches and a half in length; the tail is about an inch long; and the legs are smaller than a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s finger. It inhabits the East Indies and several of the Indian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>. It is called kantchel by the Malayes, and po-tjang by the inhabitants of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JAVA">Java</a>. The natives catch them in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> numbers, carry them in cages to market, and sell them for 2½ d. a piece. 5. The meminna, or Ceylon chevrotin, is in length 17 inches from the nose to the rump, and of a cinereous olive colour; the throat, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>, and belly, are white; the sides and haunches spotted, and barred transversely with white; and the ears are large and Meminna open: the tail is very short; and the feet have no spurious hoofs. It inhabits Ceylon and Java. 6. The javanicus, or Javan musk, is of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FERRUGINOUS">ferruginous</a> colour on the upper parts of the body, and white all along the under; the tail is long and hairy, white below and at the tip; its legs are similar to those of the pigmy musk, and furnished with very small spurious hoofs. This and the meminna seem only varieties of the pigmæus.

MOSCOW

Pages 396-400

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of the empire of Russia, deriving its name from the river Mulcova, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> Molkva, on which the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> is situated. It was from this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> that the czars of old took the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of dukes of Mytchov. The province is bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the duchies of Twere, Roitow, Sufdai, and Wododiner; on the south by Rezan, from which it is separated by the river Occa; on the east by the principality of Cacheine, and the same river Occa parting it from Nissi-novgorod; and on the west by the duchies of Rzeva, Biela, and Smolensko. It extends about 200 miles in length, and about 100 in breadth; and is watered by the Molkva, Occa, and Cleima, which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> into the Wolga: nevertheless, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is not very fertile. The <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>, however, though sharp, is salubrious; and this consideration, with the advantage of its being situated in the midst of the best provinces in the empire, induced the czars to make it their chief residence. In the western <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> of Moscow is a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> forest, from whence flows the celebrated river Nieper, or Borythines, which, traversing the duchy of Smolensko, winds in a serpentine course to Ukraine, Lithuania, and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>. Moscow, the capital of the above province, and till the beginning of the present century the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a> of all Russia, is situated in a spacious plain on the banks of the river Mulcova. The Russian antiquaries differ considerably in their opinions concerning the first foundation of Moscow; the following relation, Mr Coxe lays, is generally esteemed by the best authors the most probable account. Kiof was the metropolis, when George son of Vladimir Monomakha ascended in 1154 the Russian throne. That monarch, being insulted in a progress through his dominions by a rich and powerful nobleman named Stephen Kutchko, put him to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, and confiscated his domains, which consisted of the lands now occupied by the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Moscow and the adjacent territory. Pleased with the situation of the ground lying at the confluence of the Molkva and Neglina, he laid the foundation of a new town, which he called Molkva from the river of that name. Upon the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEMISE">demise</a> of George, the new town was not neglected by his son Andrew, who transferred the seat of empire from Kiof to Vladimir; but it fell into such decay under his immediate successors, that when Daniel, son of Alexander Nevski, received, in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the empire, the duchy of Mulkovo as his portion, and fixed his residence upon the confluence of the Molkva and Neglina, he may be said to have newly founded the town. The spot now occupied by the Kremlin was at that <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> overspread with a thick wood and a morass, in the midst whereof was a small <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> containing a single wooden hut. Upon this part Daniel constructed churches and monasteries, and various buildings, and enclosed Moscow enclosed it with wooden fortifications; he first assumed the title of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Moscow; and was so attached to this situation, that when in 1394 he succeeded his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Andrew Alexandrovich in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> duchy of Vladimir, he did not remove his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COURT">court</a> to Vladimir, but <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> his residence at Moscow, which then became the capital of the Russian dominions. His successors followed his example; among whom his son Ivan considerably enlarged the new metropolis, and in 1367 his grandson Demetrius Ivanovich Doniski surrounded the Kremlin with a brick wall. These new fortifications, however, were not strong enough to prevent <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TAMERLANE">Tamerlane</a> in 1382 from taking the town, after a short siege. Being soon evacuated by that defunct conqueror, it again came into the possession of the Russians; but was frequently invaded and occupied by the Tartars, who in the 14th and 15th centuries overran the greatest part of Russia, and who even maintained a garrison in Moscow until they were finally expelled by Ivan Vasilievitch I. To him Moscow is indebted for its <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> splendor, and under him it became the principal and most considerable city of the Russian empire. Moscow continued the metropolis of Russia until the beginning of the present century, when, to the great dissatisfaction of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, but with great advantage probably to the state, the seat of empire was transferred to Petersburgh. Notwithstanding the predilection which <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> conceived for Petersburgh, in which all the succeeding sovereigns excepting Peter II. have fixed their residence, Moscow, according to Mr Coxe, is still the most populous city of the Russian empire. Here the chief <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a> who do not belong to the court of the emperors reside: they here support a larger <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of retainers; they <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LOVE">love</a> to gratify their <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for a ruder and more expensive magnificence in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> style of feudal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a>; and are not, as at Petersburgh, eclipsed by the superior splendor of the court. Moscow is represented as the largest town in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>; its circumference within the rampart, which encloses the suburbs, being exactly 39 versts or 26 miles; but it is built in so straggling and disjointed a manner, that its <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> in no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> corresponds to its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>. Some Russian authors state its inhabitants at 500,000 souls, a number evidently exaggerated. According to a late computation, which Mr Coxe says may be depended upon, Moscow contains within the ramparts 250,000 souls, and in the adjacent villages 50,000. The streets of Moscow are in general exceedingly <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>: some of them are paved; others, particularly those in the suburbs, are formed with trunks of trees, or are boarded with planks like the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a> of a room; wretched hovels are blended with large palaces; cottages of one story stand next to the most superb and statelike mansions. Many brick structures are covered with wooden tops; some of the wooden houses are painted; others have <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-IRON">iron</a> doors and roofs. Numerous churches present themselves in every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>, built in a peculiar style of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>; some with domes of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, others of tin, gilt or painted green, and many roofed with wood. In a word, some parts of this vast city have the look of a sequestered <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a>, other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of a populous town; some of a contemptible village, others of a great capital. Moscow may be considered as a town built upon the Asiatic <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MODEL">model</a>, but gradually becoming more and more European, and exhibiting in its present state a motley mixture of discordant architecture. It is distributed into the following divisions. 1. The Kremlin. This stands in the central and highest part of the city; is of a triangular form, and about two miles in circumference; and is surrounded by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> walls of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-STONE">stone</a> and brick, which were constructed in the year 1491, under the reign of Ivan Vasilievitch I. It contains the ancient <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of the czars, several churches, two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a>, the patriarchal palace, the arsenal now in ruins, and one private <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, which belonged to Boris Godunof before he was raised to the throne. 2. Khitaigorod, or the Chinese town, is inclosed on one side by that wall of the Kremlin which runs from the Moikva to the Neglina; and on the other side by a brick wall of inferior height. It is much larger than the Kremlin, and contains the university, the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a>-house, and many other public buildings, and all the tradesmen's shops. The edifices are mostly stuccoed or <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WHITE">white</a>-washed, and it has the only street in Moscow in which the houses stand <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to one another without any intervals between them. 3. The Bielgorod, or White Town, which runs quite round the two preceding divisions, is supposed to derive its name from a white wall with which it was formerly inclosed, and of which some remains are still to be seen. 4. Semlinoigorod, which environs all the three other quarters, takes its denomination from a circular rampart of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> with which it is encompassed. These two last mentioned divisions exhibit a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GROTESQUE">grotesque</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GROUP">group</a> of churches, convents, palaces, brick and wooden houses, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> hovels, in no degree superior to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PEASANT">peasant</a>'s cottages. 5. The Sloboda, or suburbs, form a vast exterior circle round all the parts already described, and are invested with a low rampart and ditch. These suburbs contain, beside buildings of all kinds and denominations, corn fields, much open pasture, and some small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>, which give rise to the Neglina. The river Moikva, from which the city takes its name, flows through it in a winding channel; but, excepting in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, is only navigable for rafts. It receives the Yauza in the Semlinoigorod, and the Neglina at the western extremity of the Kremlin; the beds of both these last-mentioned rivulets are in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> little better than dry channels. The places of divine worship at Moscow are exceedingly numerous: including chapels, they amount to above 1000; there are 484 public churches, of which 199 are of brick, and the others of wood; the former are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> stuccoed or white-washed, the latter painted of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. The most ancient churches of Moscow are generally <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> buildings, with a cupola and four small domes, some whereof are of copper or iron gilt; others of tin, either plain or painted green. These cupolas and domes are for the most part ornamented with crosses entwined with thin chains or wires. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of the Holy Trinity, sometimes called the church of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, which stands in the Khitaigorod, close to the gate leading into the Kremlin, has a kind of high steeple and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NINE">nine</a> or ten domes. Moscow. James: it was built in the reign of Ivan Vassilievich II. The inside of the churches is mostly composed of three parts: that called by the Greeks "trapeza"; by the Russians "trapeza"; the body; and the sanctuary or shrine. Over the door of each church is the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PORTRAIT">portrait</a> of the saint to whom it is dedicated, to which the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMON">common</a> people pay their homage as they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> along by taking off their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HATS">hats</a>, crossing themselves, and occasionally touching the ground with their heads. The bells, which form no inconsiderable part of public worship in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, as the length or shortness of their peals affects the greater or lesser sanctity of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, are hung in belfreys detached from the church; they do not swing like our bells; but are fixed immovably to the beams, and are rung by a rope tied to the clapper and pulled sideways. Some of these bells are of a stupendous size; one in the tower of St. Ivan's church weighs 351 Russian pounds, or 127 English pounds. It has always been esteemed a meritorious <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> to present a church with bells; and the piety of the donor has been measured by their magnitude. According to this <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of estimation, Boris Godunof, who gave a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELL">bell</a> of 283,000 pounds to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> of Moscow, was the most pious sovereign of Russia, until he was surpassed by the empress <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>, at whose expense a bell was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> weighing 432,000 pounds, and which exceeded in bigness every bell in the known world. The height of this enormous bell is 19 feet, its circumference at the bottom 21 yards 11 inches; its greatest thickness 23 inches. The beam to which this vast machine was fastened being accidentally burnt, the bell fell <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, and a fragment was broken off towards the bottom, which left an aperture large enough to admit two persons abreast without stooping. The palace, inhabited by the ancient czars, stands at the extremity of the Kremlin. Part of this palace is old, and remains in the same state in which it was built under Ivan Vassilievich I. The remainder has been successively added at different intervals without any <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>, and in various styles of architecture, which has produced a motley pile of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, remarkable for nothing but the incongruity of the several structures. The top is thickly set, with numerous little gilded spires and globes; and a large portion of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FRONT">front</a> is decorated with the arms of all the provinces which compose the Russian empire. The apartments are in general exceedingly small, excepting one single room called the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>-chamber, in which the ancient czars used to give audience to foreign ambassadors, and which has been repeatedly described by several English travellers who visited Moscow before the Imperial residence was transferred to Petersburgh. The room is large and vaulted, and has in the centre an enormous pillar of stone which supports the ceiling. In this palace Peter the Great came into the world, in the year 1672. In that part called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a> are repolished the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, jewels, and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> robes, used at the coronation of the sovereign, besides several curiosities relative to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the country. Of the great number of churches contained in this city, two in particular, namely, that of St Michael and that of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSUMPTION">Assumption</a> of the Virgin <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, are remarkable; the one for being the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where the sovereigns of Russia were formerly interred, and the other where they are crowned. These edifices, which are situated in the Kremlin, are both in the same style of architecture; and their exterior form, though modelled according to the ancient style of the country, is not absolutely elegant. In the cathedral of St Michael, which contains the tombs of the Russian sovereigns, the bodies are not, as with us, deposited in vaults, or beneath the pavement, but are entombed in raised sepulchres, mostly of brick, in the shape of a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COFFIN">coffin</a>, and about two feet in height. When Mr Coxe visited the cathedral, the most ancient were covered with palls of red cloth, others of red velvet, and that of Peter II. with <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> tissue, bordered with silver fringe and ermine. Each <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> has at its lower extremity a small silver plate, upon which is engraved the name of the deceased sovereign, and the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DATE">date</a> of his death. The cathedral of the assumption of the Virgin Mary, which has long been appropriated to the coronation of the Russian sovereigns, is the most splendid and magnificent in Moscow. The screen is in many parts covered with plates of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> silver and gold richly worked. From the centre of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> hangs an enormous chandelier of maffy silver, weighing 294 pounds; it was made in England, and was a present from Morolof, prime minister and favourite of Alexey Michaelowitch. The sacred utensils and episcopal vestments are extraordinarily rich, but the taste of the workmanship is in general rude, and by no means equal to the materials. Many of the paintings which cover the inside walls are of a colossal size; some are very ancient, and were executed so early as in the latter end of the 15th century. It contains, amongst the rest, a head of the virgin, supposed to have been delineated by St Luke, and greatly celebrated in this country for its sanctity and the power of working <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a>. Its <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FACE">face</a> is almost <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>; its head is ornamented with a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> of precious <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, and its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> and body are gilded, which gives it a most grotesque appearance. It is placed in the screen, and enclosed within a large silver covering, which is only taken off on great festivals, or for the curiosity of strangers. In this cathedral are deposited the remains of the Russian patriarchs. The place in the Khitaigorod, where the public archives are deposited, is a strong brick building, containing several vaulted apartments with iron floors. These archives, consisting of a numerous collection of state-papers, were crowded into boxes, and thrown aside like common lumber, until the present empress ordered them to be revised and arranged. In conformity to this mandate, Mr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MULLER">Muller</a> has disposed them in chronological order with such perfect regularity, that any single <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DOCUMENT">document</a> may be inspected with little trouble. They are enclosed in separate cabinets with glass doors; those relative to Russia are all classified according to the several provinces which they concern; and over each cabinet is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a> the name of the province to which it is appropriated. In the same manner the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a> relative to foreign kingdoms are placed in separate divisions under the respective titles of Poland, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, England, France, Germany, &c. The university of Moscow, also situated in the Khitaigorod, was founded, at the instance of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> Shuvalof, by the empress <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, for 600 students; who are clothed, clothed, boarded, and instructed, at the expense of the crown. Besides this <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a>, there are two gymnasia or seminaries for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> of youth, endowed also by Elizabeth; in which are taught, by twenty-three philosophers, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>, classics, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, the Greek, Latin, Russian, German, French, Italian, and Tartar languages; history, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">geography</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, architecture, fortification, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALGEBRA">algebra</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, music, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FENCING">fencing</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-READING">reading</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>. Moscow is the centre of the inland <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> of Russia, and particularly connects the trade between Europe and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SIBERIA">Siberia</a>. The only <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a> to this city is formed by the Moskva, which falling into the Oka near Columna, communicates by means of that river with the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-VOLGA">Volga</a>. But as the Moskva is only navigable in spring upon the melting of the snows, the principal merchandise is conveyed to and from Moscow upon sledges in winter. As to the retail commerce here, the whole of it is carried on in the Khitaigorod; where, according to a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> common in Russia, as well as in most kingdoms of the East, all the shops are collected together in one spot. The place is like a kind of fair, consisting of many rows of low brick buildings; the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> between them resembling alleys. These shops or booths occupy a considerable space; they do not, as with us, make part of the houses inhabited by the tradesmen, but are quite detached from their dwellings, which for the most part are at some distance in another quarter of the town. The tradesman comes to his shop in the morning, remains there all day, and returns home to his family in the afternoon. Every trade has its separate department; and they who sell the same goods have booths adjoining to each other. Furs and skins form the most considerable article of commerce in Moscow; and the shops which vend those commodities occupy several streets. Among the curiosities of Moscow, the market for the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-SALE">sale</a> of houses is not the least remarkable. It is held in a large open space in one of the suburbs; and exhibits a great variety of ready-made houses, thickly strewed upon the ground. The purchaser who wants a dwelling, repairs to this spot, mentions the number of rooms he requires, examines the different timbers, which are regularly numbered, and bargains for that which suits him. The house is sometimes paid for on the spot, and taken away by the purchaser; or sometimes the vender contracts to transport and erect it upon the place where it is designed to stand. It may appear incredible to assert, that a dwelling may be thus bought, removed, raised, and inhabited, within the space of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a>; but we shall conceive it practicable by considering that these ready-made houses are in general merely collections of trunks of trees tenanted and mortised at each extremity into one another, so that nothing more is required than the labour of transporting and adjusting them. But this summary mode of building is not always peculiar to the meaner hovels; as wooden structures of very large dimensions and handsome appearance are occasionally formed in Russia with an expedition almost inconceivable to the inhabitants of other countries. A remarkable instance of this dispatch was displayed the last time the empress came to Moscow. Her majesty proposed to reside in the mansion of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> Galitzin, which is esteemed the completest edifice in this city; but as it was not sufficiently spacious for her reception, a temporary addition of wood, larger than the original house, and containing a magnificent suite of apartments, was begun and finished within the space of six weeks. This <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-METEOR">meteor</a>-like fabric was so handsome and commodious, that the materials which were taken down at her majesty's departure, were to be reconstructed as a kind of imperial villa upon an eminence near the city. Mr Coxe mentions an admirable <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol18.html#article-POLICE">police</a> in this city for preventing riots, or for stopping the concourse of people in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CASE">case</a> of fires, which are very frequent and violent in those parts, where the houses are mostly of wood, and the streets are laid with <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>. At the entrance of each street there is a chevaux de frise gate, one end whereof turns upon a pivot, and the other rolls upon a wheel; near it is a sentry-box in which a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAN">man</a> is occasionally stationed. In times of riot or fire the centinel shuts the gate, and all passage is immediately stopped. Among the public institutions of Moscow, the most remarkable is the Foundling <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOSPITAL">Hospital</a>, endowed in 1764 by the present empress, and supported by voluntary contributions and legacies, and other charitable gifts. In order to encourage donations, her majesty grants to all benefactors some valuable privileges, and a certain degree of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RANK">rank</a> in proportion to the extent of their liberality. Among the principal contributors must be mentioned a private merchant named Dimidoff, a person of great wealth, who has expended in favour of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> above £100,000. The hospital, which is situated in a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIRY">airy</a> part of the town upon a gentle ascent near the river Moskva, is an immense pile of building of a quadrangular shape, part of which was only finished when Mr Coxe (whose account we are transcribing) was at Moscow. It contained, at that time, 3000 foundlings; and, when the whole is completed, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a> receive 8000. The children are brought to the porter's lodge, and admitted without any recommendation. The rooms are lofty and large; the dormitories, which are separate from the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> rooms, are very airy, and the beds are not crowded; each foundling, even each infant, has a separate <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a>; the bedsteads are of iron; the sheets are changed every week, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> three times a-week. Through the whole rooms the greatest neatness prevails; even the nurseries being uncommonly clean, and without any unwholesome smells. No cradles are allowed, and rocking is particularly forbidden. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INFANTS">infants</a> are not swaddled according to the custom of the country, but looely dressed.—The foundlings are divided into separate classes, according to their respective ages. The children remain two years in the nursery, when they are admitted into the lowest class; the boys and girls continue together until they are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, at which time they are separated. They all learn to read, write, and cast accounts. The boys are taught to knit; they occasionally card <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, and work in the different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>. The girls learn to knit, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NET">net</a>, and all kinds of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a>-work; they spin and weave <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LACE">lace</a>; they are employed in cookery, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAKING">baking</a>, and house-work of all sorts. At the age of 14 the foundlings enter into the first class; when they have the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of choosing any particular branch of trade; and for this purpose there are different <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of manufactures established in the hospital, of which the principal are <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-EMBROIDERY">embroidery</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SILK">silk</a> stockings, ribbands, lace, gloves, buttons, and cabinet work. A separate room is appropriated to each trade. Some boys and girls are instructed in the French and German languages, and a few boys in the Latin tongue; others learn music, drawing, and dancing. About the age of 20, the foundlings receive a sum of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, and several other advantages, which enable them to follow their trade in any part of the empire; a very considerable privilege in Russia, where the peasants are slaves, and cannot leave their village without the permission of their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MASTER">master</a>.—The girls and boys eat separately. The dining rooms, which are upon the ground-floor, are large and vaulted, and differing from their work-rooms. The first class sit at <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TABLE">table</a>; the rest stand: the little children are attended by servants; but those of the first or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SECOND">second</a> class alternately wait upon each other. Their victuals are of the most wholesome and nourishing kinds. Each foundling has a napkin, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PEWTER">pewter</a> plate, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a>, fork, and spoon: the napkin and table-cloth are clean three times in the week. They rise at six, dine at eleven, and sup at six. The little children have <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> at seven and at four. When they are not employed in their necessary occupations, the utmost freedom is allowed, and they are encouraged to be as much in the air as possible.

MOSELLE

Pages 400-400

a river of Germany, which rises in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of Vauge in Lorraine, and, running through that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-ELECTORATE">electorate</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRIER">Trier</a>, falls into the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a> at Coblentz.

MOSES

Pages 400-401

the son of Amram and Jochebed, was born in the year 1571 before Christ. <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PHARAOH">Pharaoh</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, perceiving that the Hebrews were become a formidable <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, issued forth an edict commanding all the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MALE">male</a> children to be put to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. Jochebed, the mother of Moses, having, to avoid this cruel edict, concealed her son for three months, at length made an ark <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASKET">basket</a> of bulrushes, daubed it with pitch, laid the child in it, and exposed him on the banks of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NILE">Nile</a>. Thermuthis the king's <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>, who happened to be walking by the river's side, perceived the floating cradle, commanded it to be brought to her, and, struck with the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of the child, determined to preserve his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. In three years afterwards the princess adopted him for her own son, called his name Moses, and caused him be diligently instructed in all the learning of the Egyptians. But his father and mother, to whom he was restored by a fortunate accident, were at still greater pains to teach him the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> of his fathers. Many things are related by historians concerning the first <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of Moses's life, which are not to be found in the Old <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>. According to Josephus and Eusebius, he made <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WAR">war</a> on the Ethiopians, and completely defeated them. They add, that the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CITY">city</a> Saba, in which the enemy had been forced to take refuge, was betrayed into his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> by the king's daughter, who became deeply enamoured of him, when she beheld from the top of the walls his valorous exploits at the head of the Egyptian <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>. But as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of this expedition is more than doubtful, we shall therefore confine ourselves to the narrative of sacred writ, which commences at the fortieth year of Moses's life. He then left the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COURT">court</a> of Pharaoh, and went to visit his countrymen the Hebrews, who groaned under the ill-usage and oppression of their unfeeling masters. Having perceived an Egyptian smiting an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a>, he slew the Egyptian, and buried him in the sand. But he was obliged, in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MURDER">murder</a>, to fly into the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAND">land</a> of Midian, where he married Zipporah, daughter of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> Jethro, by whom he had two sons, Gerhohom and Eliezar. Here he lived 40 years; during which <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> his employment was to tend the flocks of his father-in-<a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAW">law</a>. Having one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> led his flock towards Mount Horeb, God appeared to him in the midst of a bush which burned with fire but was not consumed, and commanded him to go and deliver his brethren from their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONDAGE">bondage</a>. Moses at first refused to go; but was at length prevailed on by two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a> which the Almighty wrought for his conviction. Upon his return to Egypt, he, together with his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AARON">Aaron</a>, went to the court of Pharaoh, and told him that God commanded him to let the Hebrews go to offer sacrifices in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>. But the impious monarch disregarded this command, and caused the labour of the Israelites to be doubled. The messengers of the Almighty again returned to the king, and wrought a miracle in his sight, that they might move his heart, and induce him to let the people depart. Aaron having <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DOWN">down</a> his miraculous rod, it was immediately converted into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERPENT">serpent</a>; but the same thing being performed by the magicians, the king's heart was hardened more and more; and his obstinacy at last drew down the judgments of the Almighty on his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, which was afflicted with ten dreadful plagues. The first was the changing of the waters of the Nile and of all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> into blood, so that the Egyptians died of thirst. In consequence of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a>, the land was covered with innumerable swarms of frogs, which entered even into Pharaoh's <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>. By the third plague, the dust was converted into <a class="xref" href="../1823/vol0.html#article-LICE">lice</a>, which cruelly tormented both <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAN">man</a> and beast. The fourth plague was a multitude of destructive flies which spread throughout Egypt, and infected the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. The fifth was a sudden pestilence, which destroyed all the cattle of the Egyptians, without injuring those of the Israelites. The sixth produced numberless ulcers and fiery biles upon man and upon beast. The seventh was a dreadful storm of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAIL">hail</a>, accompanied with <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a>, which destroyed every thing that was in the field, whether man or beast, and spared only the land of Goshen, where the children of Israel dwelt. By the eighth plague swarms of locusts were brought into the country, which devoured every green <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HERB">herb</a>, the fruit of the trees and the produce of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a>. By the ninth plague thick darkness covered all the land of Egypt, except the dwellings of the children of Israel. The tenth and last plague was the death of the first-born in Egypt, who were all in one night cut off by the destroying angel, from the first-born of the king to the first-born of the slaves and of the cattle. This dreadful calamity moved the heart of the hardened Pharaoh, and he at length consented to allow the people of Israel to depart from his kingdom. Profane authors who have spoken of Moses, seem to have been in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> acquainted with these mighty wonders. wonders. That he performed miracles, must have been allowed by many, by whom he was considered as a famous magician; and he could scarcely appear in any other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> to men who did not acknowledge him for the messenger of the Almighty. Both Diodorus and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a> mention the distressful state to which Egypt was reduced by these terrible calamities. The Hebrews, amounting to the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of 600,000 men, without reckoning women and children, left Egypt on the 15th day of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MONTH">month</a> Nisan, which, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of this deliverance, was thenceforth reckoned the first month of their year. Scarcely had they reached the shore of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RED_SEA"><a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RED">Red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SEA">Sea</a> when Pharaoh with a powerful army set out in pursuit of them. On this occasion Moses stretched forth his rod upon the sea; and the waters thereof being divided, remained suspended on both sides till the Hebrews passed through dry-footed. The Egyptians determined to follow the same course; but God caused a violent <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> to blow, which brought back the waters to their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a>, and the whole army of Pharaoh perished in the waves. After the miraculous passage of the Red Sea, the army proceeded towards Mount <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SINAI">Sinai</a>, and arrived at Marah, where the waters were bitter; but Moses, by casting a tree into them, rendered them fit for drinking. Their tenth encampment was at Rephidim; where Moses drew <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WATER">water</a> from the rock in Horeb, by smiting it with his rod. Here likewise Amalek attacked Israel. While Joshua fought against the Amalekites, Moses stood on the top of a hill, and lifted up his hands; in consequence of which the Israelites prevailed, and cut their enemies in pieces. They at length arrived at the foot of Mount Sinai on the third day of the ninth month after their departure from Egypt. Moses having ascended several times into the Mount, received the law from the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAND">hand</a> of God himself in the midst of thunders and lightnings, and concluded the famous covenant betwixt the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> and the children of Israel. When he descended from Sinai, he found that the people had fallen into the idolatrous worship of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> calf. The messenger of God, shocked at such ingratitude, broke in pieces the tables of the law which he carried in his hands, and put 23,000 of the transgressors to the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>. He afterwards reascended into the mountain, and there obtained new tables of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-STONE">stone</a> on which the law was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a>. When Moses descended, his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FACE">face</a> shone so that the Israelites dared not to come nigh unto him, and he was obliged to cover it with a veil. The Israelites were here employed in constructing the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TABERNACLE">tabernacle</a> according to a pattern shown them by God. It was erected and consecrated at the foot of the Mount Sinai on the first day of the first month of the second year after their departure from Egypt; and it served the Israelites instead of a temple till the time of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a>, who built a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> for the God of his fathers after a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MODEL">model</a> shown him by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DAVID">David</a>. Moses having dedicated the tabernacle, he consecrated Aaron and his sons to be its ministers, and appointed the Levites to its <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. He likewise gave various commandments concerning the worship of God and the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of the Jews. This was a theocracy in the full <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of the word. God himself governed them immediately by means of his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> Moses, whom he had chosen to be the interpreter of his <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a> to the people; and he required all the honours belonging to their king to be paid unto himself. He dwelt in his tabernacle, which was situated in the middle of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>, like a monarch in his palace. He gave answers to those who consulted him, and himself denounced punishments against the transgressors of his laws. This properly was the time of the theocracy, taken in its full extent; for God was not only considered as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> who was the object of their <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> worship, but as the sovereign to whom the honours of supreme majesty were paid. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CASE">case</a> was nearly the same under Joshua; who, being filled with the spirit of Moses, undertook nothing without consulting God. Every <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, both of the leader and of the people, was regulated by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the Almighty, who rewarded their fidelity and obedience by a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of miracles, victories, and successes. After Moses had regulated every thing regarding the civil administration, and the marching of the troops, he led the Israelites to the confines of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANAAN">Canaan</a>, to the foot of Mount Nebo. Here the Lord commanded him to ascend into the mountain; whence he showed him the promised land, whereunto he was not permitted to enter. He immediately after yielded up the ghost, without sickness or pain, in the 120th year of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, and 1451 years before <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ. Moses is incontestably the author of the first five books of the Old Testament, which go by the name of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENTATEUCH">Pentateuch</a>; and which are acknowledged to be inspired, by the Jews and by <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> of every persuasion. Some, however, have denied that Moses was the author of these books; and have founded their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> on this, that he always speaks of himself in the third person. But this manner of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> is by no means peculiar to Moses: it occurs also in several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> historians; such as Xenophon, Caesar, Josephus, &c., who, possessed of more <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a> or good <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> than some <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> historians, whose egotism is altogether disgusting, have not like them left to posterity a spectacle of ridiculous vanity and self-conceit. After all, it is proper to observe, that profane authors have related many falsehoods and absurdities concerning Moses, and concerning the origin and the religion of the Jews, with which they were but little acquainted. Plutarch, in his book concerning Isis and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OSIRIS">Osiris</a>, says, that Judæus and Hierostratus were brothers, and descended from Typhon; and that the former gave his name to the country and its inhabitants, and the latter to the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> city. Others say that they came from Mount Ida in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PHRYGIA">Phrygia</a>. Strabo is the only author who speaks anything like reason and truth concerning them; tho' he too says that they were descended from the Egyptians, and considers Moses their <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LEGISLATOR">legislator</a> as an Egyptian priest. He acknowledges, however, that they were a people strictly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> and sincerely religious. Other authors by whom they are mentioned, seem not to have had the smallest acquaintance either with their laws or their worship. They frequently confound them with the Christians, as is the case with Juvenal, Tacitus, and Quintilian.

MOSHEIM

Pages 401-402

an illustrious German divine, was born in 1695, of a noble family, which might seem to open to his ambition a fair path to civil promotion; but his zeal for the interests of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, religion, his thirst after knowledge, and particularly his <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for sacred literature, induced him to consecrate his talents to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. The German <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a> loaded him with literary honours; the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a> invited him to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COPENHAGEN">Copenhagen</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BRUNSWICK">Brunswick</a> called him thence to Helmstadt, where he filled the academical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>; was honoured with the character of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> counsellor to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COURT">court</a>; and presided over the seminaries of learning in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Wolfenbuttle and the principality of Blackenburgh. When a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> was formed of giving an uncommon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of lustre to the university of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GOTTINGEN">Gottingen</a>, by filling it with men of the first <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RANK">rank</a> in letters, Dr Mosheim was deemed worthy to appear at the head of it, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>; and here he died, universally lamented, in 1755. In depth of judgment, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of learning, in purity of taste, in the powers of eloquence, and in a laborious application to all the various branches of erudition and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, he had certainly very few superiors. His Latin translation of Cudworth's Intellectual System, enriched with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> annotations, discovered a profound acquaintance with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> learning and philosophy. His illustrations of the Scriptures, his labours in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of Christianity, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> he <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> upon religion and philosophy, appear in many volumes of sacred and profane literature; and his Ecclesiastical <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, from the birth of Christ to the beginning of the present century, is unquestionably the best that is extant. This <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>, written in Latin, has been translated into English, and accompanied with notes and chronological tables by Archibald Macalpine, D.D. and from this translator's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SECOND">second</a> edition, 1758, in 5 vols 8vo, this short account is taken.

MOSKITO-COUNTRY

Pages 402-402

is situated in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, between 85 and 88 degrees of west <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a>, and between 13 and 15 degrees of north latitude; having the north <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SEA">sea</a> on the north and east, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NICARAGUA">Nicaragua</a> on the south, and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HONDURAS">Honduras</a> on the west; and indeed the Spaniards esteem it a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> of the principality of Honduras, though they have no colonies in the Mosquito <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. When the Spaniards first invaded this part of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a>, they massacred the greatest part of the natives, which gave those that escaped into the inaccessible part of the country an insuperable aversion to them; and they have always appeared ready to join any Europeans that come upon their coasts against the Spaniards, and particularly the English, who frequently come hither; and the Mosquito men being excellent marksmen, the English employ them in striking the maratee fish, &c. and many of the Mosquito Indians come to Jamaica, and sail with the English in their voyages. These people are so situated between morasses and inaccessible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, and a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COAST">coast</a> full of rocks and shoals, that no attempts against them by the Spaniards, whom they mortally hate, could ever succeed. Nevertheless, they are a mild inoffensive people, of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> morality and virtue, and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a> never trust a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAN">man</a> who has once deceived them. They have so great a veneration towards the English, that they have spontaneously put themselves and their lands under the protection and dominion of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of England. This was first done when the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBEMARLE">Albemarle</a> was governor of Jamaica, and the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">king</a> of the Moskitos received a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> from his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>, under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEAL">seal</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>; since which <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> they have not only been steady in their <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> with the English, but warm in their affections, and very useful to them on many occasions. When their king dies, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MALE">male</a> heir goes to Jamaica, to certify that he is next in blood, and receives a commission in form from the governor of Jamaica to be king of the Moskitos, till which he is not acknowledged as such by his countrymen. So fond are these people of every thing that is English, that the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMON">common</a> people are proud of every Christian <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SURNAME">surname</a> given them by our seamen, who <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> men with the titles of some of our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>.

MOSQUE

Pages 402-402

a temple <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> worship among the Mahometans. All mosques are <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> buildings, generally constructed of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-STONE">stone</a>. Before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> gate there is a square <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COURT">court</a> paved with <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WHITE">white</a> marble; and low galleries round it, whose <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> is supported by marble pillars. In these galleries the Turks wash themselves before they go into the mosque. In each mosque there is a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of lamps; and between these hang many crystal rings, ostriches eggs, and other curiosities, which, when the lamps are lighted, make a fine show. As it is not lawful to enter the mosque with stockings or shoes on, the pavements are covered with pieces of stuff sewed together, each being wide enough to hold a row of men kneeling, sitting, or prostrate. The women are not allowed to enter the mosque, but stay in the porches without. About every mosque there are six <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> towers, called minarets, each of which has three little open galleries one above another; these towers, as well as the mosques, are covered with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, and adorned with gilding and other ornaments; and from thence, instead of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELL">bell</a>, the people are called to prayers by certain officers appointed for that purpose. Most of the mosques have a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a> belonging to them, in which travellers of what <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> soever are entertained three days. Each mosque has also a place called tarbe, which is the burying-place of its founders; within which is a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> fix or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> feet <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a>, covered with green velvet or satinn; at the ends of which are two tapers, and round it several seats for those who read the koran and pray for the souls of the deceased.

MOSS

Pages 402-403
dean of Ely, was eldest son of Mr Robert Moss, a gentleman in good circumstances; and was born at Gillingham in Norfolk in 1666. He was bred at Benet-college, Cambridge; and acquired great reputation both as a disputant and a preacher. He became preacher to the society of Gray's-inn, London, in 1668; and assistant preacher to Dr Wake at St James's, Westminster, 1699. He was sworn chaplain in three succeeding reigns, to King William, Queen Anne, and George I. and being one of the chaplains in waiting when Queen Anne visited the university of Cambridge, April 5, 1705, he was then created D.D. In 1708 he was invited by the parishioners of St Lawrence Jewry, on the resignation of dean Stanhope, to accept of their Tuesday lecture, which he held till 1727, and then resigned it on account count of his growing infirmities. In 1712, on the death of Dr Roderick, he was nominated by the queen to the deanery of Ely, which was the highest, but not the last, promotion he obtained in the church; for in 1714 he was collated, by Robinson bishop of London, to Clifton, a small rectory on the eastern side of Hertfordshire. The gout deprived him of the use of his limbs for some of the last years of his life; and he died March 26, 1729, in his 63rd year; and was buried in the presbytery of his own cathedral, under a plain stone with a simple inscription. His character may be seen in the preface to the eight volumes of his Sermons, which has usually been attributed to Dr Snape, the editor of the sermons; but the credit of it has lately been transferred to Dr Zachary Grey. Dean Mos is also supposed to have been the author of a pamphlet printed in 1717, intitled, "The report vindicated from misreport: being a defence of my lords the bishops, as well as the clergy of the lower house of convocation; in a letter from a member of that house to the prolocutor concerning their late consultations about the bishop of Bangor's writings." He wrote also some poems, both Latin and English.

MOSTRA

Pages 415-415

in the Italian music, a mark at the end of a line <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> space, to show that the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> of the next line is in that <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a>: and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> this note be accompanied with a sharp or flat, it is proper to place these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> along with the motra.

MOTACILLA

Pages 415-419

in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">ornithology</a>, the WAGTAIL and Warbler: A genus of birds of the order of passerines, distinguished by a straight weak <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BILL">bill</a> of a subulated <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, a tongue lacerated at the end, and very slender legs. 1. The <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBA">alba</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WHITE">white</a> wagtail, frequents the sides of ponds and small streams, and feeds on insects and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-WORMS">worms</a>. The head, back, and upper and lower side of the neck, as far as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>, are <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>; in some the chin is white, and the throat marked with a black <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CRESCENT">crescent</a>: the breast and belly are white; the quill-feathers are dusky; the coverts black, tipped and edged with white. The tail is very <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and always in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>. Mr Willoughby observes, that this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> shifts its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> in the winter; moving from the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NORTH">north</a> to the south of England during that season. In <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> and autumn it is a constant attendant on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PLOUGH">plough</a>, for the sake of the worms thrown up by that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>. These birds make their nest on the ground, composed of dry grass, fine fibres of roots, and moss, lined within with <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> or feathers. The eggs are five in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, white, spotted with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>; and for the most <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> there is only one brood in a year. 2. The flavo, or <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> wagtail, migrates in the north of England, but in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAMPSHIRE">Hampshire</a> continues the whole year.
