In the Eastern countries it is used by burning it on the skin: a little cone of the moxa is laid upon the part, previously moistened, and set on fire at the top; it burns down with a temperate glowing heat, and produces a dark-coloured spot, the exfoliation of which is promoted by applying a little garlic; the ulcer is left to discharge, or is soon healed, according to the intention in using the moxa. See Artemisia.

MOYLE

Pages 456-456

a learned English writer in the 18th century, descended of a good family in Cornwall, where he was born in 1672. He was sent to <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, and thence removed to the temple; where he applied himself chiefly to the general and more noble parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAW">law</a>, such as led him to the knowledge of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of the English <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. In 1697 he had a share with Mr Trenchard in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> a pamphlet, intitled, "An Argument showing that a Standing <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">Army</a> is inconsistent with a Free Government, and absolutely destructive to the Constitution of the English <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MONARCHY">Monarchy</a>." He translated Xenophon's Discourse upon Improving the State of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>. He was for some <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> member of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, in which he always acted an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a>; applying himself to the improvement and regulation of trade, and the employment of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, which has so near a connection with trade. He afterwards retired to his seat at Bake in Cornwall, where he applied himself with vigour to his studies, and died in 1721. In 1726, his works were printed at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, in 2 vols 8vo. MOYR. See <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MOIRA">MOIRA</a>.

MUCILAGE

Pages 456-456

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PHARMACY">pharmacy</a>, is in general any viscid <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> glutinous liquor. Mucilage, also imports the liquor which principally serves to moisten the ligaments and cartilages of the articulations, and is supplied by the mucilaginous glands.

MUCK

Pages 457-457
or running a muck, is a practice that has prevailed time immemorial in Batavia. To run a muck, in the original sense of the word, is to get intoxicated with opium, and then rush into the streets with a drawn weapon, and kill any one that comes in the way, till the party is himself either killed or taken prisoner. If the officer takes one of these amocks or mohawks (as they have been called by an easy corruption) alive, he has a considerable reward; and the unhappy wretches are always broken alive on the wheel; but such is the fury of their desperation, that three out of four are necessarily destroyed in attempting to secure them. MUD-IGUANA. See Muræna.

MUCOR

Pages 456-456

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>: A genus of the order of fungi, belonging to the cryptogamia class of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. The fungus has vesicular heads supported by footstalks.—There are 12 <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; the most remarkable of which are, 1. The sporocephalus, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> grey round-headed mucor, growing upon rotten wood, and sometimes upon decayed plants and mosses. The stalks of this are generally <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, about a line in height; <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> each at the top a spherical <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BALL">ball</a> about the size of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIN">pin</a>'s head; its coat or rind is covered with a grey powder, and containing within a black or fulvous spongy <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DOWN">down</a>. The coat bursts with a ragged, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> margin. 2. The lichenoides, or little, black, pin-headed mucor. This species grows in groups near to each other, in chinks of the barks of old trees, and upon old <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PARK">park</a>-pales. The stalks are black, about two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> in height; bearing each a single head, sometimes a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> or treble one, of the size of mustard or poppy seeds, of a roundish <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> at first, but when burst often flatish or truncated, and of a black <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. The internal powdered down is black, with a tinge of green. 3. The mucedo, or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMON">common</a> grey mould, grows on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, plants, and other substances in a putrid state. It grows in clusters; the stalks a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of an inch <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, pellucid, hollow, and cylindrical; supporting each a single globular head, at first transparent, afterwards dark grey; which bursts with <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-ELASTIC">elastic</a> force, and ejects small round seeds discoverable by the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-MICROSCOPE">microscope</a>. 4. The glaucus, or grey clutter-headed mould, is found on rotten apples, melons, and other fruits; as also upon decayed wood, and the stalks of wheat. These are of a pellucid grey colour; the stalks generally single, supporting a spherical ball, which, when magnified, appears to be compounded of numerous, fine, moniliform, necklace-like radii. 5. The crustaceus, or fingered mould, is frequent upon corrupted food of various kinds. It is of a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WHITE">white</a> aqueous colour; the stalks single, each supporting at the top four or five necklace-like radii, diverging from the same point or centre. 6. The septicus, or <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> frothy mucor, is found on the leaves of plants, such as ivy and beech, &c., sometimes upon dry sticks, and frequently upon the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TAN">tan</a> or bark in hot-houses. It is of no certain size or figure, but of a fine yellow colour, and a substance resembling at first cream <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> up into <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FROTH">froth</a>. In the space of 24 hours it acquires a thin filmy coat, becomes dry, and full of a foamy powder adhering to downy threads. The seeds under the microscope appear to be globular. Haller ranks it under a new genus, which he terms fuligo; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of which are, that the plants contained under it are soft, and like <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a> at first, but soon change into a black foamy powder.

MUCUS

Pages 456-457

a mucilaginous liquor secreted by certain glands, Mucus glands, and serving to lubricate many of the internal cavities of the body. In its <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> state it is generally limpid and colourless; but, from certain causes, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a> often assume a thick consistence and whitish <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> like pus. As it is sometimes of very <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> importance in medicine to distinguish these two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a> from each other, this was lately proposed as the subject of a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a> disputation by the Acclapian <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>. The prize was gained by Mr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> Darwin student of medicine from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LITCHFIELD">Litchfield</a>. The conclusions drawn from his experiments were: 1. Pus and mucus are both soluble in the vitriolic acid, though in very different proportions, pus being by far least soluble. 2. The addition of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WATER">water</a> to either of these compounds decomposes it. The mucus thus separated either swims in the mixture <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> forms <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> flocculi in it; whereas the pus falls to the bottom, and forms, on agitation, an uniform turbid mixture. 3. Pus is diffusible through a diluted vitriolic acid, though mucus is not. The same also occurs with water, or with a solution of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-SALT">salt</a>. 4. Nitrous acid dissolves both pus and mucus. Water, added to the solution of pus produces a precipitate, and the fluid above becomes clear and green, while water and the solution of mucus form a turbid dirty-coloured fluid. 5. Alkaline lixivium dissolves, though sometimes with difficulty, mucus, and generally pus. 6. Water precipitates pus from such a mixture, but does not mucus. 7. Where alkaline lixivium does not dissolve pus, it still distinguishes it from mucus, as it then prevents its <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DIFFUSION">diffusion</a> through water. 8. Coagulable lymph is neither soluble in concentrated nor diluted vitriolic acid. 9. Water produces no change on a solution of serum in alkaline lixivium, until after <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a> standing, and then only a very slight sediment appears. 10. Corrosive sublimate coagulates mucus, but does not pus. From the above experiments it appears, that strong vitriolic acid and water, diluted vitriolic acid, and caustic alkaline lixivium and water, will serve to distinguish pus from mucus; that the vitriolic acid can separate it from coagulable lymph, and alkaline lixivium from serum. Hence, when a person has any expectorated <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, the decomposition of which he wishes to ascertain, let him dissolve it in vitriolic acid, and in caustic alkaline lixivium; and let him add pure water to both solutions. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> there be a fair precipitation in each, he may be assured that some pus is present. But if there be a precipitation in neither, it is a certain test that the mixture is entirely mucous. If the matter cannot be made to dissolve in alkaline lixivium by <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> and trituration, we have also reason to believe that it is pus.

MUFFLE

Pages 457-457

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a>, a vessel much used in some metallurgical operations. In <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> it represents an <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> vault, the hinder <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> of which is closed by a semicircular <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLANE">plane</a>, and the lower part or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a> of which is a rectangular plane. It is a little oven that is placed horizontally in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSAY">assay</a> and enamelling furnaces, so that its open side corresponds with the door of the fire-<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FURNACE">furnace</a>. Under this arched oven small cupsels or crucibles are placed; and the substances contained are thus exposed to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> without contact of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a>, or ashes.

MUFTI

Pages 457-457

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> order, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRIMATE">primate</a> of the mufilman <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. The authority of the mufti is very <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> in the Ottoman empire; for even the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SULTAN">sultan</a> himself, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he would prefer any appearance of religion, cannot, without hearing his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, put any person to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, or so much as inflict any corporal <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>. In all actions, especially criminal ones, his opinion is required, by giving him a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> in which the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CASE">case</a> is stated under feigned names; which he subscribes with the words, He shall, or Shall not be, punished. Such outward <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> is paid to the mufti, that the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> signior himself rises up to him, and advances <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> steps to meet him when he comes into his presence. He alone has the honour of kissing the sultan's left shoulder; whilst the prime vizier kisses only the hem of his garment. When the grand signior addresses any writing to the mufti, he gives him the following titles: To the efad, the wisest of the wise, instructed in all knowledge, the most excellent of excellents, abstaining from things unlawfuls, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> of virtue and of true science, heir of the prophetic doctrines, resolver of the problems of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, revealer of the orthodox <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KEY">key</a> of the treasures of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> to the doubtful allegories, strengthened with the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> of the supreme <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LEGISLATOR">Legislator</a> of mankind, may the Most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">High</a> God perpetuate thy virtues! The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> of the mufti is solely in the grand signior, who presents him with a vest of rich fables, &c. If he is convicted of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TREASON">treason</a>, or any great crime, he is put into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a> kept for that purpose in the Seven Towers at Constantinople, and pounded to death.

MUGGLETONIANS

Pages 457-457

a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> which arose in England about the year 1657; so denominated from their leader Lodowick Muggleton, a journeyman taylor, who, with his associate Reeves, set up for <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> prophets, pretending, as it is said, to have an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> power of saving and damning whom they pleased; and giving out that they were the two last witnesses of God that should appear before the end of the world.

MUGIL

Pages 457-458

the mullet; in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">ichthyology</a>, a genus of fishes belonging to the order of abdominales. The lips are membranaceous, the inferior one being carinated inwards; they have no <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>; the branchiofuge membrane has <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> crooked rays; the opercula are smooth and round; and the body is of a whitish <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. There are two <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, distinguished by the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of rays in the back-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIN">fin</a>. The mullet is justly ranked by <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a> among the pisces littorales, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> those that prefer the shores to the full full <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SEA">sea</a>; they are found in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> plenty on several of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> coasts of our <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, and haunt in particular those small bays that have influxes of fresh <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WATER">water</a>. They come in great shoals, and keep rooting like hogs in the sand or mud, leaving their traces in form of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> round holes. They are very cunning; and when surrounded with a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NET">net</a>, the whole shoal frequently escapes by <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LEAPING">leaping</a> over it; for when one takes the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, the others are sure to follow. This circumstance is observed by Oppian; who also informs us, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> these fishes fail to get over at the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAP">leap</a>, they never attempt a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, but <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> as if they resigned themselves to their fate. Mr Pennant says he is uncertain whether this last observation holds good or not; however, Oppian had good opportunity of examining those fish, as they sometimes swarm on the coasts of the Mediterranean. Near Martegues, in the south of France, abundance of mullets are taken in weirs made of reeds placed in the shallows. Of the milts of the males, which are there called allevents, and of the roes of females, which are called botar, is made botargo. The materials are taken out entire, covered with <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-SALT">salt</a> for four or five hours, then pressed a little between two boards or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, washed, and at last dried in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> for 13 or 14 days. This fish was sometimes made the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> of a horrible <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> for unfortunate gallants. It was used both at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a> and Rome; but it is very doubtful whether it was a legal punishment or not. By Horace it is mentioned in the following <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>: Disce tua <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TUNICA">tunica</a> fugiendum est, ac pede nudo; Ne nummi percant, aut Pyga, aut denuque fama. SAT. II, lib. i. 132. The mullet is an excellent fish for the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, but at present not a fashionable one. The albulas* is caught in great quantities about the Bahama <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> at the times they go in shoals to spawn; and is there esteemed very good eating.

MUGWORT

Pages 458-458

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>; a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTEMISIA">Artemisia</a>. An infusion of this plant in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WHITE">white</a> wine, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> a bath made of it, has been always esteemed an emmenagogue, and useful in difficult parturition. The leaves, when young and tender, are frequently made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of by the Highlanders of Scotland as a pot <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HERB">herb</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>-people in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a> drink a decoction of them for the gout.

MUID

Pages 458-458

a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> among the French, for things dry. The muid is no real vessel used as a measure, but an estimation of several other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a>; as the septier, mine, minot, bushel, &c. Muid, is also one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NINE">nine</a> casks, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> regular vessels used in France, to put wine and other liquors in. The muid of wine is divided into two demi-muids, four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>-muids, and eight half-quarter muids, containing 36 septiers.

MULATTO

Pages 458-458

a name given in the Indies to those who are begotten by a negro <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAN">man</a> on an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> woman, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> by an Indian man on a negro woman.

MULBERRY

Pages 458-458

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>. See Morus. Mulberry-Cyder, a name given by the people of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>, and some other parts of England, to a sort of cyder rendered very palatable by an admixture of mulberry juice in the making: they choose for this purpose the ripest and blackest mulberries, and pressing out their juice and mixing it with a full-bodied cyder at the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GRINDING">grinding</a> and pressing, give <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> so much of it as adds a perceptible flavour. It is very worthy the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of people who live in other countries, where strong and good cyder is made, that this renders it a sort of wine much more agreeable than any other English liquor, and might be brought into general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> advantage of the dealer. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of this liquor resembles that of the brightest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RED">red</a> wine, and the flavour of the mulberry never goes off. Phil. Trans. No 133.

MULCT

Pages 458-458

a fine of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> laid upon a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAN">man</a> who has committed some fault <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> misdemeanor.

MULE

Pages 458-461

in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ZOOLOGY">zoology</a>, a mongrel kind of quadruped, usually <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENERATED">generated</a> between an ass and a mare, and sometimes between a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> and a she-ass; but the signification of the word is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> extended to every kind of animal produced by a mixture of two different <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>. There are two kinds of these animals; one from the he-ass and mare, the other from the horse and the she-ass. We call them indifferently mules, but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> distinguished them by proper appellations. The first kind are the best and most esteemed; as being larger, stronger, and having least of the ass in their disposition. The largest and stoutest asses, and the fairest and finest mares, are chosen in those countries where these creatures are most in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>; as in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>. In the last especially, they succeeded in having very stately mules from the size of their mares, some of them 16 and some 17 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, which are very serviceable as sumpter-mules in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>. But since the Low Countries are no longer under the dominion of Spain, they breed fewer mules. These creatures are very much commended for their being stronger, surer footed, going easier, being more cheaply maintained, and lasting longer than horses. They are commonly of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> quite black, with that shining <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIST">list</a> along the back and crofs the shoulders which distinguishes asses. In former times they were much more <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> than at present; being often brought over in the days of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POPERY">Popery</a> by the Italian prelates. They <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> longest in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of millers; and are yet in use among them in some places, on account of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> loads they carry on their back. As they are capable of being trained for riding, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> burdens, and for draught, there is no doubt that they might be usefully employed in many different services. But they are commonly found to be vicious, stubborn, and obstinate to a proverb; which whether it occasions or is produced by the ill usage they meet with, is a point not easily settled. Whatever may be the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CASE">case</a> of asses, it is allowed that mules are larger, fairer, and more serviceable in mild than in warm climates. In the British American colonies, both on the continent and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, but especially in the latter, they are much used and esteemed; so that they are frequently sent to them from hence, suffer less in the passage, and die much seldomer than horses, and commonly yield, when they arrive, no inconsiderable profit. It has commonly been asserted, that animals produced by the mixture of two <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HETEROGENEOUS">heterogeneous</a> species are incapable of generating, and thus perpetuating the monstrous breed; but this, we are informed by M. Buffon, is now discovered to be a mistake. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>, says he, tells us, that the mule engenders with the mare, and that the junction produces an animal which the Greeks call binnus, or ginus. He likewise wife remarks, that the she-mule easily conceives, but seldom brings the fetus to perfection. But the most remarkable and well attested instance of this fact, is mentioned in a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> read by M. d'Alembert before the academy of sciences, which informed him that a she-mule in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of St Domingo had brought forth a foal. The fact was attested by persons of the most unquestionable veracity; and other instances, though not so well authenticated, are adduced by our author. We may therefore, continues M. Buffon, consider it as an established fact, that the he-mule can <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENERATE">generate</a> and the she-mule produce. Like other animals, they have a seminal liquor, and all the organs necessary to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a>. But mongrel animals are always less fertile and more tardy than those of a pure species. Besides, mules have never produced in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLD">cold</a> climates, seldom in warm regions, and still more seldom in temperate countries. Hence their barrenness, without being <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a>, may be regarded as positive; since their productions are so rare, that a few examples can be only collected. The translator of Buffon's works, in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> on the passage above-quoted, has given a remarkable and well authenticated instance of the prolific powers of a she-mule in the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of Scotland. Having heard that a mule, belonging to Mr <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DAVID">David</a> Tullo <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FARMER">farmer</a> in Auchtertyre, in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Forfar, had some years ago brought forth a foal, he transmitted a few queries to be put to Mr Tullo; and requested that his answers might be legally attested before a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a>. This request was cheerfully complied with; and the following is an exact copy of the queries, answers, and attestations. Interrogatories to be put to Mr Tullo tenant in Auchtertyre, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> of Newtyle, and county of Forfar, with his answers thereto. 1st. Had you ever a she-mule? At what <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>? Is it true that the mule had a foal? At what <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> was she covered; and when did she foal?—Answered by Mr Tullo: That he bought a she-mule about 20 years ago; That she was constantly in season for a horse; That, about some years thereafter, he gave her a horse; and that she thereafter gave him a foal, about the 10th of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JUNE">June</a>. The mule's price was L. 4, 5s. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-STERLING">Sterling</a>. 2nd. What was the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of the foal? Was there any thing particular in its <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>?—Answer: The foal was exactly the colour of its mother, inclined to black, with a very <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> head, big ears, and small tail; and the declarant thinks, had its head been weighed when foaled, it would have weighed nearly as much as its body. 3rd. How <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a> was the animal allowed to live?—Answer: The next <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> after the mule foaled, it was sent, with its mother, to the Loch of Lundie, in order to let the foal die, as the declarant could not want the mule's <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>, and the mother seemed not fond of the foal: That it was accordingly left, and next day came to Auchtertyre, about two miles distance, over a hill, with the cattle of Auchtertyre, that had been grazing near to that <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and was drowned in a ditch the day following. 4th. Was its skin preserved, or the head, or any other <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BONES">bones</a> of the skeleton? Could any <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> thereof be still found?—Answered: Neither the skin nor any part of the skeleton was preserved, nor can be now had; though the declarant has often regretted the not preserving the foal, as its mother always performed any work that a horse of 1 l. value could do. 5th. Is the mother still alive? What is her <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>?—Answer: The mother died about eight years ago, of an epidemic cold that was raging among the horses in this country: The mule had little, or no <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MILK">milk</a> after foaling, and the foal got some cow's milk: And this is all that he remembers of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>. David Tullo. Auchtertyre, 4th Feb. 1780. We James Small tenant in Burmouth, and Robert Ramsay tenant in Newtyle, hereby certify, That we have often seen the mule above-described; and we know that she had a foal, as is narrated by David Tullo. James Small. Rob. Ramsay. Ballantyne <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, 4th Feb. 1780. The within interrogatories were put to David Tullo tenant in Auchtertyre, anent the mule he had, and the foal she produced; to which he gave the answers subjoined to each query, and signed them; as did James Small and Robert Ramsay, attesting the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> thereof, in presence of George Watson, J.P. The original attestation is in the possession of the translator; and he lately transmitted notarial or authenticated copies of it to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COUNT">count</a> de Buffon, and to Thomas Pennant, Esq. of Downing, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FLINTSHIRE">Flintshire</a>. Mules, among gardeners, denote a sort of vegetable monsters produced by putting the farina fecundans of one species of plant into the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PISTIL">pistil</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-UTRICLE">utricle</a> of another. The carnation and sweet-william being somewhat alike in their parts, particularly their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, the farina of the one <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a> impregnate the other, and the seed so enlivened will produce a plant differing from either. An instance of this we first had in Mr Fairchild's garden at Hoxton; where a plant is seen neither sweet-william nor carnation, but resembling both equally: this was raised from the seed of a carnation that had been impregnated by the farina of the sweet-william. These couplings being not unlike those of the mare with the ass, which produce the mule, the same name is given them; and they are, like the others, incapable of multiplying their species. This furnishes a hint for altering the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> of any fruit, by impregnating one tree with the farina of another of the same class; e.g., a codlin with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEAR">pear</a>-main, which will occasion the codlin so impregnated to last a longer time than usual, and to be of a sharper taste. Or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the winter-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> be fecundated with the dust of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> kinds, they will <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RIPEN">ripen</a> before their usual time. And from this accidental coupling of the farina of one with another, it may possibly be, that an orchard where there is variety of apples, even the fruit gathered from the same tree differ in their flavour, and in the season of maturity. It is also from the same accidental coupling that the numberless varieties of fruits and flowers raised every day from seed proceed. Wild or Fecund Mule. See Equus, p. 712. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MULHAUSEN">Mulhausen</a>, an imperial and Hanseatic town of Germany, in Upper <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>, and in Thuringia, under the protection of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> of Saxony; situated... Mulhausen in a fertile country, on the river Unstruth, 15 miles north east of Eisenach, and 45 east by south of Cassel. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MULLER">Muller</a>. E. Long. 10° 49' N. Lat. 51° 13'. Mulhausen, a considerable town of Germany, in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALSACE">Alsace</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a republic in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> with the Swiss. It is populous, well built, and adorned with handsome public structures; seated in a pleasant fertile country, on an island formed by the river Ill, 15 miles north-west of Basle, and 20 east of Belfort. E. Long. 7° 24' N. Lat. 47° 48'. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MULIER">Mulier</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAW">law</a>, signifies the lawful issue born in wedlock, though begotten before. The mulier is preferred to an elder <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> born out of matrimony; as for instance, if a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAN">man</a> has a son by a woman before <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, which issue is a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASTARD">bastard</a>, and afterwards marries the mother of the bastard, and they have another son, this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SECOND">second</a> son is mulier and lawful, and shall be heir of the father; but the other can be heir to no person*. By the civil law, where a man has issue by a woman, if after that he marries her, the issue is mulier. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MULL">Mull</a>, one of the Western Islands of Scotland, about 25 miles long, and as much in breadth. It is in general rocky and barren, not producing a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of corn for the inhabitants; but a great <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of cattle are annually exported, which with the fishings and a considerable quantity of kelp are the only <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>. It is deeply indented with bays and creeks, forming in several parts good <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> harbours. There are no villages except Tobermory, near the northern point of the island, where a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a> station has been lately erected. The island was originally part of the dominions of the Lords of the Isles; but in after-times it became part of the possessions of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and valiant family of Macleans, who still retain one-half. The other is the litigated property of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Argyle, whose ancestor possessed himself of it in 1674, on account of a debt; but after the courts of law had made an adjudication in his favour, he was obliged to support their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DECREE">decree</a> by force of arms. The ruins of several ancient castles are seen on this island. Mull of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CANTYRE">Cantyre</a>. See Cantyre. Mull of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GALLOWAY">Galloway</a>. See Galloway. Mullein. See Verbascum. Muller or Regiomontanus (John), a celebrated astronomer of the 15th century, was born at Koningshoven in Franconia in 1436, and acquired great reputation by publishing an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABRIDGMENT">abridgment</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>'s Almagest, which had been begun by Paracelsus. He went to Rome to perfect himself in the Greek tongue, and to see the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Baffarion; but finding some faults in the Latin translations of George de Trebizond, that translator's son assassinated him in a second journey he made to Rome in 1476, where Pope Sextus IV. had provided for him the archbishopric of Ratibon, and had sent for him to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-REFORM">reform</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CALENDAR">calendar</a>. Others say that he died of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a>. Muller (John), a noted engraver, who flourished about the year 1600, and had been bred under Henry Goltzius, whose style he closely imitated. The facility with which he handled the graver (for he worked with that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> only) cannot be sufficiently expressed; his works must be seen, to convey a proper idea of it to the mind. His engravings are valuable, as productions of a very extraordinary <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>; exclusive of which they have a prodigious share of merit. Among his most estimable performances, may be mentioned, 1. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAND">hand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> on the wall, a middling-sized plate lengthwise, from his own <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>. 2. The <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADORATION">adoration</a> of the wise men, the same, from the same. Fine impressions of both these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTS">prints</a> are very rare. 3. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RESURRECTION">resurrection</a> of Lazarus, a large plate lengthwise, from <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABRAHAM">Abraham</a> Bloemart. He engraved also several much esteemed portraits. Muller, or Mullar, denotes a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-STONE">stone</a> flat and even at bottom, but round atop; used for <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GRINDING">grinding</a> of matters on a marble.—The apothecaries use mullers to prepare many of their tephaceous powders; and painters for their colours, either dry or in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OIL">oil</a>. Muller is an instrument used by the glass-grinders; being a piece of wood, to one end whereof is cemented the glass to be ground, whether convex in a basin, or concave in a sphere or bowl.—The muller is ordinarily about six inches long, turned round; the cement they use is composed of ashes and pitch. See Grinding. Mulleras, a town of Germany, in the circle of Upper Saxony, and marquisate of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BRANDENBURG">Brandenburg</a>, situated 38 miles south of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BERLIN">Berlin</a>, upon a canal which joins the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-ODER">Oder</a> and the Spree. This canal is 15 miles in length, 10 yards in breadth, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> feet in depth. It was eight years in making; and since that time the cities of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAMBURG">Hamburg</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BRESLAU">Breslau</a> have carried on great trade by <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WATER">water</a>. E. Long. 14° 50' N. Lat. 52° 21'. Mullet, in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">ichthyology</a>. See Mugil. Mullet, or Mollet, in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HERALDRY">heraldry</a>, a bearing in form of the rowel of a spur, which it originally represented. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MULLINGAR">Mullingar</a>, a borough or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MANOR">manor</a> in the county of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WESTMEATH">Westmeath</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LEINSTER">Leinster</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, 38 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>. It is the shire town of that county, and has a barrack for two troops of horse. It returns two members to <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GRANARD">Granard</a>. This is a poit town, N. Lat. 53° 30' W. Long. 7° 50'. Within a few miles of it are the ruins of a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, and also those of a castle. It is situated on the river Feyle. It holds a great <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> fair, and is a place of good trade. In 1227, the priory of St <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, formerly known by the name of The House of God of Mullingar, was founded here by Ralph de Petey bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MEATH">Meath</a>, for regular canons of the order of St Augustin. A Dominican friary was also founded here in 1237 by the family of Nugent; some ruins of which still remain. In 1622, the friars of Multifarnham began to erect a house here for friars of the order of St Francis, but it was never completed. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAIRS">Fairs</a> are held here 6th April, 4th and 5th <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>, 29th August, and 11th November. Mullus, the Sarmullus, in ichthyology, a genus of fishes belonging to the order of thoracici. See Plate CCCXV. This fish was highly esteemed by the Romans, and bore an exceeding high price. The capricious epicures of Horace's days valued it in proportion to its size; not that the larger were more delicious, but that they were more difficult to be got. The price that was given for one in the time of Juvenal. venal and Pliny is a striking <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a> and extravagance of the age: M. P. m. fex milibus eum Aquantum sane paribus sferetis libris e. Juv. Sat. IV. The lavish slave Six thousand pieces for a mullet gave, A solerice for each <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POUND">pound</a>.

MULTIPLE

Pages 461-461

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARITHMETIC">arithmetic</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> which comprehends some other several times: thus 6 is a multiple of 2, and 12 is a multiple of 6, 4, and 3; comprehending the first twice, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SECOND">second</a> thrice, &c. <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">Action</a> of MULTIPLEPOINDING, in Scots <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAW">law</a>. See Law, no clxxiii. 24.

MULTIPLICAND

Pages 461-461

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARITHMETIC">arithmetic</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> to be multiplied by another. See ARITHMETIC.

MULTIPLICATION

Pages 461-461

in general, the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of increasing the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of any thing. Multiplication, in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARITHMETIC">arithmetic</a>, is a rule by which any given number may be speedily increased, according to any proposed number of times. See ARITHMETIC. Multiplication, in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALGEBRA">algebra</a>. See ALGEBRA, p.401.

MULTIPLICATOR

Pages 461-461
or Multiplier, in arithmetic, the number by which any other is multiplied, or the number of times it is supposed to be taken.

MULTIPLICATUS FLOS

Pages 461-461

a luxuriant flower, whose petals are multiplied so as to exclude a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> of the stamens. A multiplied luxuriant flower differs from a full one, the highest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of luxuriance, in that the petals of the latter are so multiplied as to exclude all the flaminia; whereas those of the former are only repeated <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> multiplied, two, three, or four times, as to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EXCLUSION">exclusion</a> of only a small part of the essential organs.

MULTIPLYING-GLASS

Pages 461-461

in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OPTICS">optics</a>, a glass where-with objects appear increased in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>. See (the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a> subjoined to) OPTICS.

MULTURE

Pages 461-461

in Scots <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAW">law</a>, a certain stipulated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MEAL">meal</a> given as payment to the proprietor <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> tackman of a mill for <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GRINDING">grinding</a> the corn; and all corn ground on farms thirled to the mill is obliged to pay multure whether the corn be ground at that mill or elsewhere.

MULVIA

Pages 461-461

a river of Barbary in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, which rises in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATLAS">Atlas</a>, and divides the empire of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MOROCCO">Morocco</a> from that of Algiers, and then falls into the Mediterranean, to the westward of Marfal-quiver.

MUM

Pages 461-461

a kind of malt-liquor much drank in Germany, and chiefly brought from <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BRUNSWICK">Brunswick</a>, which is the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> for making it. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREWING">brewing</a> mum, as recorded in the town-<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CITY">city</a>, is as follows. Take 63 gallons of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WATER">water</a> that has been boiled till one-third <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> is consumed, and brew it with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> bushels of wheaten malt, one bushel of oat-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MEAL">meal</a>, and one bushel of ground beans. When it is turned, the hoghead must not be filled too full at first; as soon as it begins to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>, put into it three pounds of the inner rind of fir, one <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POUND">pound</a> of the tops of fir and beech, three handfuls of carduus benedictus, a handful <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> two of the flower of rosa folis: add burnet, betony, marjoram, avena, pennyroyal, and wild thyme, of each an handful and an half; of elder-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, two handfuls or more; seeds of cardamum bruised, 30 ounces; barberries bruised, one ounce; when the liquor has worked a while, put the herbs and seeds into the vessel; and, after they are added, let it work over as little as possible; then fill it up: lastly, when it is stopped, put into the hoghead ten new-laid eggs unbroken; stop it up <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CLOSE">close</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> it at two years end. The English brewers, instead of the inner rind of fir, use cardamum, ginger, and saffron; and also add chicampane, madder, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RED">red</a> sanders. MUMIA. See PISAPHALTUM.

MUMMIUS

Pages 461-461

a Roman <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a> sent against the Achaeans, whom he conquered B.C. 147. He destroyed Corinth, Thebes, and Chalcis, by order of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>, and obtained the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SURNAME">surname</a> of Achaeus from his victories. He did not enrich himself with the spoils of the enemy, but returned home without any increase of fortune. He was so unacquainted with the value of the paintings and works of the most celebrated artists of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> which were found in the plunder of Corinth, that he said to those who conveyed them to Rome, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they lost them <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> injured them, they should make others in their stead.

MUMMY

Pages 461-462

a body embalmed <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> dried, in the manner used by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Egyptians; or the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> with which it is embalmed. There are two kinds of bodies denominated mummies. The first are only carcases dried by the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, and by that means kept from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PUTREFACTION">putrefaction</a>: these are frequently found in the sands of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIBYA">Libya</a>. Some imagine, that these are the bodies of deceased people buried there on purpose to keep them entire without <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-EMBALMING">embalming</a>; others think they are the carcases of travellers who have been overwhelmed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a> of sand raised by the hurricanes frequent in those deserts. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SECOND">second</a> kind of mummies are bodies taken out of the catacombs near <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAIRO">Cairo</a>, in which the Egyptians deposited their dead after embalming. See EMBALMING. We have two different substances preserved for medicinal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> under the name of mummy, though both in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of the same origin. The one is the dried and preserved <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> bodies, embalmed with <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MYRRH">myrrh</a> and spices; the other is the liquor running from such mummies, when newly prepared, or when affected by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> heat or damps. The latter is sometimes in a liquid, sometimes of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> form, as it is preserved in vials well stopped, or suffered to dry and harden in the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>. The first kind of mummy is brought to us in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> pieces, of a lax and friable texture, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> and spungy, of a blackish <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, and often damp and clammy on the surface; it is of a strong but disagreeable smell. The second kind of mummy, in its liquid state, is a thick, opaque, and viscous fluid, of a blackish colour, but not disagreeable smell. In its indurated state, it is a dry solid substance, of a fine shining <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> colour, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> texture, easily broken, and of a good smell; very inflammable, and yielding a scent of myrrh and aromatic ingredients while <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BURNING">burning</a>. This, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we cannot be content without medicines from our own bodies, ought to be the mummy used in the shops; but it is very scarce and dear; while the other is so cheap, that it <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a> always be most in use. All these kinds of mummies are brought from <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>. But we are not to imagine, that any body breaks up the real Egyptian mummies, to sell them in pieces to the druggists, as they make a much better market of them in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> whole, when they can contrive to get them. What our druggists are supplied with, is the flesh of executed criminals, or of any other bodies the Jews can get, who fill them with the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMON">common</a> bitumen, so plentiful in that <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> of the world; and adding a little aloes, and two or three other cheap ingredients, send them to be baked in an oven, till the juices are exhale, and the embalming <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> has penetrated so thoroughly that the flesh will keep and bear transporting into Europe. Mummy has been esteemed resolvent and balsamic; but whatever virtues have been attributed to it, seem to be such as depend more upon the ingredients used in preparing the flesh than in the flesh itself; and it would surely be better to give those ingredients without so shocking an addition. There are found in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a> a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> mummies, or human bodies preserved without the assistance of art. These <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> in considerable numbers in some of the vast caverns in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. They are dried with the flesh and skin shrunk up almost close to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BONES">bones</a>, and are of a blackish colour. In the wars which several ages ago laid waste that country, it was common for parties of the weaker side to retire into these caves, where their enemies, if they found them out, suffocated them by burning straw, &c., at the mouth of the cavern, and then left the bodies; which, being out of the way of injuries from common accidents, have lain there ever since. Mineral Mummy. See Pissaphaltum. Mummy, among gardeners, a kind of wax used in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GRAFTING">grafting</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTING">planting</a> the roots of trees, made in the following manner: Take one <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POUND">pound</a> of black pitch, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of a pound of turpentine; put them together into an earthen pot, and set them on fire in the open air, holding something in your <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAND">hand</a> to cover and quench the mixture in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a>, which is to be alternately lighted and quenched till all the nitrous and volatile parts be evaporated. To this a little common wax is to be added; and the composition is then to be set by for use. MUMPS. See Medicine-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MUNDA

Pages 462-463

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GRANADA">Granada</a>, seated on the declivity of a hill, at the bottom of which runs a river. W. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 4° 13'. N. Lat. 48° 15'. This <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CITY">city</a> was anciently famous for a victory gained by Caesar over the two sons of Pompey, who had collected an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> in Spain after the defeat of their father at Pharafia. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Rome. The Pompeys posted their army advantageously on a rising ground, whereof one side was defended by the city of Munda, and the other by a small river which watered the plain, and by a marsh; so that the enemy could not attack them but in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FRONT">front</a>. Caesar likewise drew up his troops with <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> art, and having advanced a little way from his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>, ordered them to halt, expecting the enemy would abandon their advantageous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a>, and come to meet him. But as they did not stir, Caesar made as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he intended to fortify himself in that post; which induced the young general, who looked upon this as a sign of fear, to advance into the plain, and attack the enemy before they could secure themselves with any works. Pompey's army was by far the most numerous; for it consisted of 13 legions, 6000 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, and an incredible <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of auxiliaries, among whom were all the forces of Bocchus <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAURITANIA">Mauritania</a>, commanded by his two sons, both youths of great valour and bravery. Caesar had 80 cohorts, three legions, to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WIT">wit</a>, the third, the fifth, and the tenth, and a body of 8000 horse. As the enemy drew near, Caesar betrayed a great <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of uneasiness and concern, as if he were doubtful of the success, knowing he was to engage men no way inferior in valour and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> to his own, and commanded by officers who had on many occasions given signal proofs of their bravery and conduct. Cnecius, the elder of the two brothers, was generally looked upon as an able commander; and Labienus, who had revolted, esteemed scarce inferior to himself. However, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DICTATOR">dictator</a>, desirous to put an end to the civil <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WAR">war</a>, either by his own <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEATH">death</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> that of his rivals, gave the signal for the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, and fell upon the enemy with his usual vigour and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a>. At the first onset, which was dreadful, the auxiliaries on both sides betook themselves to flight, leaving the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> to decide their quarrel by themselves. Then the legionaries engaged with a fury hardly to be expressed; Caesar's men being encouraged by the hopes of putting an end to all their labours by this battle, and those of Pompey exerting themselves out of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> and despair, since most of them expected no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>, as having been formerly pardoned. Never was victory more obstinately disputed. Caesar's men, who had been always used to conquer, found themselves so vigorously <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> by the enemy's legionaries, that they began to give ground; and though they did not turn their backs, yet it was manifest that shame alone kept them in their posts. All authors agree, that Caesar had never been in so great danger; and he himself, when he came back to his camp, told his friends, that he had often fought for victory, but this was the first <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> he had ever fought for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. Thinking himself abandon- ed by fortune, which had hitherto favoured him, he had some thoughts of stabbing himself with his own <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, and by a voluntary death preventing the disgrace of a defeat; but returning soon to himself, and concluding it would be more to his reputation to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> by the enemy's <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAND">hand</a> at the head of his troops, than, in a fit of despair, by his own, he dismounted from his horse, and snatching a buckler from one of his legionaries, he threw himself like a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAN">man</a> in despair into the midst of the enemy; crying out to his men, Are you not ashamed to deliver your general into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of boys? At these words, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> of the tenth legion, animated by the example of their general, fell upon the enemy with fresh vigour, and made a dreadful havoc of them. But in spite of their utmost efforts, Pompey's men still kept their ground, and, though greatly fatigued, returned to the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> with equal vigour. Then the Caesarians began to despair of victory; and the dictator, running through the ranks of his disheartened legionaries, had much ado to keep them together. The battle had already lasted from the rising to the setting of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, without any considerable advantage on either side. At length a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> accident decided the dispute in favour of the dictator. Bogud, a petty king of Mauritania, had joined Caesar soon after his arrival in Spain, with some squadrons of Numidian horse; but, in the very beginning of the battle, being terrified at the shouting of the soldiers, intermingled with groans, and the clashing of their arms, he had abandoned his post, and retired with the auxiliaries under his command to a rising ground at a small distance from the enemy's camp. There he <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> an idle spectator of the battle that was fought in the plain. But towards the evening, partly out of shame and partly out of compassion for his friend Caesar, he resolved to fall upon Pompey's camp; and accordingly flew thither with all the forces he had with him. Labienus, apprised of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, hastened after him to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of the camp; which Caesar observing, cried to his legionaries, Courage, fellow soldiers! the victory at length is ours; Labienus flies. This artifice had the desired effect: Caesar's men, believing that Labienus was truly fled, made a last effort, and charged the wing he commanded so briskly, that after a most obstinate dispute they put them to flight. Though the enemy's left wing was thus entirely defeated, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> wing, where the elder Pompey commanded, still kept their ground for some time. Pompey dismounting from his horse, fought on foot like a private man in the first line, till most of his legionaries being killed, he was forced to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-SAVE">save</a> himself by flight from falling into the enemy's hands. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">Part</a> of his troops fled back to their camp, and part took shelter in the city of Munda. The camp was immediately attacked, and taken sword in hand; and as for the city, Caesar, without loss of time, drew a line of circumvallation round it. This victory was gained on the 16th of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KALENDS">kalends</a> of April, i.e., according to our way of counting, on the 17th day of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MARCH">March</a>, when the Dionysian festival, or the Liberalia, were celebrated at Rome; the very day, as Plutarch observes, in which Pompey the Great, four years before, laid out for the war. In this <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> Pompey lost 30,000 men; among whom were the famous Labienus, Attius <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-VALENS">Valens</a>, and 3000 Roman knights. Seventeen officers of distinction were taken, and all the enemy's <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-EAGLES">eagles</a> and ensigns; together with Pompey's fasces, which he had assumed as governor of Spain. On Caesar's side only 1000 men were killed and 500 wounded.

MUNDINGOES

Pages 463-463

the name of a people who live on the sides of the river <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-GAMBIA">Gambia</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, and who are of a jet <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, strong, and well-made. They have a prettily fent over every year from one of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> de Verde <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> to christen and marry.

MUNDUS PATENS

Pages 463-463

the open world, in Roman antiquity, a solemnity performed in a small temple, of a round form like the world, dedicated to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DIS">Dis</a> and the rest of the infernal gods. This temple was opened but three times in the year, viz., the 24th of August, the 4th of October, and the 7th of November. During these days, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> believed <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HELL">hell</a> was open; on these days therefore they never offered <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, fitted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, put out to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> married.

MUNICH

Pages 463-464

was the favourite of the Czarina <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNA">Anna</a>, and was concerned in all the events of her reign. Being appointed general of her armies, he gained <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> advantages over the Crimean Tartars, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> the Turks, A.D. 1739, in an engagement near Chocozim, and took that <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CITY">city</a> together with Jaffa the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MOLDAVIA">Moldavia</a>. He was afterwards prime minister to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CZAR">Czar</a> Ivan VI., but in a short <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> after he was accused of employing the power which his office conferred on him to gratify his own ambition and private resentment. The Empress <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a> brought him to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>, and he was condemned to lose his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> A.D. 1742. This <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> was mitigated to banishment into <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SIBERIA">Siberia</a>, whither many of the victims of his power had been exiled. He was recalled by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> III. A.D. 1762, and declared field-marshal. Upon the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, the Empress Catharine II. appointed him <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DIRECTOR">director</a>-general of the ports of the Baltic. He died on the 8th of October 1767, at the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 84.

MUNICIPAL

Pages 464-464

among us, is applied to the laws that obtain in any particular <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CITY">city</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>. And those are called municipal officers who are elected to defend the interests of cities, to maintain their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> and privileges, and to preserve order and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> among the citizens; such as mayors, sheriffs, consuls, &c.

MUNICIPIES

Pages 464-464

an appellation given by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> to the inhabitants of the municipia <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> municipal cities. See Municipium.

MUNICIPIUM

Pages 464-464

in Roman antiquity, a corporation, borough, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> enfranchised <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CITY">city</a> or town, where the inhabitants enjoyed their own laws and customs, and at the same <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> were honoured with the privileges of Roman citizens; but then this privilege generally reached no further than the bare <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TITLE">title</a>. Some indeed, by particular merit, obtained the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of votes, which occasioned that distinction of municipium sine suffragio, and municipium cum suffragio.—The inhabitants of the municipium sine suffragio were called barely Romani, but those of the municipium cum suffragio were called cives Romani. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between proper citizens of Rome and the inhabitants of the municipium may be thus expressed. The proper citizens of Rome were, 1. Registered in the census; 2. Had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of suffrage and of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> honours; 3. Were assessed in the poll-tax; 4. Served in the legions; 5. Used the Roman laws and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>; 6. Were called Quirites and populus Romanus; whereas the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MUNICIPES">municipes</a> enjoyed the three first of these privileges, but were denied the three last.

MUNITION

Pages 464-464

the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> with which a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is furnished in order for <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> that which follows a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAMP">camp</a> for its subsistence. MUNITION Ships, are those that have stores on board in order to supply a fleet of men of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WAR">war</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. In an engagement, all the munition-ships and victuallers attending the fleet take their station in the rear of all the rest; they are not to engage in the fight, but to attend to such directions as are sent them by the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a>.

MUNSTER

Pages 464-465

a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Germany, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a bishopric of the same name and of all Westphalia, stands at the confluence of the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AA">Aa</a> with the Ems, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7° 49' N. Lat. 52° 0'. It is of a circular form, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, and well fortified both by <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and art. It has a fine citadel called the Brille, erected by a bishop named Bernard van Galen in order to awe the burghers. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEAN">dean</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> now elect the bishop; but till the beginning of the 14th century he was nominated by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>. This city has been rendered famous by three remarkable transactions. 1. By the peace concluded here in 1648, which put an end to a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WAR">war</a> of 30 years; occasioned by the persecuting spirit of bigotted papists, who chose rather to plunge their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> into all the calamities of war than allow <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>. By this peace, how- Munychia ever, they consented, much against their inclinations, to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> them a toleration. 2. By the disorders and disturbances occasioned here in 1553, by a parcel of enthusiasts, headed by a tailor called John of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of his birth, who turned out the magistrates, and took possession of the city, where they perpetrated the most horrid villanies and cruelties. 3. For the noble, though unsuccessful, efforts it made in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of its liberties against the tyranny and usurpation of the above-mentioned turbulent and bloody-minded bishop, Bernard van Galen. In this city are a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a> and other <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> houses, many of them lately piles, and surrounded with beautiful gardens.

MUNYCHIA

Pages 465-465

an anniversary solemnity observed at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a>, on the 16th of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MONTH">month</a> Munychion. Cakes were offered on the occasion called apomonia.

MUNYCHION

Pages 465-465
