At last he settled at Vienna, where he obtained <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> appointments from the court; and lived universally esteemed for his uncommon merit, and equally valued for his personal accomplishments. He died in 1755. There were some other painters of the name of Mytens, but of inferior <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">MYTHOLOGY</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEFINITION">Definition</a>. IS a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TERM">term</a> compounded of two Greek words, and in its original import it signifies any kind of fabulous doctrine: In its more appropriated <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, it means those fabulous details concerning the objects of worship which were invented and propagated by men who lived in the early ages of the world, and by them transmitted to succeeding generations, either by written records <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORAL">oral</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a>. As the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a> and mythology of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> are almost inseparably connected, it <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a> be impossible for us to develop the latter, without often introducing some observations relating to the former. We must therefore intreat the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDULGENCE">indulgence</a> of our readers, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> upon many occasions we should hazard a few strictures on the names, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, adventures, and functions of such pagan divinities as may have furnished materials for those fabulous narrations which the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the subject may <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> us to discuss. With respect to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FABLE">fable</a>, it may be observed in general, that it is a creature of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> imagination, and derives its birth from that <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of the marvellous which is in a manner congenial to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAN">man</a>.—The appearances of nature which every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> occur, objects, actions, and events, which succeed each other, by a kind of routine, are too familiar, too obvious, and uninteresting, either to gratify curiosity or to excite admiration. On the other <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, when the most <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMON">common</a> phenomena in nature or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> are new-modelled by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PLASTIC">plastic</a> power of a warm imagination; when they are diversified, compounded, embellished, or even arranged and moulded into forms which seldom or perhaps never occur in the ordinary course of things;—<a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NOVELTY">novelty</a> generates admiration, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> always attended with delightful sensations. Here then we imagine we have discovered the very source of fiction and fable.—They originated from that powerful propensity in our nature towards the new and surprising, animated by the delight with which the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONTEMPLATION">contemplation</a> of them is generally attended. Many circumstances contributed to extend and establish the empire of fable. The <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LEGISLATOR">legislator</a> laid hold on this bias of human nature, and of course employed fable and fiction as the most effectual means to civilize a rude, unpolished world. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, the theologian, the poet, the musician, each in his turn, made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of this vehicle to convey his maxims and instructions to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> tribes. They knew that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, simple and unadorned, is not possessed of charms powerful enough to captivate the heart of man in his present corrupt and degenerate state. This consideration, which did indeed result from the character of their audience, naturally led them to employ fiction and allegory. From this was derived the allegorical <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> of the ancients, and especially of the primary sages of the east. Though almost every <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATION">nation</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FACE">face</a> of the globe, however remote from the centre of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POPULATION">population</a>, however savage and adverse from cultivation, has fabricated... and adopted its own system of mythology; the Orientals, however, have distinguished themselves in a peculiar manner, by the boldness, the inconsistency, and the extravagance of their mythology. The genial warmth of those happy climes, the fertility of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, which afforded every <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a>, every convenience, and often every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a> of life, without depressing their spirits by laborious exertions; the face of nature perpetually blooming around them, the skies smiling with uninterrupted serenity; all contributed to inspire the Orientals with a glow of fancy and a vigour of imagination rarely to be met with in less happy regions. Hence every object was swelled beyond its <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> dimensions. Nothing was great or little in moderation, but every sentiment was heightened with incredible hyperbole. The magnificent, the sublime, the vast, the marvellous, first sprung up, and were brought to maturity, in those native regions of fable and fairyland. As nature, in the ordinary course of her operations, exhibited neither objects nor effects adequate to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of their romantic imaginations, they naturally deviated into the fields of fiction and fable. Of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of detailing fabulous adventures originated in the east, and was from thence transplanted into the western countries. As the allegorical taste of the eastern nations had sprung from their propensity to fable, and as that propensity had in its turn originated from the love of the marvellous; so did allegory in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of time contribute its influence towards multiplying fables and fiction almost in infinitum. The latent import of the allegorical doctrines being in a few ages lost and obliterated, what was originally a moral or theological tenet, assumed the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of a personal adventure. The propensity towards personification, almost universal among the Orientals, was another fruitful source of fable and allegory. That the people of the east were strongly inclined to personify inanimate objects and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSTRACT">abstract</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a>, we imagine will be readily granted, when it is considered, that in the formation of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> they have generally annexed the affection of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SEX">sex</a> to those objects. Hence the distinction of grammatical genders, which is known to have originated in the eastern parts of the world. The practice of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PERSONIFYING">personifying</a> virtues, vices, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> and moral affections, was necessary to support that allegorical style which universally prevailed in those countries. This <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> was in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> reputation even in Europe some centuries ago; and to it we are indebted for some of the most noble poetical compositions now extant in our own language. Those productions, however, are but faint imitations of the original mode of writing still current among the eastern nations. The Europeans derived this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> from the Moorish inhabitants of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, who imported it from <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>, their original <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. The general use of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIEROGLYPHICS">hieroglyphics</a> in the east, must have contributed largely towards extending the empire of mythology. As the import of the figures employed in this method of delineating the signs of ideas was in a great <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> arbitrary, mistakes must have been frequently committed in ascertaining the notions which they were at the first intended to represent. When the development of these arbitrary signs happened to be attended with uncommon difficulty, the expounders were obliged to have recourse to conjecture. Those conjectural expositions were for the most <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> tinctured with that bias towards the marvellous which universally prevailed among the primitive men. This we find is the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CASE">case</a> even at this day, when moderns attempt to develop the purport of emblematical figures, preserved on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> medals, entaglions, &c. The wise men of the east delighted in obscure enigmatical sentences. They seem to have disdained every sentiment obvious to vulgar <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APPREHENSION">apprehension</a>. The words of the wife, and their dark sayings, often occur in the most ancient records both sacred and profane. The sages of antiquity used to vie with each other for the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a> of superior <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>, by propounding riddles, and dark and mysterious questions, as subjects of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a>. The contest between <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a> and Hiram, and that between Amasis king of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> and Polycrates <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-SAMOS">Samos</a>, are universally known.—As the import of those enigmatical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPOSITIONS">propositions</a> was often absolutely lost, in ages when the art of writing was little known, and till less practised, nothing remained but fancy and conjecture, which always verged towards the regions of fable. This then, we think, was another source of mythology. The Pagan priests, especially in Egypt, were probably the first who reduced mythology to a kind of system. The sacerdotal tribe, among that people, were the grand depositories of learning as well as of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. That order of men monopolised all the arts and sciences. They seem to have formed a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSPIRACY">conspiracy</a> among themselves, to preclude the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAITY">laity</a> from all the avenues of intellectual improvement. This <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> was adopted with a view to keep the laity in subjection, and to enhance their own importance. To accomplish this end, they contrived to perform all the ministrations of their religion in an unknown tongue, and to cover them with a thick veil of fable and allegory. The language of Ethiopia became their sacred dialect, and hieroglyphics their sacred character.—Egypt, of course, became a kind of fairyland, where all was jugglery, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAGIC">magic</a>, and enchantment. The initiated alone were admitted to the knowledge of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OCCULT">occult</a> mystical exhibitions, which, in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, constituted the essence of their religion. From these the vulgar and profane were prohibited by the most rigorous penalties (see <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MYSTERIES">Mysteries</a>.). The Egyptians, and indeed all the ancients without exception, deemed the mysteries of religion too sacred and solemn to be communicated to the herd of mankind, naked and unrefined; a mode by which they imagined those sacred and sublime <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-ORACLES">oracles</a> would have been defiled and degraded. "Procul, o procul eite profani—Odi profanum vulgus et arceo." Egypt was the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAND">land</a> of graven images; allegory and mythology were the veil which concealed religion from the eyes of the vulgar; fable was the groundwork of that impenetrable covering. In the earliest and most unpolished stage of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> in the east, we cannot suppose fable to have existed among men. In the ages of Fables are always tales of other times, but at this <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> mythology other times did not reach far enough backward to afford those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of the imagination sufficient time to mature. Fable requires a considerable space of time to acquire credibility, and to rise into reputation. Accordingly, we find that both the Chinese and... and Egyptians, the two most ancient nations whose annals have reached our times, were altogether unacquainted with fabulous details in the most early and least improved periods of their respective monarchies. It has been shown almost to a demonstration, by a variety of learned men, that both the one and the other people, during some centuries after the general deluge, retained and practised the primitive Noachic religion, in which fable and fancy could find no <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a>; all was genuine unsophisticated truth. As soon as the authentic tradition concerning the origin of the universe was either in a good measure lost, or at least adulterated by the inventions of men, false and fiction began to prevail. The Egyptian Thoth or Thothot, or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a> Trismegistus, and Mochus the Phoenician, undertook to account for the formation and arrangement of the universe, upon principles purely <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a>. Here fable began to usurp the place of genuine historical truth. Accordingly, we find that all the historians of antiquity, who have undertaken to give a general detail of the affairs of the world, have suffered in their <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NARRATION">narration</a> with a fabulous cosmogony. Here imagination ranged unconfined over the boundless extent of the primary <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHAOS">chaos</a>. To be convinced of the truth of this assertion, we need only look into Sanchoniathon's Cosmogony, Euseb. Prep. Evang. I. i. sub init. and Diodorus Sic. I. i. From this we suppose it will follow, that the first <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-RACE">race</a> of fables owed their birth to the erroneous opinions of the formation of the universe. Having now endeavoured to point out the origin of mythology, or fabulous traditions, we shall proceed to lay before our readers a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIEF">brief</a> detail of the mythology of the most respectable nations of antiquity, following the natural order of their situation. The Chinese, if any <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> be due to their own annals, or to the missionaries of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Rome, who pretend to have copied from them, were the first of the nations. Their fabulous records reach upwards many myriads of years before the Mosaic era of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CREATION">creation</a>. The events during that period of time, if any had been recorded, must have been fabulous as the period itself. These, however, are buried in eternal oblivion. The missionaries, who are the only sources of our information with relation to the earliest periods of the Chinese history, represent those people as having retained the religion of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NOAH">Noah</a> many centuries after the foundation of their empire. Upon this supposition, their cosmogony must have been <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> and genuine, without the least tincture of those fabulous ingredients which have both disguised and disgraced the cosmogonies of most other nations. According to the most authentic accounts, Fo-hi or Fohi laid the foundation of that empire about 4000 years ago. This emperor, according to the Chinese, was conceived in a miraculous manner. His mother, say they, one day as she was walking in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> place, was surrounded by a rainbow; and, being impregnated by this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-METEOR">meteor</a>, was in due time delivered of that celebrated legislator. This personage, like the Athenian Cecrops, was half a man and half a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERPENT">serpent</a>. His intellectual powers were truly hyperbolical. In one day he discovered so different species of poisonous herbs. He taught his countrymen the whole art of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a> in the space of a very few years. He instructed them how to sow five different sorts of grain. He invented boats and nets for <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a>, the art of fabricating <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PORCELAIN">porcelain</a>, the management of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SILK">silk</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-WORMS">worms</a>, the manufacturing of silk, &c. In a word, that wonderful personage was inspired by Heaven with knowledge, which qualified him for composing that incomparable body of laws which are even at this day the wonder of the world. Our readers will admit, that this whole detail is fabulous and chimerical. The most learned part of them will readily observe, that the Chinese, in ascribing the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of all the useful arts to their Fohi, are perfectly agreed with almost all the other nations of antiquity. The Indians ascribe every invention to <a class="xref" href="../1815/vol0.html#article-BUDHA">Budha</a>, or Vithou, or Foe; the Persians to Zerdusht or Zoroaster; the Chaldeans to their man of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, whom they call <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OANNES">Oannes</a>; the Egyptians to Thoth or Thothot; the Phoenicians to Melicertes; the Greeks to the family of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TITANS">Titans</a>; and the Scandinavians to Odin, &c. About 551 years before the Christian era, appeared the famous Chinese philosopher <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONFUCIUS">Confucius</a>, or Confucius Concerning the birth of this prince of philosophers, the Chinese have propagated the following legendary tale. His mother walking in a solitary place was impregnated by the vivifying influence of the heavens. The babe, thus produced, spoke and reasoned as soon as it was born. Confucius, however, wrought no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a>, performed no romantic exploits, but lived an austere ascetic life, taught and inculcated the doctrines of pure morality, and died, remarkable only for superior wisdom, religious, moral, and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a>. About the year of Christ 601, flourished the Secularist Laokoon. His mother carried him 30 years in her womb, and was at last delivered of him under a plum-tree. This philosopher was the Epicurus of the Chinese. His disciples, who were denominated Faosse, i.e., heavenly doctors, were the first who corrupted the religion of the Chinese. They were addicted to magic, and introduced the worship of good and bad demons. Their doctrine was embraced by a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a> succession of emperors. One of these princes, called Tou-ti, had been deprived by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of a favourite mistress, whom he loved with the most extravagant passion. The emperor, by the magical skill of one of these doctors, obtained an interview with his deceased mistress, a circumstance which riveted the whole order in the affection and esteem of the deluded prince. Here our readers will observe the exact counterpart of the fable of Eurydice, so famous in the mythology of the Greeks and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. That such a system of religious principles must have abounded with mythological adventures is highly probable; but as the missionaries, to whom we are chiefly indebted for our information relating to the religion of the Chinese, have not taken the pains to record them, we find it impossible to gratify the curiosity of our readers on that head. The worship of the idol Fo, or Foe, was transplanted from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a> into <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHINA">China</a> about the 56th year of the Christian era, upon the following occasion. One worship of the doctors of the Fao-sse had promised a prince of Fo, and of the family of Tchou, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of the emperor <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-MING">Ming</a>-ti, to make him enter into <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a> with the spirits. At his solicitation an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> was dispatched into India, in order to inquire where the true reli- There had been a tradition, say the missionaries, ever since the age of Confucius, that the true religion was to be found in the west.—The ambassador stopt short in India; and finding that the god Foe was in high reputation in that country, he collected several images of that deity painted on chintz, and with it 42 chapters of the canonical books of the Hindoos, which, together with the images, he laid on a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WHITE">white</a> elephant, and transported into his native country. At the same time he imported from the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> the doctrine of the transmigration of souls, which is firmly believed in China to this day. The doctrine and worship of Foe, thus introduced, made a most rapid progress all over China, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JAPAN">Japan</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SIAM">Siam</a>, &c. The priests of Foe are called among the Siamese, Talopains; by the Tartars, Lamas; by the Chinese, Ho-chang; and by the people of Japan, Bonzes. By this last appellation they are generally known in Europe. An infinitude of fable was invented and propagated by the disciples of Foe, concerning the life and adventures of their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MASTER">master</a>. If the earlier ages of the Chinese history are barren of mythological incidents, the later periods, after the introduction of the worship of Foe, furnish an inexhaustible store of miracles, monsters, fables, intrigues, exploits, and adventures, of the most villainous <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a>. Indeed, most of them are so absurd, so ridiculous, and at the same time so impious and profane, that we are convinced our readers will easily dispense with a detail from which they could reap neither entertainment nor instruction. Such as may find themselves disposed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RAKE">rake</a> into this abominable puddle, we must refer to the reverend fathers du Halde, Couplet, Amiot, Kircher, and other members of the propaganda, in whose writings they will find wherewithal to satisfy, and even to forfeit, their appetite. The Hindoos, like the other nations of the east, for a long time retained the worship of the true God. At length, however, idolatry broke in, and, like an impetuous <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TORRENT">torrent</a>, overwhelmed the country. First of all, the genuine history of the origin of the universe was either utterly lost, or disguised under a variety of fictions and allegories. We are told that Brimha, the supreme <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> of the Hindoos, after three several efforts, at last succeeded in creating four persons, whom he appointed to rule over all the inferior creatures.—Afterwards Brimha joined his efficient power with Bishon and Rudler; and by their united exertions they produced ten men, whose general appellation is Munier, that is, the inspired. The same being, according to another mythology, produced four other persons, as imaginary as the former; one from his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>, one from his back, one from his lip, and one from his heart. These children were denominated Bangs; the import of which word we cannot pretend to determine. According to another tradition, Brimha produced the Bramins from his mouth, to pray, to read, to instruct; the Chiltern from his arms, to draw the bow, to fight, to govern; the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BICE">Bice</a> from his belly or thighs, to nourish, to provide the necessaries of life by agriculture and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>; the Soder from his feet, for subjection to serve, to labour, to travel. The reader will see at once, in these allegorical persons, the four castes or sects into which the Hindoo nations has, time immemorial, been divided. These are some of their most celebrated mythological traditions with relation to the origin of the universe. The Hindoos have likewise some mythological opinions which seem to relate to the general deluge. They traditions tell us, that desiring the preservation of herds and of the Brahmins, of genii and of virtuous men, of vedas of &c. <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAW">law</a>, and of precious things, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> of the universe afflumed many bodily shapes; but though he pervades, like the air, a variety of beings, yet he is himself unvaried, since he has no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> in him subject to change. At the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of the last calpa, there was a general destruction, occasioned by the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> of Brahma, whence his creatures in different worlds were drowned in a vast ocean. Brahma being inclined to slumber after a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAPSE">lapse</a> of so many ages, the strong demon Hayagriva came near him, and stole the vedas which had flowed from his lips. When Heri, the preserver of the universe, discovered this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEED">deed</a> of the prince of Dainavas, he took the shape of a minute fish called Sap-hari. After various transformations, and an enormous increase of size in each of them, the Lord of the universe loving the righteous man (A) who had still adhered to him under all these various shapes, and intending to preserve him from the sea of destruction caused by the depravity of the age, thus told him how he was to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a>: "In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> days from the present time, O thou Tamer of enemies! the three worlds will be plunged in an ocean of death; but in the midst of the destroying waves a large vessel sent by me for thy life shall stand before thee." The remaining part of the mythology so nearly resembles the Mosaic history of Noah and the general deluge, that the former may be a strong <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONFIRMATION">confirmation</a> of the truth of the latter. To dry up the waters of the deluge, the power of the Deity descends in the form of a boar, the symbol of strength, to draw up and support on his tusks the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, which had been sunk beneath the ocean. Again, the same power is represented as a tortoise sustaining the globe, which had been convulsed by the violent assaults of demons, while the gods charmed the sea with the mountain Mandar, and forced it to disgorge the sacred things and animals, together with the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WATER">water</a> of life which it had swallowed. All these stories, we think, relate to the same event, shadowed by a moral, a metaphysical, and an astronomical allegory; and all three seem connected with the hieroglyphical sculptures of the old Egyptians. The Hindoos divide the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DURATION">duration</a> of the world into four Yugs or Jugs, or Joguts, each consisting of a prodigious <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of years. In each of those periods, the age and stature of the human race have been gradually diminished; and in each of them mankind has gradually declined in virtue and piety, as well as in age and stature. The present period they call the Colle, i.e. the corrupt Jogue, which they say is to last 400,000 (A) He was Sovereign of the world. His name was Mana, or Statgavirata; his patronymic name was Valvala, or Child of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">Sun</a>.

MYTHOLOGY

Pages 648-655

400,000 years, of which near 5000 years are already past. In the last <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> of the preceding Jogue, which they call the Dava <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAN">man</a> was contracted into 1000 years, as in the present it is confined to 100. From this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPORTIONAL">proportional</a> diminution of the length of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, our readers <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a> probably infer, that the two last Jogues bear a pretty near resemblance to the Mosaic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the age of the antediluvian and postdiluvian patriarchs; and that the two first are imaginary periods <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CREATION">creation</a> of the world, like those of the Chinese, Chaldeans, and Egyptians. According to the mythology of the Hindoos, the system of the world is subject to various dissolutions and resuscitations. At the conclusion of the Colla Jogue, say they, a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> revolution will take <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, when the solar system will be consumed by fire, and all the elements reduced to their original constituent atoms. Upon the back of these revolutions, Brimha, the supreme deity of the Hindoos, is sometimes represented as a new-born infant, with his toe in his mouth, floating on a camala <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WATER">water</a> flower, sometimes only on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a> of that plant, on the surface of the vast <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABYSS">abyss</a>. At other times he is figured as coming forth of a winding shell; and again as blowing up the mundane foam with a pipe at his mouth. Some of these emblematical figures and attitudes, our learned readers will probably observe, nearly resemble those of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Egyptians. But the vulgar <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> of the ancient Hindoos was of a very different complection, and opens a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> field of mythological adventures. We have observed above, that the Fo or Foe of the Chinese was imported from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a>; and now we shall give a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIEF">brief</a> detail of the mythological origin of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>. We have no certain account of the birth-place of this imaginary deity.—His followers relate, that he was born in one of the kingdoms of India near the line, and that his father was one of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. His mother brought him into the world by the left side, and expired soon after her delivery. At the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> of her <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONCEPTION">conception</a>, she dreamed that she had swallowed a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WHITE">white</a> elephant; a circumstance which is supposed to have given birth to the veneration which the kings of India have always shown for a white animal of that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>. As soon as he was born, he had strength enough to stand erect without assistance. He walked abroad at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a>, and, pointing with one <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAND">hand</a> to the heavens, and with the other to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, he cried out, "In the heavens, and on the earth, there is no one but me who deserves to be honoured." At the age of 30, he felt himself all on a sudden filled with the divinity; and now he was metamorphosed into Fo or Pagod, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> of the Hindoos. He had no sooner declared himself a divinity, than he thought of propagating his doctrine, and proving his divine mission by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of his disciples was immense; and they soon spread his dogmas over all India, and even to the higher extremities of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>. One of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> doctrines which Fo and his disciples propagated, was the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-METEMPSYCHOSIS">metempsychosis</a> or transmigration of souls. This doctrine, some imagine, has given rise to the multitude of idols reverenced in every country where the worship of Fo is established. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-QUADRUPEDS">Quadrupeds</a>, birds, reptiles, and the vilest animals, had <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a> erected for them; because, say they, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> of the god, in his numerous transmigrations, may have at one time or other inhabited their bodies. Both the doctrine of transmigration and of the worship of animals seems, however, to have been imported from <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> into India. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the intercourse between these two countries was begun at so early a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> as some very late writers have endeavoured to prove, such a supposition is by no means improbable. The doctrine of the transmigration of souls was early established among the Egyptians. It was, indeed, the only idea they formed of the soul's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMMORTALITY">immortality</a>. The worship of animals among them seems to have been still more ancient. If such an intercourse did actually exist, we may naturally suppose that colonies of Egyptian priests found their way into India, as they did afterwards into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASIA_MINOR">Asia <a cl</a>ass="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>. That colonies of Egyptians did actually penetrate into that country, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> there, many centuries before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATIVITY">nativity</a>, is a fact that cannot be called in question, for reasons which the bounds prescribed us on this article will not allow us to enumerate. We shall only observe, that from the hieroglyphical representations of the Egyptian deities seem to have originated those monstrous idols which from time immemorial have been worshipped in India, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JAPAN">Japan</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SIAM">Siam</a>, and even in the remotest parts of Asiatic <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TARTARY">Tartary</a>. Foe is often called <a class="xref" href="../1815/vol0.html#article-BUDHA">Budha</a>, Budda, and sometimes the incarnate Vishnou; perhaps, indeed, he may be distinguished by nations of many other names, according to the variety of dialects Vishnou, of the different nations among which his worship was established. An infinitude of fables was propagated by his disciples concerning him after his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. They pretended that their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MASTER">master</a> was still alive; that he had been already born 8000 times; and that he had successively appeared under the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of an ape, a lion, a dragon, an elephant, a boar, &c. These were called the incarnations of Vishnou. At length he was confounded with the supreme God; and all the titles, attributes, operations, perfections, and ensigns of the Most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">High</a> were ascribed to him. Sometimes he is called <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMIDA">Amida</a>, and represented with the head of a dog, and worshipped as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARDIAN">guardian</a> of mankind. He sometimes appears as a princely personage, issuing from the mouth of a fish. At other times, he wears a lunette on his head, in which are seen cities, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, towers, trees, in short, all that the world contains. These transformations are evidently the children of allegorical or hieroglyphical emblems, and form an exact counterpart to the symbolical worship of the Egyptians. The enormous <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of mythological traditions which have in a manner deluged the vast continent of India, would fill many volumes: We have selected the preceding <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> as a specimen only, by which our readers may be qualified to judge of the rest. If they find themselves disposed to indulge their curiosity at greater length, we must remit them to Thevenot's and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAMILTON">Hamilton</a>'s Travels, to Mons. Aquetel in his Zond, Avesla, Halhed's Introduction to his translation of the Code of Gentoo Laws, Col. Dow's History of Hindoostan, Grose's Voyage to the East Indies, Asiatic Researches, vol. i. and 2. The mythology of the Persians is, if possible, still more extravagant than that of the Hindoos. It supposes the world to have been repeatedly destroyed, and repeopled by creatures of different formation, who were successively annihilated or banished for their disobedience to the supreme Being. The monstrous griffin Sinergb tells the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HERO">hero</a> Cakerman that he had already lived to see the earth seven times filled with creatures and seven times a perfect void; that, before the creation of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADAM">Adam</a>, this globe was inhabited by a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-RACE">race</a> of beings called Peri and Dives, whose character formed a perfect <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONTRAST">contrast</a>. The Peri are described as beautiful and benevolent; the Dives as deformed, malevolent, and mischievous, differing from infernal demons only in this, that they are not as yet confined to the pit of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HELL">hell</a>. They are ever ranging over the world, to scatter <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DISCORD">discord</a> and misery among the sons of men. The Peri nearly resemble the fairies of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>; and perhaps the Dives gave birth to the giants and magicians of the middle ages. The Peri and Dives wage incessant wars; and when the Dives make any of the Peri prisoners, they shut them up in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-IRON">iron</a> cages, and hang them on the highest trees, to expose them to public view, and to the fury of every chilling blast. When the Peri are in danger of being overpowered by their foes, they solicit the assistance of some mortal hero; which produces a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of mythological adventures, highly ornamental to the strains of the Persian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARDS">bards</a>, and which, at the same time, furnishes an inexhaustible <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FUND">fund</a> of the most diversified machinery. One of the most celebrated adventurers in the mythology of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a> is Tabmuras, one of their most ancient monarchs. This <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> performs a variety of exploits, while he endeavours to recover the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAIRY">fairy</a> Merjan. He attacks the Dive Demrush in his own cave; where, having vanquished the giant or demon, he finds vast piles of hoarded wealth; these he carries off with the fair captive. The battles, labours, and adventures of Roitan, another Persian worthy, who lived many ages after the former, are celebrated by the Persian bards with the same extravagance of hyperbole with which the labours of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a> have been sung by the poets of Greece and Rome. The adventures of the Persian heroes breathe all the wildness of achievement recorded of the knights of Gothic <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ROMANCE">romance</a>. The doctrine of enchantments, transformations, &c., exhibited in both, is a characteristic symptom of one <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMON">common</a> original. Persia is the genuine classic ground of eastern mythology, and the source of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of chivalry and romance; from which they were propagated to the regions of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-SCANDINAVIA">Scandinavia</a>, and indeed to the remotest corners of Europe towards the west. Perhaps our readers may be of our <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, when we offer it as a conjecture, that the tales of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WAR">war</a> of the Peri and Dives originated from a vague <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a> concerning good and bad <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a>: nor is it, in our opinion, improbable, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FABLE">fable</a> of the wars between the gods and giants, so famous in the mythology of Greece and Italy, was imported into the former of these countries from the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>. For a more particular account of the Persian mythology, our readers may consult Dr Hyde de Relig. vet. Perf. Medor, &c. D. Herbelot's Bibl. Orient, and Mr Richard-son's introduction to his Persian and Arabic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DICTIONARY">Dictionary</a>. The mythology of the Chaldeans, like that of the Chaldean other nations of the east, commences at a period myriads of years prior to the era of the Mosaic creation. Their cosmogony, exhibited by Berothus, who was a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> of Belus, and deeply versed in the antiquities of his country, is a piece of mythology of the most extravagant <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. It has been copied by Eusebius (Chron. l. i. p. 5.) it is likewise to be found in Syncellus, copied from Alexander Polyhistor. According to this historian, there were at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BABYLON">Babylon</a> written records preserved with the greatest care, comprehending a period of fifteen myriads of years. These writings likewise contained a history of the heavens and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, of the earth, and of the origin of mankind. "In the beginning (says Berothus, copying from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OANNES">Oannes</a>, of whom we shall give a brief account below) there was nothing but darkness and an abyss of water, wherein resided most hideous beings produced from a twofold principle. Men appeared with two wings; some with two and some with four faces. They had one body, but two heads; the one of a man the other of a woman. Other human figures were to be seen, furnished with the legs and horns of goats. Some had the feet of horses behind, but before were fashioned like men, resembling hippocentaurs." The remaining part of this mythology is much of the same complexity; indeed so extravagant, that we imagine our readers will readily enough dispense with our translating the sequel. "Of all these (says the author) were preserved delineations in the temple of Belus at Babylon. The person who was supposed to preside over them was called Omorea. This word, in the Chaldean <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, is Thalath, which the Greeks call θαλάττης, but it more properly imports the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MOON">moon</a>. Matters being in this situation, their god (says Eusebius), the god (says Syncellus) came and cut the woman inunder; and out of one half of her he formed the earth, and out of the other he made the heavens; and, at the same time, he destroyed the monsters of the abyss." This whole mythology is an allegorical history copied from hieroglyphical representations, the real purport of which could not be deciphered by the author. Such, in general, were the consequences of the hieroglyphical style of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>. Oannes, the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> civilizer and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LEGISLATOR">legislator</a> of the Chaldeans, according to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOLLODORUS">Apollodorus</a>, who copied from Berothus, was an amphibious animal of a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HETEROGENEOUS">heterogeneous</a> appearance. He was endowed with reason and a very uncommon acuteness of parts. His whole body resembled a fish. Under the head of a fish he had also another head, and feet below similar to those of a man, which were subjoined to the tail of the fish. His <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> and language were articulate and perfectly intelligible, and there was a figure of him still extant in the days of Berothus. He made his appearance in the Erythrean or <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RED_SEA"><a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RED">Red</a> Sea, where it borders upon <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BABYLONIA">Babylonia</a>. This monstrous being conversed with men by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>; but at night he plunged into the sea, and remained concealed in the water till next morning. He taught the Babylonians the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of letters and the knowledge of all the arts and sciences. He instructed them in the method of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> houses, constructing temples, and all other edifices. He taught them to compile laws. laws and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> ceremonies, and explained to them the principles of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>. In a word, he communicated to them everything necessary, useful, and ornamental; and so universal were his instructions, that not one single article had ever been added to them since the time they were first communicated. Helladius is of opinion that this strange personage, whoever he was, came to be represented under the figure of a fish, not because he was actually believed to be such, but because he was clothed with the skin of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEAL">seal</a>. By this account our readers will see that the Babylonian Oannes is the exact counterpart of the Pho-hi of the Chinese, and the Thoth or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a> Trismegistus of the Egyptians. It is likewise apparent, that the idea of the monster <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> of the man and the fish has originated from some hieroglyphic of that form grafted upon the appearance of man. Some <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> mythologists have been of opinion, that Oannes was actually <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NOAH">Noah</a> the great preacher of righteousness; who, as some think, settled in Shinar or Chaldea after the deluge, and who, in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of his connection with that event, might be properly represented under the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-EMBLEM">emblem</a> of the Man of the Sea. The nativity of Venus, the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LOVE">love</a>, is another piece of mythology famous among the Babylonians and Assyrians. An <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-EGG">egg</a>, say they, of a prodigious size, dropt from heaven into the river <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EUPHRATES">Euphrates</a>. Some doves settled upon this egg, after that the fishes had rolled it to the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BANK">bank</a>. In a short time this egg produced Venus, who was afterwards called the Dea <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, the Syrian goddess. In consequence of this tradition (says Hyginus), pigeons and fishes became sacred to this goddess among the Syrians, who always abstained from eating the one or the other. Of this imaginary being we have a very exact and entertaining history in the treatise De Dea Syria, generally ascribed to Lucian. In this mythological tradition our readers will probably discover an allusion to the celebrated Mundane egg; and at the same time the story of the fishes will <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> them to anticipate the connection between the sea and the moon. This same deity was the Atargatis of Alcalon, described by Diodorus the Sicilian; the one-half of her body a woman, and the other a fish. This was no doubt a hieroglyphic figure of the moon, importing the influence of that planet upon the sea and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SEX">sex</a>. The oriental name of this deity evidently <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POINTS">points</a> to the moon; for it is compounded of two <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> words (a), which import "the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOST">host</a> of heaven." The fable of Semiramis is nearly connected with the preceding one. Diodorus Siculus has preferred the mythological history of this deity, which he and all the writers of antiquity have confounded with the Babylonian princess of the same name. That historian informs us, that the word Semiramis, in the Syrian dialect, signifies "a wild pigeon;" but we apprehend that this <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TERM">term</a> was a name or epithet of the moon, as it is compounded of two words (c) of an import naturally applicable to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LUNAR">lunar</a> planet. It was a general practice among the Orientals to denominate their sacred animals from that deity to which they were consecrated. Hence the moon being called Semiramis, and the pigeon being sacred to her divinity, the latter was called by the name of the former. As the bounds prescribed, this article renders it impossible for us to do <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> to this interesting piece of mythology, we must beg leave to refer our readers for farther information to Diod. Sic. I. ii. Hyginus Poet. Astron. tab. 197. Pharnutus de Nat. Deor. Ovid. Metam. I. iv. Athen. in Apol. Izetzes Chil. ix. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 275. Seld. de Diis Syr. Syrii. ii. p. 183. We should now proceed to the mythology of the Little Arabians, the far greatest part of which is, however, known of buried in the abyss of ages; though, when we reflect on Arabian genius and character of that people, we must be convinced that they too, as well as the other nations of the east, abounded in fabulous relations and romantic compositions. The natives of that country have always been enthusiastically addicted to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, of which fable is the essence. Wherever the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MUSES">muses</a> have erected their thrones, fables and miracles have always appeared in their train. In the Koran we meet with frequent allusions to well-known traditional fables. These had been transmitted from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a> to generation by the bards and rhapsodists for the entertainment of the vulgar. In <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>, from the earliest ages, it has always been one of the favourite entertainments of the common people, to assemble in the serene evenings around their tents, or on the platforms with which their houses are generally covered, or in large halls erected for the purpose, in order to amuse themselves with traditional narrations of the most distinguished actions of their most remote <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>. Oriental imagery always embellished their romantic details. The glow of fancy, the love of the marvellous, the propensity towards the hyperbolic, and the vast, which constitute the essence of oriental <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>, must ever have drawn the relation aside into the devious regions of fiction and fairy-<a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAND">land</a>. The religion of Mahomet <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the original fabric of idolatry and mythology together. The Arabian fables current in modern times are borrowed or imitated from Persian compositions; Persia being still the grand nursery of romance in the east. In Egypt we find idolatry, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>, and mythology, almost inseparably blended together. The inhabitants of this region, too, as well as of others in the vicinity of the centre of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POPULATION">population</a>, adhered for several centuries to the worship of the true God. At last, however, conscious of their own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-IMPURITY">impurity</a>, imperfection, and total unfitness to approach an infinitely perfect Being, distant, as they imagined, and invisible, they began to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> about for some beings more exalted and more perfect than themselves, by whose mediation they might prefer their prayers to the supreme Majesty of heaven. The immortals of heaven, which they imagined were animated bodies, naturally presented themselves. These were splendid and glorious beings. They were thought to partake of the divine nature; they were revered as the satraps, prefects, (a) Adar or Hadar, "magnificus;" and Gad, "exercitus turmi." (c) Shem or Sem, "a sign;" and ramah, "high." prefects, and representatives of the supreme <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> of the universe. They were visible, they were benevolent; they dwelt nearer to the gods, they were near at hand, and always accessible. These were, of course, employed as mediators and intercessors between the supreme Divinity and his humble subjects of this lower world. Thus employed, they might claim a subordinate share of worship, which was accordingly assigned them. In <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of time, however, that worship, which was originally addressed to the supreme Creator by the mediation of the heavenly bodies, was in a great <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> forgotten, and the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADORATION">adoration</a> of mankind ultimately terminated on those illustrious creatures. To this circumstance, we think, we may ascribe the origin of that species of idolatry called Zabism, or the worship of the host of heaven, which overpread the world early and almost universally. In Egypt this <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of worship was adopted in all its most absurd and most enthusiastic forms; and at the same time the most heterogeneous mythology appeared in its train. The mythology of the ancient Egyptians was so various and multifrom, so complicated and so mysterious, that it would require many volumes even to give a superficial account of its origin and progress, not only in its mother country, but even in many other parts of the eastern and western world. Besides, the idolatry and mythology of that wonderful country are so closely connected and so inseparably blended together, that it is impossible to describe the latter without at the same time developing the former. We hope, therefore, our readers will not be disappointed if, in a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> of this nature, we touch only upon some of the leading or most interesting articles of this complicated subject. The Egyptians confounded the revolutions of the heavenly bodies with the reigns of their most early monarchs. Hence the incredible number of years included in the reign of their eight superior gods, who, according to them, filled the Egyptian throne successively in the most early periods of time. To these, according to their system, succeeded twelve demigods, who likewise reigned an amazing number of years. These imaginary reigns were no other than the periodical revolutions of the heavenly bodies preserved in their almanacks, which might be carried back, and actually were carried back, at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>. Hence the fabulous antiquity of that <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. The imaginary exploits and adventures of these gods and demigods furnished an inexhaustible fund of mythological romances. To the demigods succeeded the kings of the cynic cycle, personages equally chimerical with the former. The import of this epithet has greatly perplexed critics and etymologists. We apprehend it is an oriental word importing <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, elevation of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RANK">rank</a>. This appellation intimated, that the monarchs of that cycle, admitting that they actually existed, were more powerful and more highly revered than their successors. After the princes of the cynic cycle comes another race, denominated Nekyos, a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TITLE">title</a> likewise implying royal, splendid, glorious. These cycles figure high in the mythological annals of the Egyptians, and have furnished materials for a variety of learned and ingenious disquisitions. The wars and adventures of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OSIRIS">Osiris</a>, Orus, Typhon, and other allegorical personages who figure in the Egyptian rubric; the wanderings of Isis, the sister and wife of Osiris; the transformation of the gods into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> kinds of animals; their birth, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, peregrinations, and exploits—compose a body of mythological fictions so various, so complicated, so ridiculous, and often so apparently absurd, that all attempts to develop and explain them have hitherto proved unsuccessful. All, or the greater part, of those extravagant fables, are the offspring of hieroglyphical or allegorical emblems devised by the priests and sages of that <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, with a view to conceal the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a> of their religion from that class of men whom they stigmatized with the name of the uninformed rabble. The worship of brute animals and of certain vegetables universal among the Egyptians, was another exuberant source of mythological adventures. The Egyptian priests, many of whom were likewise profound philosophers, observed, or pretended to observe, a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANALOGY">analogy</a> between the qualities of certain animals and vegetables, and those of some of their subordinate divinities. Such animals and vegetables they adopted, and consecrated to the deities to whom they were supposed to bear this analogical resemblance; and in process of time they considered them as the visible emblems of those divinities to which they were consecrated. By these the vulgar addressed their archetypes; in the same manner, as in other countries, pictures and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> were employed for the very same purpose. The mob, in process of time, forgetting the emblematical character of those <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-BRUTES">brutes</a> and vegetables, addressed their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a> immediately to them; and of course these became the ultimate objects of vulgar adoration. After that these objects, animate or inanimate, were consecrated as the visible symbols of the deities, it soon became fashionable to make use of their figures to represent those deities to which they were consecrated. This practice was the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> consequence of the hieroglyphical style which universally prevailed among the ancient Egyptians. Hence <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMMON">Ammon</a> was represented under the figure of a ram, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APIS">Apis</a> under that of a cow, Osiris of a bull, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAN">Pan</a> of a goat, Thoth or Mercury of an ibis, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BUBASTIS">Bubastis</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a> of a cat, &c. It was likewise a common practice among those deluded people to dignify these objects, by giving them the names of those deities which they represented. By this mode of dignifying these sacred emblems, the veneration of the rabble was considerably enhanced, and the ardour of their devotion inflamed in proportion. From these two sources, we think, are derived the fabulous transformations of the gods, so generally celebrated in the Egyptian mythology, and from it imported into Greece and Italy. In consequence of this practice, their mythological system was rendered at once enormous and unintelligible. Their Thoth, or Mercury Trismegistus, was, in our opinion, the inventor of this unhappy system. This Trismegistus, according to the Egyptians, was the original author of letters, geometry, astronomy, music, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>; in a word, of all the elegant and useful Egyptian arts, and of all the branches of science and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>. He it was who first discovered the analogy between the divine affections, influences, appearances, operations, and the corresponding properties, qualities, and instincts. instincts of certain animals, and the propriety of dedicating particular kinds of vegetables to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of particular deities. The priests, whose <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> it was to expound the mysteries of that allegorical hieroglyphical religion, (see Mysteries), gradually lost all knowledge of the primary import of the symbolical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>. To supply this defect, and at the same time to veil their own ignorance, the sacerdotal instructors had recourse to fable and fiction. They heaped fable upon fable, till their religion became an accumulated <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHAOS">chaos</a> of mythological absurdities. Two of the most learned and most acute of the ancient philosophers have attempted a rational explication of the latent import of the Egyptian mythology; but both have failed in the attempt; nor have the moderns, who have laboured in the same department, performed their part with much better success. Instead, therefore, of prosecuting this inexplicable subject, which would swell this article beyond all proportion, we must beg leave to refer those who are desirous of further information to the following authors, where they will find enough to gratify their curiosity, if not to inform their judgment: <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a>, lib. ii. Diodorus Siculus, lib. i. Plut. Isis and Osiris; Jamblichus de Myth. Egypt. Horapollo Hieroglyph. Egypt. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACROBI">Macrobi</a>. Sat. cap. 23. among the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>; and among the moderns, Kircher's Oedip. Voss. de orig. et prog. Idol. Mr Bryant's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALYSIS">Analysis</a> of Anc. Mythol. Mons Gebelin Monde prim.; and above all, to the learned Jablonski's Panth. Egyptianum. The elements of Phoenician mythology have been preserved by Eusebius, Prep. Evang. sub init. In the large extract which that learned father hath copied from Philo Bithyni's translation of Sanchoniathon's History of Phoenicia, we are furnished with several articles of mythology. Some of these throw considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> on several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> of the sacred history; and all of them are strictly connected with the mythology of the Greeks and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. There we have preserved a brief but entertaining detail of the fabulous adventures of Uranus, Cronus, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DAGON">Dagon</a>, Thoth or Mercury, probably the same with the Egyptian hero of that name. Here we find Muth or Pluto, Æpheceus or Vulcan, Æsculapius, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEREUS">Nereus</a>, Poseidon or <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol7.html#article-NEPTUNE">Neptune</a>, &c. Astarte, or Venus <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-URANIA">Urania</a>, makes a conspicuous figure in the catalogue of Phoenician worthies; Pallas or <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a> is planted on the territory of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTICA">Attica</a>; in a word, all the branches of the family of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TITANS">Titans</a>, who in after ages figured in the rubric of the Greeks, are brought upon the stage, and their exploits and adventures briefly detailed. By comparing this fragment with the mythology of the Atlantidae and that of the Cretans preserved by Diodorus the Sicilian, lib. v. we think there is good reason to conclude, that the family of the Titans, the several branches of which seem to have been both the authors and objects of a great part of the Grecian idolatry, originally emigrated from Phoenicia. This conjecture will receive additional strength, when it is considered, that almost all their names recorded in the fabulous records of Greece, may be easily traced up to a Phoenician original. We agree with Herodotus, that a considerable part of the idolatry of Greece may have been borrowed from the Egyptians; at the same time, we imagine it highly probable, that the idolatry of the Egyptians and Phoenicians were, in their original <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, nearly the same. Both systems were Sabellian, or the worship of the host of heaven. The Pelagri, according to Herodotus, learned the names of the gods from the Egyptians; but in this conjecture he is certainly warped by his partiality for that people. Had those names been imported from Egypt, they would no doubt have bewrayed their Egyptian original; whereas, every etymologist will be convinced that every one is of Phoenician <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EXTRACTION">extraction</a>. The adventures of Jupiter, Juno, Mercury, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a>, Diana, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MARS">Mars</a>, Minerva or Pallas, Venus, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CERES">Ceres</a>, Procerpine, Pluto, Neptune, and the other descendants and coadjutors of the ambitious family of the Titans, furnish by far the greatest part of the mythology of Greece. They left Phoenicia, we think, about the age of Moses; they settled in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a>, a large and fertile <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>; from this region they made their way into Greece, which, according to the most authentic accounts, was at that time inhabited by a race of savages. The arts and inventions which they communicated to the natives; the mysteries of religion which they inculcated; the laws, customs, polity, and good order, which they established; in short, the blessings of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> and civilization, which they everywhere disseminated, in process of time inspired the unpolished inhabitants with a kind of divine admiration. Those ambitious mortals improved this admiration into divine homage and adoration. The greater part of that worship, which had been formerly addressed to the luminaries of heaven, was now transferred to those illustrious personages. They claimed and obtained divine honours from the deluded rabble of enthusiastic Greeks. Hence sprung an inexhaustible fund of the most inconsistent and irreconcilable fictions. The foibles and frailties of the deified mortals were hence transmitted to posterity, incorporated as it were with the pompous attributes of supreme divinity. Hence the heterogeneous mixture of the mighty and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> which chequers the characters of the heroes of the Iliad and Odyssey. The Greeks adopted the oriental fables; the import of which they did not understand. These they accommodated to heroes and illustrious personages, who had figured in their own country in the earliest periods. The labours of Hercules originated in Egypt, and evidently relate to the annual progress of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ZODIAC">zodiac</a>, though the vain-glorious Greeks accommodated them to a hero of their own, the reputed son of Jupiter and Alcmene. The expedition of Otris they borrowed from the Egyptians, and transferred to their Bacchus, the son of Jupiter and Semele the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CADMUS">Cadmus</a>. The transformation and wanderings of Io are evidently transcribed from the Egyptian romance of the travels of Isis in quest of the body of Osiris, or of the Phoenician Astarte, drawn from Sanchoniathon. Io or Lib is in reality the Egyptian name of the moon, and Astarte was the name of the same planet among the Phoenicians. Both these fables are allegorical representations of the anomalies of the lunar planet, or perhaps of the progress of the worship of that planet in different parts of the world. The fable of the conflagration occasioned by Phaethon is clearly of oriental extraction, and alludes to an excessive drought which in the early period... periods of time scorched Ethiopia and the adjacent countries. The fabulous adventures of Perseus are said to have happened in the same regions, and are allegorical representations of the influence of the solar luminary; for the original Perseus was the sun. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RAPE">rape</a> of Proserpine and the wanderings of Ceres; the Eleusinian mysteries; the orgies or sacred <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> of Bacchus; the rites and worship of the Cabiri—were imported from Egypt and Phoenicia; but strangely garbled and disfigured by the Hierophants of Greece. The gigan- tomachia, or war between the gods and the giants, and all the fabulous events and varieties of that war, form an exact counterpart to the battles of the Peri and Divs, celebrated in the romantic annals of Per- fia. The Greeks signifant of oriental languages. A considerable part of the mythology of the Greeks sprung from their ignorance of the oriental languages. They disdained to apply themselves to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of languages spoken by people whom, in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a> of their heart, they stigmatised with the epithet of barbarians. This aversion to every foreign dialect was highly detrimental to their progress in the sciences. The same neglect or aversion has, we imagine, proved an irreparable injury to the republic of letters in all succeeding ages. The soi-disant or strolling bands laid hold on those oriental legends, which they sophificated with their own additions and improvements, in order to accommodate them to the popular <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>. These wonderful tales figured in their rhapsodical compositions, and were greedily swallowed down by the credulous vulgar. Those fictions, as they rolled down, were constantly augmented with fresh materials, till in process of time their original import was either forgotten or buried in impenetrable darkness. A multitude of these fables had collected in his Theogonia, or generation of the gods, which unhappily became the religious creed of the illiterate part of the Greeks. Indeed, fable was so closely interwoven with the religion of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIRY">airy</a> volatile people, that it seems to have contaminated not only their religious and moral, but even their <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> tenets. The far-famed oracle of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DODONA">Dodona</a> was copied from that of Ammon of Thebes in Egypt: The oracle of Apollo at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DELPHI">Delphi</a> was an emanation from the same source: The celebrated Apollo Pythius of the Greeks was no other than Ob or Aub of the Egyptians, who denominated the basilisk or royal snake Ov Gai, because it was held sacred to the sun. Ob or Aub is still retained in the Coptic dialect, and is one of the many names or epithets of that luminary. In short, the groundwork of the Grecian mythology is to be traced in the east. Only a small part of it was fabricated in the country; and what was imported pure and genuine was miserably sophificated by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> through which it passed, in order to give it a Grecian <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>, and to accommodate its style to the Grecian taste. To enlarge upon this topic would be altogether superfluous, as our learned readers must be well acquainted with it already, and the unlearned may without much trouble or expense furnish themselves with books upon that subject. The Roman mythology was borrowed from the Greeks. That people had addicted themselves for many centuries to the arts of war and civil polity. Science and philosophy were either neglected or un- N° 236. known. At last they conquered Greece, the native land of science, and then "Graecia capta ferum victorem cepit arte et intulit agresti Latio." This being the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CASE">case</a>, their mythology was, upon the whole, a transcript from that of Greece. They had indeed gleaned a few fables from the Pelasgi and Hetruscans, which, however, are of so little consequence, that they are scarce worth the trouble of transcribing. The mythology of the Celtic nations is in a good measure lost.
