There may possibly still remain some vestiges of the Druidical <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a> in the remotest parts of the Highlands and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> of Scotland; and perhaps in the uncivilized places of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>. These, we presume, would afford our readers but little entertainment, and still less instruction. Instead therefore of giving a detail of those uninteresting articles, we shall beg leave to refer our readers to <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OSSIAN">Ossian</a>'s Poems, and Col. Valency's Collections of Irish Antiquities, for satisfaction on that subject. The mythology of the northern nations, i.e., of the Norwegians, Danes, Swedes, Icelanders, &c., are not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> curious and entertaining. The Edda and northern Voluppa contain a complete collection of fables which have not the smallest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFFINITY">affinity</a> with those of the Greeks and Romans. They are wholly of an oriental <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a>, and seem almost congenial with the tales of the Persians above described. The Edda was compiled in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ICELAND">Iceland</a> in the 1st century. It is a kind of system of the Scandinavian mythology; and has been reckoned, and we believe justly, a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMENTARY">commentary</a> on the Voluppa, which was the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a> of the northern nations. Odin or Othin, or Woden or Waden, was the supreme divinity of those people. His exploits and adventures furnish the far greatest part of their mythological creed. That hero is supposed to have emigrated from the east; but from what country or at what period is not certainly known. His achievements are magnified beyond all credibility. He is represented as the god of battles, and as slaughtering thousands at a blow. His <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> is called Valhalla; it is situated in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Midgard, where, according to the fable, the souls of heroes who had bravely fallen in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> enjoy supreme felicity. They spend the day in mimic hunting-matches, or imaginary combats. At night they assemble in the palace of Valhalla, where they feast on the most delicious viands, drested and served up by the Valkyries, virgins adorned with celestial charms, and flushed with the bloom of everlasting youth. They solace themselves with drinking <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MEAD">mead</a> out of the skulls of enemies whom they killed in their days of nature. Mead, it seems, was the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NECTAR">nectar</a> of the Scandinavian heroes. Sleepner, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> of Odin, is celebrated along with his master. Hela, the hell of the Scandinavians, affords a variety of fables equally shocking of the and heterogeneous. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LOKE">Loke</a>, the evil genius or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEVIL">devil</a> of the northern people, nearly resembles the Typhon of the Egyptians. Sigma or Sinna is the comfort of Loke; from this name the English word sin is derived. The giants Weynur, Ferbanter, Belophor, and Hel-lunda, perform a variety of exploits, and are exhibited in the most frightful attitudes. One would be tempted to imagine, that they perform the exact counterpart of the giants of the Greek and Roman mythologies. Instead of glancing at these ridiculous and uninteresting fables, fables, which is all that the limits prescribed us would permit, we shall take the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to lay before our readers a brief account of the contents of the Voluppa, which is indeed the text of the Scandinavian mythology. The word *Voluppa* imports, "the prophecy of Vola or Fola." This was perhaps a general name for the prophetic ladies of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, as Sybil was appropriated to women endowed with the like <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> in the south. Certain it is, that the ancients generally connected madness with the prophetic faculty. Of this we have two celebrated examples: the one in Lycophron's Alexandra, and the other in the Sybil of the Roman Poet. The word *vola* signifies "mad or foolish;" whence the English words *fool*, *foolish*, *folly*. *<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPA">Spa</a>*, the latter part of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, signifies "to prophesy," and is still current among the common people in Scotland, in the word *Spa*, which has nearly the same fig- The Voluppa consists of between 200 and 300 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>. The prophetess having imposed silence on all intelligent beings, declares that she is about to reveal the works of the Father of nature, the actions and operations of the gods, which no mortal ever knew before herself. She then begins with a description of the chaos; and then proceeds to the formation of the world, the creation of the different species of its inhabitants, giants, men, and dwarfs. She then explains the employments of the fairies or destinies, whom the northern people call *nornir*; the functions of the deities, their most memorable adventures, their disputes with Loki, and the vengeance that ensued. She at last concludes with a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a> and indeed animated description of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FINAL">final</a> state of the universe, and its <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> by a general conflagration. In this catastrophe, Odin and all the rabble of the pagan divinities, are to be confounded in the general ruin, no more to appear on the stage of the universe. Out of the ruins of the former world, according to the Voluppa, a new one shall <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> up, arrayed in all the bloom of celestial beauty. Such is the doctrine exhibited in the fabulous Voluppa. So congenial are some of the details therein delivered, especially their relating to the final dissolution of the present system, and the succession of a new heaven and a new earth, that we find ourselves strongly inclined to suspect, that the original fabrication of the work was a semi-pagan writer, much of the same complexion with the authors of the Sibylline <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-ORACLES">oracles</a>, and of some other apocryphal pieces which appeared in the world during the first ages of Christianity. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, the only mythological countries must be <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PERU">Peru</a>. The other parts of that large continent were originally inhabited by savages, most of them as remote from religion as from civilization. The two vast empires of Mexico and Peru had existed about 400 years only before the Spanish invasion: In neither of them was the use of letters understood; and of course the ancient opinions of the natives relating to the origin of the universe, the changes which succeeded, and every other monument of antiquity, was obliterated and lost. Clavigero has indeed enumerated a vast canaille of sanguinary gods worshipped by the Mexicans; but produces nothing either entertaining or interesting with respect to their mythology. The information to be derived from any other quarter is little to be depended upon. It passes through the hands of bigoted missionaries or other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a>, who were so deeply tinctured with fanaticism, that they viewed every <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, every sentiment, every <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>, every religious opinion and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> of those half-civilized people, through a false medium. They often imagined they discovered resemblances and analogies between the rites of those savages and the dogmas of Christianity, which nowhere existed but in their own heated imagination. The only remarkable piece of mythology in the annals of the Peruvians, is the pretended extraction of Manco Capac the first Inca of Peru, and of Mama Oculla his consort. These two illustrious personages appeared first on the banks of the lake Titicaca. They were persons of a majestic stature, and clothed in decent garments. They declared themselves to be the children of the Sun, sent by their beneficent <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PARENT">parent</a>, who beheld with pity the miseries of the human race, to instruct and to reclaim them. Thus we find these two legislators availed themselves of a pretence which had often been employed in more civilized regions to the very same purposes. The idolatry of Peru was gentle and benevolent, that of Mexico gloomy and sanguinary. Hence we may see, that every mode of superstition, where a divine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REVELATION">revelation</a> is not concerned, borrows its complexion from the characters of its professors. In the course of this article, our readers will observe, that we have not much enlarged upon the mythology of the Greeks and Romans; that subject, we imagine to be so universally known by the learned, and so little valued by the vulgar, that a minute discussion of it would be altogether superfluous. Besides, we hope it will be remembered, that the narrowness of the limits prescribed us would scarce admit of a more copious detail. We would flatter ourselves, that in the course of our disquisition, we have thrown out a few reflections and observations, which may perhaps prove more acceptable to both descriptions of readers.

MYTILUS

Pages 655-661

the Mussel, in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">ichthyology</a>; a genus of animals, belonging to the order of vermes testacea. The animal is an ascidia; the shell bivalve; often affixed to some substance by a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARD">beard</a>; the hinge without a tooth, marked by a longitudinal hollow line. Of these animals there are a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> many <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, some of them inhabiting the seas, others the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> and ponds. Several of them are remarkable for the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of their internal shell, and for the pearls which are sometimes found in them. 1. The edulis, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> edible mussel, has a strong shell, slightly incurved on one side, and angulated on the other. other. The end near the hinge is pointed; the other rounded. When the epidermis is taken off, it is of a deep blue <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. It is found in immense beds, both in deep <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WATER">water</a> and above low-water mark. The finest mussels in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> are those called Hambleton hookers, from a village called Hambleton in that <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>. They are taken out of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and placed in the river Wier, within reach of the tide, where they grow very fat and delicious. This species inhabits the European and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> seas. Between the tropics it is largest, and smallest within the polar circle. It is said to be hurtful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> too often eaten, or in too great quantities; and is even sometimes poisonous. 2. The modiolus, or great mussel, with a strong shell, blunted at the upper end; one side angulated near the middle; from thence dilating towards the end, which is rounded. It dwells in the Mediterranean, Indian, European, and American seas; and its <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>, which is a deep <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a> colour, is eatable. It is the greatest of the mussels known in Britain; being from six to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> inches in length; it lies at great depths; often seizes the baits of ground-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, and is taken up with the hooks. 3. The cygnus, or swan mussel, with a thin brittle shell, very <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> and convex, marked with concentric striae; attenuated towards one end, dilated towards the other; decorticated about the hinge; the colour a dull green; the length six inches, breadth three and a half. It is an inhabitant of the European rivers, frequenting chiefly their mouths. 4. The anatinus, or duck mussel, has a shell more <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> and less convex than the last; is very brittle and semitransparent; the space round the hinges like the last; the length about five inches, breadth two. It is found in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> in fresh waters. Both it and the cygnus are devoured by swans and ducks; whence their names: crows also feed on these mussels, as well as on different other shell fish; and it is diverting to observe, that when the shell is too hard for their bills, they fly with it to a great height, drop the shell on a rock, and pick out the meat when the shell is fractured by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>. 5. The cryphagalli, or cock's-comb mussel, has the shell folded or plicated as it were, spiny, and both lips rugged. It makes its abode in the coral beds of the Indian ocean. 6. The margaritiferus, or <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PEARL">pearl</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> mussel, has the shell compressed and flat, nearly orbicular, the base transverse, and imbricated with dentate coats. It dwells in the ocean of either <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a>. This is the mater perlariae of Rumphius, or mother-of-pearl shell. On the inside it is exquisitely polished, and of the whitestens and water of pearl itself. It has also the Mytilus fame lustre on the outside after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> laminae have been taken off by aquafortis and the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAPIDARY">lapidary</a>'s mill. Mother-of-pearl is used in inlaid works, and in several toys, as snuff-boxes, &c. 7. The lithophagus, or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-STONE">stone</a>-eating mussel, has the shell cylindric, the extremities both ways being rounded. It inhabits the Indian, European, and Mediterranean seas, penetrating and eating away marbles, corals, &c. The Indian shell is softer and nearly tough like <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, but the European is more brittle. 8. The violacea, or violet mussel, has the shell longitudinally furrowed, the rim very obtuse, somewhat formed like the mytilus edulis, but considerably larger and more flattened, of a beautiful violet colour. Inhabits the southern ocean. There are about 50 other species. Mussels not only open and shut their shells at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, but they have also a progressive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>; they can fasten themselves where they please; they retire water like the fishes; and some even flutter about on its surface so as to inhale <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>. If they <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> in shallow places, a small circular motion is seen above the heel of the shell; and a few moments after, they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> out the water by one single stroke at the other end of the shell. The mouth is situated near the sharp <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> of the animal, and is furnished with four floating fringes in the shape of multichios, which may perhaps answer the purpose of lips. The barbs which surround the edge of almost half the mussel, are a wonderful web of hollow fibres which serve as fins or organs of respiration, as vessels for the circulation of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a>, and probably, as some philosophers suppose, as wedges for opening their shells; for we observe two <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> muscles or tendons for the purpose of shutting them; but we in vain look for their antagonists, or those which are destined to open them. When the mussel wishes to open itself, it relaxes the two muscles or tendons, and swells the fringes, which <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> as wedges and separate the shells. The animal shuts up itself by the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONTRACTION">contraction</a> of two thick <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIBROUS">fibrous</a> muscles which are fixed internally to each end of the shells; and these shells are lined all around with a membrane or epidermis, which unites them so closely together when they are soaked in water, that not the smallest drop can escape from the muscle. When mussels choose to walk (a), they often contrive to raise themselves on the sharp edge of their shells, and put forth a fleshy substance susceptible of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENSION">extension</a>, which serves them as a leg to drag themselves along, in a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GROOVE">groove</a> or furrow which they form in the sand or mud, and which supports the shell on both sides. In ponds, these furrows are very observable. From the same member or leg hang the threads. (a) The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMON">common</a> sea or edible mussel has, from its being for the most <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> found fastened to the rocks, been supposed by many wholly incapable of progressive motion; but this M. Reamur has shown to be an erroneous <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>. It is a common practice in France, at such seasons of the year as do not afford <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> enough to make <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, to throw the common sea-mussels, which the fishermen catch about the coasts, into the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BRINE">brine</a>-pits. They have an opinion that this renders their flesh the more tender and delicate, as the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> which falls at these seasons makes the water of the pits much less salt than the common sea-water. The mussels are on this occasion thrown carelessly in, in several different parts of the pits; yet, at whatever distances they have been thrown in, the fishermen, when they go to take them out, always find them in a clutter together; and as there is no current of water in these places, nor any other power of motion, which can have brought the mussels together, it seems threads by which the animals fasten (a) themselves to rocks or to one another. According to the observations of M. Mery of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> Academy, and the subsequent experiments of other naturalists, mussels are all androgynous; and, from a peculiar generative organization, each individual is of itself capable of propagating its species, and annually does it without the intercourse of any other. This is altogether singular, and different from what takes <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in snails, earthworms, and other hydrogenous or hermaphroditical animals; for though each individual of these contains the parts of both sexes, yet there is always a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONGRESS">congress</a> of two animals for the propagation of the species. The parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a> are seems very evident that they must voluntarily have marched from the places where they were at first, to have met thus together. This progressive motion is wholly performed by means of what we call the tongue of the mussel, from its shape; but, from its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in this <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CASE">case</a>, appears rather to merit the name of a leg, or an arm, as by laying hold of any distant substance, and then forcibly contracting itself again, it draws along the whole body of the animal. The same part, when it has moved the animal to a proper place, serves also to fix it there, being the organ by which it spins the threads which we call its beard, by which it is held to a rock, or to another mussel. The motion of the mussel, by means of this part, is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> the same with that of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAN">man</a> laid flat on his belly, who would draw himself along by laying hold of anything with one <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and then <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> himself to it. (a) Mussels are well known to have a power of fastening themselves either to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, or to one another's shells, in a very strong and firm manner; but the method of doing this was not well understood till the observations of Mr Reaumur explained it. Every one who opens and examines a common mussel, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a> find, that in the middle of the fish there is placed a little blackish or brownish body resembling a tongue. This in large mussels is near half an inch <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and a little more than a sixth of an inch in breadth, and is narrower at the origin than at the extremity: from the root of this tongue, or that part of it which is fastened to the body of the fish, there are produced a great <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of threads, which, when fixed to any <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> substance, hold the mussel firmly in its place: these threads are usually from an inch to two inches in length, and in thickness from that of a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> to that of a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOG">hog</a>'s bristle. They issue out of the shell in that part where it naturally opens, and fix themselves to any thing that lies in their way, to stones, to fragments of shells, or, which is the most common case, to the shells of other mussels; whence it happens that there are usually such large quantities of mussels found together. These threads are expanded on every side, and are usually very numerous, having been found issuing from one shell: they serve the office of so many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CABLES">cables</a>; and, each pulling in its proper <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>, they keep the mussel fixed against any force that can be offered from whatever part it come. The filaments are well known to all who eat mussels, who ever carefully separate them under the name of the beard; and Mr Reaumur has found, that while the animal is living in the sea, if they are all torn away by any accident, the creature has a power of substituting others in their room: he found, that if a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of mussels were detached from one another and put into a vessel of any kind, and in that plunged into the sea, they in a little <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> fastened themselves both to the sides of the vessel and to one another's shells; the extremity of each thread seemed in this case to serve in the manner of a hand to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> upon anything that it would fix to, and the other part, which was slenderer and smaller, to do the office of an arm in conducting it. To know the manner of the mussels performing this operation, this diligent observer put some mussels into a vessel in his chamber, and covered them with sea water; he there <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAW">saw</a> that they soon began to open their shells, and each put forth that little body before described by its resemblance to a tongue, and at the root of which these threads grow; they extended and shortened this part several times, and thrust it out every way, often giving it not less than two inches in length, and trying before, behind, and on every side with it, what were the proper places to fix their threads at: at the end of these trials they let it remain fixed for some time on the spot which they chose for that purpose, and then drawing it back into the shell with great quickness, it was easy to see that they were then fastened by one of these threads to the spot where it had before touched and remained fixed for a few minutes; and in repeating this workmanship the threads are increased in number one at every time, and being fixed in different places they sustain the fish at rest against any common force. The several threads were found to be very different from one another; the new formed ones being ever whiter, more glossy, and more transparent than the others; and it appeared on a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a>, that it was not, as might have been most naturally supposed, the office of the tongue to convey the old threads one by one to the new places where they were now to be fixed, but that these in reality were now become useless; and that every thread we see now formed, is a new one made at this time; and in fine, that <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> has given to some sea-fishes, as well as to many <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAND">land</a>-insects, a power of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPINNING">spinning</a> those threads for their necessary uses; and that mussels and the like fish are under water, what caterpillars and spiders are at land.—To be well assured of this, however, Mr Reaumur cut off the beard or old threads of a mussel as close as he could, without injuring the part; and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of the opinion of their spinning new ones at pleasure was now brought to this easy <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>, whether these mussels, so deprived of their old ones, could fix themselves as soon as others which were possessed of theirs, and could throw out their threads to as considerable distances. two ovaries and two seminal vesicles. Each ovary and vesicle has its proper duct. It is through these four channels that the eggs and the seed of the mussel are conveyed to the anus, where those two principles unite at their issue, which answers the purpose of generation. It is in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> that mussels lay their eggs; there being none found in them but in winter. M. Lewenhoek, in several mussels which he dissected, discovered numbers of eggs or embryo mussels in the ovarium, appearing as plainly as if he had seen them by the naked eye, and all lying with their sharp ends fastened to the string of vessels by which they receive nourishment. The minute eggs, or embryos, are by the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PARENT">parent</a> placed in due order, and in a very close arrangement on the outside of the shell, where, by means of a gluey <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, they adhere very fast, and continually increase in size and strength, till becoming perfect mussels, they fall off and shift for themselves, leaving the holes where they were placed behind them. This abundance the mussel shells very plainly show, when examined by the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-MICROSCOPE">microscope</a>, and sometimes the number is 2000 or 3000 in one shell: but it is not certain that these have been all fixed there by the mussel within; for these fish usually lying in great numbers near one another, the embryos of one are often affixed to the shell of another. The fringed edge of the Mytilus mussel, which Lewenhoek calls the beard, has in every minute part of it such variety of motions as is inconceivable; for being composed of longish fibres, each <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FIBRE">fibre</a> has on both sides a vast many moving particles. The mussel is infested by several enemies in its own element; according to Reaumur it is in particular the prey of a small shell-fish of the trochus kind. This animal attaches itself to the shell of the mussel, pierces it with a round hole, and introduces a sort of tube five or six lines long, which it turns in a spiral direction, and with which it sucks the substance of the mussel. Mussels are also subject to certain diseases, which have been supposed to be the cause of those bad effects which sometimes happen from the eating of them. These are stated by Dr Moehring, in the 7th vol. of the German Ephemerides, to be the moths and the scab. The roots of the moths being introduced into the shell, the water penetrates through the openings, and gradually dissolves the mussel. The scab is formed by a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TUBERCLES">tubercles</a> which are produced by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> of the shell. Certain small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CRABS">crabs</a>, which are sometimes found in mussels, likewise tend to make them unwholesome. The experiment proved the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of the conjecture; for those whose beards or old threads were cut off, fixed themselves as soon as those in which they were left, and spread their threads to as great a distance every way. When the mechanism of this manufacture was thus far understood, it became a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> desire to inquire into the nature of the part by which it was performed. This has hitherto been mentioned under the name of the tongue, from its shape; but it is truly the arm of the fish; and whenever it happens to be loosened from its <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, or fixed in a wrong place, it serves the animal to drag its whole body shell and all along, and to perform its several motions. It fixes itself to some solid body; and then strongly contracting its length, the whole fish must necessarily follow it, and be pulled toward the place where it is fixed. This is an use, however, that this part is so rarely put to, that it is not properly to be esteemed a leg or an arm for this; but, according to its more frequent employment, may much better be denominated the organ by which the threads are spun. Though this body is flat in the manner of a tongue for the greater part of its length, it is however rounded or cylindric about the base or insertion, and it is much smaller there than in any other part: there are several muscular ligaments fastened to it about the root or base, which hold it firmly against the middle of the back of the shell; of these ligaments there are four which are particularly observable, and which serve to move the body in any direction. There runs all along this body a slit or crack, which pierces very deeply into its substance, and divides it as it were into two longitudinal sections; this is properly a canal, and along this is thrown the liquor which serves to form the threads; and it is in this canal or slit that these threads are moulded into their form. Externally, this appears only a small crack or slit, because the two fleshy sections of the parts almost meet and cover it; but it is rounded and deep within, and is surrounded with circular fibres. This canal is carried regularly on from the tip of the tongue, as it is called, to its base, where it becomes cylindric; the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CYLINDER">cylinder</a> in this part being no other than a close tube or pipe, in which this open canal terminates. The cylindric tube contains a round oblong body, of the nature of the threads, except that it is much larger; and from the extremity of this all the threads are produced, this serving as a great cable to which all the other little cordages dispersed towards different parts are fixed. The tube or pipe in which this large thread is lodged, seems the reservoir of the liquor of which the other threads are formed; all its internal surface being furnished with glands for its secretion. The mussel, like many other sea-fishes, abounds in this liquor; and if at any time one touch with a finger the base of this spinning organ, one draws away with it a viscid liquor in form of several threads, like those of the caterpillar, spider, and the other spinning land-animals. The threads fix themselves with equal ease to the most smooth and glossy, as to rougher bodies; if the mussels are kept in glass-jars of sea-water, they as firmly fasten themselves to the glass as to any other body. Mussels, be they ever so young, have this <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of spinning; and by this means they fasten themselves in vast numbers to anything which they find in the sea. Mr Reaumur has seen them, when as small as millet-seeds, spin plentifully, though their threads, proportioned to their own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, are much finer and smaller than those of larger mussels. The eating of mussels has sometimes produced erysipelas, inflammations, cutaneous eruptions, inapplicable itching all over the body, great restlessness and agitation; and though these complaints are easily removed by <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MILK">milk</a>, and emetics, and have seldom or never proved mortal, yet they have an alarming aspect, and make the patient suffer grievously. These noxious effects have been supposed to be owing to the mussels or part of them having been diseased. Some authors, however, have pretended that those effects never take place but between the vernal and autumnal equinox; and M. Beunie, physician at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTWERP">Antwerp</a>, in a memoir on this subject, seems inclined to adopt this opinion; for he recommends <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSTINENCE">abstinence</a> from mussels during the months of May, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JUNE">June</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>, and August. The cause of these noxious effects in the mussel is, according to this author, altogether accidental. They are occasioned, he says, by a kind of Stella marina, a little sea insect pretty common about the mouth of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHELDT">Scheldt</a>, which sometimes lodges itself in the mussel in quest of food; and whose spawn is so caustic and inflammatory, that, even when applied outwardly to the skin, it produces itching and swellings that are painful in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>. The itching occasioned by touching the spawn of the Stella marina is removed by <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a>; and this known fact induced Dr Beunie to prescribe the internal use of vinegar, after bleeding, evacuations, and emetics. His method consists in recommending a large quantity of refreshing <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEVERAGE">beverage</a>, and, every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>, three ounces of vinegar diluted in water. This remedy, however, seems rather to confirm the opinion of those who impute the disorder in question to an unperceived commencement of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PUTREFACTION">putrefaction</a> in the mussel; as vinegar is known to be a powerful antiseptic, and there is no sort of putrefaction more noxious and offensive than that of fish.—Upon the whole, the edulis, or eatable mussel, though a rich food, is difficult of digestion. In its best state it is even noxious to some constitutions; and when affected by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> is in some degree poisonous. Mussels are apt to do most harm when eaten raw. They ought always to be boiled with onions, well washed with vinegar, and seasoned with <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PEPPER">pepper</a>; and even thus qualified, they should not be eaten to excess or too frequently. Fresh-water mussels are not so good eating as the sea-mussel. The river mussel, according to M. Poupart, swims in the water, and sometimes appears to flutter on its surface. But we believe it more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> creeps in the mud, where it remains almost always at rest. The pond mussel is always larger than that which is found in rivers; and it is a more solitary animal. In its motion it makes tracks in the sand and mud, as already observed; and it penetrates into it two or three inches, and sometimes more. Pearls of considerable beauty are found in several river-mussels; of this kind are the Scots mussels, those of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-VALOGNES">Valognes</a> in Lorraine, of St Savinier, of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAVARIA">Bavaria</a>, and of the marshes near Augsburg.

MYTTOTON

Pages 661-661

a coarse kind of food, used by the labouring people among the Greeks, and sometimes among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. It was made of garlic, onions, eggs, cheese, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a>, and reckoned very wholesome.

MYUS

Pages 661-661

one of the twelve <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-IONIA">Ionia</a>; seated on the Meander, at the distance of 30 stadia from the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. In Strabo's <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> it was incorporated with the Milesians, on account of the paucity of its inhabitants, from its being formerly overwhelmed with <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WATER">water</a>; for which reason the Ionians consigned its suffrage and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> ceremonies to the people of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MILETUS">Miletus</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTAXERXES">Artaxerxes</a> allotted this town to Themistocles, in order to furnish his <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TABLE">table</a> with meat; <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAGNESIA">Magnesia</a> was to support him in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>, and Lampacus in wine. The town now lies in ruins.

MYXINE

Pages 661-662

the Hag; a genus of insects belonging to the order of vermes intestini. It hath a slender body, carinated beneath; mouth at the extremity, ciliated; the two jaws pinnated; an adipose <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> rayless <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIN">fin</a> round the tail and under the belly. The only remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> is the glutinoa, about eight inches <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a>. It inhabits the ocean; enters the mouths of fish when on the hooks of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> that remain a tide under <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and totally devours the whole, except skin and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BONES">bones</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-SCARBOROUGH">Scarborough</a> fishermen often take it in the robbed fish, on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> up their lines. Linnaeus attributes to it the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> water into <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-GLUE">glue</a>. N: N, A liquid consonant, and the 13th <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> of the Greek, Latin, English, &c. alphabets. The n is a nasal consonant: its <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> is that of a d, passed through the nose; so that when the nose is flopped by a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, or the like, it is usual to pronounce d for n. M. l'Abbe de Dangeau observes, that in the French, the n is frequently a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> nasal vowel, without any thing of the consonant in it. He calls it the Slavonic vowel. The Hebrews call their n <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUN">nun</a>, which signifies child, as being supposed the offspring of m; partly on account of the resemblance of sound, and partly on that of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>. Thus from the m, by omitting the last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLUMN">column</a>, is formed n; and thus from the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> N, by omitting the first column, is formed the Greek minuscule. Hence for bennies, &c., the Latins frequently <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> binus, &c. and the same people convert the Greek v, at the end of a word, into an m, as φαρμακον, pharmacum, &c. See M. N before p, b, and m, the Latins change into m, and frequently into l and r; as in in-ludo, illudo; in- NAB rigo, irigo, &c.: in which they agree with the Hebrews, who, in lieu of nun, frequently <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> the following <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSONANTS">consonants</a>; and the Greeks do the same; as when for Manlius, they write Mannaio, &c. The Greeks also, before η, ρ, χ, changed the into γ; in which they were followed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>; who, for Angulus, wrote Aggulus; for anepos, agepos, &c. The Latins retrench the n from Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOUNS">nouns</a> ending in ον; as Αυγος, Leo; Δρακον, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DRACO">Draco</a>: on the contrary, the Greeks add it to the Latin ones ending in o; as Κατος, Nippos, Cato, Nero. N, among the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, was a numeral letter, signifying 900; according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> in Baronius, N, quoque nongentos numero designat habendos. And when a line was struck over it, N, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NINE">nine</a> thousand. Among the ancient lawyers N.L. stood for non liquet, i.e., the cause is not clear enough to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> upon. N, or No, in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, &c., is used as an abbreviation of numero, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>.

NAARDA

Pages 662-662

Nearda, Neerda, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> Neardao, (anc. geog.), a town situated on the confines of Melopotamia and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BABYLONIA">Babylonia</a>; populous, and with a rich and extensive territory, not easily to be attacked by an enemy, being surrounded on all sides by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EUPHRATES">Euphrates</a> and strong walls (Josephus). In the lower <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> the Jews had a celebrated school there.

NAAS

Pages 662-662

a borough and port town of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KILDARE">Kildare</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LEINSTER">Leinster</a>. It is the shire town of that county, and alternately with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATHY">Athy</a> the assizes town. It is distant above 15 miles south west of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>, in N. Lat. 53° 10' W. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 6° 50'. It sends two members to <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>; and gives <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of viscount to the family of Burke. It has five <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a> in the year.—This <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a> was anciently the residence of the kings of Leinster: the name signifies "the place of elders," for here the states of that province assembled during the 6th, 7th, and 8th centuries, after the Naasfeighan of Carmen had been anthematized by the Christian clergy. On the arrival of the English it was fortified; many castles were erected, the ruins of which are partly visible; and parliaments were held there. At the foot of the mount <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> rath are the ruins of a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> founded in 1484, for eremites of the order of St Augustin. In the 12th century the baron of Naas founded a priory dedicated to St John the Baptist, for Augustinian regular canons. In the centre of this town the family of Euflace erected a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> for Dominican friars, dedicated to St Euflachius; and it appears that their possessions in Naas were granted them in the year 1355. This place was a strong hold during the civil wars.

NABATENE

Pages 662-662
or Regio Nabataeorum, according to Jerome, comprised all the country lying between the Euphrates and the s="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RED">Red Sea, and thus contained Arabia Deserta, with a part of the Petraea: so called from Nabaioth, the first born of Ishmael. According to Diodorus, it was situated between Syria and Egypt. The people Nabatei (Maccabees, Diodorus Siculus); inhabiting a desert and barren country; they lived by plundering their neighbours according to Diodorus. Nabathaesus the epithet.

NABIS

Pages 662-662
tyrant of Sparta, reigned about 254 B.C.; and is reported to have exceeded all other tyrants so far, that, upon comparison, he left the epithets of gracious and merciful to Dionysius and Phalaris. He is said to have contrived an instrument of torture in the form of a statue of a beautiful woman, whose rich drapery concealed a number of iron spikes in her bosom and arms. When any one therefore opposed his demands, he would say, "If I have not talents enough to prevail with you, perhaps my woman Apgea may persuade you." The statue then appeared; which Nabis taking by the hand, led up to the person, who, being embraced by it, was thus tortured into compliance. To render his tyranny less unpopular, Nabis made an alliance with Flamininus the Roman general, and pursued with the most inveterate enmity the war which he had undertaken against the Achaeans. He besieged Gythium, and defeated Philopoemen in a naval battle. His triumph was short, the general of the Achaeans soon repaired his losses, and Nabis was defeated in an engagement, and killed as he attempted to save his life by flight, about 194 years before the Christian era.

NABLUM

Pages 662-662

in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a>, Nebel, was an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> of music among the Jews. It had strings like the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARP">harp</a>, and was played upon by both <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. Its form was that of a Greek lyre. In the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SEPTUAGINT">Septuagint</a> and Vulgate, it is called nablum, psalterion, lyra; and sometimes citbara.

NABLUS

Pages 662-662

a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a> anciently celebrated under the name of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-SAMARIA">Samaria</a>. Its <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, likewise called Nablous, is situated near to Sichem on the ruins of the Niepolis of the Greeks, and is the residence of a sheik, who is subordinate to the pache of Damascus, from whom he farms the tribute of the province.

NABO

Pages 662-662
or NEBO, in mythology, a deity of the Babylonians, who possessed the next rank to Bel. It is mentioned by Isaiah, chap. xlviii. Voilus apprehends that Nabo was the moon, and Bel the sun; but Grotius supposes that Nabo was some celebrated prophet of the country; which opinion is confirmed by the etymology of the name, signifying, according to Jerom, "one that profises over prophecy."

NABOB

Pages 662-662

properly NAVAB, the plural of Naib, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a>. As used in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENGAL">Bengal</a>, it is the same as Nazim. It is a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TITLE">title</a> also given to the wives and daughters of princes, as well as to the princes themselves.

NABONASSAR

Pages 662-662

first <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">king</a> of the Chaldeans <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> Babylonians; memorable for the Jewish era which bears his name, which is generally fixed in 3257, beginning on Wednesday February 26th in the 3967th of the Julian <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, 747 years before Christ. The Babylonians revolting from the Medes, who had overthrown the Assyrian <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a>, did, under Nabonassar, found a dominion, which was much increased under <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEBUCHADNEZZAR">Nebuchadnezzar</a>. It is probable, that this Nabonassar is that Baladan in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SECOND">second</a> of Kings xx. 12. father of Merodach, who sent ambassadors to Hezekiah. See 2 Chron. xxxii.

NABOPOLASSAR

Pages 662-662
king of Babylon: he joined with Ashyages the Mede, to destroy the empire of Assyria; which having accomplished, they founded the two empires of the Medes under Ashyages, and the Chaldeans under Nabopolassar, 627 B.C.

NABUCHADNEZZAR

Pages 662-663
or Nabuchodonosor II. king of Assyria, son of Nabopolassar, and styled the Great, was associated by his father in the empire, 607 B.C. and the following year he took Jehoiakim king king of Judah prisoner, and proposed to carry him and his subjects in captivity into Babylon; but upon his submission, and promising to hold his kingdom under Nabuchodonosor, he was permitted to remain at Jerusalem. In 603 B.C., Jehoiakim attempted to shake off the Assyrian yoke, but without success; and this revolt brought on the general captivity. Nabuchadnezzar having subdued the Ethiopians, Arabians, Idumaeans, Philistines, Syrians, Persians, Medes, Assyrians, and almost all Asia; being puffed up with pride, caused a golden statue to be set up, and commanded all to worship it; which Daniel's companions refusing to do, they were cast into the fiery furnace. But as he was admiring his own magnificence, by divine sentence he was driven from men, and in the scripture it is said to have eaten grass as oxen: i.e., he was seized with the disease called by the Greeks lycomathy, which is a kind of madness that causes persons to run into the fields and streets in the night, and sometimes to suppose themselves to have the heads of oxen, or to be made of glass. At the end of seven years his reason returned to him, and he was restored to his throne and glory. He died 562 B.C. in the 43rd year of his reign; in the 5th of which happened that eclipse of the sun mentioned by Ptolemy, which is the surest foundation of the chronology of his reign.

NADIR

Pages 663-663

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a> that point of the heavens which is diametrically opposite to the zenith <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> point directly over our heads.

NAENIA

Pages 663-663

the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> of funerals at Rome. Her temple was without the gates of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CITY">city</a>. The songs which were sung at funerals were also called nenia. They were generally filled with the praises of the deceased; but sometimes they were so unmeaning and improper, that the word became proverbial to signify nonsense.

NAERDEN

Pages 663-663

a strong town of the United Provinces in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, seated at the head of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>. The foundations of it were laid by William of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAVARIA">Bavaria</a>, in 1350. It was taken by the Spaniards in 1572, and by the French in 1672; but it was retaken by the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a> the next year. It stands at the south end of the Zuider Zee, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5. N. Lat. 51. 22.

NAEVUS

Pages 663-663

a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MOLE">mole</a> on the skin, generally called a mother's mark; also the tumour known by the name of a wen. All preternatural tumours on the skin, in the form of a wart <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> tubercle, are called excrescences; by the Greeks they are called acrothymia; and when they are born with a person, they are called navi materni, or marks from the mother. A <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> tumour depending from the skin is denominated sarcoma. These appear on any <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> of the body: some of them differ not in their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> from the rest of the skin; whilst others are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RED">red</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, &c. Their shapes are various; some resembling strawberries, others <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a>, &c. Heifer advises their removal by means of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGATURE">ligature</a>, a cautery, or a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a>, as circumstances best <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUIT">suit</a>. As to the tumour called a wen, its different <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> are distinguished by their contents. They are encysted tumours; the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> contained in the first three following is inflamed lymph, and that in the fourth is only fat. Monk Littre was the first who particularly described the fourth kind; and to the following purpose he speaks of them all. A wen is said to be of three sorts, according to the kind of matter it contains: those whose contents resemble boiled <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, or curds, or a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>-poultice, is called atheroma; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it resembles <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, it is named melicera; and if it is like fat, it is denominated fleatoma: but there is a fourth sort, which may be called lipome, because of its fat contents resembling grease. He says that he has seen one on the shoulders of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAN">man</a>, which was a thin bag, of a tender texture, full of a soft fat, and that it had all the qualities of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMON">common</a> grease. And though the fat in the lipome resembles that in the fleatoma, yet they cannot be the same: for the matter of the fleatoma is not inflammable, nor does it melt; or if it does, it is with <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> difficulty and imperfectly; whereas it is the contrary with the lipome. When the man who had the above-named lipome was fatigued, or had drank freely of strong liquors, his lipome was inflamed for some days after, and its contents rarefying increased the size of the tumour. The lipome seems to be no other than an enlargement of one or more of the cells of the adipose membrane, which is filled only with its <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> contents. Its softness and largeness distinguish it in general from the other species, though sometimes the fatty contents <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a> be so hard as to deceive. As this kind of wen does not run between the muscles, nor is possessed of any considerable blood-vessels, it may always be cut off with ease and safety. As to the other kind of wens, their extirpation may or may not be attempted, according as their situation is with respect to adjacent vessels, the wounding of which would endanger the patient's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>.

NAGERA

Pages 663-663
or NAGARA, a town of Spain, in Old Castile, and the territory of Rioja, with the title of a duchy and fortress; famous for a battle fought in its neighbourhood in 1369. It is situated in a fertile country, on a brook called Nagerilla. W. Long. 2. 20. N. Lat. 42. 25.

NAGRACUT

Pages 663-664

a town of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of the same name in the dominions of the NAI <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> Mogul, with a rich temple to which the Indians go in pilgrimage. It is seated on the river Ravi. E. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 78. 10. N. Lat. 33. 12.

NAHUM

Pages 664-664
or the Prophecy of Nahum, a canonical book of the Old Testament. Nahum, the seventh of the 12 lesser prophets, was a native of Elkoshai, a little village of Galilee. The subject of his prophecy is the destruction of Nineveh, which he describes in the most lively and pathetic manner; his style is bold and figurative, and cannot be exceeded by the most perfect masters of oratory. This prophecy was verified at the siege of that city by Assyrians, in the year of the world 3378, 622 years before Christ.

NAIADES

Pages 664-664

certain inferior deities who presided over <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WELLS">wells</a>, and fountains. The Naiades generally inhabited the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and resorted to the woods <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> meadows near the stream over which they presided. They are represented as young and beautiful virgins, often leaning upon an urn, from which flows a stream of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WATER">water</a>. Aegle was the fairest of the Naiades, according to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>. Their name seems to be derived from *vare*, to flow. They were held in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> veneration among the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>; and often sacrifices of goats and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAMBS">lambs</a> were offered to them, with libations of wine, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OIL">oil</a>. Sometimes they received only offerings of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MILK">milk</a>, fruit, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>.

NAIANT

Pages 664-664

in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HERALDRY">heraldry</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TERM">term</a> used in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLAZONING">blazoning</a> fishes, when borne in an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> posture, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWIMMING">swimming</a>.

NAIAS

Pages 664-664

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>: A genus of the monandra order, belonging to the dioecia class of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking with those of which the order is doubtful. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MALE">male</a> calyx is cylindrical and bifid; the corolla quadridif; there is no filament; nor is there any <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> calyx <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> corolla; there is one <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PISTIL">pistil</a>; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPSULE">capsule</a> is ovate and unicellular.

NAILS

Pages 664-664

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, &c., small spikes of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>, &c., which being drove into wood, serve to bind several pieces together, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> to fasten something upon them. Nails were made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Hebrews for cancelling bonds: and the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> was performed by striking them through the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>. This seems to be alluded to in scripture, where God is said by our crucified Saviour to have "blotted out the handwriting of ordinances that was against us, and to have taken it out of the way, nailing it to his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>." Col. ii. 14. For the cause and ceremony of driving the annual nail, or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CLAVUS">clavus</a> annalis, among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, see Annalis Clavus. Nail, is also a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of length, containing the 1/6th <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> of a yard. NAILING of Cannon. When circumstances make it necessary to abandon cannon, or when the enemy's <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a> are seized, and it is not however possible to take them away, it is proper to nail them up, in order to render them useless; which is done by driving a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> nail or iron spike into the vent of a piece of artillery, to render it unserviceable. There are various contrivances to force the nail out, as also sundry <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a> invented for that purpose, but they have never been found of general use; so that the best method is to drill a new vent. One Gaspér Vimercatus was the first who invented the nailing of cannon. He was a native of Bremen, and made use of his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> first in nailing up the artillery of Sigismund Malatesta.

NAIN

Pages 664-664

one of the most learned and judicious critics and historians France has produced, was the son of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the request, and born at <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1637. At ten years old he went to school at Port <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a>, and became one of the best writers of that <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a>. Sacy, his intimate friend and counsellor, prevailed with him in 1676 to receive the priesthood; which, it seems, his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> humility would not before suffer him to aspire to. This virtue he seems to have possessed in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a>; so that Bossuet, seeing one of his letters to father Damé, with whom he had some little dispute, behooved him merrily, "not to be always upon his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNEES">knees</a> before his adversary, but raise himself now and then up." He was solicited to push himself in the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, and Buzanval, bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAUVAIS">Beauvais</a>, wished to have him for his successor; but Nain, regardless of dignities, wished for nothing but retirement. In this he did indeed most effectually <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BURY">bury</a> himself; and, joining the mortifications of a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> to an indefatigable pursuit of letters, he wore himself entirely out, so as to die in 1698, aged 61, though he was formed for a longer life. His <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> works are, 1. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the first ages of the church, 16 vols 4to. 2. The history of the emperors, 6 vols 4to. These works are deduced from original sources, and composed with the utmost fidelity and exactness. Nain, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> Naim, situated at the bottom of mount Hermon on the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NORTH">north</a> side, was anciently a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the tribe of Issachar, in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Galilee. It was near the gates of this city that our Saviour restored to life the only son of a widow, and where he inspired <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> Magdalen to come and mourn for her sins at his feet. These circumstances alone make this <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a> worthy of notice; for at present Nain is only a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAMLET">hamlet</a> inhabited by <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, Mahometans, and Hebrews, where there is not a single monument to attract the curiosity of the traveller.

NAIRES

Pages 664-664

NAHERS, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> NAYERS, in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a name which is given by the Malabarians to the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, who form a very numerous class or tribe, out of which the sovereigns of Malabar choose their body-<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GUARD">guard</a>.

NAIRN

Pages 664-665

a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Scotland, comprehending the west <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> of Murray. It is bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by Murray frith, on the west and south by <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-INVERNESS">Inverness</a>, and on the east by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-ELGIN">Elgin</a>. The length of it amounts to 20 miles, and the breadth to 14. The <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> is temperate and salubrious, and the winters are remarkably mild. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FACE">face</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is rough and mountainous; yet there are some fruitful straths, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> valleys, which produce good crops of oats and barley; but in general the country is much better adapted for pasturage. Here are also <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> woods of fir, and other trees, that afford shelter to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAME">game</a>, of which there is <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> plenty. A strath is a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a>, narrow valley, with a river running through the bottom. Of these, the most remarkable remarkable in this county, are Strathnairn, on the river of that name, in the south-west part of the shire; and on the south-east side, Stratherin, on both sides of Findhorne river. Nairn is well watered with streams, rivulets, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>, abounding with fish. In the southern part there is a small lake, called Moy, surrounding an <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, on which there is a castle belonging to the laird of McIntosh; but the greater part of the thire is peopled by the Fraers, a warlike Highland clan, whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Lovat, lost his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> on a scaffold for having been concerned in the late rebellion. Here are a great <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of villages; but no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> except Nairn, supposed to be the Taeis of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>, situated at the mouth of the river which bears the same name; a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> borough, which gave a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of lord to an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family, forfeited in the rebellion of 1715. The harbour, which opened in the Murray frith, is now choked up with sand; and the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> of the town is too inconsiderable to deserve notice. The people in general subsist by feeding sheep and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> cattle. About four miles from Nairn stands the castle of Calder, on the river of that name, belonging to a branch of the family of Campbell. In this neighbourhood we find a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-QUARRY">quarry</a> of freestone, and many signs of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>. About six miles to the north-west of Nairn, a new fort hath been lately built by order of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, at a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a> called Ardsier, a small isthmus upon the Murray frith, which it is intended to command.

NAISSANT

Pages 665-665

in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HERALDRY">heraldry</a>, is applied to any animal issuing out of the midst of some ordinary, and showing only his head, shoulders, fore-feet, and legs, with the tip of his tail; the rest of his body being hid in the shield, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> some <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> upon it; in which it differs from issuant, which denotes a living creature arising out of the bottom of any ordinary or charge.

NAISSUS

Pages 665-665

a town of Dardania, a district of Moesia Superior, said to be the birth-<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of Constantine the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>, which seems probable from his often residing at that place. Naissiani, the people (<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">Coin</a>). Now called Niša, a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SERVIA">Servia</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 23° N. Lat. 43°. NAKED seeds, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>, those that are not inclosed in any pod <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CASE">case</a>.

NAKIB

Pages 665-665

in the oriental dignities, the name of an officer who is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a> to the caliph, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a>, as he may be called, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, appointed by the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> signior. His office is to carry the standard of Mahomet.

NAKOUS

Pages 665-665

an Egyptian musical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>, made like two plates of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>, and of all sizes, from two inches to a foot in diameter; they hold them by strings fastened to their middles, and strike them together so as to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a>. They are used in the Coptic churches and in the Mahometan processions.

NAME

Pages 665-666

denotes a word whereby men have agreed to express some idea; <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> which serves to denote or signify a thing or subject spoken of. See Word. This the grammarians usually call a noun, nomen, though their noun is not of quite so much <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> as our name. See Noun. Seneca, Lib. II. de Beneficiis, observes, that there are a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of things which have no name; and which, therefore, we are forced to call by other borrowed names. Ingens est (says he) rerum copia sine nomine, quas cum propriis appellationibus figuere non possumus, alienis accommodatis utimur: which may show why, in the course of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DICTIONARY">dictionary</a>, we frequently give <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> senses to the same word. Names are distinguished into proper and appellative. Proper Names, are those which represent some individual thing or person, so as to distinguish it from all other things of the same <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; as, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a>, which represents a certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>. Appellative or General Names, are those which signify <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a>; or which are common to several individuals of the same species; as, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, animal, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAN">man</a>, oak, &c. Proper names are either called Christian, as being given at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a>; or surnames: The first imposed for distinction of persons, answering to the Roman praenomen; the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, for the distinction of families, answering to the nomen of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, and the patronymicum of the Greeks. Originally every person had but one name; as among the Jews, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADAM">Adam</a>, &c. among the Egyptians, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BUSIRIS">Busiris</a>; among the Chaldees, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NINUS">Ninus</a>; the Medes, Abysse; the Greeks, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DIOMEDES">Diomedes</a>; the Romans, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ROMULUS">Romulus</a>; the Gauls, Diviciacus; the Germans, Ariovitus; the Britons, Cafliblan; the English, Hengist, &c. And thus of other nations, except the savages of Mount <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATLAS">Atlas</a>, whom Pliny and Marcellinus represent as anonyme, "nameless." The Jews gave the name at the circumcision, viz. eight days after the birth; the Romans, to females the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, to males the ninth; at which <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> they held a feast, called nominalia. Since Christianity has obtained, most nations have followed the Jews, baptizing and giving the name on the eighth day after the birth; except our English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>, who, till of late, baptized and gave the name on the birth-day. The first imposition of names was founded on different views, among different people; the most common was to mark the good wishes of the parents, or to entitle the children to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a> a happy name seemed to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a>. Hence, Victor, Caesar, Faustus, Statius, Probus, &c. Accordingly, we find such names, by Cicero called <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BONA">bona</a> nomina, and by Tacitus fausta nomina, were first enrolled and ranged in the Roman muster; first called to serve at the sacrifices, in the foundation of colonies, &c.—And, on the contrary, Livy calls Atrius Umber, abominandi omnis nomen: and Plautus, on occasion of a person named Lyco, i.e. "greedy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WOLF">wolf</a>," says; Vosmet nunc facile conjecturam ceterum Quid id sit hominis, cui Lyco nomen fiet. Hence, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a> recommends it to men to be careful in giving happy names; and the Pythagoreans taught expressly, that the minds, actions, and successe of men, were according to their names, genius, and fate. Thus Nam.
