Panormitan, ex bono nomine oritur bona praesumptio; and the common proverb, Bonum nomen bonum <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OMEN">omen</a>: and hence the foundation of the onomomantia. See Onomomantia. It is an observation deserving <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, says the Abbé Barthélemy, that the greater <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> of names found in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a> are marks of distinction. They were given in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the qualities most esteemed in the heroic ages. From the word polemos, which signifies <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WAR">war</a>, have been formed Telipolemus and Archeptolemus, the names of two heroes mentioned in the Iliad. The former name signifies able to support, and the latter, able to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a>, the labours of war. By adding to the word mache, or butle, certain prepositions and different parts of speech, which modify the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> in a manner always <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a>, are composed the names Amphimachus, Antimachus, Promachus, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TELEMACHUS">Telemachus</a>. Proceeding in the same way with the word honorea, "strength or intrepidity," they formed the names Agapenor, "he who esteems valour;" Agenor, "he who directs it." From thoes, "swift," are derived, Alcaiboeus, Pantboes, Periboeus, &c. From nous, "mind or intelligence," come Alynos, Arinos, Autenos, &c. From medes, "counsel," Agamedes, Eumedes, Lyconides, Thrasymedes; and from elos, "<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-GLORY">glory</a>," Amphielos, Agaelos, Iphielos, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PATROCLUS">Patroclus</a>, Cleobulus, with many others. Hence Camden takes it for granted, that the names, in all nations and languages, are significative, and not simple sounds for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> distinction sake. This holds not only among the Jews, Greeks, Latins, &c. but even the Turks; among whom, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABDALLA">Abdalla</a> signifies God's <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a>; Soliman, peaceable; Mahomet, glorified, &c. And the savages of Hispaniola, and throughout <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, who, in their languages, name their children, Glittering <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">Light</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">Sun</a> Bright, Fine <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GOLD">Gold</a>, &c.; and they of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONGO">Congo</a>, by the names of precious <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, &c. To suppose names given without any meaning, however by the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> of languages their signification may be lost, that learned author thinks is to reproach our ancestors; and that contrary to the sense of all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> writers. Porphyry notes, that the barbarous names, as he calls them, were very emphatical, and very concise: and accordingly it was esteemed a duty to be ingeniorum, or sui nominis homines: as Severus, Probus, and Aurelius, are called sui nominis imperatores. It was the usual way of giving names, to wish the children might discharge their names. Thus when Gunthram <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">king</a> of France named Clotharius at the font, he said, Crescat puer, &c. hujus fit hominis executor. The ancient Britons, Camden says, generally took their names from colours, because they painted themselves; which names are now lost, or remain hid among the Welsh. When they were subdued by the Romans, they took Roman names, some of which still remain, corrupted; though the greatest part became extinct upon the admission of the English Saxons, who introduced the German names, as Crida, Penda, Oswyld, Edward, &c.—The Danes, too, brought with them their names; as Suayne, Harold, Knute, &c. The Normans, at the Conquest, brought in other German names, as originally using the German tongue; such as Robert, William, Richard, Henry, Hugh, &c. after the same manner as the Greek names: Apollonius, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOETHIUS">Boethius</a>, Symmachus, &c. were introduced into <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> upon the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the empire. After the Conquest, our <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, which had ever been averse to foreign names, as deeming them unlucky, began to take <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> names; as Matthew, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DAVID">David</a>, Sampson, &c. The various names anciently or at present obtaining among us, from what <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> or people forever borrowed, are explained by Camden in his Remains. As to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> when names began to be multiplied, and surnames introduced, &c. see <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SURNAME">Surname</a>. Of late years it has obtained among us to give surnames for Christian names; which some dislike, on account of the confusion it may introduce. Camden relates it as an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that the practice first began in the reign of Edward VI. by such as would be godfathers, when they were more than half fathers. Upon which some were persuaded to change their names at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONFIRMATION">confirmation</a>; which, it seems, is usual in other countries.—Thus, two sons of Henry II. of France, christened Alexander and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>, changed them at confirmation into Henry and Francis. In monasteries, the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> assume new names at their admittance, to show they are about to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> a new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and have renounced the world, their family, and even their name: e.g. sister <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> of the Incarnation, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Henry of the Holy Sacrament, &c. The popes also changed their names at their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXALTATION">exaltation</a> to the pontificate; a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> first introduced by Pope Sergius, whose name till then, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLATINA">Platina</a> informs us, was Swinefoot. But Omphurus refers it to John XII. or XIII. and at the same time adds a different reason for it from that of Platina, viz. that it was done in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of St <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> and St Paul, who were first called Simon and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAUL">Saul</a>. Among the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, those deified by the Heathen consecrations had new names given them; as Romulus was called Quirinus; Melicertes, Portunus or Portumnus, &c. New names were also given in adoptions, and sometimes by <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TESTAMENT">testament</a>; thus L. Aemilius, adopted by Scipio, took the name of Scipio Africanus; and thus Augustus, who at first was called G. Octavius Thurinus, being adopted by the testament of Julius Caesar into his name and family, took the name of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAIUS">Caius</a> Julius Caesar Octavianus. Names were also changed at enfranchisements into new cities. Thus Lucumo, at his first being made free of Rome, took the name Lucius Tarquinius Priscus, &c.; and slaves, when made free, usually assumed their masters names. Those called to the equestrian order, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they had base names, were always new named, nomine ingeniorum veterumque Romanorum. And among the primitive <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, it was the practice to change the names of the catechumens: Thus the renegade <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUCIANUS">Lucianus</a>, till his baptism, was called Lucius. Toward the middle of the 15th century, it was the fancy of the wits and learned men of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, particularly in Italy, to change their baptismal names for classical ones. As Sannazarius, for instance, who altered his own plain name Jacopo to Atius Syncerus. Numbers did the same, and among the rest Platina the historian at Rome, who, not without a solemn <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CEREMONIAL">ceremonial</a>,

NAMPTWICH

Pages 666-667
or Nantwich, a town of Chester in England, situated on the Weaver river, 14 miles S.E. from Chester and 162 miles from London. It lies in the Vale-Royal, and is one of the largest and best built towns in the county, the streets being very regular, and adorned with many gentlemen's houses. The inhabitants drive a trade, not only by its large market on Saturday for corn and cattle, and its great thoroughfare to Ireland, but by its cheese and its fine white salt, which are made here to the greatest perfection; and by shoes made here and sent to London to the warehouses. It is governed by a constable, &c. who are guardians of the salt-springs. It is divided by the Weaver into two equal parts, which is not navigable any farther than Winsford bridge. The Chester canal, lately completed, terminates in a handsome broad basin near this place. In this town were several religious foundations, now no more. The church is a handsome pile of building in the form of a cross, with an octagonal tower in the middle. There are here three fairs.

NAMUR

Pages 667-667

a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, lying between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Sambre and Maas; bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by Brabant, on the east and south by the bishopric of Leige, and on the west by Hainault. It is pretty fertile; has several forests, marble quarries, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, and pit-coal; and is about 30 miles <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a> and 20 <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>. Namur is the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> town. Namur, a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, rich, and very strong town of the Netherlands, capital of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Namur, with a strong castle, several forts, and a bishop's see. The most considerable forts are, Fort-Wilhelm, Fort-Maas, Fort-Quatrefoil, and Fort-Espinor. The castle is built in the middle of the town, on a craggy rock. It was besieged by <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">king</a> William in 1695, who took it in the fight of an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of 100,000 French, though there were 60,000 men in garrison. Namur is now a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARRIER">barrier</a>-town, and has a Dutch garrison. It was ceded to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a> in 1713, but taken by the French in 1746; and restored by the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIX">Aix</a>-la-Chapelle. It is situated between two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, at the confluence of the rivers Maas and Sambre, in E. Long. 4° 57'. N. Lat. 50° 25'.

NAN-KING

Pages 667-668

a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">King</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAN">man</a>, is said to have been formerly one of the most beautiful and flourishing cities in the world. When the Chinese speak of its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, they say, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> two horsemen should go out by the same gate, and ride round it on full speed, taking different directions, they would not meet before night. This account is evidently exaggerated: but it is certain, that Nan-k'ing surpasses in extent all the other cities of China. We are assured that its walls are five leagues and a half in circumference. This city is situated at the distance of a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> from the river <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-YANG_TSE_KIANG">Yang-tse-kiang</a>: it is of an <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> which are within its circumference having prevented its being built on a regular <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>. It was formerly the imperial city; for this reason it was called Nan-King, which signifies, "the Southern <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COURT">Court</a>;" Nan-king Court; but since the six <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> tribunals have been transferred from hence to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEKING">Peking</a>, it is called Kiang-ning in all the public acts. Nan-king has lost much of its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> splendour: it had formerly a magnificent <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, no vestige of which is now to be seen; an <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OBSERVATORY">observatory</a> at present neglected, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>, tombs of the emperors, and other superb monuments, of which nothing remains but the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-REMEMBRANCE">remembrance</a>. A third of the city is deserted, but the rest is well inhabited. Some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of it are extremely populous and full of business; particularly the manufacture of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of cotton cloth, of which <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> quantities are imported into <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> under the name of Nankin. The streets are not so <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> as those of Peking; they are, however, very beautiful, well-paved, and bordered with rich shops. In this city resides one of those great mandarins called T'ong-gou, who takes cognizance of all important affairs, not only of both the governments of the province, but also of those of the province of Kiang-si. The Tartars have a numerous garrison here, commanded by a general of their own <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATION">nation</a>; and they occupy a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of the city, separated from the rest by a plain wall. The palaces of the mandarins, whether Chinese <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> Tartars, are in this city neither larger nor better built than those in the capital cities of other provinces. Here are no public edifices corresponding to the reputation of so celebrated a city, excepting its gates, which are very beautiful, and some temples, among which is the famous <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PORCELAIN">porcelain</a> tower. It is 200 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, and divided into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NINE">nine</a> stories by plain boards within, and without by cornices and small projections covered with green varnished tiles. There is an ascent of 40 steps to the first story; between each of the others there are 21. The breadth and depth of the river Yang-tse-kiang formerly rendered the port of Nan-king very commodious; but at present <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> barks, or rather Chinese junks, never enter it; whether it be that it is shut up by sand-banks, or that the entrance of it has been forbidden, in order that navigators may infensibly lose all knowledge of it. In the months of April and May a great <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of excellent fish are caught in this river near the city, which are sent to court; they are covered with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ICE">ice</a>, and transported in that manner by barks kept entirely on purpose. Although this city is more than 200 leagues from Peking, these boats make such expedition, that they arrive there in eight or nine days. This city, though the capital of the province, has under its particular jurisdiction only eight cities of the third class. The number of its inhabitants are said to be 1,000,000, without comprehending the garrison of 40,000 men. E. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 119. 25. N. Lat. 32. 46.

NAN-TCHANG-FOU

Pages 667-667

the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Kiang-si, a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHINA">China</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CITY">city</a> has no trade but that of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PORCELAIN">porcelain</a>, which is made in the neighbourhood of Jao-tcheou. It is the residence of a viceroy, and comprehends in its district eight cities; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> of which are of the third class, and only one of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SECOND">second</a>. So much of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is cultivated, that the pastures left are scarcely sufficient for the flocks.

NANCI

Pages 667-667

a town of France, and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Lorraine, is situated on the river Meuse, in the centre of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>. It is divided into the Old and New <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">Towns</a>. The first, though irregularly built, is very populous, and contains the ducal <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>; the streets of the New Town are as straight as a line, adorned with handsome buildings, and a very fine <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> is a magnificent structure, and in that of the Cordeliers are the tombs of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> dukes. The two towns are separated by a canal; and the new town was very well fortified, but the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">king</a> of France has demolished the fortifications. It has been taken and retaken several times; particularly by the French, to whom it was ceded in 1736, to enjoy it after the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Stanislaus.

NANI

Pages 667-667

was born in 1616. His father was procurator of St Mark, and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> to Rome. He was educated with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, and made considerable improvement. Urban VIII., a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> valuer of merit, soon perceived that of young Nani. He was admitted into the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of senators in 1641, and was shortly after nominated ambassador in France, where he signalized himself by his compliant manners. He procured considerable succours for the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WAR">war</a> of Candia against the Turks; and became, after his return to Venice, superintendent of the war-office and of finances. He was afterwards ambassador to the empire; where he rendered those services to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> which, as a zealous and intelligent citizen, he was well qualified to discharge. He was again sent into France in 1660 to solicit fresh succours for Candia; and on his return was appointed procurator of St Mark. He died November 5, 1678, at the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 63, much regretted by his countrymen. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> had appointed him to write the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the Republic; which he executed to the satisfaction of the Venetians, although the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> was less admired by foreigners, who were not proper judges of the accuracy with which he stated the facts, of the purity of his diction, nor of the simplicity of his style; although it must be acknowledged that his narrative is much interrupted by too frequent parentheses. In <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> his history of Venice he has given an universal history of his times, especially with respect to the affairs of the French in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. This history, which is <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> from 1613 to 1671, was printed at Venice in 2 vols 4to, in the years 1662 and 1679.

NANSIO

Pages 668-668

an <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of the Archipelago, a little to the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of the island of Santorino, 16 miles in circumference; but has no harbour. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> are nothing but bare rocks, and there are not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> sufficient to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WATER">water</a> the fields. There are a vast <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of partridges, whose eggs they destroy every year to preserve the corn, and yet vast numbers of them are always produced. The ruins of the temple of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a> are yet to be seen, and consist chiefly of marble columns. E. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 26. 20. N. Lat. 36. 15.

NANTES

Pages 668-668

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>, rich, and very considerable town of France, in Bretagne, with a bishop's see, an university, and a mint. It is one of the most considerable places in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>; contains the richest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>; and was formerly the residence of the dukes of Bretagne, where they built a very strong castle on the side of the river, and which is strongly fortified. There are several parishes, and a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> many <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> houses, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> contains the tombs of the ancient dukes. There are several fine bridges over the river <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LOIRE">Loire</a>, which is navigable. The suburbs are so <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, on account of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of people that come from all parts to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> here, that they exceed the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CITY">city</a>. The Spaniards trade here with wine, fine <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, oranges, and lemons; and they carry back cloth, stuffs, corn, and hardware. The Dutch send <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-SALT">salt</a> fish, and all sorts of spices; and in return have wine and brandy. The Swedes bring <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>; and the English, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, tin, and pit-coal. It was in this <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a> that Henry IV. promulgated the famous edict in 1598, called the Edict of Nantes, and which was revoked in 1685. Nantes was anciently, like almost every considerable city in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, very strongly fortified. <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> de <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DREUX">Dreux</a>, one of the dukes of Bretagne, surrounded it with walls, which have only been demolished within these few years. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> is an object of curiosity. It is near a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MILE">mile</a> and a half in length, being <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> across all the little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> in the Loire, from <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NORTH">north</a> to south. The territory of Nantes lies on both sides the Loire, and feeds a great number of cattle. Large vessels can come no higher than Port Launai, which is 12 miles from Nantes. W. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1. 31. N. Lat. 47. 13.

NANTUELL

Pages 668-669

the celebrated designer and engraver to the cabinet of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIV., was born at <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RHEIMS">Rheims</a> in 1630. His father, though but a petty shopkeeper, gave his son a liberal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>; who, having a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a>, cultivated it with such success, that he became the admiration of the whole town; but marrying young, and not being able to maintain his family, he took a journey to <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, where he made his talents known by a stratagem.—Seeing several abbés at the door of an eating-<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, he asked the mistress for an ecclesiastic of Rheims, whose name he had forgot, but that she might easily know him by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> of him which he showed: the abbés crowding round, were so charmed with it, that he feigned the opportunity of offering to draw any of their pictures for a small <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>. Customers came so fast, that he soon raised his price, and brought his family to Paris, where his reputation was quickly established. He applied himself particularly to taking portraits in crayons, which he afterwards engraved for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of academical thieves; and in this way he did the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PORTRAIT">portrait</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">king</a>, and afterwards engraved it as big as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; a thing never before attempted. The king was so pleased with it, that he created the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of designer and engraver to the cabinet for him, with a pension of 1000 livres. He died in 1678; and an entire collection of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTS">prints</a> amounts to upwards of 240. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-NANTWICH">NANTWICH</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NAMPTWICH">NAMPTWICH</a>. NAPÆA, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>: A genus of the polyandria order, belonging to the polydelphia class of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 37th order, Columniferae. The calyx is single and cylindric; Naphtha: the arilli coalited and monospermous. There are two <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; both of them with perennial roots, composed of many thick fleshy fibres, which strike deep into the ground, and are connected at the top into <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> heads; the stalks grow to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> eight feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, producing <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, tubulous at bottom, but spreading open at top, and dividing into five obtuse segments. Both these plants are natives of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VIRGINIA">Virginia</a> and other parts of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>: from the bark of some of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> kinds a sort of fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a> might be procured, capable of being woven into very strong cloth. They are easily propagated by seed, which <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a> thrive in any situation.

NAPHTHA

Pages 669-669

an inflammable substance of the bituminous kind, of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, and incapable of decomposition, though frequently adulterated with <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HETEROGENEOUS">heterogeneous</a> mixtures. By <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a> keeping it hardens in the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> into a substance resembling a vegetable resin; and in this state it is always of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> colour, whether pure <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> mixed with other bodies. According to Mongez, there are three kinds of naphtha, the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, reddish, and green or deep-coloured; and it is in fact a true petrol or rock <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, of which the lightest and most inflammable is called naphtha. It is said to be of an extremely fragrant and agreeable smell, though very different in this respect from vegetable oils. It is also transparent, extremely inflammable, dissolves resins and balsams, but not <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GUM">gum</a>-resins nor <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-ELASTIC">elastic</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GUMS">gums</a>. It dissolves in the essential oils of thyme and lavender, but is insoluble in spirit of wine and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ETHER">ether</a>. It burns with a bluish <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FLAME">flame</a>, and is as inflammable as ether; like which it also attracts <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AQUA">aqua</a>-regia. Naphtha, according to Cronstedt, is collected from the surface of some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WELLS">wells</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>; but Mr Kirwan informs us, that it issues out of white, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, or black clays, in Persia and Media. The finest is brought from a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> in the Caspian <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>, called by Kempfer okhira. It issues out through the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> into cisterns and wells, purposely excavated for collecting it at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BAKU">Baku</a> in Persia. Different kinds of this substance are also found in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MODENA">Modena</a>, and in Mount Ciaro, 12 leagues from Plaisance. The formation of naphtha and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETROLEUM">petroleum</a> is by most naturalists and chemists ascribed to the decomposition of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> bitumens by the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of subterranean fires; naphtha being the lightest oil, which the fire disengages first; what follows gradually acquiring the colour and consistence of petrol. Lastly, the petrolea, united with some earthy substances, or altered by <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ACIDS">acids</a>, assume the appearance of mineral pitch, pila-phaltum, &c. This <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> seems to be supported by the phenomena attending the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISTILLATION">distillation</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBER">amber</a>; where the first liquor that rises is a true naphtha; then a petroleum of a more or less brown colour; and lastly, a black substance like jet, which being farther urged by the fire, leaves a dry friable <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, &c. It is further observed, that <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> frequently produces all the different kinds of petrolea near the same spot; of which we have an instance at Mount Testin in the duchy of Modena in Italy. Some, however, are of opinion, that these mineral oils or bitumens are formed from the vitriolic acid, and various oily and fat substances found in the bowels of the earth.

NAPHTHALI

Pages 669-669
or Nephtali (Josh. xix.), one of the tribes of Israel; having Zabulon on the south, Asher on the west, the Jordan on the east, and on the north Antilibanus.

NAPIER

Pages 669-671

baron of Merchiston in Scotland, inventor of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LOGARITHMS">logarithms</a>, was the eldest son of Sir Archibald Napier of Merchiston, and born in the year 1550. Having given early discoveries of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> parts, his father was careful to have them cultivated by a liberal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>. After going through the ordinary courses of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> at the university of St Andrew's, he made the tour of France, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and Germany. Upon his return to his native <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, his literature and other fine accomplishments soon rendered him conspicuous, and might have raised him to the highest offices in the state; but declining all civil employments, and the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COURT">court</a>, he retired from the world to pursue literary researches, in which he made an uncommon progress, so as to have favoured mankind with sundry useful discoveries. He applied himself chiefly to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>; but at the same <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> did not neglect that of the Holy Scriptures. In both these he hath discovered the most extensive knowledge and profound penetration. His <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-ESSAY">essay</a> upon the book of the Apocalypse, indicates the most acute <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a>, and an uncommon strength of judgment; though time hath discovered, that his calculations concerning particular events had proceeded upon fallacious <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DATA">data</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> has been printed abroad in several languages; particularly in French at <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ROCHELLE">Rochelle</a> in the year 1693, 8vo, announced in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TITLE">title</a> as revised by himself. Nothing, says <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BUCHAN">Buchan</a>, could be more agreeable to the Rochellers <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HUGUENOTS">Huguenots</a> of France at this time, than the author's annunciation of the pope as antichrist, which in this book he has endavoured to set forth with much zeal and erudition.—But what has principally rendered his name famous, was his great and fortunate discovery of logarithms in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TRIGONOMETRY">trigonometry</a>, by which the ease and expedition in calculation have so wonderfully assisted the science of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a> and the arts of practical <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>. That he had begun about the year 1593 the train of enquiry which led him to that great achievement in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARITHMETIC">arithmetic</a>, appears from a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to Crugerus from Kepler in the year 1624; wherein, mentioning the Canon Mirificus, he writes thus: "Nilhautem supra Neperianam rationem esse puto: et si Scotus quidem literis <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AD">ad</a> Tychonem, anno 1594, scriptis jam spem fecit Canonis illius mirifici;" which allusion agrees with the idle story mentioned by Wood in his Athene Oxoni, and explains it in a way perfectly consonant to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> of Napier as the inventor. When Napier had communicated to Mr Henry <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BRIGGS">Briggs</a>, mathematical professor in Gresham <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, his wonderful canon for the logarithms, that learned professor set himself to apply the rules in his Imitatio Neperiana; and in a letter to archbishop Usher in the year 1615, he writes thus: "Napier, baron of Merchiston, hath set my head and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> at work with his new and admirable logarithms. I hope to see him this <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it please God; for I never <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAW">saw</a> a book which pleased me better, and made me more wonder." The following passage from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of Lilly the astrologer is quoted by Lord Buchan as giving a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a>. resque view of the meeting betwixt Briggs and the inventor of the logarithms at Merchiston near <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>. "I <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a> acquaint you (says Lilly) with one memorable story related unto me by John Marr, an excellent mathematician and geometrician, whom I conceive you remember. He was <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">King</a> James I. and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I. When Merchiston first published his logarithms, Mr Briggs, then reader of the astronomy lectures at Gresham college in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, was so much surprised with admiration of them, that he could have no quietness in himself until he had seen that noble person whose only <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> they were: he acquaints John Marr therewith, who went into Scotland before Mr Briggs, purposely to be there when these two learned persons should meet. Mr Briggs appoints a certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> when to meet at Edinburgh; but failing thereof, Merchiston was fearful he would not come. It happened one day as John Marr and the baron Napier were speaking of Mr Briggs; 'Ah, John (said Merchiston), Mr Briggs will not now come.' At the very instant one knocks at the gate; John Marr hasted <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, and it proved to be Mr Briggs to his great contentment. He brings Mr Briggs up to the Baron's chamber, where almost one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> was spent, each beholding other with admiration before one word was spoken. At last Mr Briggs began: 'Sir, I have undertaken this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a> journey purposely to see your person, and to know by what engine of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WIT">wit</a> or ingenuity you came first to think of this most excellent help into astronomy, viz. the logarithms; but, Sir, being by you found out, I wonder nobody else found it out before, when now being known it appears so easy.' He was nobly entertained by baron Napier; and every summer after that, during the laird's being alive, this venerable <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAN">man</a> Mr Briggs went purposely to Scotland to visit him." There is a passage in the life of Tycho Brahe by Gassendi, which may mislead an attentive reader to suppose that Napier's method had been explored by Herwart at Hoenburg: It is in Gassendi's Observations on a Letter from Tycho to Herwart of the last day of August 1599. "Dixit Hervartus nihil morari se solvendi cujusquam trianguli difficulatem; folere se enim multiplicationum, ac divisionum vice additiones solum, subtractiones 93 ufuppare (quod ut fieri posset, docuit postmodum fuo Logarithmorum Canone Nepereus.)" But Herwart here alludes to his work afterwards published in the year 1610, which solves triangles by prosthapheresis; a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MODE">mode</a> totally different from that of the logarithms. Kepler dedicated his Ephemerides to Napier, which were published in the year 1617; and it appears from many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> in his letter about this time, that he held Napier to be the greatest man of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> in the particular department to which he applied his abilities. "And indeed (says our noble biographer), if we consider that Napier's discovery was not like those of Kepler or of Newton, connected with any analogies or coincidences which might have led him to it, but the fruit of unassisted reason and science, we shall be vindicated in placing him in one of the highest niches in the temple of fame. Kepler had made many unsuccessful attempts to discover his canon for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIODIC">periodic</a> motions of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol11.html#article-HIT">hit</a> upon it at last, as he himself candidly owns on the 15th of May 1618; and Newton applied the palpable tendency of heavy bodies to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> to the system of the universe in general; but Napier sought out his admirable rules by a slow scientific progress, arising from the gradual <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EVOLUTION">evolution</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>." The last literary exertion of this eminent person was the publication of his Rabdologia and Promptuary in the year 1617, which he dedicated to the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHANCELLOR">Chancellor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SETON">Seton</a>; and soon after died at Merchiston on the 3rd of April O.S. of the same year, in the 68th year of his age and 23d of his happy invention.—The particular titles of his published works are: 1. A plain discovery of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REVELATION">Revelation</a> of St John. 2. Mirifici ipsius canonis <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> et logarithmorum, ad naturales illorum numeros habitudines. 3. Appendix de alia atque praestantiori logarithmorum specie confinienda, in qua sciuntur unitas logarithmus eft. 4. Rhabdologie, seu numerationis per virgulas, libri duo. 5. Propositiones quaedam eminentissime, ad triangula sphærica mira facultate refolventa. To which may be added, 6. His Letter to Anthony <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BACON">Bacon</a> (the original of which is in the archbishop's library at Lambeth), intitled, "Secret inventions, profitable and necessary in these days for the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, and notwithstanding strangers enemies to God's truth and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>?" which the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Buchan has caused to be printed in the Appendix to his Account of Napier's Writings. This letter is dated <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 2. 1596, about which time it appears the author had set himself to explore his logarithmic canon. This eminent person was twice married. By his first wife, who was a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Sir James Stirling of Keir, he had only one son named Archibald, who succeeded to the estate. By his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SECOND">second</a> wife, a daughter of Sir James Chisholm of Cromlix, he had a numerous issue.—Archibald Napier, the only son of the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, was a person of fine parts and learning. Having more a turn to public business than his father had, he was raised to be a privy counsellor by James VI. under whose reign he also held the offices of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a>-depute, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>-clerk, and senator of the college of justice. By Charles I. he was raised to the peerage by the title of Lord Napier. Napier's Rods, or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BONES">Bones</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> invented by Baron Napier, whereby the multiplication and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> numbers is much facilitated. As to the Construction of Napier's Rods: Suppose the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TABLE">table</a> of multiplication to be made upon a plate of metal, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a>, or pasteboard, and then conceive the several columns (standing downwards from the digits on the head) to be cut asunder; and these are what we call Napier's rods for multiplication. But then there must be a good <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of each; for as many times as any <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> is in the multiplicand, so many rods of that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> (i.e. with that figure on the top of it) must we have; though six rods of each species will be sufficient for any example in common affairs: there must be also as many rods of o's. But before we explain the way of using these rods, there is another thing to be known, viz. that the figures on every rod are written in an order different from that in the table. Thus the little <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> space or division in which the several products of every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLUMN">column</a> are written, is divided into two parts by a line across from the upper <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to the lower on the left; and if the product is a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DIGIT">digit</a>, it is set in Napier's lower division; if it has two places, the first is set in the lower, and the second in the upper division; but the spaces on the top are not divided; also there is a rod of digits, not divided, which is called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDEX">index</a> rod, and of this we need but one single rod. See the figure of all the different rods, and the index, separate from one another, in Plate CCCXLIV. Multiplication by Napier's Rods. First lay down the index-rod; then on the right of it set a rod, whose top is the figure in the highest <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of the multiplicand: next to this again, set the rod whose top is the next figure of the multiplicand; and so on in order to the first figure. Then is your multiplicand tabulated for all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NINE">nine</a> digits; for in the same line of squares standing against every figure of the index rod, you have the product of that figure; and therefore you have no more to do but to transfer the products and sum them. But in taking out these products from the rods, the order in which the figures stand obliges you to a very easy and small addition: thus, begin to take out the figure in the lower <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a>, or units place, of the square of the first rod on the right; add the figure in the upper part of this rod to that in the lower part of the next, and so on; which may be done as fast as you can look on them. To make this practice as clear as possible, take the following example: Example: To multiply 4768 by 385. Having set the rods together for the number 4768 (ibid. n° 2.) against 5 in the index, I find this number, by adding according to the rule, \[ \begin{<a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARRAY">array</a>}{c} \text{Against 5, this number} & 23840 \\ \text{Against 8, this number} & 38144 \\ \text{Against 3, this number} & 14324 \\ \end{array} \] Total product 183,680 To make the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the rods yet more regular and easy, they are kept in a flat square box, whose breadth is that of ten rods, and the length that of one rod, as thick as to hold six (or as many as you please) the capacity of the box being divided into ten cells, for the different species of rods. When the rods are put up in the box (each species in its own <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CELL">cell</a> distinguished by the first figure of the rod set before it on the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FACE">face</a> of the box near the top), as much of every rod stands without the box as shows the first figure of that rod: also upon one of the flat sides without and near the edge, upon the left <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, the index rod is fixed; and along the foot there is a small ledge; so that the rods when applied are laid upon this side, and supported by the ledge, which makes the practice very easy; but in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CASE">case</a> the multiplicand should have more than nine places, that upper face of the box may be made broader. Some make the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a> with four different faces, and figures on each for different purposes. Division by Napier's Rods. First tabulate your divisor; then you have it multiplied by all the digits, out of which you may choose such convenient divisors as will be next less to the figures in the dividend, and write the index answering in the quotient, and so continually till the work is done. Thus 2179788, divided by 6123, gives in the quotient 356. Having tabulated the divisor 6123, you see that 6123 cannot be had in 2179; therefore take five places, and on the rods find a number that is equal or next less to 21797, which is 18369; that is, 3 times the divisor: wherefore set 3 in the quotient, and subtract 18369 from the figures above, and there will remain 34288; to which add 8, the next figure of the dividend, and seek again on the rods for it, or the next less, which you will find to be five times; therefore set 5 in the quotient, and subtract 30615 from 34288, and there will remain 3673; to which add 8, the last figure in the dividend, and finding it to be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> 6 times the divisor, set 6 in the quotient. \[ \begin{array}{c} 6123 \times 2179788 = 356 \\ 18369 \\ 34288 \\ 30615 \\ 3673 \\ 30738 \\ \end{array} \]

NAPLES

Pages 671-682

a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, comprehending the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> countries of Samnium, Campania, Apulia, and Magna Graecia. It is bounded on all sides by the Mediterranean and Adriatic, except on the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east, where it terminates on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">Ecclesiastical</a> state. Its greatest length from south-east to north-west is about 235 English miles; and its breadth from north-east to south-west, from 96 to 120. The ancient <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> falls under the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> ROME and ITALY; the present state of it, as well as of the rest of Italy, is owing to the conquests of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLEMAGNE">Charlemagne</a>. When that monarch put an end to the kingdom of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LOMBARDS">Lombards</a>, he obliged the dukes of Friuli, Spoleto, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENEVENTO">Benevento</a>, to acknowledge him as <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">king</a> of Italy; but allowed them to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> the same power and authority which they had enjoyed before his conquest. Of these three dukedoms of Benevento was by far the most powerful and extensive, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> as it comprehended almost all the present kingdom of Naples; that <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> of Farther <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CALABRIA">Calabria</a> beyond the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SARNO">Sarno</a> and Peto, a few <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> cities in Hither Calabria, with the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Acripoli, and the promontory in its neighbourhood called Capo di Liqo; and lastly, the dukedoms of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAETA">Gaeta</a>, Naples, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMALFI">Amalfi</a>, which were very inconsiderable, and extended along the shore only about 100 miles, and were interrupted by the Gaitaldate <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAPUA">Capua</a>. This flourishing and extensive dukedom was at this <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> governed by Arechis, who had married one of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Benevento, and likewise built Salerno on the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, surrounding it with a very strong and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> wall. He engaged in several wars with the Greeks, whom he sometimes obliged to give him hostages; but having invaded the territories of the pope, whom Pepin could not affright, Charlemagne was prevailed on to return to Italy. Arechis, unable to oppose such a formidable enemy, sent his eldest son, Romuald, to Rome, with an offer of submission; but, at the instigation of the pope, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> refused the offer. offer, and detained his son prisoner; after which he ravaged the country, and made himself <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of Capua. Other deputies, however, proved more successful; and, in the year 787, a peace was concluded on these conditions: That Arechis and the Beneventans should renew their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">allegiance</a> to the Franks; that he should pay a yearly tribute to Pepin; deliver up all his <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a>; and give his son Grimoald and his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> Adelgisa, with twelve others, as hostages for his fidelity: however, after many treaties, Adelgisa was restored to her father. Charles had no sooner left Italy, than Arechis forgot all his engagements, and began to negotiate with Irene, empress of Constantinople, and her son Constantine, for expelling the Franks out of Italy. For himself, he desired the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of patriciate, and the dukedom of Naples with all its dependencies; and, in return, promised to acknowledge the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> as his sovereign, and to live after the manner of the Greeks. He required, however, to be supported by a Greek <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>; and that his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>-in-<a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAW">law</a> Adalgisus, son to Desiderius the last king of the Lombards, should be sent over into Italy, to raise a party among his countrymen. These conditions were readily accepted, on condition that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> Romuald should be sent as an hostage; ambassadors were sent to Naples with the ensigns of the patrician order, namely the mantle of cloth of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, the comb, and the sandals; but before the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> could be performed, prince Romuald died, and soon after him his father; whose <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEATH">death</a> was supposed to have been hastened by that of his son. After the death of Arechis, the Beneventans sent a most submissive embassy to Charlemagne, intreating him to send them Grimoald, the late king's son, and only lawful heir to his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>; threatening at the same time to revolt <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> their prince was denied them. Charles readily granted their request, and allowed Grimoald to depart, after he had agreed to the following conditions, viz. That he should oblige the Lombards to shave their beards; that, in writings, and on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, the name of the king should be put before that of the prince; and that he should cause the walls of Salerno, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACERENZA">Acerenza</a>, and Confa, to be entirely demolished. The new king was received by his subjects with the utmost joy; and for some time <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> faithful to his engagements, excepting only the last article, which he either neglected or eluded. So far, however, was he from afflicting the Greeks, that he gave notice of their machinations to Pepin king of Italy; raised an army to oppose his uncle Adalgisus; and being joined by Hildebrand duke of Spoleto, and Vinigife the general of Pepin, he attacked the Greeks in Calabria soon after they had landed, entirely defeated and took his uncle prisoner, and, as is said, put him to a cruel death. Yet in a short time Grimoald contracted an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> with the Greek emperor by marrying his niece Wanzia; and in the fifth year of his reign a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WAR">war</a> broke out between him and Pepin, which continued for twelve years; at the end of which time a truce was concluded. Grimoald survived this pacification only three years, and was succeeded by his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a> Grimoald II. who submitted to Charlemagne after the death of Pepin; and from this time the Beneventans were looked upon as tributaries of the western emperors. As yet, however, the city of Naples did not own allegiance to the dukes of Benevento, but was held by the eastern emperors; and frequent wars took <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a> between the Beneventans and Neapolitans. This happened to be the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CASE">case</a> when Grimoald II. ascended the throne. He concluded a peace with them; which however, was of no <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a> continuance; for Theodore, governor of Naples, having granted protections to Dauferius a noble Beneventan, who had been concerned in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSPIRACY">conspiracy</a> against his prince, Grimoald marched against the city of Naples, and invested it by sea and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAND">land</a>. Theodore still refused to deliver up the traitor, and a general engagement both by land and sea was the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>; in which the Neapolitans were defeated with so <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> slaughter, that the sea was stained with their blood for more than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> days. Theodore then consented to deliver up Dauferius, with 8000 crowns for the expenses of the war; and Grimoald not only pardoned Dauferius, but received him into favour; the traitor, however, reflecting on the heinousness of his crime, was seized with remorse; and went a pilgrimage to the holy land, carrying a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-STONE">stone</a> in his mouth, by way of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENANCE">penance</a>, which he never took out but at his meals. In the year 821, Grimoald was murdered by Radelchis <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COUNT">count</a> of Confa, and Sico gaftald of Acerenza, and the latter of whom succeeded to the dukedom of Benevento. Radelchis being soon after seized with remorse, became a monk; while Sico associated his son Sicardo with him in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>; and both, being of an ambitious and restless disposition, sought a pretence for attacking the Neapolitans. This was soon found, and the city was invested by sea and land. The walls were furiously battered; and part of them being <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, Sico prepared for a general assault. Stephen, at that time duke of Naples, pretended to submit; but, that he might prevent the city from being pillaged, intreated Sico to put off his entry till the morning, and in the meantime sent out his mother and his two children as hostages. Sico consented to his request; but next morning found the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREACH">breach</a> built up, and the Neapolitans prepared for their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>. Exasperated at their perfidy, he renewed his attacks with vigour, but without any success; the besieged defending themselves with the utmost obstinacy. At last, perceiving that they should not be able to hold out much longer, they consented to a peace on the following conditions, viz. That the Neapolitans should pay an annual tribute to the princes of Benevento, and confess to the tranporting of the body of St. Janarius from his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> without the walls of Naples to Benevento. These conditions being ratified, Sico returned with great honour to Benevento; but soon after renewed the war, under pretence that the Neapolitans had neglected to pay the stipulated sum; and hostilities continued till his death, which happened in 833. Sico was succeeded in the government of Benevento by his son Sicardo, who had married the daughter of successor Dauferius; and being influenced by the evil counsels of Roffrid his wife's brother, oppressed his subjects to such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> that they conspired against his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. He besieged Naples with a powerful army, and took possession of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACERRA">Acerra</a> and Atella, both of which he fortified. But Bonus, the Neapolitan duke, defended himself himself so vigorously, that the Beneventans were obliged to retire, and even to abandon Accera and Atella, the fortifications of which were immediately demolished. At last Sicardo agreed to a peace for five years, on the intercession of Lothaire, emperor and king of Italy; but his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> was thought to have been the fear of the Saracens, whom the duke of Naples had called over from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a> to his assistance: for no sooner were they sent back than Sicardo attempted to delay the conclusion of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a>; but the emperor interfering his authority, a peace was concluded in the year 836, after the war had continued, with very little intermission, for 16 years. Soon after the conclusion of this peace, the Saracens landed at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BRINDISI">Brindisi</a>; and having made themselves masters of the place, ravaged all the neighbouring country. Sicardo marched against them with a numerous army; but the Saracens having dug a great <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of ditches which they slightly covered over, found means to draw the Beneventans in among them, whereby they were repulsed with great loss. However, Sicardo, having reinforced his army, marched again to attack them; but the Saracens, despairing of success, pillaged and burnt Brindisi, and then retired with their booty, and a great many captives, to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>. Sicardo then, without any apparent provocation, attacked the city of Amalfi, levelled its walls with the ground, carried off all its wealth, and the body of its tutelar saint Triphomen. A great many of the inhabitants were transported to Salerno; and by promoting alliances between the inhabitants of both places, he endeavoured to unite Amalfi to his own principality as firmly as possible. During all these transactions, Sicardo had tyrannized over his subjects in such a manner, that at last he became intolerable. Among other acts of injustice, he imprisoned his own brother Siconolphus; compelled him to turn <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>; and afterwards sent him bound to Tarento, where he caused him to be shut up in an old tower that had been built for a citadel. By such acts of tyranny his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a> were provoked to conspire against him; and in the year 839 he was murdered in his <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TENT">tent</a>. On the death of Sicardo, Radelchis, his secretary or treasurer, was unanimously elected prince of Benevento; but Siconolphus, the last king's brother, having regained his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, formed a great party against the new prince. Radelchis did not fail to oppose him with a formidable army; and a most ruinous civil war ensued. Both parties by turns called in the Saracens; and these treacherous allies acted sometimes against one, and sometimes against the other; or turned their arms against both, as seemed most suitable to their own <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>. Thus the war continued with the utmost animosity for 12 years, during which time the principality was almost entirely ruined; till at last the emperor <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> interfered, and obliged the competitors to agree to a partition of the principality. By this treaty, Radelchis promised to acknowledge Siconolphus and his successors as lawful princes of the principality of Salerno, which was declared to contain Tarento, Latiniano, Caflano, Cofenzo, Laino, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LUCANIA">Lucania</a>, Conisa, Montella, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ROTA">Rota</a>, Salerno, Sarno, Ciratium, Furculo, Capua, Feano, Sora, and the half of the Gaetaldate of Acerenza, where it joins Latiano and Conisa. The boundary betwixt Benevento and Capua was fixed at St. Angelo <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AD">ad</a> Cerros; Alli Perigrini was made the boundary betwixt Benevento and Salerno, and Staffilo betwixt Benevento and Conisa. The monasteries of Monte Cassino and St Vincent were declared to be immediately under the protection of the emperor: both princes stipulated that no hostilities should be committed by either against the subjects of each other; and promised to join their forces in order to drive out the Saracens. Soon after this pacification, however, both Radelchis and Siconolphus died; the former appointing his son Radelgarius, or Radelcar, to succeed him; and the latter leaving an infant son, Sico, to the care of his godfather, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>. The war with the Saracens proved very unsuccessful; neither the united efforts of the princes, nor the full war assistance of the emperor Lewis himself, being able to expel the infidels; and, in 854, Adelgife the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SECOND">second</a> son of Radelchis, who had now succeeded, on the death of his brother Radelcar, to the principality of Benevento, was obliged to pay them an annual subsidy. Two years after, Lando, count of Capua, revolted from the prince of Salerno, and could not be reduced. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time, Sico, the lawful prince of Salerno, had been poisoned by Count Lando, and the principality usurped by Ademarius, the son of Peter above mentioned; but in 861, Ademarius himself was seized and imprisoned by Gausferius, the son of Dauerius formerly mentioned. This was occasioned by his cruelty and rapaciousness, which entirely alienated the hearts of his subjects from him, and encouraged Gausferius to become the head of the conspirators. The Saracens in the mean time committed terrible ravages throughout the Beneventan territories; which at last obliged Adelgife to enter into an alliance with Gausferius, and both together sent a most humble embassy to the emperor Lewis, requesting him to take them under his protection. About the same time an embassy arrived from Constantinople, proposing a junction of the forces of the eastern and western empires against the infidels; upon which Lewis gave orders for assembling a formidable army. But in the mean time Adelgife fell off from his alliance, and made peace with the Saracens; nay, according to some, he encouraged them in their incursions, and it was at his desire that they invaded the duchy of Capua, and afterwards that of Naples, which they ravaged in a most barbarous manner. The Neapolitans, in conjunction with the duke of Spoleto and the count of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MARS">Mars</a>, endeavoured to oppose them; but being defeated, the Saracens continued their ravages with redoubled fury, and retired to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARI">Bari</a>, which was their <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> city, with an immense booty. In 866, Lewis arrived at Sora with his army; and having marched to Capua, was there joined by Landulph, the bishop and count, with a body of Capuans; but Landulph soon after persuading his countrymen to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a>, Lewis marched against that city, which he took after a siege of three months, and almost totally destroyed. In the end of the year he was joined by Gausferius with his quota of troops, having ordered the eyes of Ademarius to be put out in his absence. Lewis confirmed him in the principality, and marched with his army to Benevento, where Adelgife received ceived him with great respect. Having reduced some inconsiderable places belonging to the Saracens, Lewis soon after invested Bari; but as the Saracens received continual supplies from their countrymen settled in Sicily, and besides were protected by the Neapolitans, he could not reduce the place till the year 871, though he had received considerable assistance from his brother Lotharius, and the Greek emperor had sent him a fleet of 200 sail. The expulsion of the Saracens was completed the same year by the taking of Tarento; after which the emperor returned with great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> to Benevento, resolving next to carry his arms into Sicily, and expel the infidels from thence also. But his future schemes of conquest were frustrated by a quarrel between him and Adelgiso. The latter, pretending to have been insulted by the empress, and oppressed by the French, seized the emperor himself, and kept him prisoner for 40 days. His imprisonment would probably have been of much longer continuance, had not a body of Saracens arrived from Africa, who, being joined by such of their countrymen as had concealed themselves in Italy, laid siege to Salerno with an army of 30,000 men, ravaging the neighbouring country at the same time with the utmost barbarity. By this new invasion Adelgiso was so much alarmed, that he set the emperor at liberty, but first obliged him to swear that he would not <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> the insult that had been offered him, and that he would never return to Benevento. Lewis having then joined his forces to those of the prince of Salerno, soon obliged the Saracens to raise the siege of Salerno; but though they were prevented from taking that city, they entirely destroyed the inhabitants of Calabria, leaving it, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> of one of the historians of that time, "as desolate as it was at the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a>." In the year 873, Lewis being absolved from his oath by the pope, went to Benevento, and was reconciled to Adelgiso; but soon after this reconciliation he died, and the Saracens continued their ravages to such a degree that the inhabitants of Bari were constrained to deliver up their city to the Greeks. At the same time, the Salernitanos, Neapolitanos, Cajetanos, and Amalfitanos, having made peace with the Saracens, were compelled to agree to their proposal of invading the territories of the Roman pontiff. His <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOLINESS">holiness</a> exerted himself to the utmost, both with spiritual and temporal weapons, in order to defend his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>; but was at last reduced to the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of becoming a tributary to the infidels, and promising to pay them a large sum annually. In the mean time, all Italy was thrown into the greatest confusion by the death of Charles the Bald, who died of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POISON">poison</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PAVIA">Pavia</a>, as he was coming to the pope's assistance. Sergius duke of Naples continued a firm friend to the infidels; nor could he be detached from their interests even by the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a> of a papal <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EXCOMMUNICATION">excommunication</a>; but unluckily happening to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of his brother Athanasius bishop of Naples, the zeal of that prelate prompted him to put out his eyes, and send him a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> prisoner to Rome; for which the highest encomiums were bestowed on him by the holy father. In 876, Adelgiso was murdered by two of his nephews; one of whom, by name Gaiderius, seized the principality. About the same time Landolph bishop of Capua dying, a civil war ensued among his children, though their father's dominions had been divided among them according to his <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a>. The princes of Salerno and Benevento, the duke of Spoleto, and Gregory the Greek governor of Bari and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OTRANTO">Otranto</a>, took different sides in the quarrel, as they thought most proper; and to complete the confusion, the new bishop was expelled, and his brother, though a layman, chosen to that office, and even consecrated by the pope, who wrote to Gaufurius, forbidding him to attack Capua under pain of excommunication. But though Gaufurius was, in general, obedient to the pope's commands, he proved refractory in this particular, and laid siege to Capua for two years successively. Thus the Capuan territories were reduced to the most miserable situation; being obliged to maintain at the same time the armies of the prince of Benevento and the duke of Spoleto.
