Claudius Aquaviva, a famous general of the Jesuits, who died in 1615, was of this family.

NARDUS

Pages 684-685

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>: A genus of the monogynia order, belonging to the triandra class of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 4th order, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GRAMINA">Gramina</a>. There is no calyx; the corolla is bilved. This plant was highly valued by the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, both as an article of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a> and medicine. The *unguentum nardinum* was used at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a> and feasts as a favourite <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PERFUME">perfume</a>. Its value is evident from that passage of scripture, where our Saviour's head was anointed with a box of it, with which Judas found fault. From a passage in Horace it appears that this ointment was so valuable among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, that as much as could be contained in a small box of precious <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-STONE">stone</a> was considered as a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> for a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> vessel of wine, and a proper quota for a guest to contribute at an entertainment, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>: --- *Nardo <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VINA">vina</a> merere.* *Nardi parvus onyx elicit cadum.* The plant had a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> character among the ancients as a medicine, both internally taken and externally applied. It has a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIST">list</a> of all antidotes from those of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIPPOCRATES">Hippocrates</a> (given on the authority of Mephisto and Nicholas Alexandrinus) to the officinals which have kept their ground till lately, under the names of *Mithridate* and *<a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> treacle*. Galen and Alexander Trallian recommend it in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DROPSY">dropsy</a> and gravel; Celsus and Galen in pains of the stomach and bowels, both internally given and externally applied. Galen prescribed the oleum nardinum to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Marcus Aurelius when afflicted with a cholera morbus. It was externally applied to the stomach on <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>; and the success was so great, that he ever afterwards enjoyed the highest confidence of that emperor. In a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> attributed to Galen, also, it is mentioned that a medicine composed of this and some other aromatics was found useful in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a> protracted fevers; and the natives of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a> at present consider it as a very efficacious remedy in fevers. Its sensible qualities, indeed, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> it to be of considerable efficacy in some <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, as it has a pungency of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> superior to contrayerva, and little inferior to terpentaria. But though the name of this plant, with the uses and virtues of it, has long been familiar in the writings of botanists and physicians, the genus and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of the plant have only been ascertained very lately. In the Philosophical Transactions for 1790, Dr. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLANE">Blane</a> gives an account of it from a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> sent him by his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LUCKNOW">Lucknow</a>, dated in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1786.—According to this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>'s relation, being one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> on a hunting party with the nabob visier, after crossing the river Rapti, about 20 miles from the foot of the northern <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, he was surprised to find the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> perfumed with an aromatic smell, which, as he was told, proceeded from the roots of the grass that were bruised <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> torn out of the ground by the nabob's elephants and horses. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> was wild, uncultivated, and entirely covered with this kind of grass, which grew in large tufts <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to each other, and from three to four feet long. As none of it was in flower, it being then the winter season, and the grass having besides been burnt <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DOWN">down</a> by order of the nabob, our author caused some of the roots to be dug up, in order to plant it in his garden at Lucknow.—Here it prospered exceedingly; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> up spikes to the height of six feet. A specimen was sent to Sir <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> Banks, who found it to belong to the genus of andropogon, different from any species hitherto described by botanists. "There is great reason, however (says Dr Blanc), to think that it is the true nardus Indica of the ancients; for, 1. The circumstance of its discovery corresponds in a striking manner with an occurrence related by Arrian in his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Alexander's Expedition into India. During the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MARCH">march</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HERO">hero</a> through the deserts of Gedrosia, the air was perfumed by the spikenard, which was trampled under foot by the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>; and the Phoenicians, who accompanied them, collected great quantities of it, as well as of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MYRRH">myrrh</a>, to carry them into their own country to make merchandise of them. This last circumstance seems further to ascertain it to have been the true nardus; for the Phoenicians, who even in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WAR">war</a> appear to have retained their true genius for <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, could no doubt distinguish the proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of this commodity. I am informed by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAJOR">major</a> Rennel, that Gedroa answers to the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> Mackran, or Kedge-mackran, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, situated between Kermou (the ancient Carmania), and the river <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-INDUS">Indus</a>, being of course the frontier province of Persia towards India; and that it appears from Arrian's account, and from a Turkish map of Persia, that this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> lies in the middle tract of country between the river Indus and the Persian <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GULF">gulf</a>, and within a few days' march of the Arabian or Erythraean <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. By this the ancients meant the northern <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> of the Ethiopic ocean, which washes the southern coasts of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a> and Persia; not what we now call the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RED_SEA"><a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RED">Red</a> Sea, as its name would seem to imply, for this by the ancients was called the Arabian Gulf. 2. Though the accounts of the ancients concerning this plant are very defective, it is plain that it was of the natural order of graminae; for the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TERM">term</a> arista, so often applied to it, was appropriated by them to the fructification of grains and grasses, and seems to be a word of Greek original, to denote the most excellent portion of those plants, which are the most useful in the vegetable <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CREATION">creation</a> for the sustenance of animal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> has also kindly made them the most abundant in all parts of the habitable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. Galen says, that though there are various sorts of nardus, the term ναρδος σκυλος, or spikenard, should not be applied to any but the nardus Indica. It would appear that the nardus Celtica was a plant of a quite different <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>, and is supposed to have been a species of valeriana. "The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of the Nardus Indica by Pliny does not indeed correspond with the appearance of our specimen; for he says it is frutex radice pingui et crassa, whereas ours has small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIBROUS">fibrous</a> roots. But as <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> is very remote from the native country of this plant, it is reasonable to suppose that others more easily procurable used to be substituted for it; and the same author says, that there were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NINE">nine</a> different plants by which it could be imitated and adulterated. There is a Nardus Africana mentioned by Horace; and Dioscorides mentions the Nardus Syriaca as a species different from the India, which certainly was brought from some of the remote parts of India; for both Dioscorides and Galen, by way of fixing more particularly the country from whence it came, call it the Nardus Gangites. 3. Garcia <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AB">ab</a> Horto, a Portuguese who resided many years at Goa in the 16th century, has given a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of the roots, or rather of the lower parts of the stalks, which corresponds with our specimen; and he says that there is but one species of nardus known in India, either for the consumption of the natives, or for <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a> to Persia and Arabia. 4. The sensible qualities of this are superior to what <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> passes for it in the shops, being possessed both of more fragrance and pungency, which seems to account for the preference given to it by the ancients. "There is a question, concerning which Matthiolus, the commentator of Dioscorides, bestows a good <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of argument, viz. whether the roots or stalks were the parts esteemed for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, the testimony of the ancients themselves on this head being ambiguous. The roots of this specimen are very small, and possess sensible qualities inferior to the rest of the plant; yet it is mentioned in the account above recited, that the virtues reside principally in the hulky roots. It is evident, that by the hulky roots must here be meant the lower parts of the stalks and leaves, where they unite to the roots; and it is probably a slight ambiguity of this kind that has given occasion to the ambiguity that occurs in the ancient accounts." The sensible qualities of this plant do not depend upon an essential <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, but on some fixed principle like those of cardamoms or ginger. Dr Blanc tried to extract its virtues with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WATER">water</a>, maceration in wine or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> spirits; but it yielded them sparingly and with difficulty to any of these menstrua. The Indians gave an infusion of it in hot water, with a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PEPPER">pepper</a> as a febrifuge.

NAREA

Pages 685-686

the most southerly <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of the empire of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABYSSINIA">Abyssinia</a>; a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> still governed by its own princes, who have the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Beneros. Its territory was formerly more extensive than at present, the Galla having almost quite surrounded it, especially on the south-east and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NORTH">north</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> to the west is the most unknown <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>; the kingdom itself stands like a fortified <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the middle of a plain, being an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> and mountainous country. A <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, rising in the fourth and fifth degrees of north latitude, spread themselves over the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> part of the country, and fill it with marshes all the way from south by east to north, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> north-west. These marshes are bounded by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, of which those nearest the marshes are overgrown with coffee-trees, the largest, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not the only ones, which grow in this country. The kingdom of Narea Proper is interspersed with small, unwholesome, but very fertile valleys. Narca, valleys. The mountainous country of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAFFA">Caffa</a> adjoins immediately to Narca, and is said to be governed by a separate <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>; but the Galla having settled themselves in all the flat ground to the very edge of the marshes, have in a great <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> cut off the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> with Abyssinia for a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> past. The Nareans who inhabit the mountainous country have the lightest <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a> of any people in Abyssinia; but those who inhabit the borders of the marshes are perfectly <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, and have the features and woolly heads of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a>; but the mountaineers of Narca, and much more those of Caffa, are fair-complexioned, more so than even the Neapolitans or Sicilians. It is said that snow has been seen to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> on some of the mountains of Caffa; but Mr Bruce imagines this to be a mistake, and thinks that it must have been <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAIL">hail</a>. Narca abounds with cattle, grain, and all kinds of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, both in the high and low country. The medium of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> is <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, which they sell by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>; but the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of trade are coarse cotton cloths, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANTIMONY">antimony</a>, beads, and incense, which are carried from this country to the kingdom of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGOLA">Angola</a>, and the parts of the African continent towards the Atlantic. The people are exceedingly brave; and though they have been driven out of the low country by multitudes of Galla, they now bid them defiance, and drive them from their frontiers whenever they come too near. The Narean prisoners taken in these skirmishes are sold to the Mahometan <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> at Gondar; and at Constantinople, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAIRO">Cairo</a>, or in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, the women are more esteemed than those of any other part of the world. Both sexes have a cheerful, kind disposition, and attach themselves inviolably to their masters, if properly treated. The people of Narca and Caffa speak a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> peculiar to themselves.

NARRATION

Pages 686-693

in oratory, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a recital <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> rehearsal of a fact as it happened, or as it is supposed to have happened. See ORATORY, n° 26. 123: Concerning **Narration** and **<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">Description</a>**, we have the following rules and observations in the Elements of Criticism. 1. The first rule is, That in history the reflections ought to be chaste and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOLID">solid</a>; for while the mind is intent upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, it is little disposed to the operation of the imagination. Strada's Belgic history is full of poetical images, which, being discordant with the subject, are unpleasant; and they have a still worse effect, by giving an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> of fiction to a genuine history. Such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> ought to be scattered with a sparing <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, even in epic poetry; and at no rate are they proper till the reader be warmed, and by an enlivened imagination be prepared to relish them: in that state of mind, they are agreeable; but while we are sedate and attentive to an historical chain of facts, we reject with disdain every fiction. 2. Vida, following Horace, recommends a modest commencement of an epic poem; giving for a reason, that the writer ought to husband his fire. Besides, bold thoughts and figures are never relished till the mind be heated and thoroughly engaged, which is not the reader's <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CASE">case</a> at the commencement. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a> introduces not a single simile in the first book of the Iliad, nor in the first book of the Odyssey. On the other hand, Shakespeare begins one of his plays with Narration—a sentiment too bold for the most heated imagination: > <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEDFORD">Bedford</a>. Hung be the heav'ns with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, yield <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> to night! > > <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMETS">Comets</a>, importing change of times and states, > Brandish your crystal tresses in the sky, > And with them scourge the bad revolving stars, > That have consented unto Henry's <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEATH">death</a>! > Henry the Fifth, too famous to live <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a>! > England ne'er lost a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">king</a> of so much worth. *First <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> Henry VI.* The passage with which Strada begins his history, is too poetical for a subject of that kind; and at any rate too <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> for the beginning of a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a> performance. 3. A third rule or observation is, That where the subject is intended for entertainment solely, not for instruction, a thing ought to be described as it appears, not as it is in reality. In running, for example, the impulse upon the ground is proportioned in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> to the celerity of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>; though in appearance it is otherwise, for a person in swift motion seems to skim the ground, and scarcely to touch it. <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, with <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, describes quick running according to appearance; and raises an image far more lively than by adhering scrupulously to truth: > Hos super adventit Volscæ de gente Camilla, > Agmen agens equitum et florentes eae catervas, > Bellatrix: non illa colo calathifive Minervæ > Femineas affluet manus; fed praia virgo > Dura pati, curisque peium praveitere ventos. > Illa vel intactæ segetis per funnum volaret > Granina: nec teneras cursu laxefact aristas: > Vel mare per medium, flunctu supensa tumenti, > Ferret iter: celere nec tingeret æquore plantas. *Enniid. vii. 803.* 4. In narration as well as in description, objects ought to be painted so accurately as to form in the mind of the reader distinct and lively images. Every useless circumstance ought indeed to be suppressed, because every such circumstance loads the narration; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a circumstance be necessary, however slight, it cannot be described too minutely. The force of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> consists in raising complete images, which have the effect to transport the reader as by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAGIC">magic</a> into the very <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of the important <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, and to convert him as it were into a spectator, beholding every thing that passes. The narrative in an epic poem ought to rival a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> in the liveliness and accuracy of its representations: no circumstance must be omitted that tends to make a complete image; because an imperfect image, as well as any other imperfect <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONCEPTION">conception</a>, is <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLD">cold</a> and uninteresting. We shall illustrate this rule by several examples, giving the first place to a beautiful passage from Virgil: > Qualis populus merens Philomela sub umbra > Amphis queritur fontis, quos durus arator > Observans nido implurum detraxit. *Georg. lib. 4. l. 511.* The poplar, plowman, and unledged young, though not essential in the description, tend to make a complete image, and upon that account are an embellishment. Again: The following passage is scarce inferior to either of Narration, those mentioned: "Far before the rest, the son of Offian comes: bright in the smiles of youth, fair as the full beams of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>. His long <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> waves on his back; his dark brow is half beneath his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HELMET">helmet</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> hangs loose on the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HERO">hero</a>'s side; and his spear glitters as he moves. I fled from his terrible eye, King of high Tenora." Fingal. The Henriade of Voltaire errs greatly against the foregoing rule: every incident is touched in a sum- <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MARY">mary</a> way, without ever descending to circumstances. This manner is good in a general history, the purpose of which is to record important transactions; but in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FABLE">fable</a> it is cold and uninteresting; because it is imprac- ticable to form distinct images of persons or things re- presented in a manner so superficial. It is observed above, that every useless circumstance ought to be suppressed. The crowding such circum- stances is, on the one hand, not less to be avoided, than the conciseness for which Voltaire is blamed, on the other. In the Æneid, Barce, the nurse of Si- chaus, whom we never hear of before nor after, is in- troduced for a purpose not more important than to call <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNA">Anna</a> to her litter Dido; and that it might not be thought unjust in Dido, even in this trivial circum- stance, to prefer her husband's nurse before her own, the poet takes care to inform his reader, that Dido's nurse was dead. To this may be opposed a beautiful passage in the same book, where, after Dido's last speech, the poet, without detaining his readers by de- scribing the manner of her death, hastens to the la- mentation of her attendants: Dixerat: atque illam media inter talia ferro Collapsam afsicium comites, ensenique cruore Spumantem, sparafaque manus. It clamor <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AD">ad</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTA">alta</a> Atria, concussam bacchatur fana per urbem; Lamentis gemitique et feminco ululatu Tecta fremunt, resonat magnis plangoribus æther. Lib. 4. l. 663. As an appendix to the foregoing rule, may be added the following observation, That to make a sudden and strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a>, some single circumstance, happily selected, has more power than the most laboured de- scription. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MACBETH">Macbeth</a>, mentioning to his lady some voices he heard while he was murdering the King, says, There's one did laugh in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a>, and one cry'd <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MURDER">Murder</a>! They wak'd each other; and I stood and heard them; But they did say their prayers, and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> them Again to sleep. Lady. There are two lodg'd together. Macbeth. One cry'd, God bless us! and, Amen! the other; As they had seen me with these hangman's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. Listening their fear, I could not say, Amen, When they did say, God bless us. Lady. Consider it not so deeply. Macbeth. But wherefore could not I pronounce Amen? I had most need of blessing, and Amen. Stuck in my throat. Lady. Lady. These deeds must not be thought After these ways; so, it <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a> make us mad. Macbeth. Methought I heard a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> cry, Sleep no more! Macbeth doth murder sleep, &c. Describing <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> Henry: I <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAW">saw</a> young Harry, with his beaver on, His cuisses on his thighs, gallantly arm'd, Ride from the ground like feather'd <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a>; And vaulted with such ease into his seat, As if an angel dropt <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DOWN">down</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a>, To turn and <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> a fiery Pegasus, And witch the world with noble <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HORSEMANSHIP">horsemanship</a>. First part Henry IV. <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> 4. sc. 2. King Henry, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a>, if thou think'st on Heaven's bliss, Hold up thy hand, make signal of thy hope. He dies, and makes no sign! <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SECOND">Second</a> part Henry VI. act 3. sc. 10. The same author, speaking ludicrously of an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> debilitated with diseases, says, "Half of them dare not shake the snow from off their casocks, lest they shake themselves to pieces." "I have seen the walls of Balcutha, but they were defoliate. The flames had resounded in the halls: and the voice of the people is heard no more. The stream of Clutha was removed from its place by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> of the walls. The thistle shook there its lonely head: the moos whistled to the wind. The fox looked out from the windows; and the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RANK">rank</a> grass of the wall waved round his head. Defoliate is the dwelling of Morna: silence is in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of her fathers." Fingal. To draw a character is the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MASTER">master</a> stroke of description. In this Tacitus excels: his portraits are <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> and lively, not a feature wanting or misplaced. Shake- speare, however, exceeds Tacitus in liveliness; some characteristical circumstance being generally invented or laid hold of, which paints more to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> than many words. The following instances will explain our meaning, and at the same <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> prove our observation to be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a>. Why should a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAN">man</a>, whose blood is warm within, Sit like his grandfire cut in alabaster? Sleep when he <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WAKES">wakes</a>, and creep into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JAUNDICE">jaundice</a>, By being peevish? I tell thee what, Anthonio, (I <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LOVE">love</a> thee, and it is my love that speaks), 'There are a sort of men, whose visages Do cream and mantle like a standing pond; And do a wilful stillness entertain, With purpose to be drest'd in an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> Of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>, gravity, profound conceit; As who should say, I am Sir Oracle, And when I ope my lips, let no dog bark! O my Anthonio! I do know of those, That therefore only are reputed wife, For saying nothing. Merchant of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, act 1. sc. 2. Again: "Gratiano speaks an infinite <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of nothing, more than any man in all Venice: his reasons are two grains of wheat hid in two bushels of chaff; you shall seek all day ere you find them; and when you have them, they are not worth the search." Ibid. N° 236. In the following passage, a character is completed by Narrator a single stroke: Shallow. O the mad days that I have spent; and to see how many of mine old acquaintance are dead. Silence. We shall all follow, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COUSIN">cousin</a>. Shallow. Certain, 'tis certain, very sure, very sure; Death (as the Psalmist <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>) is certain to all; all shall die. How good a yoke of bullocks at <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-STAMFORD">Stamford</a> fair? Slender. Truly, cousin, I was not there. Shallow. Death is certain. Is old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">Double</a> of your town living yet? Silence. Dead, Sir. Shallow. Dead! see, see; he drew a good bow; and dead. He <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> a fine shoot. How a score of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EWES">ewes</a> now? Silence. Thereafter as they be. A score of good ewes may be worth ten pounds. Shallow. And is old Double dead? Second Part Henry IV. act 3. sc. 3. Describing a jealous husband: "Neither press, coffer, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHEST">chest</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a>, well, vault, but he hath an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSTRACT">abstract</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-REMEMBRANCE">remembrance</a> of such places, and goes to them by his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>. There is no hiding you in the house." Merry Wives of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WINDSOR">Windsor</a>, act 4. sc. 3. Congreve has an inimitable stroke of this kind in his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a> of Love for Love: Ben <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LEGEND">Legend</a>. Well, father, and how do all at home? how does <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Dick, and brother Val? Sir Sampson. Dick, body o' me, Dick has been dead these two years. I writ you word when you were at <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LEGHORN">Leghorn</a>. Ben. Mfs, that's true; marry, I had forgot. Dick's dead, as you say. Act 3. sc. 6. Falstaff speaking of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> Pistol: "He's no swaggerer, hol'less; a tame cheater i'faith; you may stroak him as gently as a puppy-greyhound; he will not swagger with a Barbary hen, if her feathers turn back in any show of resistance." Second part Henry IV. act 2. sc. 9. Offian among his other excellencies is eminently suc- cessful in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>; and he never fails to de- <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> his reader with the beautiful attitudes of his he- roes. Take the following instances: "O Oscar! <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BEND">bend</a> the strong in arm; but spare the feeble hand. Be thou a stream of many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIDES">tides</a> against the foes of thy people; but like the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-GALE">gale</a> that moves the grass to those who ask thine aid.—So Trenmor lived; such Trathal was; and such has Fingal been. My arm was the support of the injured; and the weak rested behind the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a> of my <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-STEEL">steel</a>." "We heard the voice of joy on the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, and we thought that the mighty Cathmor came. Cathmor the friend of strangers! the brother of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RED">red</a>-haired Cairbar! But their souls were not the same; for the light of hea- ven was in the bosom of Cathmor. His towers rose on the banks of Atha; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> paths led to his halls; seven chiefs stood on these paths, and called the stranger to the feast. But Cathmor dwelt in the wood to avoid the voice of praise." "Dermid and Oscar were one: they reaped the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> together. Their friendship was strong as their steel;" They rush on the foe like two rocks falling from the brow of Ardven. Their words are stained with the blood of the valiant; warriors faint at their name. Who is equal to Oscar but Dermid? who to Dermid but Oscar?" "Son of Comhal, replied the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>, the strength of Morni's arm has failed: I attempted to draw the sword of my youth, but it remains in its place: I throw the spear, but it falls short of the mark: and I feel the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of my shield. We decay like the grass of the mountain, and our strength returns no more. I have a son, O Fingal! his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> has delighted in the actions of Morni's youth; but his sword has not been fitted against the foe, neither has his fame begun. I come with him to battle, to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> his arm. His renown will be a fun to my soul, in the dark <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> of my departure. O that the name of Morni were forgot among the people! that the heroes would only say, Behold the father of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a>." Some writers, through <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of imagination, fall into <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a>; some are guilty of downright absurdities; and some even rave like madmen. Against such <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> errors one cannot be more effectually warned than by collecting instances; and the first shall be of a contradiction, the most venial of all. Virgil speaking of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol7.html#article-NEPTUNE">Neptune</a>, Interea magno misceri murmure pontum, Emissamque hycenum senit Neptunus, et imis Stagna refusa vadis: graviter commotus, et alto Propiciens, summa placidum caput extulit unda. Aeneid. i. 128. Again: When first young Maro, in his boundless mind, A <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> 'toulaft immortal Rome <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>'d. <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-ESSAY">Essay</a> on Criticism, l. 30. The following examples are of absurdities. "Alli pulsis e tormento catenis disceripti sectique, Dimidiatore corpore pugnabat fibi superflites, ac peremptae partes ulteres." Strada, dec. 2. l. 2. Il pover huomo, che non sen' era accorto, Andava combattendo, ed era morto. Berni. He fled, but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLYING">flying</a>, left his life behind. Iliad, xi. 443. Full through his neck the weighty falchion sped: Along the pavement roll'd the mutt'<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a> head. Odyssey, xxii. 365. The last article is of raving like one mad. Cleopatra speaking to the apic, Welcome, thou kind deceiver, Thou best of thieves; who, with an easy <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KEY">key</a>, Dost open life, and unperceiv'd by us Ev'n fleal us from ourselves; discharging so Death's dreadful office, better than himself; Touching our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a> so gently into slumber, That Death stands by, deceiv'd by his own image, And thinks himself but sleep. Dryden, All for Love, act 5. Having discussed what observations occurred upon the thoughts or things expressed, we proceed to what more peculiarly concerns the language or verbal drets. As words are intimately connected with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> they represent, the emotions raised by the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> and by the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> ought to be concordant. An elevated subject requires an elevated style; what is familiar, ought to be familiarly expressed: a subject that is serious and important, ought to be clothed in plain nervous language: a description, on the other hand, addressed to the imagination, is susceptible of the highest ornaments that sounding words and figurative <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> can bestow upon it. We shall give a few examples of the foregoing rules. A poet of any genius is not apt to dress a high subject in low words; and yet blemishes of that kind are found even in classical works. Horace, observing that men are satisfied with themselves, but seldom with their condition, introduces <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> indulging to each his own choice: Jam faciam quod vultis; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ERIS">eris</a> tu, qui modo miles, Mercator: tu, consultus modo, rusticus: hinc vos, Vos hinc mutatis dilucidate paribus: cia, Quid statis? nolint: atqui licet effe beatas. Quid causae est, merito quin illis Jupiter ambas Tratus buccas inflet? neque se fore pothae Tam facilem dicat, votis ut prebeat aurem? Sat. lib. i. sat. 1. l. 16. Jupiter in wrath puffing up both <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEEKS">cheeks</a>, is a low and even ludicrous expression, far from suitable to the gravity and importance of the subject: every one must feel the discordance. The following couplet, sinking far below the subject, is no less ludicrous: Not one looks backward, onward still he goes, Yet ne'er looks forward farther than his nose. Essay on Man, ep. iv. 223. On the other hand, to raise the expression above the tone of the subject, is a fault than which none is more <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMON">common</a>. Take the following instances: Orcan le plus fidèle à servir ses desseins, Ne sous le ciel brûlant des plus noirs Africains. Bajac, act 3. sc. 8. Les ombres par trois fois ont obscurci les cieux Depuis que le sommeil n'est entré dans vos yeux; Et le jour a trois fois chassé la nuit obscure Depuis que votre corps languit sans nourriture. Phedra, act 1. sc. 3. Affueris. Ce mortel, qui montra tant de zèle pour moi, Vit-il encore? Asph.—Il voit l'astre qui vous éclaire. Ephor, act 2. sc. 3. Oui, c'est Agamemnon, c'est ton roi qui t'éveille; Viens, reconnais la voix qui frappe ton oreille. Iphigenie. No jocund <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a> drinks to-day, But the great cannon to the clouds shall tell; And the king's rowse the heav'n shall bruit again, Repeaking earthly <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAMLET">Hamlet</a>, act 1. sc. 2. In the inner room I spy a winking <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAMP">lamp</a>, that weakly strikes The ambient air, scarce kindling into light. Southerne, Fate of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAPUA">Capua</a>, act 3. In the funeral orations of the bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MEAUX">Meaux</a>, the following <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> are raised far above the tone of the subject: "L'Ocean etonné de se voir traversé tant de fois, en The passage we have in view begins l. 116. But let me now a while survey, &c. and ends at l. 135. It is proper to be observed upon this head, that writers of inferior rank are continually upon the stretch to enliven and enforce their subject by exaggeration and superlatives. This unluckily has an effect contrary to what is intended: the reader, disgusted with language that swells above the subject, is led by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONTRAST">contrast</a> to think more meanly of the subject than it may possibly deserve. A man of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a>, beside, will be no less careful to husband his strength in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> than in walking: a writer, too liberal of superlatives, exhausts his whole stock upon ordinary incidents, and reserves no share to express, with greater energy, matters of importance. Many writers of that kind abound so in epithets, as if poetry consisted entirely in high-founding words. Take the following instance: When black-brow'd night her dusky mantle spread, And wrapt in solemn gloom the sable sky; When soothing sleep her opiate dews had shed, And feal'd in silken slumber every eye: My waking thought admits no balmy rest, Nor the sweet bliss of soft oblivion share: But watchful wo distracts my aching <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>, My heart the subject of corroding care: From haunts of men with wandering steps and slow I solitary steal, and soothe my pensive wo. Here every substantive is faithfully attended by some tumid epithet. We proceed to a second remark, not less important than the former. No person of reflection but must be sensible, that an incident makes a stronger impression on an eye-witness, than when heard at second-hand. Writers of genius, sensible that the eye is the best avenue to the heart, represent every thing as passing in our sight; and, from readers or hearers, transform us as it were into spectators: a skilful writer conceals himself, and presents his personages: in a word, everything becomes dramatic as much as possible. Plutarch, de gloria Atheniensium, observes, that <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-THUCYDIDES">Thucydides</a> makes his reader a spectator, and inspires him with the same passions as if he were an eye-witness. In the fine arts, it is a rule to put the capital objects in the strongest point of view; and even to present them oftener than once, where it can be done. In history-<a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> is placed in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FRONT">front</a>, and in the best light: an equestrian statue is placed in a centre of streets, that it may be seen from many places at once. In no <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> is there greater opportunity for this rule than in writing: ——— Sequitur pulcherrimus Astur, Astur equo sidens et versicoloribus armis. ——— Full many a lady I've ey'd with best regard, and many a time Th' <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> of their tongues hath into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONDAGE">bondage</a> Brought my too diligent <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-EAR">ear</a>: for several virtues Have I lik'd several women; never any With so full soul, but some defect in her Did quarrel with the noblest <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> she ow'd, And put it to the foil. But you, O you, So perfect, and so peerless, are created Of every creature's best. Tempest, act 3., l. 1. Orlando. Orlando.—Whate'er you are That, in the defart inaccessible, Under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a> of melancholy boughs, Lose and neglect the creeping hours of time; If ever you have look'd on better days; If ever been where bells have knoll'd to <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>; If ever sat at any good man's feast; If ever from your eye-lids wip'd a tear, And know what 'tis to pity, and be pity'd; Let gentleness my strong enforcement be, In the which hope I blush, and hide my sword. <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DUKE">Duke</a> sen. True is it that we have seen better days; And have with holy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELL">bell</a> been knoll'd to church; And fat at good men's feasts; and wip'd our eyes Of drops that sacred pity had engender'd: And therefore sit you down in gentleness, And take upon command what help we have, That to your wanting may be ministr'd. As you like it. With the conversing I forgot all time; All seasons and their change, all paeans alike. Sweet is the breath of morn, her rising sweet, With <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHARM">charm</a> of earliest birds; pleasant the sun When first on this delightful <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAND">land</a> he spreads His orient beams on herbs, tree, fruit, and flow'r Glistening with <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEW">dew</a>; fragrant the fertile <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> After soft show'rs; and sweet the coming on Of grateful ev'n'ning mild, the silent night With this her solemn <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIRD">bird</a>, and this fair <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MOON">moon</a>, And these the gems of heav'n, her starry train: But neither breath of morn, when she ascends With charm of earliest birds, nor rising sun On this delightful land, nor <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HERB">herb</a>, fruit, flow'r, Glistening with dew, nor fragrance after show'rs, Nor grateful ev'n'ning mild, nor silent night, With this her solemn bird, nor walk by moon, Or glittering <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-STAR">star</a>-light, without thee is sweet. Paradise Lost, book 4. l. 634. "What <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> ye, that ye <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> this proverb, The fathers have eaten four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a>, and the children's <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> are set on edge? As I live, saith the Lord God, ye shall not have occasion to use this proverb in Israel. If a man keep my judgments to deal truly, he is just, he shall surely live. But if he be a robber, a shedder of blood; if he have eaten upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, and defiled his neighbour's wife; if he have oppressed the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POOR">poor</a> and needy, have spoiled by violence, have not restored the pledge, have lift up his eyes to idols, have given forth upon usury, and have taken increase: shall he live? he shall not live: he shall surely die; and his blood shall be upon him. Now, lo, if he beget a son, that feeth all his father's sins, and confedereth, and doth not such like; that hath not eaten upon the mountains, hath not lifted up his eyes to idols, nor defiled his neighbour's wife, hath not oppressed any, nor withheld the pledge, neither hath spoiled by violence, but hath given his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> to the hungry, and covered the naked with a garment; that hath not received usury nor increase, that hath executed my judgments, and walked in my statutes: he shall not die for the iniquity of his father; he shall surely live. The soul that sinneth, it shall die; the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, neither shall the father bear the iniquity of the son; the righteous deeds of the righteous shall be upon him, and the wickednesses of the wicked shall be upon him. Have I any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> that the wicked should die, saith the Lord God; and not that he should return from his ways, and live?" <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EZEKIEL">Ezekiel</a> xviii. A concise comprehensive style is a great ornament in narration; and a superfluity of unnecessary words, not less than of circumstances, a great nuisance. A judicious selection of the striking circumstances, clothed in a nervous style, is delightful. In this style, Tacitus excels all writers, ancient and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MODERN">modern</a>. Instances are numberless: take the following specimen: "Cerebra hinc pralia, et saepius in modum latrocinii: per saltus, per paludes; ut cuique fors aut virtus: temere, proviso, ob iram, ob praedam, iuveni, et aliquando ignarisi ducibus." Annal. lib. i. § 29. After Tacitus, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OSSIAN">Ossian</a> in that respect justly merits the place of distinction. One cannot go wrong for examples in any part of the book. If a concise or nervous style be a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, tautology must be a blemish; and yet writers, fettered by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>, are not sufficiently careful to avoid this slovenly practice: they may be pitied, but they cannot be justified. Take for a specimen the following instances, from the best poet, for verification at least, that England has to boast of: High on his helm celestial lightnings play, His beamy shield emits a living ray; Th' unwearied blaze incessant streams supplies, Like the red star that fires the autumnal skies. Iliad v. 5. Strength and omnipotence invest thy throne. Ibid. viii. 576. So silent fountains, from a rock's tall head, In fable streams soft trickling waters shed. Ibid. ix. 19. His clanging armour rung. Ibid. xii. 94. Fear on their cheek, and horror in their eye. Ibid. xv. 4. The blaze of armour flash'd against the day. Ibid. xvii. 736. As when the piercing blasts of Boreas blow. Ibid. xix. 380. And like the moon, the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> resplendent shield Blaz'd with long rays, and gleam'd athwart the field. Ibid. xix. 402. No—could our swiftness o'er the winds prevail, Or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> the pinions of the western gale, All were in vain— Ibid. xix. 604. The humid sweat from ev'ry pore descends. Ibid. xxiii. 829. We <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> this article with a curious inquiry. An object, however ugly to the sight, is far from being so when represented by colours or by words. What is the cause of this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>? With respect to painting, the cause is obvious: a good picture, whatever the subject be, is agreeable by the pleasure we take in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a>; and this pleasure overbalancing the disagreeableness of the subject, makes the picture upon the whole agreeable. With respect to the description of an ugly object, the cause follows. To connect individuals in the social state, no particular contributes more than language, by the power it possesses of an expeditious <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> of thought, and a lively representation of transactions. But <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> hath not been been satisfied to recommend language by its utility merely: independent of utility, it is made susceptible of many beauties, which are directly felt, without any intervening reflection. And this unfolds the mystery; for the pleasure of language is so great, as in a lively description to overbalance the disagreeableness of the image raised by it. This, however, is no encouragement to choose a disagreeable subject; for the pleasure is incomparably greater where the subject and the description are both of them agreeable. The following description is upon the whole agreeable, though the subject described is in itself dismal: <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NINE">Nine</a> times the space that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> day and night To mortal men, he with his horrid crew Lay vanquish'd, rolling in the fiery <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GULF">gulf</a>, Confounded though immortal! but his doom Reserved him to more wrath; for now the thought Both of lost <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> and lasting pain Torments him; round he throws his baleful eyes That witness'd huge affliction and dismay: Mix'd with obdurate <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a> and steadfast hate: At once as far as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a> ken he views The dismal situation waste and wild: A dungeon horrible, on all sides round As one great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FURNACE">furnace</a> flamed; yet from those flames No light, but rather darkness visible Serv'd only to discover sights of woe, Regions of sorrow, doleful shades, where peace And rest can never dwell, hope never comes That comes to all; but torture without end Still urges, and a fiery deluge, fed With ever-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> sulphur unconsum'd! Such place eternal <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> had prepar'd For those rebellious. *Paradise Lost*, book 1. l. 50. An unmanly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEPRESSION">depression</a> of spirits in time of danger is not an agreeable sight; and yet a fine description or representation of it will be relished: *K. Richard*. What must the king do now? must he submit? The king shall do it: must he be depos'd? The king shall be contented: must he lose The name of king? o' God's name let it go; I'll give my jewels for a set of beads; My gorgeous <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, for a hermitage; My gay apparel, for an almsman's <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GOWN">gown</a>; My hir'd goblets, for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISH">dish</a> of wood; My sceptre, for a palmer's walking-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STAFF">staff</a>; My subjects, for a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of carved saints; And my <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, for a little grave; A little, little grave,—an obscure grave. Or I'll be <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BURY">bury</a>'d in the king's highway; Some way of common <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREAD">tread</a>, where subjects feet May hourly trample on their sovereign's head; For on my heart they tread now, whilst I live; And, bury'd once, why not upon my head? *Ricbard II.*, act 3., sc. 6. Objects that strike terror in a spectacle, have in poetry and painting a fine effect. The picture, by raising a slight <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMOTION">emotion</a> of terror, agitates the mind; and in that condition every beauty makes a deep im- pression. May not contrast heighten the pleasure, by opposing our present security to the danger of en- countering the object represented? The other shape, If shape it might be call'd that shape had none— Distinguishable in member, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JOINT">joint</a>, or limb; Or substance might be call'd that shadow seem'd, For each seem'd either; black it stood as night, Fierce as ten furies, terrible as <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HELL">hell</a>, And shook a dreadful dart. *Par. Lost*, b. 2. l. 665. Now storming fury rose, And clamour such as heard in heaven till now Was never: arms on clamour clashing bray'd Horrible <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DISCORD">discord</a>, and the madding <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a> Of brazen <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHARIOTS">chariots</a> rage; dire was the noise Of conflict; overhead the dismal hills Of fiery darts in flaming volleys flew, And flying vaulted either hoist with fire, So under fiery cope together rush'd Both battles main, with ruinous assault And inextinguishable rage: all heaven Resounded, and had earth been then, all earth Had to her centre shook. *Ibid.* book 6. l. 207. Ghost. But that I am forbid To tell the secrets of my prison-house, I could a tale unfold, whose lightest word Would <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARROW">harrow</a> up thy soul, freeze thy young blood, Make thy two eyes, like stars, start from their spheres, Thy knotty and combined locks to part, And each particular hair to stand on end, Like quills upon the fretful porcupine: But this eternal blazon must not be To ears of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> and blood. *Hamlet*, act 1. sc. 8. *Gratiano*. Poor Desdemona! I'm glad thy father's dead: Thy <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MATCH">match</a> was mortal to him; and pure grief Shore his old thread in twain. Did he live now, This flight would make him do a deifyrate turn: Yea, curse his better angel from his side, And fall to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-REPROBATION">reprobation</a>. *Othello*, act 5. sc. 8. Objects of horror must be excepted from the fore- going <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-THEORY">theory</a>; for no description, however lively, is sufficient to overbalance the disgust raised even by the idea of such objects. Every thing horrible ought therefore to be avoided in a description. *NARSES*, the eunuch who rivalled Delilah in heroism under the reign of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Julian, em- erged from obscurity A.D. 538. From the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DOME">dome</a>- stic <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the palace, and the administration of the private revenue, he was suddenly exalted to the head of an army. He is ranked among the few eu- nuchs who have rescued that unhappy name from the contempt and hatred of mankind. A feeble diminu- tive body concealed the soul of a statesman and a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WAR">war</a>- rior. His youth had been employed in the manage- ment of the loom and distaff, in the cares of the house- hold, and the service of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a>; but, while his hands were busy, he secretly exercised the faculties of a vigorous and discerning mind. A stranger to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>, he studied in the palace to dif- ferentiate, to flatter, and to persuade; and as soon as he approached the person of the emperor, Julian listened with surprise and pleasure to the manly coun- cils of his chamberlain and private <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a>. The talents of Narves were tried and improved in frequent embassies; he led an army into <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, acquired a prac- tical tical knowledge of the war and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and pre- sumed to strive with the genius of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELISARIUS">Belisarius</a>. Twelve years after his return, the eunuch was chosen to at- chieve the conquest which had been left imperfect by the first of the Roman generals. Instead of being dazzled by vanity or emulation, he seriously declared, that unless he were armed with an adequate force, he would never consent to risk his own <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> and that of his sovereign. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTINIAN">Justinian</a> granted to the favourite what he might have denied to the hero; the Gothic war was rekindled from its ashes, and the preparations were not unworthy of the ancient majesty of the em- pire. Narves defeated the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOTHS">Goths</a>, the Franks, and the Alemanni; the Italian cities opened their gates to the conqueror; he entered the capital in triumph; and having established the seat of his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> at Ra- venna, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> 15 years to govern Italy under the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXARCH">Exarch</a>. His virtues, we are told, were stained with avarice; and in this <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROVINCIAL">provincial</a> reign he accumulated a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver which surpassed the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a> of a private fortune. His government was oppressive or unpopular; and the general discontent was expressed with freedom by the deputies of Rome. Before the throne of Justinian they boldly declared, that their Gothic servitude had been more tolerable than the des- potism of a Greek eunuch; and that unless their ty- rant were instantly removed, they would confute their own happiness in the choice of a master. Thus was his disgrace the effect of the people's disaffection; and his death, though in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of old <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, was unseasonable and premature, since his genius alone could have repaired the last and fatal <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-ERROR">error</a> of his life. He died about the year 567, and, as some say, at the advanced age of 95; but this does not appear very probable. See Gibbon's Rom. Hist. vol. iv. 4to edit. p. 194, 298 &c.

NARVA

Pages 693-693

a strong town of the Russian empire, in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIVONIA">Livonia</a>, with a castle and a harbour. It was taken by the Muscovites from the Danes in 1558, by the Swedes in 1581, and they defeated the Muscovites near it in 1700; but it was retaken by the Russians in 1704 by storm, and the inhabitants sent to Astrakhan. It is seated on the river Narva, 95 miles S.W. of Wil- burg, and 172 N.E. of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGA">Riga</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 29° O. N. Lat. 59° 8'.

NASSAU-SIEGEN

Pages 693-693

a small principality of Ger- many in the Welterwalde, is in general a mountain- ous woody <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, with some arable and pasture ground, and a good breed of cattle. Its manufac- tures are chiefly those of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-IRON">iron</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-STEEL">steel</a>, having an iron mine in the neighbourhood of Siegen. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> John the Younger, in 1626, embraced the Roman Catho- lic <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, and endeavoured to introduce it into the country; but the principality, upon the extinction of the line of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NASSAU">Nassau</a>-Siegen in 1743, falling to the line of Nassau-Dietz, and therein to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-STADTHOLDER">stadtholder</a> of the United Provinces, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> were delivered from their apprehensions of Popish tyranny and bigotry. The prince, on account of these territories, has a seat and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> at the diets of the empire and circle in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of princes. His assessment in the matricula for Nassau Siegen is 773 florins monthly; and towards the maintenance of the chamber-judicatory, 50 rix-dollars six kruitzers and a half each <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TERM">term</a>. The revenue of this principality is estimated at 100,000 rix-dollars. Nassau-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DILLENBURG">Dillenburg</a>, a principality of Germany, si- tuated near the former. It has not much arable <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAND">land</a>, but plenty of wood, good quarries of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, some sil- ver and vitriol, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, with store of iron, for the working and smelting of which there are many forges and founderies in the country; and by these, and the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-SALE">sale</a> of their iron, the inhabitants chiefly subsist. Calvinism is the religion of the principality, which contains five <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> and two boroughs, and be- longs entirely to William V. prince of Orange, and hereditary stadtholder of the United Provinces, whose father succeeded to a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> of it in 1739 on the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of prince Christian, and to the rest in 1743 on the death of prince William Hyacinth of Siegen. The prince, on account of this principality also and Dietz, has a seat and voice in the college of princes, at the diets of the empire and circle. His assessment in the matricula, for Nassau-Dillenburg, is 102 florins monthly; and to the chamber-judicatory, 50 rix-dol- lars six and a half kruitzers, each term. His revenue from this principality is computed at above 130,000 florins. Nassau-Hadamar, a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Germany, which, till the year 1711, had princes of its own; but now be- longs wholly to William V. prince of Orange. Nassau, prince of Orange. See Maurice.

NATES

Pages 693-693

in anatomy, a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TERM">term</a> expressing those two fleshy exterior parts of the body vulgarly called the buttocks. See Anatomy. Nates Cerebri, are two circular protuberances of the brain, situated on the back-side of the medulla oblongata, near the cerebellum.

NATION

Pages 693-697

a collective <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TERM">term</a>, used for a consider- able <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of people inhabiting a certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAND">land</a>, confined within fixed limits, and under the same <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. NATIONAL DEBT: the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> owing by go- vernment. Our limits permit us to give but a very general sketch of this subject: However, as it is of considér- able importance to every inhabitant of these kingdoms, we shall endeavour to give as clear and comprehensive a view of it as the bounds necessarily prescribed us <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a> admit. In order to this, it may not be improper to refer back to the times that have gone before us, that we may the better discover the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of public revenues, the manner of their expenditure, and the causes of public debt. In that rude state of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> which precedes the ex- tension of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> and the improvements of manu- factures, when those expensive luxuries which com- merce and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> can alone introduce, are alto- gether unknown; the person who possesses a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> re- venue can spend <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> enjoy that revenue in no other way than by maintaining nearly as many people as it can maintain. Among our feudal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a> Smith's <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> during which estates used to continue in the same wealth of family, sufficiently demonstrates the general disposition Natu- ral of people to live within their income. Though the noble hospitality constantly exercised by the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> landholders may not to us in the present times seem consistent with that order which we are apt to consider as inseparably connected with good economy, yet we must certainly allow them to have been at least so far frugal as not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> to have spent their whole income. Some <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> of this money, perhaps, they spent in purchasing the few objects of vanity and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a> with which the circumstances of the times could furnish them; but some part of it they seem commonly to have hoarded. They could not well indeed do anything else but hoard whatever money they saved. To trade was disgraceful to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>; and to lend money at <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>, which at that time was considered as usury and prohibited by <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAW">law</a>, would have been still more so. The same disposition to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-SAVE">save</a> and to hoard prevailed in the sovereign as well as in the subjects. Among nations to whom commerce and manufactures are little known, the sovereign is in a situation which naturally disposes him to the parsimony requisite for accumulation. In that situation the expense even of a sovereign cannot be directed by that vanity which delights in the gaudy finery of a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COURT">court</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> of the times affords but few of the trinkets in which that finery consists. Standing armies are not then necessary; so that the expense even of a sovereign, like that of any other great <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LORD">lord</a>, can be employed in scarce anything but bounty to his tenants and hospitality to his retainers. But bounty and hospitality very seldom <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> to extravagance; though vanity almost always does. All the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> sovereigns of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> accordingly had treasuries. Every Tartar <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> in the present times is said to have one. In a commercial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> abounding with every sort of expensive luxury, the sovereign, in the same manner as almost all the great proprietors in his dominions, naturally spends a great part of his revenue in purchasing those luxuries. His own and the neighbouring countries supply him abundantly with all the costly trinkets which compose the splendid but insignificant pageantry of a court. His ordinary expense becomes equal to his ordinary revenue, and it is well <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it does not frequently exceed it. The amassing of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a> can no longer be expected; and when extraordinary exigencies require extraordinary expenses, he must necessarily call upon his subjects for an extraordinary aid. The late <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a> and his father are the only great princes of Europe who, since the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Henry IV. of France in 1610, are supposed to have amassed any considerable treasure. The parsimony which leads to accumulation has become almost as rare in republican as in monarchical governments. The Italian republics, the United Provinces of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, are all in debt. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CANTON">canton</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BERNE">Berne</a> is the single republic in Europe which has amassed any considerable treasure. The other Swiss republics have not. The <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for some sort of pageantry, for splendid buildings at least and other public ornaments, frequently prevails as much in the apparently sober <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of a little republic as in the dissipated court of the greatest king. The want of parsimony in time of peace imposes the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of contracting debt in time of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WAR">war</a>. When war comes, there is no money in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a> but what is necessary for carrying on the ordinary expense of the peace establishment. In war an establishment of three or four times that expense becomes necessary for the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of the state, and consequently a revenue three or four times greater than the peace revenue. Supposing that the sovereign should have, what he scarce ever has, the immediate means of augmenting his revenue in proportion to the augmentation of his expense; yet still the produce of the taxes, from which this increase of revenue must be drawn, will not begin to come into the treasury till perhaps ten or twelve months after they are imposed. But the moment in which war begins, or rather the moment in which it appears likely to begin, the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> must be augmented, the fleets must be fitted out, the garrisoned <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> must be put into a posture of defence; that army, that fleet, those garrisoned towns, must be furnished with arms, ammunition, and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>. An immediate and great expense must be incurred in that moment of immediate danger, which will not wait for the gradual and slow returns of the new taxes. In this exigency government can have no other resources but in borrowing. The same commercial state of society which, by the operation of moral causes, brings government in this manner into the necessity of borrowing, produces in the subjects both an ability and an inclination to lend. If it commonly brings along with it the necessity of borrowing, it likewise brings along with it the facility of doing so. A country abounding with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> and manufacturers, necessarily abounds with a set of people whose whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> not only their own capitals, but the capitals of all those who either lend them money or trust them with goods, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> as frequently or more frequently than the revenue of a private <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAN">man</a>, who without trade or business lives upon his income, passes through his hands. The revenue of such a man can regularly pass through his hands only once in a year. But the whole amount of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> of a merchant who deals in a trade of which the returns are very quick, may sometimes pass through his hands two, three, or four times in a year. A country abounding with merchants and manufacturers, therefore, necessarily abounds with a set of people who have it at all times in their power to advance, if they choose to do so, a very large sum of money to government. Hence the ability in the subjects of a commercial state to lend.
