The progress of the enormous debts which at present oppresses, and will in the long run probably ruin, all the great nations of Europe, has been pretty uniform. In England, after the Revolution, when new connections with Europe introduced a new system of foreign politics, the expenses of the nation, not only Blackett, in settling the new establishment, but in maintaining Comment, long wars, as principals, on the continent, for the security of the Dutch <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARRIER">barrier</a>, reducing the French <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a>, settling the Spanish succession, supporting the house of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>, maintaining the liberties of the Germanic body, and other purposes, increased to an unusual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>: insomuch, that it was not thought advisable to raise all the expenses of any one year by taxes to be levied within that year, lest the unaccustomed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of them should create murmurs among the people. It was therefore the policy of the times to anticipate the revenues of their posterity, by borrowing immense sums. sums for the current <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the state, and to lay no more taxes upon the subject than would suffice to pay the annual interest of the sums so borrowed; by this means converting the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> debt into a new <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, transferable from one man to another at any time and in any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>. This system indeed seems to have had its original in the state of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>, A.D. 1344; which government then owed about L.60,000 <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-STERLING">Sterling</a>; and being unable to pay it, formed the principal into an aggregate sum, called metaphorically a mount or <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BANK">bank</a>, the shares whereof were transferable like our stocks, with interest at 5 per cent., the prices varying according to the exigencies of the state. This laid the foundation of what is called the national debt; for a few long <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ANNUITIES">annuities</a> created in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. will hardly deserve that name. Nations, like private men, have generally begun to borrow upon what may be called personal credit, without assigning or mortgaging any particular <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FUND">fund</a> for the payment of the debt; and when this resource has failed them, they have gone on to borrow upon assignments or mortgages of particular funds. What is called the unfunded debt of Great <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, is contracted in the former of those two ways. It consists partly in a debt which bears, or is supposed to bear, no interest, and which resembles the debts that a private man contracts upon account; and partly in a debt which bears interest, and which resembles what a private man contracts upon his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BILL">bill</a> or promissory <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>. The debts which are due either for extraordinary services, or for services either not provided for or not paid at the time when they are performed; part of the extraordinary of the army, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>, and ordnance, the arrears of subsidies to foreign princes, those of seamen's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WAGES">wages</a>, &c. usually constitute a debt of the first kind. Navy and exchequer bills, which are issued sometimes in payment of a part of such debts, and sometimes for other purposes, constitute a debt of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SECOND">second</a> kind; exchequer bills <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> interest from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> on which they are issued, and navy bills six months after they are issued. The bank of England, either by voluntarily discounting those bills at their current value, or by agreeing with government for certain considerations to circulate exchequer bills, that is, to receive them at par, paying the interest which happens to be due upon them, keeps up their value, and facilitates their circulation, and thereby frequently enables government to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> a very large debt of this kind. During the great reconnoitre in King William's time, when the bank of England thought proper to put a stop to its usual transactions, exchequer bills and tallies are said to have sold from 25 to 60 per cent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCOUNT">discount</a>; owing partly, no doubt, to the supposed instability of the new government established by the Revolution, but partly too to the want of the support of the bank of England. When this resource is exhausted, and it becomes necessary, in order to raise money, to assign or mortgage some particular branch of the public revenue for the payment of the debt, government has upon different occasions done this in two different ways. Sometimes it has made this assignment or mortgage for a short <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of time only, a year or a few years, for example; and sometimes for perpetuity. In the one <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CASE">case</a>, the fund was supposed sufficient to pay within the limited time both principal and interest of the money borrowed: in the other, it was supposed sufficient to pay the interest only, or a perpetual annuity <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> to the interest; government being at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to redeem at any time this annuity upon paying back the principal sum borrowed. When money was raised in the one way, it was said to be raised by anticipation; when in the other, by perpetual funding, or, more shortly, by funding. In the reign of King William, when the debt began to be amassed, and during a great part of that of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>, before we had become so familiar as we are now with the practice of perpetual funding, the greater part of the new taxes were imposed but for a short period of time (for four, five, six, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years only), and a great part of the grants of every year consisted in loans upon anticipation of the produce of those taxes. The produce being frequently insufficient for paying within the limited term the principal and interest of the money borrowed, deficiencies arose; to make good which it became necessary to prolong the term. On the 31st of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1697, the funded and unfunded debts amounted to L.21,515,742:13:8½; at the same time, in 1714, they were L.53,681,076:18:6½. In 1755, before the breaking out of the war, they amounted to L.72,239,673; and on the 5th of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1763, at the conclusion of the peace, they had accumulated to L.122,603,336:8:2½ of funded debt, and of unfunded L.13,027,589:2:2 more. In 1775, they were very nearly 130 millions; and the last American war added upwards of 120 millions more to that enormous sum: to pay the interest of which, and the charges of management, amounting annually to nearly eight millions and a half, the extraordinary revenues elsewhere enumerated† (excepting only the land-tax and annual malt-tax) are in the first <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a> venue mortgaged and made perpetual by <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. Perpetual we say; but still redeemable by the same authority that imposed them: which, if it at any time can pay off the capital, will abolish those taxes which are raised to discharge the interest. By this means, then, the quantity of property in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> is greatly increased in idea compared with former times; yet, if we coolly consider it, not at all increased in reality. We may boast of large fortunes, and quantities of money in the funds. But where does this money exist? It exists only in name, in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, in public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, in parliamentary security: and that is undoubtedly sufficient for the creditors of the public to rely on. But then what is the pledge which the public faith has pawned for the security of these debts? The land, the trade, and the personal industry of the subject; from which the money must arise that supplies the several taxes. In these therefore, and these only, the property of the public creditors does really and intrinsically exist; and of course the land, the trade, and the personal industry of individuals, are diminished in their true value <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> so much as they are pledged to answer. If A's income amounts to L.100 per annum; and he is so far indebted to B, that he pays him L.50 per annum for his interest; one half of the value of A's property is transferred to B the creditor. The creditor's property exists in the demand which he has upon the debtor, and nowhere else; and the debtor is only a trustee to his creditor for one half of the value of his income. In short, the property of a creditor of the public consists in a certain portion of the national taxes; by how much therefore he is the richer, by so much the nation, which pays these taxes, is the poorer. The only advantage that can result to a nation from public debts, is the increase of circulation, by multiplying the cash of the kingdom, and creating a new species of currency, assignable at any time and in any quantity; always therefore ready to be employed in any beneficial undertaking, by means of this its transferable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>; and yet producing some profit even when it lies idle and unemployed. A certain proportion of debt seems to be highly useful to a trading people; but what that proportion is, it is not for us to determine. This much is indubitably certain, that the present magnitude of our national incumbrances very far exceeds all calculations of commercial benefit, and is productive of the greatest inconveniences. For, first, the enormous taxes that are raised upon the necessaries of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> for the payment of the interest of this debt, are a hurt both to trade and manufactures, by raising the price as well of the artificer's subsistence as of the raw material, and of course, in a much greater proportion, the price of the commodity itself. Nay, the very increase of paper-circulation itself, when extended beyond what is requisite for commerce or foreign <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a>, has a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> tendency to increase the price of provisions as well as of all other merchandise. For as its effect is to multiply the cash of the kingdom, and this to such an extent that much must remain unemployed, that cash (which is the universal <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of the respective values of all other commodities) must necessarily sink in its own value, and every thing grow comparatively dearer. Secondly, if part of this debt be owing to foreigners, either they draw out of the kingdom annually a considerable quantity of specie for the interest; or else it is made an argument to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> them unreasonable privileges in order to induce them to reside here. Thirdly, if the whole be owing to subjects only, it is then charging the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> and industrious subject, who pays his share of the taxes to maintain the indolent and idle creditor who receives them. Lastly, and principally, it weakens the internal strength of a state, by anticipating those resources which should be reserved to defend it in case of necessity. The interest we now pay for our debts would undoubtedly be sufficient to maintain the most vigorous war that any national motives could possibly require. If indeed our ancestors in King William's time had annually paid, so long as their exigencies lasted, a far less sum than we now annually raise upon their accounts, they would not in time of war have borne so great burdens as they have bequeathed to and settled upon their posterity in time of peace; and might have been eased the instant the exigence was over. See Funds. On the whole, then, the national debt is undoubtedly a subject of vast importance, and as such it has been always considered; for much has been said and written upon it, and many schemes have been proposed at various times and by various persons for gradually removing it, it being considered by the most judicious as a most pernicious incumbrance to a commercial country. Some, we are aware, think it of vast utility; but this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> is too eccentric, and in our estimation too feebly supported, to be convincing. The public debt is indisputably a great grievance; and every lover of his country must surely wish to see it removed: the period, however, when this blessing shall take place, if indeed it ever arrive, must at least be very distant. It is neither our business nor intention (even if the limits prescribed to the article did not prevent it) to be minute on the subject, or to propose any schemes for alleviating the burdens of the nation. That indeed has been already done by far abler hands than we profess to be: we must therefore refer such as wish for farther information on this interesting topic to those (and they are not a few) who have treated of it at full length. Smith's Wealth of Nations, and Sir John Sinclair's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the Revenue, go to the bottom of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>. The writings of Dr Price likewise deserve considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, especially as one of his plans for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REDUCTION">reduction</a> of the debt has in fact been adopted, and in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> established, by the legislature: His three plans may be found in a late pamphlet by William Morgan, intitled, A Review of Dr Price's Writings on the Subject of the Finances of this Kingdom. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATIVITY">Nativity</a>, or <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-NATAL">Natal</a> day, the day of a person's birth. The word nativity is chiefly used in speaking of the saints; as, the nativity of St John the Baptist, &c. But when we say the Nativity, it is understood of that of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ, or the feast of Christmas. Nativity, nativitas, in ancient law-books, signifies <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONDAGE">bondage</a> or servitude. Nativity, in astrology, the theme or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of the heavens, and particularly of the twelve houses, at the moment when a person was born; called also the horoscope. Calling the nativity, or by calculation seeking to know how long the queen should live, &c. was made felony, an. 23 Eliz. c. 2. Nativo habendo, in law, a writ directed to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a>, for a lord who claimed inheritance in any villain, when a villain was run away from him, for the apprehending and restoring him to the lord. Nativix, in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY">natural history</a>, a name given by some old writers to the nerita. Natalia, the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> name of the Lesser <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, being the most westerly part of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> in Asia, and consisting of a large <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a>, which extends from the river <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EUPHRATES">Euphrates</a> as far as the Archipelago, the seas of Marmora, the straits of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALIPOLI">Galipoli</a> and of Constantinople, which separate it from Europe on the west. It is bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BLACK_SEA"><a class=</a>"xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and on the south by the Mediterranean. Natrix, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>, the name given by Rivinius to a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> nearly allied to the anonis, and comprehended with it in one genus by Linnæus, under the name of anonis. See Rest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARROW">harrow</a>. Natrix, in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ZOOLOGY">zoology</a>, the name of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMON">common</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WATER">water</a>-snake, called also torquata, from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a> about its neck. It is not a water animal, properly speaking, but a land one, which being able to swim very well, often takes the water to hunt about for frogs, which are its principal food. It grows to be much longer and larger than the viper, and does not bring forth live young ones, but great numbers of eggs, which it lays in dunghills to be hatched by the warmth of the place, or by the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>.

NATRUM

Pages 697-697

the nitre of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, is a genuine, pure, and native <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, extremely different from our nitre, and indeed from all the other native salts, it being a fixed alkali, plainly of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of those made by fire from vegetables, yet capable of a regular <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CRYSTALLIZATION">crystallization</a>, which those salts are not. It is found on the surface of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> at very small depths within it; and is naturally formed into thin and flat cakes or crusts, which are of a spongy or cavernous substance, very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> and friable, and, when pure, of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> brownish <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WHITE">white</a>; but as its spongy texture renders it very subject to be fouled by earth received into its pores, it is often met with of a deep dirty <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>, and not unfrequently reddish. Natrum, whether native or purified, dissolves in a very small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WATER">water</a>; and this solution is, in many parts of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, used for washing; where it is also made into <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOAP">soap</a>, by mixing it with <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OIL">oil</a>. Natrum reduced to powder, and mixed with sand or flints, or with any other <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-STONE">stone</a> of which crystal is the basis, make them readily run into glaigs. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GOLD">Gold</a> heated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RED">red</a>-hot, and sprinkled with a small quantity of this salt, melts in the same manner; as does also <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, and the regulus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANTIMONY">antimony</a>; which melt much more easily than they otherwise would do. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a> cannot be mixed with it by any art, and indeed <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a> not amalgamate with <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-METALS">metals</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> only a little of this salt be added. It is found in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> abundance in many parts of Asia, where the natives <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SWEEP">sweep</a> it up from the surface of the ground, and call it soap-earth. The earliest account we have of it is in the scriptures, where we find that the salt called nitre in those times would ferment with <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a>, and had an abrasive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, so that it was used in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a> and in washing things. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a> compares the fingering of songs with a heavy heart, to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONTRARIETY">contrariety</a> of vinegar and nitre; and Jeremiah says, that if the sinner wash himself with nitre, his sin is not cleansed off. These are properties that perfectly agree with this salt, but not at all with our <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SALTPETRE">saltpetre</a>.

NATURAL

Pages 697-698

in general, something that relates to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. See NATURE. Natural children, are those born out of lawful wedlock. See <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASTARD">BASTARD</a>. Natural Functions, are those actions whereby the aliments are changed and assimilated so as to become a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> of the body. Natural, in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HERALDRY">heraldry</a>, is used where animals, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, &c. are blazoned with the colours they naturally have, though different from the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMON">common</a> colours of heraldry; and this is to prevent their armories being accused of falsity, when blazoned with the names of colours unknown in heraldry. Natural <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">Note</a>, in music, is used in opposition to flat and sharp notes, which are called <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> notes. See NOTE, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-SCALE">SCALE</a>, &c. Natural is also used for something coming immediately out of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of nature: in which <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> it stands opposed to fictitious <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> artificial, which signifies something wrought by art. See ARTIFICIAL. Bishop Wilkins observes, that there appears a world of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between natural and artificial things, when viewed with microscopes. The first ever appear adorned with all imaginable elegance and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>; the latter, though the most curious in their kind, infinitely rude and unhewn: the finest <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a> appears a rough <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAR">bar</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-IRON">iron</a>; and the most accurate engraving or confinement, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> done with a mattock or a trowel. Natural Beauty, or the beauty of natural objects, is that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> or those qualities in the works of nature, or more properly of God, which are calculated to excite pleasing sensations in the minds of all such persons of true <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> as attentively observe them. It <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a> not, we trust, be deemed improper or impertinent, therefore, to introduce a few observations on this subject, previous to our treating of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY">natural <a clas</a>s="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>.—To many, it is hoped, it will appear to be a very proper introduction to that important article. "That <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SENSIBILITY">sensibility</a> to beauty, which, when cultivated and improved, we <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TERM">term</a> taste, is universally diffused through the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; and it is most uniform with respect to those objects, which being out of our power are not liable to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a> from accident, caprice, or fashion. The verdant <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAWN">lawn</a>, the shady <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GROVE">grove</a>, the variegated landscape, the boundless ocean, and the starry firmament, are contemplated with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> by every attentive beholder. But the emotions of different spectators, though similar in kind, differ widely in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>; and to relish with full delight the enchanting scenes of nature, the mind must be uncorrupted by avarice, sensuality, or ambition; quick in her sensibilities; elevated in her sentiments; and devout in her affections. He who possesses such exalted powers of perception and enjoyment, may almost say, with the poet, I care not, Fortune! what you me deny; You cannot rob me of free Nature's <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>; You cannot shut the windows of the sky, Through which <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AURORA">Aurora</a> shows her brightening <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FACE">face</a>; You cannot bar my constant feet to trace The woods and lawns, by living stream, at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVE">eve</a>: Let <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> my nerves and finer fibres brace, And I their toys to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> children leave: Of fancy, reason, virtue, nought can me bereave. "Perhaps such ardent enthusiasm may not be compatible with the necessary tools and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> offices which <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a> has assigned to the generality of men. But there are none to whom some portion of it may not prove advantageous; and if it were cherished by each individual, in that degree which is consistent with the indispensible duties of his station, the felicity of human <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> would be considerably augmented. From this source, the refined and vivid pleasures of the imagination are almost entirely derived: and the elegant arts owe their choicest beauties to a taste for the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONTEMPLATION">contemplation</a> of nature. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PAINTING">Painting</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a> are express imitations of visible objects; and where would be the charms of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, if divested of the imagery and embellishments which she borrows from rural scenes? Painters, statuaries, and poets, therefore, are always anxious to acknowledge themselves the pupils of nature; and as their skill increases, they grow more and more delighted with every view of the animal and vegetable world. But the pleasure resulting from admiration is transient; and to cultivate taste, without regard regard to its influence on the passions and affection, is to rear a tree for its blossoms, which is capable of yielding the richest and most valuable fruit. Physical and moral beauty bear so intimate a relation to each other, that they may be considered as different gradations in the scale of excellence; and the knowledge and relish of the former should be deemed only a step to the nobler and more permanent enjoyments of the latter. "Whoever has visited the Leafeows, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WARWICKSHIRE">Warwickshire</a>, must have felt the force and propriety of an inscription which meets the eye at the entrance into those delightful grounds. Would you then taste the tranquil <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-SCENE">scene</a>? Be sure your bosoms be serene: Devoid of hate, devoid of strife, Devoid of all that poisons life; And much it vailes you, in their <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, To graft the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of human <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-RACE">race</a>. "Now such scenes contribute powerfully to inspire that serenity which is necessary to enjoy and to heighten their beauties. By a secret contagion, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> catches the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> which the contemplates; and the frame within assimilates itself to that which is without. For, Who can forbear to smile with Nature? Can The stormy passions in the bosom roll, While every <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-GALE">gale</a> is peace, and every grove Is <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-MELODY">melody</a>? "In this state of sweet composure, we become susceptible of virtuous impressions, from almost every surrounding object. The patient ox is viewed with generous complacency; the guileless sheep with pity; and the playful lamb raises emotions of tenderness and love. We rejoice with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> and exemption from toil, while he ranges at <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> through enamelled pastures; and the frolics of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLT">colt</a> would afford unmixed delight, did we not recollect the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONDAGE">bondage</a> which he is soon to undergo. We are charmed with the song of birds, foreshadowed with the buzz of insects, and pleased with the sportive motions of fishes, because these are expressions of enjoyment; and we exult in the felicity of the whole animated <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CREATION">creation</a>. Thus an equal and extensive benevolence is called forth into exertion; and having felt a common <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> in the gratifications of inferior beings, we shall be no longer indifferent to their sufferings, or become wantonly instrumental in producing them. "It seems to be the intention of Providence, that the lower order of animals should be subservient to the comfort, convenience, and sustenance of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAN">man</a>. But his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of dominion extends no farther; and if this right be exercised with mildness, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, the subjects of his power will be no less benefited than himself. For various species of living creatures are annually multiplied by human art, improved in their perceptive powers by human culture, and plentifully fed by human industry. The relation, therefore, is <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RECIPROCAL">reciprocal</a> between such animals and man; and he may supply his own wants by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of their labour, the produce of their bodies, and even the sacrifice of their lives, whilst he co-operates with all gracious Heaven in promoting <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a>, the great end of existence. "But though it be true, that partial evil, with respect to different orders of sensitive beings, may be universal good; and that it is a wise and benevolent intuition of nature, to make destruction itself, within certain limitations, the cause of an increase of life and enjoyment; yet a generous person will extend his compassionate regards to every individual that suffers for his sake; and, whilst he sighs Even for the kid or lamb that parts its life Beneath the bloody <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a>, he will naturally be solicitous to mitigate pain, both in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DURATION">duration</a> and degree, by the gentlest modes of inflicting it. "We are inclined to believe, however, that this sense of humanity would soon be obliterated, and that the heart would grow callous to every soft <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a>, were it not for the benignant influence of the smiling face of nature. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COUNT">count</a> de Lauzun, when imprisoned by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIV. in the castle of Pignerol, amused himself during a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> with catching flies, and delivering them to be devoured by a rapacious spider. Such an entertainment was equally singular and cruel; and inconsistent, we believe, with his former character, and his subsequent turn of mind. But his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CELL">cell</a> had no window, and received only a glimmering <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> from an aperture in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ROOF">roof</a>. In less unfavourable circumstances, may we not presume, that instead of sporting with misery, he would have released the agonizing flies, and bid them enjoy that freedom of which he himself was bereaved? "But the taste for natural beauty is subservient to higher purposes than those which have been enumerated: and the cultivation of it not only refines and humanizes, but dignifies and exalts the affections. It elevates them to the admiration and love of that Being who is the author of all that is fair, sublime, and good in the creation. Scepticism and irreligion are hardly compatible with the sensibility of heart which arises from a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> and lively relish of the wildness, harmony, and order subsisting in the world around us; and emotions of piety must <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> up spontaneously in the bosom that is in unison with all animated nature. Actuated by this divine <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-INSPIRATION">inspiration</a>, man finds a fane in every grove; and, glowing with devout fervour, he joins his song to the universal chorus, or mutes the praise of the Almighty, in more expressive silence. Thus they Whom Nature's works can <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHARM">charm</a>, with God himself Hold <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONVERSE">converse</a>; grow familiar, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> by day, With his conceptions; <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> upon his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>; And form to his, the relish of their souls." On the whole then, it certainly appears, that the advantages resulting from a taste for natural beauties are great and important: it is equally certain, that as it is useful, so it is a continual source of real enjoyment; for a more rational pleasure cannot possibly occupy the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> or captivate the affections of mankind, than that which arises from a due consideration of the works of nature. Pleasure, we know, is a necessary ingredient in human life, in order in some <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> to counterbalance the pains, the evils, and little necessities, which are at times perhaps unavoidable, and in order to render life tolerable. It is the part then of

Vertebre. | Ord. | Gen. | Sp. | |------|------|-----| | Intestina | 21 | 384 | | <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOLLUSCA">Mollusca</a> | 31 | 438 | | Tetraca | 36 | 2525 | | Zoophita | 15 | 498 | | Infloria | 15 | 191 | Total: 118 4036 In the new French Encyclopédie par oide de Matieret, the editors promised to give a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of more than 18,000 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. Dr Berkenhout, in the last edition of his Synopsis, says, that in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a> there are about 54 <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAMMALIA">mammalia</a>, 210 of birds, 50 of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMPHIBIA">amphibia</a>, 600 of insects, 150 of fishes, and 1600 species of plants; but in every class he is probably much within the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY"><a class="xref" hr</a>ef="vol12.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">Philosophy</a>. Natural philosophy is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> defined to be that art <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> science which considers the powers and properties of natural bodies, and their mutual actions on one another. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MORAL_PHILOSOPHY">moral philosophy</a> is the mind of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAN">man</a>; its inquiries and researches are into the intellectual world. Natural philosophy, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, is only concerned with the material <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CREATION">creation</a>. The Moralist's business is to inquire into the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of virtue, the causes and effects of vice, to propose remedies for it, and to point out the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of attaining <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a>, which only can be the result of virtuous conduct. The Naturalist, on the contrary, has nothing to do with spirit; his business is solely about body or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>; and he ought to have a full and accurate knowledge of all material substances, together with their affections and properties; and, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> possible, he is to investigate the reasons of such and such appearances. Indeed, the first and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> part of this science is to collect all the manifest and sensible appearances of things, and reduce them into a body of natural <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. Philosophy, it has often been said, and it is even now very generally thought, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> an inquiry into all the causes of things; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> informs us, that though we are acquainted with a good number of effects, we can trace but few of their causes; so that philosophy itself <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a> really be found to be in general but a collection of facts. Still, however, it differs from natural history in its appropriated <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>; the business of which is only to observe the appearances of natural bodies separately, and from these appearances to clas them with other bodies: natural philosophy goes farther, and recites the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of two or more bodies of the same or different kinds upon one another; and though it can neither investigate nor point out the causes of those effects, whatever they are, yet, from mathematical reasoning combined with experience, it can be demonstrated, that in such circumstances such effects must always take <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. There are evidently two ways of making observations on the material world: the first is, when we view things nearly as they happen to turn up, without any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> or intervention of our own; in which way, indeed, no great improvements can be expected in this art, because chance having the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>, only exhibits occasional or extraordinary properties. The other method is, when, after a thorough acquaintance with bodies, we apply them to other bodies equally known, diligently attending to the result, and observing whether any thing new arises. Such seems to be in general the nature of our article; nor is it our intention to be much more particular at present. We must therefore refer our readers respectfully to those parts of the subject, respecting which they wish for more satisfaction and minute details. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> definitions of the word philosophy, together with its origin, as well as the manner of philosophising in former times as well as at present, with the gradual improvement of science, particularly natural, we shall introduce, we think, more properly under the words PHILOSOPHY and PHYSICS. We need only add under the present article, what however is well known, that natural philosophy was till lately divided only into four parts, commonly called the four branches, viz. 1. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MECHANICS">Mechanics</a>; 2. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HYDROSTATICS">Hydrostatics</a>; 3. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OPTICS">Optics</a>; and 4. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>; and these again are subdivided into various parts. Modern discoveries have added, however, two more parts to the number, viz. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAGNETISM">magnetism</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-ELECTRICITY">electricity</a>, whose properties and effects, &c. have been wonderfully unfolded of late years. It is remarkable, that in the English <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a> these two latter branches are never taken notice of in lecturing on natural philosophy, the old <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> being still retained, without any mention of these two important <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>. The reason may be, that they are only subject to experiment, and not yet reduced to mathematical reasoning; which is the method of teaching philosophy in one of those celebrated seminaries. Of these branches of this extensive science, it is not our intention to take even a general view in this place. We mult must therefore refer our readers to each particular article, where they will find them treated at considerable length—See <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-EXPERIMENTAL_PHILOSOPHY">Experimental Philosophy</a>.

NATURALIZATION

Pages 719-719

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAW">law</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of naturalizing an alien, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> putting him into the condition of a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> born subject, and intitling him to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> and privileges thereof. But none can be naturalized unless they have received the sacrament within one <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MONTH">month</a> before the bringing in of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BILL">bill</a>, and taken the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OATHS">oaths</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">allegiance</a> and supremacy in the presence of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. A person who is naturalized may have lands by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a>, as heir at law, as well as obtain them by purchase; but he is disallowed from being a member of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRIVY_COUNCIL">privy <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> or parliament; or from holding offices, 7 Jac. I. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 2. 12 <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">Will</a>. III. cap. 2. All children born out of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">king</a>'s dominions, whose fathers were or are subjects of this <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> at the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> of their birth, are adjudged to be natural born subjects of this realm, except children of parents attainted of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TREASON">treason</a>, or that are in the actual <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of a foreign <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> at enmity with us, 4 Geo. II. cap. 21. Every foreign seaman, who in time of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WAR">war</a> serves two years on board an English ship, is ipso facto naturalized, 3 Geo. II. cap. 3. And all foreign <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> and Jews, upon their residing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years in any of the British colonies, without being absent above two months at a time, or serving two years in a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> capacity there, are upon taking the oaths naturalized to all intents and purposes, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they had been born in this kingdom; and therefore are admissible to all such privileges, and no other, as Protestants or Jews born in this kingdom are entitled to. See Alien and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DENIZEN">Denizen</a>. In France, before the Revolution, naturalization was the king's <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PREROGATIVE">prerogative</a>; in England it is only done by act of parliament. In the former of those places, before their <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> was overturned, Swiss, Savoyards, and Scots, did not require naturalization, being reputed regnicoles, or natives.

NATURE

Pages 719-719

according to Mr Boyle, has eight different significations; it being used, 1. For the Author of nature, whom the schoolmen call Natura Naturans, being the same with God. 2. By the nature of a thing, we sometimes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> its essence; that is, the attributes which make it what it is, whether the thing be corporeal <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> not; as when we attempt to define the nature of a fluid, of a triangle, &c. 3. Sometimes we confound that which a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAN">man</a> has by nature with what accrues to him by birth; as when we say, that such a man is noble by nature. 4. Sometimes we take nature for an internal principle of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>; as when we say, that a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-STONE">stone</a> by nature falls to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. 5. Sometimes we understand, by nature, the established course of things. 6. Sometimes we take nature for an aggregate of powers belonging to a body, especially a living one; in which <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> physicians say, that nature is strong, weak, or spent; or that, in such or such diseases, nature left to herself <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a> perform the cure. 7. Sometimes we <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TERM">term</a> nature for the universe, or whole system of the corporeal works of God; as when it is said of a phoenix, or chimera, that there is no such thing in nature. 8. Sometimes too, and that most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a>, we express by the word nature a kind of semi-deity, or other strange kind of being. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a>, says the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, I were to propose a notion of nature, less ambiguous than those already mentioned, and with regard to which many axioms relating to that word may be conveniently understood, I should first distinguish between the universal and the particular nature of things. Universal nature I would define to be the aggregate of the bodies that make up the world in its present state, considered as a principle by virtue whereof they <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> and suffer, according to the laws of motion prescribed by the Author of all things. And this makes way for the other subordinate notions, since the particular nature of an individual consists in the general nature applied to a distinct portion of the universe; or, which is the same thing, it is a particular assemblage of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> properties of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, as <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, motion, &c. Kingdoms of Nature. See Kingdoms. Conduct or Operations of Nature. See <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>.

NAUCLERUS

Pages 721-721

descended of a noble family of Swabia, was provost of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Suringia, and professor of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAW">law</a> in the university of that <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CITY">city</a>. His original name was Vergennus; but this name, which in German signifies "sailor," he changed into Naucerus, a word of the same signification in Greek. He was alive in 1501. We have from him a Latin <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHRONICLE">Chronicle</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADAM">Adam</a> to the year 1500, of which Basilus wrote a continuation <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to 1514, and Surius to 1564. It possesses greater accuracy than any historical compilation which had appeared <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> to his <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a>; but still it is only a compilation. It is chiefly valued for what regards the occurrences of the 15th century. It was printed at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOGNE">Cologne</a> in folio in 1564 and 1579.

NAUCRARI

Pages 721-721

among the Athenians, was the name given to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> magistrates of the "boroughs <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> townships," called Naucrarii; because each was obliged, besides two horsemen, to furnish out one ship for the public <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>.

NAUCRATES

Pages 721-721

a Greek poet, who was employed by <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTEMISIA">Artemisia</a> to write a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PANEGYRIC">panegyric</a> upon Mausolus. An orator who endeavoured to alienate the cities of Lycia from the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of Brutus.

NAUCRATIS

Pages 721-722

a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> on the left side of the Canopic mouth of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NILE">Nile</a>. It was celebrated for its <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, and no ship was permitted to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAND">land</a> at any other <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, but was obliged to fail directly to the city, there to deposit its cargo. It gave birth to Athenaeus. NAUCRATITES Nomos (anc. geog.), Pliny; Vol. XII. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">Part</a> II. NAU formed a most rich library, which he raised from the first volume in the space of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years to the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of 40,000. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> was nearly completed before the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> gave him two small benefices, a canonry of Verdun and the priory of Artige in the Limousin; and we know how much this ungenerosity affected him, from a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> of Patin to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> Spon, dated <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 22, 1648, where he writes thus of our librarian: "I have seen one thing in him which I am very sorry for; especially as I have known him all along hitherto at a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> distance from such a disposition: it is, that he begins to complain of his fortune, and of his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MASTER">master</a>'s avarice, from whom he had never received any more than 1200 livres a year in benefices; not forgetting to declare, that his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> was sacrificed for too small a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>. I think (continues Patin) what grieves him is, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APPREHENSION">apprehension</a> of dying before he has raised something for his brothers and his nephews, of whom he has a great number." However that be, Naude had the grief to see this library, which he had collected with so much pains and care, totally dispersed. Upon the disgrace of Mazarine it was sold; and Patin, in a letter of March 5, 1651, observes, that Naude had bought all the books in physic for 3500 livres. <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHRISTINA">Christina</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, who set herself to draw into her dominions all the literati of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, procured a proposal to be made to Naude of being her library keeper; and as he was then out of all employ, he accepted the proposal, and went to Cop.—But he soon grew out of humour with his residence in Sweden: the manners of the people, so very different from his, gave him great disgust; and seeing France become more quiet than it had been, he resolved to return. Accordingly he quitted Sweden loaded with presents from the queen, and several persons of distinc- tion: but the fatigue of the journey threw him into a fever, which obliged him to stop at <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABBEVILLE">Abbeville</a>; and he died there <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 29, 1652. As to his character, he was very prudent and regular in his conduct, sober, never drinking anything but <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WATER">water</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">Study</a> was his <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> occupation, and he was indeed a true Helluo librorum; so that he undertook them perfectly well. He spoke his mind with great freedom, and that freedom sometimes showed itself upon <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> subjects, in such a manner as might have occasioned some disadvantageous thoughts of him; but the Christian sentiments in which he died left room to believe that his heart was never corrupted, and had no share in the free expressions which sometimes escaped from him; especially in the philosophical railleries which passed sometimes between him, Guy Patin, and Gailendi. He wrote a great number of books, a catalogue of which may be seen in Niceron's Memoires, tom. ix. Voltaire says, that "of all his books, the Apologie des grands Hommes acusés de Magie is almost the only one which continues to be read."

NAULUM

Pages 837-838

a piece of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> put into the mouth of a person deceased among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, to enable him to pay <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHARON">Charon</a> the ferryman for his passage. It was to be of the current <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a> of the reigning empe- NAUPLIA had been driven from <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PELOPONNESUS">Peloponnesus</a> by the Macedonians. It became the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of the Macedonians after the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Aegospotamos, and it was restored to the Locri. <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACEDONIA">Macedonia</a> afterwards took it, and gave it to the Epirots; from which circumstance it has generally been called one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> cities of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 22. 20. N. Lat. 38. 0. There was on the shore a temple of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol7.html#article-NEPTUNE">Neptune</a>, and near it a cave filled with offerings, and dedicated to Venus, where widows resorted to request new husbands of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a>. Pausan. lib. 10. p. 898.

NAUPLION

Pages 838-838

(anc. geog.), a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PELOPONNESUS">Peloponnesus</a>. It was the naval station of the Argives. The fountain Canathos was in its neighbourhood. NAUPlius, (fab. hist.), a son of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol7.html#article-NEPTUNE">Neptune</a> and Amymons, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-ELIS">Elis</a>. He was the father of the famous <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PALAMEDES">Palamedes</a>, who was so unjustly sacrificed to the artifice and resentment of Ulysses by the Greeks at the Trojan <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WAR">war</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Palamedes highly enraged Nauplius; and to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> the injustice of the Grecian princes, he endeavoured to debauch their wives, and ruin their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>. When the Greeks returned from the Trojan war, Nauplius was pleased to see them distressed in a storm on the coasts of Euboea; and to make their distress still more universal, he lighted fires on such places as were surrounded with the most dangerous rocks, that the fleet might be shipwrecked upon the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COAST">coast</a>. This had the desired effect; but Nauplius was so disappointed when he <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAW">saw</a> Ulysses and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DIOMEDES">Diomedes</a> escape from the general distress, that he threw himself into the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. According to some mythologists there were two persons of this name, a native of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARGOS">Argos</a>, who went to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLCHIS">Colchis</a> with Jason. He was son of Neptune and Amymons.—The other was king of Euboea, and lived about the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the Trojan war. He was, as some observe, son of Clytonas, one of the descendants of Nauplius the Argonaut. The Argonaut was remarkable for his knowledge of sea affairs and of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>. He built the town of Nauplia, and sold Ange <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Alcides to king Teuthras, to screen her from her father's resentment.

NAUPORTUS

Pages 838-838
or NAUPORTUM, (anc. geog.), a town on a cognominal river, towards its source, in Pannonia Superior. The reason of the name, according to Pliny, is, that the ship Argo, after coming up the Danube, the Save, and the Laubach, was thence carried on men's shoulders over the Alps into the Adriatic. The river Nauportus rises in the Alps, near Longaticum, at the distance of six miles from the town Nauportum; which was a colony of the Taurici, a people on the confines of Noricum. Now Upper Laubach in Carinthia, on the river Laubach. E. Long. 14. 40. N. Lat. 46. 28.

NAUSCOPY

Pages 838-841

the art of discovering the approach of ships <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> the neighbourhood of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAND">land</a> at a considerable distance. This pretended art was invented by M. Bottineau, employed in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">King</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMPANY">Company</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of France, from the year 1782 to 1784; and the account of it is given by the inventor as follows: "This knowledge is not derived either from the undulation of the waves, or from the futility of sight, nor from any particular <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a>; but merely from observation of the horizon, which discovers signs indicating the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROXIMITY">proximity</a> of ships or of land. "On the approximation of a ship towards the land, or towards another ship, there appears in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-METEOR">meteor</a> of a particular <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, visible to everyone without any painful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>. It is not by any kind of accident that this meteor appears under these circumstances; on the contrary, it is the necessary result of the approximation of one vessel towards another, or towards the land. The existence of the meteor, and the knowledge of its different modifications, are what constitute the certainty and the precision of my observations. "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> I am asked, how it is possible that the approach of a ship towards land should give birth to any meteor whatsoever in the atmosphere, and what connection there can be between two objects at such a distance from each other? I reply, that I am not obliged to give an account of the hows and the wheresof; that it is sufficient for me to have discovered the fact, without being obliged to account for its principle." The writer concludes, by defining to be called on for experimental proofs, and by promising in future a complete treatise of Nauscopy, with maps, plates, &c. This complete treatise, as far as we know, has not yet been published, nor do we expect ever to see such a treatise on the subject as <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a> satisfy the minds of those who are persuaded that every effect must have an adequate cause. The administrators of the island, who gave to M. Bottineau what he calls a report, containing the most authentic and most explicit testimony of the reality of the discovery, seem to be of our <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>; and yet they speak of this discovery with doubt, and with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of respect to which we think it can lay no claim. Their report is in the form of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> directed to the Maréchal de Caffres; and that our <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-INFIDELITY">infidelity</a> may not deprive the public of what, in the immense catalogue of possibilities, may <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> to a useful discovery, we shall here subjoin a copy of it. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORT_LOUIS">Port <a cl</a>ass="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a>, Island of France, the 18th February 1784. "My <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>, A letter which you have written on the 6th of April to M. Bottineau, employed in the King and Company's service in this colony, obliges us not to refuse him one for you, of which he proposes being himself the bearer. The desire only of being useful to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, is (as he says) the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> which determines him to take this step. He would be angry with himself were he to conceal a discovery which hath hitherto escaped the most enlightened persons, and of which he only is in possession. This discovery is the art of announcing the presence of one or several ships, at 100, 150, and as far as 20 leagues distanced. This is by no means the result of his studies, nor the fortunate application of the principles of any particular science; his science is in his eyes only, and he can have no other: what we call penetration and genius cannot make up to him what he is deficient in from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>. He perceives (as he says) in nature, some signs which indicate to him the presence of the vessels, as we know that there is a fire in a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a> when we perceive the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> which comes from it. This is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> which he makes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of himself to those who have conversed with him about his art: this (though he has kept his secret to himself) NAU Nauscopy self) is the plainest thing he has said, in order to make it be understood that he hath not made this discovery by the knowledge of any art or science, which had been the object of his application, or of his former studies. "It is according to him the effect of chance; he hath taken nature in the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a>, and hath discovered his secret; so that his science, or rather the first elements of it, hath not cost him the least trouble: but the thing which hath cost him a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of labour, and which may be really called his own, is the art of judging of the exact distance. "According to him, the signs very clearly indicate the presence of ships; but none but those who can well read these signs can draw any conclusions from them with regard to distances; and this art of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-READING">reading</a> them well, is, according to him, a true and very laborious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a>: for this reason he hath himself, for a very <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a>, been the dupe of his science. It is at least 15 years since he first foretold here the arrival of ships. At first this was regarded only as a frolic. Wagers were laid on both sides. He often lost, because the ships did not arrive at the time prescribed by him. From thence came his application to find out the cause of these mistakes; and the perfection of his art is the result of this application. "Since the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WAR">war</a>, his informations have greatly increased, and probably were sufficiently exact to excite the attention of the public. The noise of them reached us with the degree of enthusiasm which is always excited by the marvellous. He himself spoke of the reality of his science with the tone of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAN">man</a> convinced. It would have been too cruel to have dismissed him as a visionary. "Besides, every thing depended upon proofs, and we required that he should produce some: in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>, he hath regularly sent us, for eight months, the informations which he thought he might venture to send us; and the result is, that several of the ships he announced are arrived at the time he foretold, after several days of information. "Others have come later than was expected, and some have not appeared at all. "With regard to some of these, it hath been ascertained, that their delay had been occasioned by calms or by currents. M. Bottineau is persuaded, that those which never appeared were foreign vessels which went on; and accordingly we have learned, that some English ships were arrived in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, which might perhaps have been in sight of the island at the time indicated. But this is no more than a conjecture, which our occupations have not allowed us to investigate. What we can ascertain is, that in general it appears that M. Bottineau hath made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> observations: whether it is owing to chance or to his abilities, it might be, perhaps, imprudent to determine. It is however certain, that the fact is so extraordinary, under whatever <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> it is considered, that we have not thought ourselves able either to affirm or deny it; and we have wished the Sieur Bottineau to compel us to take one or the other side of the question, by trusting his secret to some trusty and able person.—But this he hath refused, being probably afraid that he should not acquire by the discovery all the benefit which he imagines he may reap from it." Vol. XII. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">Part</a> II. "Supposing the reality of the discovery, we do not believe that its utility can be as important as M. Bottingeau persuades himself it is; but it might perhaps throw a great light upon <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. In order to be useful it would be necessary that the discovery should be confined to one <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, and remain unknown to all others. This will be impossible, if every fleet, every vessel, and every privateer, is obliged to carry a man on board who is in possession of this secret.—We remain, with respect, my Lord, yours, &c. Le Vce. de Souillac, Chevreau."

NAUSEA

Pages 841-841
or sickness; a retching or propensity and endeavour to vomit, arising from something which irritates the stomach.

NAUTILUS

Pages 841-842

in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ZOOLOGY">zoology</a>; a genus belonging to the order of vermes testacea. The shell consists of one spiral <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-VALVE">valve</a>, divided into several apartments by partitions. There are 17 <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, chiefly distinguished by particularities in their shells. Bonatius observes, that this genus of shell-fish is very well named from the Greek nautilos, which signifies both "a ship" and "a sailor;" for that the shells of all the nautili carry the appearance of a ship with a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> poop. Different authors, both <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MODERN">modern</a>, have called the nautilus by the names of pompilus, nauplius, nauticus, ovum polypi, polypus testaceus; and the French call it le voilier. It is by some imagined, that men first learned the art of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a> from this animal. The most remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the nautili is into the thin and thick-shelled kinds. The first is called nautilus papyraceus; and its shell is indeed no thicker than a piece of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> when out of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WATER">water</a>. This species is not at all fastened to its shell; but there is an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, as old as the days of Pliny, that this creature creeps out of its shell, and goes on shore to feed. When this species is to fail, it expands two of its arms on high, and between these supports a membrane, which it throws out on this occasion: this serves for its sail, and the two other arms it hangs out of its shell, to serve occasionally either as oars <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> as a steerage; but this last office is generally served by the tail. When the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SEA">sea</a> is calm, it is frequent to see numbers of these creatures diverting themselves in this manner: but as soon as a storm rises, or any thing gives them disturbance, they draw in their legs, and take in as much water as makes them specifically heavier than that in which they float; and then they sink to the bottom. When they rise again, they void this water by a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of holes, of which their legs are full. The other nautilus, whose shell is thick, never quits that habitation. This shell is divided into 4 or more partitions, which grow smaller and smaller as they approach the extremity or centre of the shell: between every one of these cells and the adjoining ones there is a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> by means of a hole in the centre of every one of the partitions. Through this hole there runs a pipe of the whole length of the shell. It is supposed by many, that by means of this pipe the fish occasionally passes from one <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CELL">cell</a> to another; but this seems by no means probable, as the fish must undoubtedly be crushed to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEATH">death</a> by passing through it. It is much more likely that the fish always occupies the largest chamber in its shell; that is, that it lives in the cavity between the mouth and the first partition, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NAVY">Navy</a> Some authors call this shell the *concha margaritifera*; but this can be only on account of the fine <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> on its inside, which is more beautiful than any other mother-of-<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PEARL">pearl</a>; for it has not been observed that this species of fish ever produced pearls. It must be observed, that the polypus is by no means to be confounded with the paper-fuelled nautilus, notwithstanding the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> resemblance in the arms and body of the inclosed fish; nor is the cornu ammonis, so frequently found fossil, to be confounded with the thick-shelled nautilus, though the concatenations and general structure of the shell are alike in both; for there are great and essential differences between all these genera. There is a pretty copious and minute account of this curious animal in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">Gentleman</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAGAZINE">Magazine</a>, vol. xxii. p. 6, 7, 8, and 301, and vol. xxv. p. 128.

NAVAL

Pages 719-721

something relating to a ship; whence, NAVAL <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>. See Ship-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BUILDING">Building</a>. NAVAL <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAMP">Camp</a>, in antiquity, a fortification, consisting of a ditch and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARAPET">parapet</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAND">land</a> side, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> a wall built in the form of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEMICIRCLE">semicircle</a>, and extended from one point of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SEA">sea</a> to another. This was sometimes defended with towers, and beautified with gates, through which they issued forth to attack their enemies. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a> hath left us a remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of the Grecian fortifications of this sort, in the Trojan <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WAR">war</a>, beginning at v. 436. Iliad.
