(anc. geog.), a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> mountain, a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> Abarim, and their highest top, whither Moses was ordered to ascend to take a view of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAND">land</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANAAN">Canaan</a>, and there die. Situated in the land of Moab, over-against <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JERICHO">Jericho</a>; with a cognominal town at its foot (Isaiah) belonging to the Reubenites, which afterwards returned to the Moabites; in Jerome's <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> desolate; eight miles to the south of Heshbon.

NEBULY

Pages 847-847
or NEBULEE, in heraldry, is when a coat is charged with several little figures, in form of words running within one another, or when the outline of a bordure, ordinary, &c., is indented or waved.

NECESSITY

Pages 847-849

whatever is done by a cause <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> power that is irresistible; in which <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> it is opposed to freedom. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAN">Man</a> is a necessary <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGENT">agent</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> all his actions be so determined by the causes preceding each <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, that not one past action could possibly not have come to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a>, or have been otherwise than it hath been; nor one future action can possibly not come to pass, or be otherwise than it shall be. But he is a free agent, if he be able, at any <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a>, under the circumstances and causes he then is, to do different things; or, in other words, if he be not unavoidably determined in every point of time, by the circumstances he is in, and the causes he is under, to do that one thing he does, and not possibly to do any other thing. Whether man is a necessary or a free agent, is a question which has been debated with much ingenuity by writers of the first eminence, from Hobbes and Clarke, to Priestley and Gregory. See <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-METAPHYSICS">METAPHYSICS</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">Part</a> III. chap. 5. and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PREDESTINATION">PREDESTINATION</a>. Necessity, in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">mythology</a>, a power superior to all other powers, and equally irresistible by gods and by men. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a>, as he is quoted by Cudworth, mentions an oracle which declared that "God himself could not thus his destined fate." And among the fragments of Philemon collected by Le Clerc, is the following <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a>: "We are subject to kings, kings to the gods, and God to necessity." Hence it is, that, in the Iliad, we find Jove himself, the fire of gods and men, regretting that he was restrained by necessity from rescuing his favourite son from the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PATROCLUS">Patroclus</a>. Nay to such a height was this impiety carried in the earliest ages of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, that we find <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HESIOD">Hesiod</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a> teaching that the gods themselves were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENERATED">generated</a> by necessity, of night and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHAOS">chaos</a>. This power, though always represented as <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLIND">blind</a> and unintelligent, was however worshipped as a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> in her <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAND">hand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-IRON">iron</a>-nails, wedges, anchors, and melted <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, as emblems of the inflexible severity of her <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. "In the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Corinth she had a temple, in which the goddess Violence likewise resided, and into which no person was ever permitted to enter but the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> who officiated in sacris." Learned men have exercised their ingenuity in vain attempts to trace this portentous notion to its origin. Some, who wished to interpret it in a pious sense, have supposed that the gods who were subject to necessity were only those who were the ministers of the supreme numen; and that by necessity itself was meant nothing more than divine <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROVIDENCE">providence</a>. But this is not consistent with Hesiod and Homer's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a> of the gods, or with the epithets fusa necessitas, dura necessitas, by which this power was perpetually distinguished. Others, and among them Moheim, have supposed that this monstrous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FABLE">fable</a> was invented by the pagan priests, and diligently inculcated upon the minds of the people, in order to excuse the villanies of the objects of their worship. For, says he, who could be indignant at <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>'s numberless adulteries, after it was known that in all his actions he was the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> of blind necessity? In the thefts of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a>, the whoredoms of Venus, and the frequent squabbles of the other gods, there could be no moral turpitude, if they were under the influence of a superior power. Numina cum videas duris obnoxia fatis, Invicta positis exonere deos†. This account of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> is at least as plausible as any other which is usually given; but the real <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CASE">case</a> undoubtedly was, that when men "did not like to retain God in their knowledge, God gave them over to a reprobate mind to do those things which are not convenient; when their foolish heart was darkened, and professing themselves to be wise, they became fools." See PARCEL. Necessity, in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAW">law</a>, as it implies a defect of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a>, excuses from the guilt of crimes. See CRIME. Compulsion and inevitable necessity are a constraint upon the will, whereby a man is urged to do that which his judgment disapproves; and which, it is to be presumed, his will (if left to itself) would reject. As punishments are therefore only inflicted for the abuse of that free-will which God has given to man, it is highly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> and equitable that a man should be excused for those acts which are done through unavoidable force and compulsion. 1. Of this nature, in the first <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, is the obligation of civil subjection, whereby the inferior is constrained by the superior to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> contrary to what his own reason and inclination would suggest: as when a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LEGISLATOR">legislator</a> establishes iniquity by a law, and commands the subject to do an act contrary to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> or found morality. How far this excuse will be admitted in foro conscientiae, or whether the inferior in this case is not bound to obey the divine rather than the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> law, it is not our business to decide; though, among the causists, it is believed the question will hardly bear a doubt. But, however that may be, obedience to the laws in being is undoubtedly a sufficient extenuation of civil guilt before the municipal tribunal. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a> who burnt Latimer and Ridley, in the bigoted days of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, was not liable to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a> for executing so horrid an office; being justified by the commands of that magistracy which endeavoured to restore <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SUPERSTITION">Superstition</a>, under the holy auspices of its merciless sister, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PERSECUTION">Persecution</a>. As to persons in private relations, the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> case where constraint of a superior is allowed as an excuse for criminal misconduct, is with regard to the matrimonial subjection of the wife to her husband; for... for neither a son nor a servant are excused for the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> of any crime, whether <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> or otherwise, by the command or coercion of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PARENT">parent</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MASTER">master</a>; though in some <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CASES">cases</a> the command or authority of the husband, either express or implied, will privilege the wife from punishment, even for capital offences. And therefore, if a woman commit theft, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BURGLARY">burglary</a>, or other civil offences against the laws of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, by the coercion of her husband, or even in his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, which the law construes a coercion, she is not guilty of any crime; being considered as acting by compulsion, and not of her own will. Which doctrine is at least 1000 years old in this <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, being to be found among the laws of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">King</a> Ina the West-Saxon. And it appears, that, among the northern nations on the continent, this privilege extended to any woman transgressing in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONCERT">concert</a> with a man, and to any servant that committed a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> offence with a freeman: the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MALE">male</a> or freeman only was punished, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> or slave dismissed; procul dubio quod alterum libertas, alterum necessitas impellere. But (besides that, in our law, which is a stranger to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a>, no impunity is given to servants, who are as much free agents as their masters) even with regard to wives, this rule admits of an exception in crimes that are mala in se, and prohibited by the law of nature; as <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MURDER">murder</a>, and the like: not only because these are of a deeper dye, but also, since in a state of nature no one is in subjection to another, it would be unreasonable to screen an offender from the punishment due to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> crimes, by the refinements and subdivisions of civil society. In <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TREASON">treason</a> also (the highest crime which a member of society can, as such, be guilty of), no <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PLEA">plea</a> in coverture shall excuse the wife; no presumption of the husband's coercion shall extenuate her guilt: as well because of the odiousness and dangerous <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the crime itself, as because the husband, having broken through the most sacred tie of social <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a> by rebellion against the state, has no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to that obedience from a wife, which he himself as a subject has forgotten to pay. In inferior misdemeanors also, we may remark another exception, that a wife may be indicted and set in the pillory with her husband, for keeping a brothel: for this is an offence touching the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> economy or <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, in which the wife has a principal share; and is also such an offence as the law presumes to be generally conducted by the intrigues of the female <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SEX">sex</a>. And in all cases where the wife offends alone, without the company or coercion of her husband, she is responsible for her offence as much as any female. 2. Another <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of compulsion or necessity is what our law calls dures per minas; or threats and menaces, which induce a fear of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEATH">death</a> or other bodily harm, and which take away for that reason the guilt of many crimes and misdemeanors, at least before the human tribunal. But then that fear which compels a man to do an unwarrantable action ought to be just and well-grounded; such, "qui cadere posset in virum constanter, non timidum et meticuloformis," as Bracton expresses it, in the words of the civil law. Therefore, in time of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WAR">war</a> or rebellion, a man may be justified in doing many treasonable acts by compulsion of the enemy or rebels, which would admit of no excuse in the time of peace. This, however, seems only, or at least principally, to hold as to positive crimes, so created necessity, by the laws of society, and which therefore society may excuse; but not as to natural offences, so declared by the law of God, wherein human magistrates are only the executioners of divine punishment. And therefore though a man be violently assaulted, and hath no other possible means of escaping death but by killing an innocent person, this fear and force shall not acquit him of murder; for he ought rather to die himself than escape by the murder of an innocent. But in such a case he is permitted to kill the assailant; for there the law of nature, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SELF_DEFENCE">self-<a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> its primary canon, have made him his own protector. 3. There is a third species of necessity, which may be distinguished from the actual compulsion of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> force or fear, being the result of reason and reflection, which act upon and constrain a man's will, and oblige him to do an action which without such obligation would be criminal. And that is, when a man has his choice of two evils set before him, and, being under a necessity of choosing one, he chooses the least pernicious of the two. Here the will cannot be said freely to exert itself, being rather <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSIVE">passive</a> than <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a>; or, if active, it is rather in rejecting the greater evil than in choosing the less. Of this sort is that necessity, where a man by the commandment of the law is bound to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARREST">arrest</a> another for any capital offence, or to disperse a riot, and resistance is made to his authority: it is here justifiable, and even necessary, to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a>, to wound, or perhaps to kill, the offenders, rather than permit the murderer to escape, or the riot to continue. For the preservation of the peace of the kingdom, and the apprehending of notorious malefactors, are of the utmost consequence to the public; and therefore excuse the felony, which the killing would otherwise amount to. 4. There is yet another case of necessity, which has occasioned <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> speculation among the writers upon general law; viz. whether a man in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> want of food or clothing may justify stealing either, to relieve his present necessities. And this both Grotius and Puffendorf, together with many other of the foreign jurists, hold in the affirmative; maintaining by many ingenious, humane, and plausible reasons, that in such cases the community of goods, by a kind of tacit concession of society, is revived. And some even of our lawyers have held the same; though it seems to be an unwarranted doctrine, borrowed from the notions of some civilians; at least it is now antiquated, the law of England admitting no such excuse at present. And this its doctrine is agreeable not only to the sentiments of many of the wisest <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, particularly Cicero, who holds, "that si quis cuicumque in omnium rerum eß, potius quam de aliorum commodiis detrahae; but also to the Jewish law, as certified by King <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a> himself: "If a thief steal to satisfy his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> when he is hungry, he shall restore sevenfold, and shall give all the substance of his house;" which was the ordinary punishment for theft in that kingdom. And this is founded upon the highest reason: for men's properties would be under a strange insecurity, if liable to be invaded according to the wants of others; of which wants no man can possibly be an adequate judge, but the party himself who pleads them. In England especially, there would be a peculiar impropriety in admitting so dubious an excuse; for by the laws such sufficient provision is made for the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POOR">poor</a> by the power of the civil <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a>, that it is impossible that the most needy stranger should ever be reduced to the necessity of thieving to support nature. The case of a stranger is, by the way, the strongest instance put to Baron Puffendorf, and whereon he builds his principal arguments: which, however they may hold upon the continent, where the parsimonious industry of the natives orders every one to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> or starve, yet must lose all their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> and efficacy in England, where <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> is reduced to a system, and interwoven in our very <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>. Therefore our laws ought by no means to be taxed with being unmerciful, for denying this privilege to the necessitous; especially when we consider, that the king, on the representation of his ministers of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, hath a power to soften the law, and to extend mercy in cases of peculiar hardship. An advantage which is wanting in many states, particularly those which are democratical: and these have in its stead introduced and adopted, in the body of the law itself, a multitude of circumstances tending to alleviate its rigour. But the founders of our constitution thought it better to vest in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> the power of pardoning particular objects of compassion, than to countenance and establish theft by one general undistinguishing law.

NECHO

Pages 849-849
king of Egypt, began his reign 690 B.C., and was killed eight years after by Sabacon king of Ethiopia. Piamenticus his son succeeded him, and was the father, as Herodotus informs us, of Necho II., who reigned in the 616 B.C. This Necho II. is celebrated in history for attempting, though in vain, to cut a canal from the Nile to the Arabian gulf. He carried his arms as far as the Euphrates, and conquered the city of Carchemish. This prince is not only known in scripture under the name of Necho, but also in profane history. He no sooner succeeded to the crown than he raised great land armies, and fitted out vast fleets, as well upon the Mediterranean as upon the s="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RED">Red Sea: he gave battle to the Syrians near the city of Migdol; routed them, and made himself master of the city of Cadytis. The learned, however, are not agreed about this city Cadytis. Some will have it to be Cades in Arabia Petraea, others Jerusalem; and others say it is the city of Cedes, or Kedesh, in Galilee, in the tribe of Naphtali. The scriptures acquaint us with the whole expedition of Necho in all its particulars. 2 Kings xxiii. 29-30, &c. and 2 Chr. xxxv. 20, 21, &c. In the year of the world 3394, this prince having drawn out his army into the field to make war with the Assyrians or Babylonians, and to take the city of Carchemish, otherwise called Circeium, upon the Euphrates, Josiah king of Judah, who was a tributary to the king of Babylon, marched to oppose his passage. Necho, who had no designs against him, sent to tell him, What have I to do with you, king of Judah? It is not against you that I am come forth; but against another people, against whom the Lord has commanded me to make war. Leave off therefore to set yourself against me, for fear the Lord should punish you for your resistance. But Josiah would not hearken to the remonstrances of Necho, but gave him battle at Megiddo, where he received the wound of which he died. The people of Jerusalem set up Jehoahaz for king of Judah, and Necho soon passed forwards, without making any longer stay in Judea. But at his return from his expedition, which was very successful, he halted at Riblah in Syria; and sending for Jehoahaz king of the Jews, he deposed him, loaded him with chains, and sent him into Egypt. Then coming to Jerusalem, he set up Eliakim, or Jehoiakim, in his place, and exacted the payment of 100 talents of silver and one talent of gold from the country. Jeremiah (xlvii. 2.) acquaints us, that the city of Carchemish was taken from Necho by Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, in the fourth year of Jehoiakim king of Judah; so that Necho did not enjoy his conquest above four years. Josephus adds, that the king of Babylon pursuing his victory, brought under his dominion all the country which is between the Euphrates and Egypt, excepting Judea. Thus Necho was again reduced within the limits of his own country.

NECOPHORON

Pages 849-849

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>, a name used by Pliny and other authors for the Smilax aspera, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> rough bindweed.

NECROLIUM

Pages 849-849

a word used by some of the alchemical writers to express a remedy almost always capable of averting <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, and continuing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> to its utmost <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>.

NECROLOGY

Pages 849-849

necrolagium, formed of νεκρός, "dead," and λογία, "discourse <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> enumeration," a book anciently kept in churches and monasteries, wherein were registered the benefactors of the same, the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> of their deaths, and the days of their commemoration; as also the deaths of the priors, abbots, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a>, canons, &c. This was otherwise called <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CALENDAR">calendar</a> and obituary.

NECROMANCY

Pages 849-852

the art of revealing future events by a pretended <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> with the dead. This superstitious and impious imposture appears to have had its origin at a very early <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, and to have been thence propagated in every <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATION">nation</a> with the manners of which <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> has made us acquainted. The conquests of Sesostris might introduce it into <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a>; the Israelites would naturally borrow it from the people among whom they sojourned 400 years; and it would easily find its way into Phoenicia, from the vicinity of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAND">land</a> of its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATIVITY">nativity</a>. From the Egyptians and Phoenicians it was adopted, with the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> of paganism, by the Greeks; and it was imported into Rome with Grecian literature and Grecian manners. It was not however confined to the pagan nations of antiquity; it spread itself through all the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> nations of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, and took such deep root as to be <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a> retained even after those nations were averted to the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>. Of its early antiquity we have complete <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> in the writings of Moses, where it is severely condemned as an abomination to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>; and though Deut. it appears to have been even then spread into Phenicia, we might yet conclude its birth-<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to have been Egypt, because, at their exodus, the Israelites were corrupted. Necromancy seems to be one of those whor- doms which the prophet <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EZEKIEL">Ezekiel</a> represents his coun- trymen as having brought with them from Egypt, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to practise till they were carried <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>- tives into <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BABYLON">Babylon</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> from sacred we proceed to consult profane au- thors, we shall find them not only affirming Egypt to have been the birth-place of necromancy, but in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> accounting for the origin of so impious a de- lusion. From Diodorus the Sicilian we learn, that the Grecian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FABLE">fable</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHARON">Charon</a> the ferry-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAN">man</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HELL">hell</a>, of Styx, Cocytus, the Elysian Fields, Tartarus, the judge- ment of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MINOS">Minos</a>, and Radamanthus, &c. with the whole scenery of the infernal regions, were imported from Egypt into <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Egyptians, and in- <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEED">deed</a> all the people of the east, made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of caves for burying places, which were well suited to the solemn sadness of the surviving friends, and proper receptacles for those who were never more to behold the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>. In Egypt, many of those subterranean cavities being dug out of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> rock, still remain and command the admiration of travellers; and near to the pyramids in particular there are some apartments of a wonderful fabric, which though they extend in length 4400 feet, and are about 30 feet in depth, appear to have been, if not entirely dug, at least reduced to form by the chisel <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> pick-axe of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a>. From the practice of burying in such caverns sprung the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that the infernal mansions were situated somewhere near the centre of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, which by the Egyptians was believed to be not very distant from its surface. In these dreary mansions, it was very easy for such adepts as the priests of Egypt to fabri- cate <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-EREBUS">Erebus</a>, Tartarus, the Elysian Fields, and all those scenes which were displayed before the initiated (see <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MYSTERIES">Mysteries</a>), and by them described to the million of the people. As it was in those dark abodes that ne- cromancy was practised, it would be no difficult <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> for such magicians as withstood Moses to impose so far upon the credulous vulgar, as to make them believe, that in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of their avocations they actually <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAW">saw</a> the ghosts of their friends ascend out of the earth. It appears from the book of Exodus, that the Israel- itish women were, even in the wilderness, well acquaint- ed with the use of the mirror, which was therefore un- doubtedly known to the Egyptians. But a mirror of a particular form and properly illuminated at the in- stant required, might easily be made to reflect, in a ca- avern from which all other light was carefully excluded, the image of the deceased, who was called upon by the necromancer; and we can readily conceive, that with respect to the question to be propounded, a person might be concealed, prepared to give such ambiguous answers as would satisfy the inquirer, and at the same <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-SAVE">save</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> of the oracle. The terrified imagi- nations of the spectators would aid the delusion, and make a very slight resemblance <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> for the ghost or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECTRE">spectre</a> of their departed friend; or the necromancer might assign plausible reasons why a spectre, after hav- ing dwelt for some time in the infernal regions, should lose something of its resemblance to the body which it animated. Such juggling tricks, though performed by artists less accomplished than Jannes and Jambres, have gained credit among people much more en- lightened than the Egyptians can possibly have been when the science of necromancy was invented by their priests. That the Israelites, notwithstanding the prohibition of their <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LEGISLATOR">legislator</a>, continued to practise the rites of necromancy, is apparent from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAUL">Saul</a>'s transaction with the witch of Endor (see <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAGIC">Magic</a>). From the same transaction, it is likewise apparent that the witches of Israel, and therefore in all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> the necromancers of Egypt, pretended to evocate the ghosts of the dead by a demon or familiar spirit, which they had at their com- mand to employ upon every emergency. This demon was called ob; and therefore Saul defies his servants, to find him a woman who was mistress of an ob (A). It is probable that those wretched impostors had in their pay some persons who occasionally acted the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> of the demon, and when the execution of the plot required their agency, emitted, by means of a cavity dug for that purpose, a low hollow <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> from below the ground. Hence we find Isaiah, in his de- nunciations against Ariel*, saying, "Thou shalt be brought <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, and shalt speak out of the ground; and thy speech shall be low out of the dust, and thy voice shall be as one that hath a familiar spirit (an ob) out of the ground, and thy speech shall whisper out of the dust." But though the Egyptian priests were undoubtedly the inventors of the whole mystery of necromancy, and though it was from them imported into Greece by the Selli or priests of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DODONA">Dodona</a>, it does not ap- <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEAR">pear</a> that the Grecian necromancers pretended to be masters of obs or familiar spirits. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MOPSUS">Mopsus</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORPHEUS">Orpheus</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LINUS">Linus</a>, Eumolpus, &c. who either travelled into E- gypt in quest of knowledge, or were actually natives of that country, instructed the early Greeks in this <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OCCULT">occult</a> science; but whatever might be the practice of these apostles themselves, their disciples professed to do (A) The original, or radical, signification of this word occurs in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JOB">Job</a> xxxii. ver. 19; where Elihu compares his belly to new bottles, which he calls oboth, the plural of ob. But as bottles were then made of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, new bottles filled with wine and ready to burst, as Elihu describes them, would of course be of a form nearly globular. Hence it may be inferred that the original import of ob was round or globular; but b and p being labials, are often changed into each other; and therefore from the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> ob is derived the Greek οβούς, οβούς, οβός, and the Latin opis, a name under which the earth was worshipped. Opis was a name of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a> or the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MOON">moon</a>; the father of one of the Dianas was likewise opis; but this opis was undoubtedly the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>. Now the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between opis and opis is nothing; hence we are led to believe that as they are all derived from ob, this word was employed by the early idolaters of Egypt to denote the first and greatest of Pagan gods, the sun. If so, those wretches who pretended to be mistresses of obi, were exactly the same kind of impostors with the Pythoesses of the Greeks. all the feats of magic by performing certain rites, by offering certain sacrifices, by muttering a certain form of words, by charms, spells, and exorcisms. By these they pretended to evoke the dead as certainly as the Egyptians and Jews did by their familiar spirits. By a small display of critical learning this might be easily proved from the popular story of Orpheus and Euridice, which certainly was founded on one of these necromantic deceptions exhibited in a cave near Dodona, where the priests had a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HADES">hades</a> or infernal mansion, in humble <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of those with which the first of them were well acquainted in Egypt. It is indeed evident, without the aid of criticism: no man of any letters is ignorant, that whatever superstitions of this kind prevailed among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> were borrowed from the Greeks. But we all know that <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a> makes one of his shepherds, by means of certain herbs, poisons, and senecio's charms, raise up ghosts from the bottoms of their graves; and Lucan has fabricated a story of this kind, which may be considered as an exact <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to the witch of Endor. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">Just</a> before the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PHARSALIA">Pharsalia</a> he makes young Pompey travel by night to a Thessalian sorceress, and anxiously inquire of her the issue of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WAR">war</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> necromancer, by a tedious <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of charms and incantations, conjures up the ghost of a soldier who had been lately slain. The phantom, after a long preamble, denounces a prediction much of the same kind with that which the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">king</a> of Israel received from Samuel at Endor; and though we have elsewhere shown, that nothing but the spirit of God could have foreseen the inevitable destruction of Saul, his sons, and his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> (see Magic), it was very easy for any man of tolerable sagacity to foresee the defeat of Pompey's raw and undisciplined troops by the hardy veterans of the victorious Caesar. It would be endless to enumerate all the fallacious evocations of ghosts, and the ambiguous responses returned by those pretended spirits, of which we have accounts from the poets and historians of the celebrated nations of antiquity. We shall therefore proceed to mention a few which occur in the fabulous history of more modern nations, and then leave the subject to the meditation of our readers. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MALLET">Mallet</a>'s northern antiquities, we have the following account of a necromantic exploit, between which, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> of the ancient heroes into hell, it is impossible not to remark a striking similitude. "Odin the sovereign of man arises. He saddles his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> Sleipner; he mounts, and is conveyed to the subterranean abode of Hela. The dog which guards the gates of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEATH">death</a> meets him. His breath and his jaws are stained with blood. He opens his voracious mouth to bite, and barks a long time at the father of magic. Odin pursues his way; and the infernal cavern resounds and trembles under his horse's hoofs. At length he reaches the deep abode of death, and stops near the eastern gate, where stands the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> of the prophetess. He flings with a voice adapted to call up the dead; he looks towards the world; he engraves Runic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> on her tomb; he utters mysterious words; and he demands an answer, until the prophetess is constrained to arise and thus utter the words of the dead.—'Who is this unknown that <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DARES">dares</a> to disturb my repose, and drag me from the Necromantian <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a>, in which I have been dead so long, all covered with snow, and moistened with the rains?' &c. The Gallic <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DRUIDS">druids</a> pretended to be masters of the same secret. This is evident from the name of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DIVINATION">divination</a>, not uncommon among the Scotch Highlanders so lately as in the beginning of the present century. By a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> excellently versed in the antiquities of that people, and a steady friend to the writer of this article, we have been informed, that not many years ago some of the Highlanders relied implicitly upon certain oracular responses, called in their <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> taghairm. This word seems to be compounded of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TA">ta</a>, which in some parts of the Highlands is still used to denote a spirit or ghost, and ghaire, which signifies calling upon or invoking. Taghairm, therefore, in its original import, is necromancy in the most proper <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of that word. There were different kinds of taghairm, of which one was very lately practised in Sky. The diviner covered himself with a cow's hide, and repaired at night to some deep-founding cave, whither the person who consulted him followed soon after without any attendants. At the mouth of the cave he proposed aloud the questions of which he wanted solutions; and the man within pronounced the responses in a tone of voice similar to that with which the ois, or pretended demons of antiquity, gave from beneath the ground their oracular answers. That in the latter days of taghairm, the Gallic diviners pretended to evoke ghosts, and from them to extort solutions of difficulty; proposed, we have no positive evidence; but that such was the original pretence, there can be little doubt, when we reflect either upon the place where this species of divination was practised, or upon the import of the word by which it was denominated. As we have been led to mention taghairm, we shall beg leave to make a few observations on another species of it, called taghairm an uighe, or "taghairm by <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WATER">water</a>." This too was last practised in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> of Sky, by a man of the name of McCuidean, whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> had long been famous for the art. He lived near a beautiful cascade on a small river; and when consulted on any matter of consequence, he covered his whole body with a cow's hide, that necessary implement of Highland divination, and placed himself between the water of the cascade and the rock over which it flowed. Then another man with a heavy pole gave repeated strokes to the water, and the diviner behind it crying out now and then in Gaelic, "Is this a flock of arm?" This operation was continued till McCuidean was perceived to be frantic or furious, when he was considered as in a condition to answer the most important questions. He was frequently consulted about futurity; and though he could not, in the proper sense of the word, be called a necromancer, his responses were listened to as proceeding from something more than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUMAN">human</a>. A degree of frenzy, either real or affected, seems to have accompanied the predictions of certain kinds of diviners in all ages; and we cannot help remarking the similarity between the madness of McCuidean and that of the Sybil in the fifth book of the Æneid; though we cannot cannot suppose the one to have been borrowed from the other. At, Phœbi nondum patient, immanis in antro Baccatur vaes, magnum fit petiore polvit Encyclis Deum: tanto magis ille fatigat Os rabidum, fera corda domans, fingitque premendo. Struggling in vain, impatient of her load, And lab'<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a> underneath the pond'rous god; The more she strove to shake him from her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>, With more and far superior force he press'd. Dryden. That all these pretences, whether ancient or modern, To the power of divination by means of familiar spirits, Or by the art of necromancy, were groundless As well as impious, it would be affronting the understandings of our readers to offer any <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROOF">proof</a>. Under the article MAGIC we have said enough on the subject, and perhaps more than enough, to those who know that demons, if they have any existence, and the departed spirits of good and bad men, are all under the control of Him who governs the intellectual as well as material world by fixed and equal laws.—These details of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>, however, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a> not be useless, if, by showing how <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POOR">poor</a> and wretched a creature man becomes when left to his own inventions, they shall make any one grateful for the benefits of good <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, and the blessings of revealed <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>.

NECROPOLIS

Pages 852-852

a suburb of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>. It signifies "the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CITY">City</a> of the Dead;" wherein there were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>, gardens, and superb mausoleums. Here Cleopatra is said to have applied the apic to her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>, to prevent being led in triumph by Augustus, who endeavoured to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-SAVE">save</a> her.

NECROSIS

Pages 852-852

νεκρότης, in medicine, a complete mortification of any <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a>; called also foderatio and sphacelus.

NECTANEBUS

Pages 852-852
or Nectanabis, a king of Egypt, who defended his country against the Persians. His grandson of the same name made an alliance with Agesilaus king of Sparta, and with his assistance he quelled a rebellion of his subjects. Some time after he was joined by the Sidonian, Phoenicians, and inhabitants of Cyprus, who had revolted from the king of Persia. This powerful confederacy was soon attacked by Darius the king of Persia, who marched at the head of his troops. Nectanebus, to defend his frontiers against so dangerous an enemy, levied 20,000 mercenary soldiers in Greece, the same number in Libya, and 60,000 were furnished in Egypt. This numerous body was not equal to the Persian forces, and Nectanebus, defeated in a battle, gave up all hopes of resistance, and fled into Ethiopia, where he found a safe asylum. His kingdom of Egypt became from that time tributary to the king of Persia.

NECTAR

Pages 852-852

among <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> poets, the drink of the fabulous deities of the heathens; in contradistinction from their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> food, which was called ambrosia.

NECTARINE

Pages 852-852

a fruit differing in nothing from the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMON">common</a> peach, of which it is a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, than in having a smoother rind and a firmer pulp. See Persica.

NECTARIUM

Pages 852-853

from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NECTAR">nectar</a>, the fabled "drink of the gods;" defined by Linnaeus to be a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> of the corolla, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> appendage to the petals, appropriated for containing the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of vegetable <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-SALT">salt</a> under Nectarium, a fluid form, that oozes from the plant, and is the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> food of bees and other insects. Notwithstanding this <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a>, which seems to consider the nectarium as necessary a part of the corolla as the petals; it is certain that all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> are not provided with this appendage, neither indeed is it essential to fructification. There is, besides, a manifest impropriety in terming the nectarium a part of the corolla. Linnaeus, Milne's Bot. Dict., with equal propriety, have termed it a part or appendage of the stamens, calyx, or pointal, as the appearance in question is confined to no particular part of the flower, but is as various in point of situation as of form. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> is, the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TERM">term</a> nectarium is exceedingly vague; and, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> any determinate meaning can be affixed to it, is expressive of all the singularities which are observed in the different parts of flowers. The tube, or lower part of flowers with one petal, Linnaeus considers as a true nectarium, because it is generally found to contain the sweet liquor formerly mentioned. This liquor Pontedura compares to that called amnios in pregnant animals, which enters the fertile or impregnated seeds: but that this is not at least its sole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, is evident from this circumstance, that the honey or liquor in question is to be found in flowers where there are either no seeds, or those which, from the want of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MALE">male</a> organs, cannot be impregnated. Thus the male flowers of nettle and willow, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> flowers of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-side laurel and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> bryony, the male and female flowers of clutia, higgleria, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BUTCHER">butcher</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BROOM">broom</a>, all abound with the honey or nectar alluded to. Dr Vaillant was of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that the nectarium was an essential part of the corolla; for which reason he distinguished the singular appearances in fennel-flower and columbine by the name of petals: the coloured leaves which are now termed the petals he designates the flower cup. That the nectarium, however, is frequently distinct from the petals, is evident both from the well-known examples <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> mentioned, as likewise from the flowers of monkshood, hellebore, fopyrum, fennel-flower of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a>, barrowwort, gras of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PARNASSUS">Parnassus</a>, chocolate-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NUT">nut</a>, cherleria, and fauvagellia. These general observations being premised, we proceed to take a nearer and more particular view of the principal diversities, both in form and situation, of this striking appendage to the flower. 1. In many flowers the nectarium is shaped like a spur or <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HORN">horn</a>; and that either in flowers of one petal, as valerian, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WATER">water</a>-milfoil (urticularia), <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a>-wort, and calves-foot; or in such as have more than one, as lark-spur, violet, fumitory, balsam, and orchis. 2. In the following <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, the nectarium is properly a part of the corolla, as lying within the substance of the petals: ranunculus, lily, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-IRIS">iris</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>-imperial, water-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a>, moule-tail, ananas or pine-apple, dog's tooth violet, piperidge bush, valliflora, hermannia, uvularia, and swertia. 3. The nectarium is frequently placed in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> or row within the petals, though entirely unconnected with their fulness. In this situation it often resembles a cup, as in narcissus. A nectarium of this kind is said by Linnaeus to crown the corolla. The following are examples: daffodil, sea-daffodil, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAMPION">campion</a>, viscous cam- pion, Nectarium pion, swallow-wort, stapelia, cynanchum, nepenthes, cherleria, balsam-tree, African spira, witch-hazel, olax, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> flower. 4. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CRESTS">crests</a>, buckler, mustard, Barbadoes cherry, and monotropa, the nectarium is situated upon or makes part of the calyx. 5. The nectarium in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASTARD">bastard</a> flower-<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FENCE">fence</a> is seated upon the antherae or tops of the flamina; whence the name glandularia, or glandular anthera, which has been given to this genus of plants. In the following <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIST">list</a> it is placed upon the filaments; bean-caper, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>, fraxinella, marvell of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PERU">Peru</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELL">bell</a>-flower, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>-wort, rocella, and commelina. 6. In hyacinth, flowering-rush, stock <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>-flower, and rocket, the nectarium is placed upon the seed-bud. 7. In honey-flower, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a>, buck-wheat, collinsonia, lathraea, navel-wort, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a>, clutia, kiggelaria, sea-side laurel, and African spira, it is attached to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMON">common</a> receptacle. Lastly, in ginger, nettle, dyer's weed, heart-seed, costus, turmeric, grewia, bastard-orange, vanello, skrew-tree, and willow, the nectarium is of a very singular <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a>, and cannot properly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> under any of the foregoing heads. In discriminating the genera, the nectarium often furnishes an essential character. Plants which have the nectarium distinct from the petals, that is, not lodged within their substance, are affirmed by Linnæus to be generally poisonous. The following are adduced as examples: monk's hood, helioboe, columbine, fennel-flower, gras of Parsafus, harren-wort, oleander, marvell of Peru, bean caper, succulent swallow-wort, fraxinella, and honey flower.

NECUIA

Pages 853-853

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>, a name given by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Greeks to a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of mullein. The Greeks and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> both used the stalks of a peculiar kind of mullein, called thryallis by Nicander. For the making of wicks of lamps we have a kind of mullein called lychnites, and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CANDLE">candle</a>-wick mullein, from the λυχνίτης of Dioscorides; but it is not certain that ours is the same plant. The <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> used the stalks of many different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> for the wicks of their candles and lamps. The rush, stripped of its bark, was as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> with them as with us for this purpose; and they also used the nettle, this mullein, and many other plants, whose stalks were composed of tough filaments, for the same purpose; <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> them out like <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, and when dry <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DIPPING">dipping</a> them in melted resin, and other such inflammable substances. When thus prepared, they are readily inflammable, like our <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FLAMBEAU">flambeau</a>; and this mullein, having stalks more <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, and more firm than all the others, was used to make those lights with which they set fire to the funeral pile, for consuming the ashes of their dead friends.

NECYDALIS

Pages 853-853

in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ZOOLOGY">zoology</a>, a genus of insects belonging to the order of coleoptera. The feelers are setaceous; the elytra are shorter and narrower than the wings; the tail is simple. There are 11 <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, chiefly distinguished by the size and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of their elytra. Barbut says, "Its head is <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, eyes are <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and prominent, jaws are of a dark <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>. The antennæ placed on the top of the head between the eyes have their first articulation <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a> and raised upright, the rest bent and turned aside. The antennæ vary as to length and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. In individuals whose thorax is <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, they are brown, and equal only to two-thirds of the body in length. On the contrary, in those whose thorax is black, they are likewise black, and somewhat longer than the body. The thorax is margined; in some it is yellow and longer; in others it is black, shorter, and edged only with a little yellow. The elytra are blackish, something clearer in the middle, and terminating in a lemon coloured spot. The wings are rather black, something longer than the body, exceed the clytra by one-third, and are crossed one over the other. In those that have their thorax yellow, the legs and under <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> of the belly are so likewise. In individuals with a black thorax, the legs are black as well as the belly, which has only a little yellow on the sides. I suspect the latter to be the males. The larva is as yet unknown."

NEDHAM

Pages 853-855

an English satirical writer, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BURFORD">Burford</a> Oxon, about the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of August 1620. His father died in 1621; but the following year his mother was again married to one Christopher Glynn, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-VICAR">vicar</a> and schoolmaster of Burford; who perceiving his son-in-<a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAW">law</a>'s pregnancy of parts and genius, took him under his own tuition, and at the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 14 sent him to All Souls <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a>, Oxon. Here he was made one of the choristers, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> till 1637, when, having taken the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of A.B., which made it inconvenient to continue in that office, he went to St <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HALL">Hall</a> till he became an usher in Merchant Taylor's school, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. About the beginning of the civil wars, he became clerk to an attorney at Gray's Inn, where, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> a good <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COURT">court</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, he obtained a decent subsistence. Not <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a> after this, he began a weekly <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, under the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Mercurius <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BRITANNICUS">Britannicus</a>, on the side of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>; it commenced about the middle of August 1643, coming out on Mondays, in one sheet, and continued till the end of 1646. It procured him popularity, and being an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAN">man</a> he was distinguished by the title of Capt. Nedham of Gray's Inn. Of these mercuries (for there were a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of them published on both sides of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> question which then divided the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATION">nation</a>), it is well observed by Johnson, that they taught many to talk whom they could not teach to judge. Nedham's was, indeed, addressed as much to the passions as the reason; and, by telling every man that he was equal to his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">king</a>, he flattered vulgar <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a>, that his licentious opinions were received as the dictates of an oracle. About this <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> he studied physic, and in 1645 began to practise; by which, and his <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> writings, he supported a genteel <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>. But, for some scorn and affront put upon him, he suddenly left his party, and obtaining the favour of a royalist, was introduced into the king's presence at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAMPTON">Hampton</a>-court in 1647, and asking <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a> upon his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNEES">knees</a> readily obtained it; so that being admitted to the king's favour, he wrote soon after another paper, entitled Mercurius Pragmaticus; which being equally witty with the former, as satirical against the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRESBYTERIANS">Presbyterians</a>, and full of loyalty, made him known and admired by the wits of that side. However, being narrowly sought after, he left London, and for a time lay concealed at the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Dr <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> Heylin, at Mintler-Lovell, near Burford, till at length being discovered, he was imprisoned in Newgate, and in danger of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. Lenthall, the speaker of the House of Commons, who knew him and his relations, relations well, and Bradshaw, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>-court of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, treated him favourably, and not only got his pardon, but with <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> of rewards and places persuaded him to change his side once more for the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-INDEPENDENTS">independents</a>, who then were the uppermost party. In this temper he published a third weekly paper, called *Mercurius Politicus*, which came out every Wednesday, in two sheets 4to, commencing with the 9th of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1649, and ending with the 6th of June 1650, which being Thursday, he began again with number 1 from Thursday June 6, to Thursday June 13, 1650, beginning, "Why should not the commonwealth have 'a fool, as well as the king had, &c.'" This paper, which contained many discourses against <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a>, and in behalf of a free state, especially those that were published before Cromwell was made protector, was carried on without any interruption till about the middle of April 1660, when, as several times before, it was prohibited by an order of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of state. Upon the return of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II, our author lay hid, till, by virtue of some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> well placed, he obtained his pardon under the great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEAL">seal</a>; after which he exercised the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> of physic among the Dissenters, which brought him in a considerable benefit till his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, which happened suddenly in 1678. Wood, who knew him, tells us that he was a person endowed with quick <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> parts, was a good humanist, poet, and boon driller; and, had he been constant to his calculating principles, would have been beloved and admired by all; but being mercenary, and preferring his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a>, friendship, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LOVE">love</a> to his <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, was much hated by the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> party to the last. In short, there was no depending on this scurrilous ill-natured author. He followed whenever interest <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> led, and remains a notorious instance of the danger of brilliant parts, of which he certainly was possessed, without judgment or integrity to control them. Wood, who in his Athen. Oxon. quoted above, gives a very copious account of him, says: "At length this most factious, mutable, and railing author, Mr. Needham, died suddenly, in the house of one Kidder, in D'Eurcux-court near Temple-<a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAR">bar</a>, London, in 1678, and was buried near the entrance of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCEL">chancel</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of St Clement Danes." **NEEDHAM (John Tuberville)**, was born at London the 16th of September in the year 1713. His parents were descended from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and noble families. His father, who had once possessed a considerable patrimony at Hilton, in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Monmouth, was of the younger and Catholic branch of the Needham family; the head of the elder and Protestant branch was <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LORD">lord</a> Kilmorey, created viscount in the year 1625. The father of Mr. Needham died young, and left but a small fortune to his four children. His eldest son, who is the subject of this article, prosecuted his studies under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECULAR">secular</a> clergy of the English college of Douai, where he took orders, taught <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a> for several years, gave eminent proofs of sagacity and genius, and surpassed all the other professors of that seminary in the knowledge of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-EXPERIMENTAL_PHILOSOPHY">experimental <a class="</a>xref" href="vol14.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>. In 1740, he was engaged by his superiors in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the English mission, and was entrusted with the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the school erected at Twyford, near <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WINCHESTER">Winchester</a>, for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> of the Roman Catholic youth. In 1744, he was appointed professor of philosophy in the English college at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LISBON">Lisbon</a>, where, on account of his bad <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, he remained only 15 months. After his return, he passed several years at London and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, which were principally employed in microscopical observations, and in other branches of experimental philosophy. The results of these observations and experiments were published in the Philosophical Transactions of the Royal <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> of London in 1749, and in a volume in 1750 at Paris in 1750; and an account of them was also given by M. de Buffon, in the first volumes of his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY">Natural <a clas</a>s="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>. There was an intimate connection between this illustrious French naturalist and Mr. Needham; they made their experiments and observations together; though the results and systems which they deduced from the same objects and operations were totally different. Mr. Needham was admitted to a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the Royal Society of London in the year 1747, and in the Antiquarian Society some time after. From the year 1751 to 1767 he was chiefly employed in finishing the education of several English and Irish noblemen, by attending them as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a> in their travels through France, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and other countries. He then retired from this wandering life to the English seminary at Paris, and in 1768 was chosen by the Royal Academy of Sciences in that <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CITY">city</a> a corresponding member. When the regency of the Austrian <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, in order to the revival of philosophy and literature in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, formed the project of an Imperial academy, which was preceded by the erection of a small literary society to prepare the way for its execution, Mr. Needham was invited to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BRUSSELS">Brussels</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> Cobenzel and the president Neny, and was appointed successively <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DIRECTOR">director</a> of both these foundations. He held this place, together with some <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> preferments in the Low Countries, until his death, which happened the 30th of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1781. "His piety, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPERANCE">temperance</a>, and purity of manners (we follow the expressions of the Abbé Mann) were eminent: his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to the doctrines and duties of Christianity was inviolable. His zealous opposition to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> infidels was indefatigable and even passionate. His probity was untainted. He was incapable of every <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of duplicity; his beneficence was universal, and his unfailing candour rendered him often a dupe to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PERJURY">perjury</a>." These and other good qualities the panegyrists attributes to his deceased friend; and the learned authors of the Monthly Review, to whom Mr. Needham was known, admit the judgements of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PANEGYRIC">panegyric</a>. He was undoubtedly (say they) both an honest man and a worthy citizen; but though his death be a real loss to the literary world, yet he died pleasantly for himself; for had he lived to see <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> the II, and the Great making to free with the paint, patches, and trinkets of the mother church, confiscating her lands, abolishing her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a>, suppressing her holidays, introducing <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> into her worship, erecting political conductors to disperse the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a> of the Vatican, and achieving many other things in this style of improvement, it would have vexed full before his feeling heart. For this honest man was narrow even to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a> and bigotry in his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> system; and we never knew a man in whom there was such an unaccountable Needham, unaccountable mixture of implicit <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> and philosophical curiosity as in Mr Needham. He was a keen and judicious observer of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, had a peculiar dexterity in confirming his observations by experiments, and he was always occupied (sometimes indeed with too much fancy and precipitation) in generalizing facts, and reducing them to his system. "His <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PEN">pen</a> (says Abbé Mann) was neither remarkable for fecundity nor method; his writings are rather the great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> of a subject expressed with energy, and thrown upon paper in a hurry, than finished treatises." His works are well known both in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> and in France.

NEEDHAM

Pages 855-855

in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SUFFOLK">Suffolk</a>, 73 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, stands on the Orwell, 9 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-IPSWICH">Ipswich</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ROAD">road</a> to Huntingdonshire. Its market is on Wednesday, and fair in October 28.

NEEDLE

Pages 855-856

a very <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMON">common</a> little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> utensil made of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-STEEL">steel</a>, pointed at one end, and pierced at the other, used in sewing, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-EMBROIDERY">embroidery</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TAPESTRY">tapestry</a>, &c. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NEEDLES">Needles</a> make a very considerable article in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, though there is scarce any commodity cheaper, the consumption of them being almost incredible.—The sizes are from no. 1, the largest, to no. 25, the smallest. In the manufacture of needles, German and Hungarian steel are of most repute. In the making of them, the first thing is to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> the steel through a coal fire, and under a hammer, to bring it out of its <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> into a cylindrical one. This done, it is drawn through a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> hole of a wire-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, and returned into the fire, and drawn through a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SECOND">second</a> hole of the iron smaller than the first; and thus successively from hole to hole, till it has acquired the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of fineness required for that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of needles; observing every <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> it is to be drawn, that it be greased over with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARD">lard</a>, to render it more manageable. The steel thus reduced to a fine wire, is cut in pieces of the length of the needles intended. These pieces are flattened at one end on the anvil, in order to form the head and eye: they are then put into the fire, to soften them farther; and thence taken out and pierced at each <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> of the flat <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> on the anvil, by force of a puncheon of well-tempered steel, and laid on a leaden <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLOCK">block</a> to bring out, with another puncheon, the little piece of steel remaining in the eye. The corners are then filed off the square of the heads, and a little cavity filed on each side of the flat of the head; this done, the point is formed with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FILE">file</a>, and the whole filed over: they are then laid to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RED">red</a> hot on a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a> narrow iron, crooked at one end, in a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHARCOAL">charcoal</a> fire; and when taken out thence, are thrown into a bath of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLD">cold</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WATER">water</a> to harden. On this operation a good <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> depends; too much heat burns them, and too little leaves them soft; the medium is learned by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>. When they are thus hardened, they are laid in an iron shovel on a fire more or less brisk in proportion to the thickness of the needles; taking care to move them from time to time. This serves to temper them, and take off their brittleness; <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> care here too must be taken of the degree of heat: They are then straightened one after another with the hammer, the coldness of the water used in hardening them having twisted the greatest part of them. The next <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> is the polishing them. To do this, they take 12,000 or 15,000 needles, and range them in little heaps against each other on a piece of new buckram sprinkled with <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-EMERY">emery</a>-dust. The needles thus disposed, emery-dust is thrown over them, which is again sprinkled with <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OIL">oil</a> of olives; at last the whole is made up into a roll, well bound at both ends.
