This roll is then laid on a polishing <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, and over it a thick plank loaded with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, which two men <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> backwards and forwards a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> and a half, or two days, successively; by which means the roll thus continually agitated by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the plank over it, the needles withinside being rubbed against each other with oil and emery, are infinitely polished. After polishing, they are taken out, and the filth washed off them with hot water and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOAP">soap</a>: they are then wiped in hot bran, a little moistened, placed with the needles in a round box, suspended in the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> by a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CORD">cord</a>, which is kept stirring till the bran and needles be dry. The needles thus wiped in two or three different brans, are taken out and put in wooden vessels, to have the good separated from those whose <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POINTS">points</a> or eyes have been broken either in polishing or wiping; the points are then all turned the same way, and smoothed with an emery <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-STONE">stone</a> turned with a wheel. This operation finishes them, and there remains nothing but to make them into packets of 250 each. Needles were first made in England by a native of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a> in 1545; but the art was lost at his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEATH">death</a>: it was, however, recovered by Christopher Greening in 1560, who was settled with his three children, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, John, and Thomas, by Mr Damar, ancestor of the present <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MILTON">Milton</a>, at Long Crendon in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BUCKS">Bucks</a>, where the manufactory has been carried on from that time to this present day. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIPPING_NEEDLE"><a class="xref</a>" href="vol6.html#article-DIPPING">Dipping</a>-Needle, or Inclinatory Needle, a magnetic needle, so hung, as that, instead of playing horizontally, and pointing out <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NORTH">north</a> and south, one end dips, or inclines to the horizon, and the other points to a certain degree of elevation above it. The dipping-needle was invented in the year 1575 by one Robert Norman a compass-maker at Wapping. The occasion of the discovery, according to his own account, was, that it being his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> to finish and hang the needles of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPASSES">compasses</a> before he touched them, he always found, that immediately after the touch, the north-point would <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BEND">bend</a> or incline downward, under the horizon; insomuch that, to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a> the needle again, he was always forced to put a piece of wax on the south end as a counterpoise. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSTANCY">constancy</a> of this effect led him at length to observe the precise <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of the dip, or to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> which the needle would make with the horizon; and this at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONDON">London</a> he found to be 71° 50′. In 1723 Mr Graham made a great many observations on the dipping-needle, and found the angle to be between 71° and 75° degrees. Mr Nairne, in 1722, found it to be somewhat above 72°. It is not certain whether the dip varies, as well as the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>, in the same <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. The trifling <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between Mr Norman and Mr Nairne would <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> us to imagine that the dip was unalterable; but Mr Graham, who was a very accurate observer, makes the difference more considerable. It is certain, however, from a great <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of experiments and observations, that the dip is variable in different latitudes, and that it increases in going northwards. It appears from a table of observations made with the marine dipping-needle in a voyage... voyage towards the north pole in 1733, that in lat. 60° 18', the dip was 75°; and in lat. 70° 45', it was 77° 52'; in lat. 80° 12', it was 81° 52'; and in lat. 80° 27', it was 82° 2½'. Several authors have endeavoured to apply this discovery of the dip to the finding of the latitude; and Mr Bond attempted to apply it to the finding of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a> also; but for want of observations and experiments he could not make any progress. The affair was farther prosecuted by Mr Whiston, who published a treatise on the longitude, and for some time imagined it was possible to find it exactly by means of the dip of the needle; yet he at last despaired of it, for the following reasons: 1. The weakness of the magnetic power. 2. The concussion of the ship, which he found it exceeding difficult to avoid so much as was necessary for the accuracy of the experiments. 3. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> objection was an irregularity in the motions of all magnetic needles, both horizontal and dipping, by which they, within the compass of about a degree, vary uncertainly backward and forward; even sometimes, in a few hours time, without any evident cause. For a particular account of these variations both of the horizontal and dipping needle, see the article <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VARIATION">VARIATION</a>. Mr Nairne made a dipping-needle in 1772 for the board of longitude, which was used in the voyage towards the north-pole. This is represented Plate CCCXLV, fig. 2. The needle <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AA">AA</a> is 12 inches long, and its axis, the ends BB of which are made of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> alloyed with <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, rests on friction-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a> CCCC, of four inches diameter, each end on two friction-wheels; which wheels are balanced with great care. The ends of the axes of the friction-wheels are likewise of gold alloyed with copper, and moved in small holes made in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELL">bell</a>-metal; and opposite to the ends of the axes of the needle and the friction-wheels, are flat agates, set in at DDD, finely polished. The magnetic needle vibrates within a circle of bell-metal, EEE, divided into degrees and half degrees; and a line, passing through the middle of the needle to the ends, points to the divisions. The needle of this instrument was balanced before it was made magnetic; but by means of a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>, the ends of which are FFFFF (contrived by the reverend Mr Mitchell) fixed on the axis of the needle, on the arms of which are cut very fine screws to receive small buttons, that may be screwed nearer or farther from the axis, the needle may be adjusted both ways to a great variety, after being made magnetic, by reversing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a>, and changing the sides of the needle. GG are two levels, by which the line of 0 degrees of the instrument is set horizontal, by means of the four adjusting screws LLLL; H is the perpendicular axis, by which the instrument may be turned, that the divided <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FACE">face</a> of the circle may <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FRONT">front</a> the east or west; to this axis is fixed an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDEX">index</a> I, which points to an opposite line on the horizontal plate K when the instrument is turned half round; MMMM are screws which hold the glass cover to keep the needle from being disturbed by the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>. When this needle is constructed for <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, it is suspended by an universal <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> on a triangular stand, and adjusted vertically by a plumb-line and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BUTTON">button</a> above the divided circle, and the dovetail work at the upper go; and the divisions on the circle are adjusted so as to be perpendicular to the horizon by the same plumb-line, and an adjoining screw; and when it is adjusted, a pointer annexed to a screw, which serves to move the divided circle, is fixed at the lowest go. Whenever the instrument is used to find the dip, it must be so placed that the needle may vibrate exactly in the magnetic meridian.

NEGOMBO

Pages 860-860

a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port town of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, on the west <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Ceylon. It has a fort built by the Portuguese, which was taken from them by the Dutch in 1640. E. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 80° 25'. N. Lat. 17° 0'.

NEGRO

Pages 860-864

Homo peli nigra, a name given to a variety of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, who are entirely <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, and are found in the Torrid zone, especially in that <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a> which lies within the tropics. In the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a> we meet with many various shades; but they likewise differ far from other men in all the features of their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FACE">face</a>. Round <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEEKS">cheeks</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> cheek-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BONES">bones</a>, a forehead somewhat elevated, a short, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, flat nose, thick lips, small ears, ugliness, and irregularity of shape, characterize their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> appearance. The negro women have the loins greatly depressed, and very <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> buttocks, which gives the back the shape of a saddle. Vices the most notorious seem to be the portion of this unhappy <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-RACE">race</a>: idleness, treachery, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a>, cruelty, impudence, stealing, lying, profanity, debauchery, nastiness, and intemperance, are said to have extinguished the principles of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAW">law</a>, and to have silenced the reproofs of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a>. They are strangers to every sentiment of compassion, and are an awful example of the corruption of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAN">man</a> when left to himself. The origin of the negroes, and the cause of their remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> from the rest of the human species, has much perplexed the naturalists. Mr Boyle has observed, that it cannot be produced by the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>: for though the heat of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> may darken the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of the skin, yet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> does not show that it is sufficient to produce a new blackness like that of the negroes. In Africa itself, many nations of Ethiopia are not black; nor were there any blacks originally in the West Indies. In many parts of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, under the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> with the African region inhabited by the blacks, the people are but tawny. He adds, that there are negroes in Africa beyond the southern tropic; and that a river sometimes parts nations, one of which is black, and the other only tawny. Dr Barriere alleges, that the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-GALL">gall</a> of Negroes is black, and being mixed with their blood is deposited between the skin and scarfskin. However, Dr Mitchel of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VIRGINIA">Virginia</a>, in the Philosophical Transactions no 476, has endeavoured by many learned arguments to prove, that the influence of the sun in hot countries, and the manner of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of their inhabitants, are the remote causes of the colour of the Negroes, Indians, &c. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Kames, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and such philosophers as he, whose genius and imagination are too lively to submit to a dry and painful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a> of facts, have contended, that no physical cause is sufficient to change the colour, and what we call the regular features of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WHITE">white</a> men, to the dark hue and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEFORMITY">deformity</a> of the woolly-headed negro. Their arguments have been examined with much acuteness and ingenuity by Dr Stanhope Smith of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEW_JERSEY">New <a cla</a>ss="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JERSEY">Jersey</a>, Dr Hunter, and professor Zimmerman, who have made it in a high <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> probable, that the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of the sun is the original and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> cause of the black colour, as well as distorted features, of the negro. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">AMERICA</a>, no 48—51. and COMPLEXION. True negroes are found in no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of the globe where the heat of the climate is not very <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a>. They exist nowhere but in the Torrid zone, and only in three regions situated in that zone, to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WIT">wit</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SENEGAL">Senegal</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a>, and on the western shores of Africa, in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUBIA">Nubia</a>, and the Papous <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAND">land</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> what is called New Guinea. In all these regions the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a> is scorching, and the heat excessive. The inhabitants of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NORTH">north</a> are whitest; and as we advance southwards towards the line, and those countries on which the sun's rays <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> more perpendicularly, the complexion gradually assumes a darker <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a>. And the same men, whose colour has been rendered black by the powerful action of the sun, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they remove to the north, gradually become whiter (at least their <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POSTERIOR">posterior</a>), and lose their burnt colour. Whites, when transported into the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> regions of the Torrid zone, are at first subject to fever; the skin of the face, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, and feet, becomes burnt, hardens, and falls off in scales. Hitherto the colour of negroes appears to be only local, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXTRINSIC">extrinsic</a>, and accidental, and their short frizzled frizzled and sparse <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> is to be accounted for in the very same manner. Climate possesses great and evident influence on the hair, not only of men, but of all other animals. If in one <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CASE">case</a> these transmutations are acknowledged to be consistent with identity of kind, they ought not in the other to be esteemed criterions of different species. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURE">Nature</a> has adapted the pliancy of her <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> to the situations in which she may require it to be placed. The beaver and sheep removed to the warm latitudes <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a>, the one its fur, and the other its <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, for a coarse hair that preserves the animal in a more moderate temperature. The coarse and black hair of the bear is converted, in the arctic regions, into the finest and whitest fur. The colour of the hair is likewise changed by climate. The bear is white under the arctic circle; and, in high northern latitudes, foxes, hares, and rabbits, are found white. Similar effects of climate are discernible on mankind. The hair of the Danes is generally <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RED">red</a>; of the English, fair or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>; and of the French, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> black. The hair of all people of colour is black, and that of the African negroes is likewise sparse and curled in a manner peculiar to themselves; but this peculiarity is analogous to the effect which a warm climate has on almost every other animal. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLD">Cold</a>, by obstructing the perspiration, tends to throw out the perspirable <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> accumulated at the skin in an additional coat of hair. A warm climate, by opening the pores, evaporates this matter before it can be concreted into the substance of hair; and the laxness and aperture of the pores render the hair liable to be easily eradicated by innumerable incidents. Its curl may result in part from the nature of the secretion by which it is nourished, and in part from external heat. That it depends in some degree on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of the secretion is rendered highly probable from its appearance on the chin and other parts of the human body. Climate is as much distinguished by the nature and proportion of the secretions as by the degree of heat. (See Physiology, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a>. 6.) Whatever be the nutriment of the hair, it is evidently combined in the torrid zone of Africa with some fluid of a highly volatile or ardent quality, which produces the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RANK">rank</a> smell of many African nations. Saline secretions tend to curl and to burn the hair. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EVAPORATION">evaporation</a> of any volatile spirit would render its surface dry and disposed to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a>; whilst the centre continuing distended by the vital <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, these opposite dilatations and contractions, would necessarily produce a curve, and make the hair grow involved. External and violent heat parching the extremities of the hair, tends likewise to involve it. A hair held near the fire instantly coils itself up. Africa is the hottest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> on the globe; and the influence of its heat, either external or internal, or both, in giving the peculiar form to the hair of the natives, appears, not only from its sparseness and its curl, but from its colour. It is not of a shining, but of an adult black; and its extremities tend to brown, as if it had been scorched by the fire. The peculiarities of the negro-features and form may likewise be accounted for from the excessive heat of the climate and the state of African <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>. Being savages, they have no arts to protect them from the rays of a burning sun. The heat and leniency of the sky preserving the lives of the children without much care of the parents, they seem of course to be, in the interior parts of the country, negligent of their offspring. Able Negroes themselves to endure the extremes of that ardent climate, they injure their children to it from their most tender <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. They suffer them to roll in the dust and sand, beneath the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> rays of a vertical sun. The mother, if she be engaged, lays <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the infant on the first spot she finds, and is seldom at the pains to seek the miserable shelter of a barren shrub, which is all that the inferior country affords. When we reflect on the influence of a glare of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> upon the eye, and on the contortions of countenance produced by our efforts to repel or prevent it, we need not wonder that the plaintive features of a negro-infant should, by constant exposure, acquire that permanent irregularity which we <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TERM">term</a> their characteristic ugliness. But besides the climate, food and clothing and modes of life have prodigious effects on the human form and features. This is apparent even in polished <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a>, where the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POOR">poor</a> and labouring part of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a> are much more coarse in their features, and ill-formed in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a>, than persons of better fortune and more liberal means of subsistence. What an immense difference exists in Scotland, for instance, between the chiefs and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONALTY">commonalty</a> of the Highland clans? If they had been separately found in different countries, they would have been ranged by some philosophers under different species. A similar distinction takes <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a> between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> and peasantry of France, of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and of Germany. That food and clothing, and the different modes of life, have as great an influence upon the shapes and features of the Africans as upon the natives of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, is evident from the different appearances of the negroes in the southern republics of America according to the stations in which they are employed. "The field slaves (says Dr Smith) are badly fed, clothed, and lodged. They live in small huts on the plantations, where they labour, remote from the society and example of their superiors. Living by themselves, they retain many of the customs and manners of their African <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> servants, on the other hand, who are kept near the persons, or employed in the families of their masters, are treated with great lenity; their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> is light; they are fed and clothed like their superiors; they feel their manners, adopt their habits, and infensibly receive the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of elegance and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>. The field slaves are, in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>, slow in changing the aspect and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of Africa. The domestic servants have advanced far before them in acquiring the agreeable and regular features, and the expressive countenance of civil society. The former are frequently ill-shaped. They preserve, in a great degree, the African lips, nose, and hair. Their genius is dull, and their countenance sleepy and stupid. The latter are straight and well proportioned; their hair extended to three, four, and sometimes even to six or eight inches; the size and shape of the mouth handsome, their features regular, their capacity good, and their look animated." Upon the whole, we hope that the reader, who shall candidly weigh in his own mind what we have said at present and under the article Complexion, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a> agree with us, that the black colour in the torrid zone, the sparse crisp hair of the negroes, and the peculiarities of their features and form, proceed from causes altogether extrinsic; that they depend on local temperature and the state of society; and that they are as accidental as the various various shades of colour which characterize the different nations of Europe. If the whites be considered as the stock whence all others have sprung, it is easy to conceive how they have degenerated into negroes. Some have conjectured that the complete change may have taken place at the end of three centuries, whilst others have thought that it could not be effected in less than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> that <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>. Such conjectures can be formed from no certain <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DATA">data</a>; and a much greater length of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> is undoubtedly necessary before negroes, when transplanted into our temperate countries, can entirely lose their black colour. By crossing the breed with whites, every taint of the negro-colour may be expelled, we believe, from the fifth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a> (A). But the most serious <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> brought against the poor negroes is, that of the vices said to be natural to them. If they be indeed such as their enemies represent them, treacherous, cruel, revengeful, and intemperate, by a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of nature, they must be a different race from the whites; for though all these vices abound in Europe, it is evident that they proceed not from nature, but from wrong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, which gives to the youthful mind such deep impressions as no future exertions can completely eradicate. Let us inquire coolly if the vices of the negroes may not have a similar origin. In every part of Africa with which the nations of Europe have any <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a> prevails of the worst kind. Three-fourths of the people are slaves to the rest, and the children are born to no other inheritance. "Most parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COAST">coast</a> differ in their governments; some are <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> monarchies, while others draw near to an aristocracy. In both the authority of the chief or chiefs is unlimited, extending to life, and it is exercised as often as criminal <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CASES">cases</a> require, unless <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEATH">death</a> is committed into slavery; in which case the offender is sold, and if the shipping will not buy the criminal, he is immediately put to death. Fathers of free condition have power to sell their children, but this power is very seldom enforced." In <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONGO">Congo</a>, however, a father* will sell a son or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>, or perhaps both, for a piece of cloth, a collar or girdle of coral or beads, and often for a bottle of wine or brandy. A husband may have as many wives as he pleases, and repudiate or even sell them, though with child, at his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>. The wives and concubines, though it be a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> crime for the former to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> the conjugal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, have a way to rid themselves of their husbands, if they have let their affections upon a new gallant, by accusing them of some crime for which the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> is death. In a word, the bulk of the people in every state of Africa are born slaves to great men, reared as such, held as <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, and as property sold (see Slavery). There are indeed many circumstances by which a free man may become a slave: such as being in debt, and not able to pay; and in some of such cases, if the debt be large, not only the debtor, but his family likewise, become the slaves of his creditor, and may be sold. <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADULTERY">Adultery</a> is commonly punished in the same manner, both the offending parties being sold, and the purchase-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> paid to the injured husband. Obi, or pretended <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WITCHCRAFT">witchcraft</a> (in which all the negroes firmly believe, see Witchcraft), is another, and a very <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMON">common</a> offence, for which slavery is adjudged the lawful punishment; and it extends to all the family of the offender. There are various other crimes which subject the offender and his children to be sold; and it is more than probable, that if there were no buyers, the poor wretches would be murdered without mercy. In such a state of society, what dispositions can be looked for in the people, but cruelty, treachery, and revenge? Even in the civilized nations of Europe, blest with the lights of law, science, and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, some of the lower orders of the community consider it as a very trivial crime to defraud their superiors; whilst almost all look up to them with stupid malevolence or rancorous envy. That a depraved people, when they get power into their hands, are revengeful and cruel, the present age affords a dreadful <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> in the conduct of the demagogues of a neighbouring <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATION">nation</a>; and is it wonderful that the negroes of Africa, unacquainted with moral principles, blinded by the cruellest and most abject superstitions, and whose customs tend to eradicate from the mind all natural affection, should sometimes display to their lordly masters of European <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EXTRACTION">extraction</a> the same spirit that has been so generally displayed by the lower orders of Frenchmen to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a>, their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a>, and the family of their murdered sovereign! When we consider that the majority of the negroes groan under the cruellest slavery, both in their own country and in every other where they are to be found in considerable numbers, it can excite no surprise that they are in general treacherous, cruel, and vindictive. Such are the caprices of their tyrants at home, that they could not preserve their own lives or the lives of their families for any length of time, but by a perpetual vigilance, which must necessarily degenerate, first into cunning, and afterwards into treachery; and it is not conceivable that habits formed in Africa should be instantly thrown off in the West Indies, where they are the property of men whom some of them must consider as a different race of beings. (A) 1. A white man with a negro woman, or a negro man with a white woman, produce a mulatto, half white and half black, or of a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>-blackish colour, with black, short, frizzled hair. 2. A white man with a mulatto woman, or a negro with a mulatto woman, produce a quadroon, three fourths white and one fourth black, or three fourths black and one fourth white, or of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> yellow than the former. In America, they give the name of cabres to those who are descended from a black man and a mulatto woman, or a mulatto man and a black woman, who are three fourths black and one fourth white, and who are not so black as a negro, but blacker than a mulatto. 3. A white man with a quadroon woman, or a negro with a quadroon woman, produce a mestiço, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> eighths white and one eighth black, or seven eighths black and one eighth white. 4. A white man with a mestiço woman, or a negro with a mestiço woman, produce, the one almost perfect white, the other almost a perfect black, called a quinteroon. This is the last gradation, there being no visible difference between the fair quinteroons and the whites; and the children of a white and quinteroon consider themselves as free from all taint of the negro race. But the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> is, that the ill qualities of the negroes have been greatly exaggerated. Mr Edwards, in his valuable <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the West Indies, affirms us that the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MANDINGO">Mandingo</a> negroes display such gentleness of disposition and demeanour, as would seem the result of early education and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>; were it not that, generally speaking, they are more prone to theft than any of the African tribes. It has been supposed that this propensity, among other vices, is natural to a state of slavery, which degrades and corrupts the human mind in a deplorable manner; but why the Mandingoes should have become more vicious in this respect than the rest of the natives of Africa in the same condition of life, is a question he cannot answer. "The circumstances which (according to the same author) distinguish the Koromantyn or <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GOLD">Gold</a> Coast negroes from all others, are firmness both of body and mind; a ferocity of disposition; but withal, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a>, courage, and a stubbornness, or what an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Roman would have deemed an elevation of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>, which prompts them to enterprises of difficulty and danger, and enables them to meet death, in its most horrible shape, with fortitude or indifference. They sometimes take to labour with great promptitude and alacrity, and have constitutions well adapted for it; for many of them have undoubtedly been slaves in Africa. But as the Gold Coast is inhabited by various tribes, which are engaged in perpetual warfare and hostility with each other, there cannot be a doubt that many of the captives taken in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, and sold in the European settlements, were of free condition in their native country, and perhaps the owners of slaves themselves. It is not wonderful that such men should endeavour, even by means the most desperate, to regain the freedom of which they have been deprived; nor do I conceive that any further circumstances are necessary to prompt them to action, than that of being sold into <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a> in a distant country. One cannot surely but lament (says our author), that a people thus naturally intrepid, should be sunk into so deplorable a state of barbarity and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>; and that their spirits should ever be broken down by the yoke of slavery! Whatever may be alleged concerning their ferocity and implacability in their present notions of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> and wrong, I am persuaded that they possess qualities which are capable of, and well deserve, cultivation and improvement. "Very different from the Koromantyns are the negroes imported from the Bight of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENIN">Benin</a>, and known in the West Indies by the name of Eboes. So great is their constitutional timidity and dependency of mind as to occasion them very frequently to seek, in a voluntary death, a refuge from their own melancholy reflections. They require therefore the gentlest and mildest treatment to reconcile them to their situation; but if their confidence be once obtained, they manifest as great fidelity, affection, and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a>, as can reasonably be expected from men in a state of slavery. The females of this nation are better labourers than the men, probably from having been more hardly treated in Africa. "The natives of Whidah, who, in the West Indies, are generally called Papaws, are unquestionably the most docile and best-disposed slaves that are imported from any part of Africa. Without the fierce and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> manners of the Koromantyn negroes, they are also happily exempt from the timid and desponding temper of the Eboes. The cheerful acquiescence with which these people apply to the labours of the field, and their constitutional aptitude for such employment, arise, without doubt, from the great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> paid to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a> in their native country. Botman speaks with rapture of the improved state of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of villages, and the industry, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RICHES">riches</a>, and obliging manners of the natives. He observes, however, that they are much greater thieves than those of the Gold Coast, and very unlike them in another respect, namely, in the dread of pain, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APPREHENSION">apprehension</a> of death. They are, says he, so very apprehensive of death, that they are unwilling to hear it mentioned, for fear that alone should hasten their end; and no man <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DARES">dares</a> to speak of death in the presence of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">king</a>, or any great man, under the penalty of suffering it himself, as a punishment for his presumption. He relates further, that they are addicted to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAMING">gaming</a> beyond any people of Africa. All these propensities are observable in the character of the Papaws in a state of slavery in the West Indies. That punishment which excites the Koromantyn to rebel, and drives the Ebo negro to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SUICIDE">suicide</a>, is received by the Papaws as the chastisement of legal authority, to which it is their duty to submit patiently. The case seems to be, that the generality of these people are in a state of absolute slavery in Africa, and, having been habituated to a life of labour, they submit to a change of situation with little reluctance." Having recited such observations as occurred to him on contemplating the various tribes of negroes from each other, Mr Edwards thus estimates their general character, influenced as they are by circumstances which soon efface the native and original impressions which distinguish one nation from another when newly imported into the West Indies. "Notwithstanding what has been related of the firmness and courage of the natives of the Gold Coast, it is certain that the negroes in general in our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> (such of them at least as have been any length of time in a state of servitude) are of a dilatory and cowardly disposition. So degrading is the nature of slavery, that fortitude of mind is lost as free agency is restrained. To the same cause probably must be imputed their propensity to conceal or violate the truth; which is so general, that the vice of falsehood is one of the most prominent features in their character. If a negro is asked even an indifferent question by his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, he seldom gives an immediate reply; but, affecting not to understand what is said, compels a repetition of the question, that he may have time to consider, not what is the true answer, but what is the most politic one for him to give. The proneness observable in many of them to the vice of theft has already been noticed; and I am afraid (says our author), that evil <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> makes it almost general. It is no easy matter, I confess, to discriminate those circumstances which are the result of proximate causes, from those which are the effects of national customs and early habits in savage life; but I am afraid that cowardice and diffimulation have been the properties of slavery in all ages, and will continue to be so to the end of the world. It is a situation that necessarily suppresses many of the best affections of the human heart." heart.—If it calls forth any latent virtues, they are those of sympathy and compassion towards persons in the same condition of life; and accordingly we find that the negroes in general are strongly attached to their countrymen, but above all, to such of their companions as came in the same ship with them from Africa. This is a striking circumstance: the term "comrade" is understood among them as signifying a relationship of the most endearing nature; perhaps as recalling the time when the sufferers were cut off together from their common country and kindred, and awakening <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RECIPROCAL">reciprocal</a> sympathy from the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-REMEMBRANCE">remembrance</a> of mutual affliction. But their benevolence, with very few exceptions, extends no further. The foster virtues are seldom found in the bosom of the enslaved African. Give him sufficient authority and he becomes the most remorseless of tyrants. Of all the degrees of wretchedness endured by the sons of men, the greatest, assuredly, is the misery which is felt by those who are unhappily doomed to be the slaves of slaves; a most unnatural relation, which sometimes takes place in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a> plantations. The same observation may be made concerning their conduct towards the animal <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CREATION">creation</a>. Their treatment of cattle under their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> is brutal beyond <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a>. Even the useful and social qualities of the dog secure to him no kind usage from an African master. One of the most pleasing traits in their character is the respect and attention which they pay to their aged countrymen. The whole body of negroes on a plantation must be reduced to a deplorable state of wretchedness, if, at any time, they suffer their aged companions to want the common necessaries of life, or even many of its comforts, as far as they can procure them. They seem to be actuated on these occasions by a kind of involuntary impulse, operating as a primitive law of nature, which scorns to wait the cold dictates of reason: among them, it is the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of a common duty, which courts no observation, and looks for no applause." As the colour, and features, and moral qualities of the negroes may be thus easily accounted for by the influence of climate and the modes of savage life, so there is good reason to believe that their intellectual endowments are equal to those of the whites who have been found in the same circumstances. Of those imitative arts in which perfection can be attained only in an improved state of society, it is natural to suppose that they have but little knowledge; but the fabric and colours of the Guinea cloths are a proof of their native ingenuity. In the West Indies many of them are expert carpenters, some watchmakers, and one or two have successfully practised physic; whilst others have figured both in Latin and English <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, so that we cannot doubt but that "God, who made the world, hath made of one blood all nations of men," and animated them with minds equally rational.

NEGROLAND

Pages 864-865
or NIGERIA, a country of Africa, lying next to Guinea towards the north, and extending from 18° of west to 23° of east longitude, and from 9° to 25° of north latitude. On the north it is bounded by Zara or the Desert; on the east, by countries unknown; on the south, by Guinea; and on the west, by the Atlantic Ocean; and is watered by the great river Niger or Senegal, which runs through it from east to west. The Europeans have settlements on the coasts of this country, especially near the mouths of the Niger and Gambia, which last is supposed to be a branch of the former. A great many nations inhabit the banks of the rivers, some Pagans, some Mohammedans, of different languages, and independent of one another. The country is fruitful, especially along the rivers; abounding in rice, Guinea grain, and Indian corn, where it is cultivated; and with cocoa-nuts, plantains, pulle, palm-trees, and tropical fruits; nor is it destitute of cattle, and a variety of other animals, particularly such as abound in Guinea. See Guinea. Negroland is fertilized by the overflowing of its rivers the Senegal and Gambia, as Egypt is by the Nile. It hath not yet been ascertained whether the Gambia is a branch of the Senegal or not. As far as the Europeans have penetrated up the country, they appear to be distinct; and the Mundingo Negroes report that the Gambia has a different origin. The entrance into the Niger or Senegal river is narrow and somewhat difficult, by reason of its immovable bar and sandy shoals, as well as the several islands at the mouth of it, and the several canals and marshes that clog it; but after failing up eight or ten leagues, it is found broad and deep, and fit to carry large vessels; and, excepting about five or six leagues on each side above the mouth, which is sandy and barren ground, the banks are covered with flatly trees and villages, and the country in general is fertile and well watered; for, like the Nile, this river overflows its banks for many leagues, and enriches the land to a great degree, though, for want of skill, the inhabitants do not reap the advantages which they might obtain from its fertility. The people on both sides of the river live as near to it as they can, and feed great herds of cattle, sowing large and small millet, the former of which is called by us Turkey wheat, in great quantities, and with great increase. If the river fails of overflowing at its usual season, a great scarcity ensues in the adjacent country; and, even when it overflows regularly, it breeds such vast flights of grasshoppers and insects, as quite darken the air, and frequently devour all the produce of the earth: in which case the people kill those insects and eat them; which they do either by pounding in leather bags, and then boiling them in milk, or, which is reckoned the more delicious method, by frying or broiling them over a light blaze in a frying pan full of holes. Thus the legs and wings of the insects are burnt off, and the rest of the body is sufficiently roasted to be eaten as a dainty, which they look upon to be very wholesome and nourishing. To the east, northeast, and south east of the island of Senegal, the country, as far as it is known, is overrun with woods and marshes; the Senegal, Gambia, and Sherbro, which are looked upon by some as branches of one immense river, passing through it in their way to the Atlantic Ocean. During the rainy months, which begin in July, and continue to October, they lay the whole country under water; and indeed the sudden rise of these rivers is incredible to such as are not acquainted with the violent rains that fall between the tropics. At Galam, 900 miles from the mouth of the Senegal, the waters rise 150 feet perpendicular from the bed of the river. At the island of Senegal, the river rises gradually, during the rainy season, Negroes, season, above 20 feet perpendicular over part of that Negropont flat coast; which of itself so freshens the water, that ships lying at anchor, at the distance of three leagues from its mouth, generally make use of it, and fill their water there for their voyage home. When the rains are at an end, which soon happens in October, the intense heat of the sun usually dries up those stagnating waters which lie on the higher parts, and the re- mainder from lakes and marshes, in which are found all sorts of dead animals. At last, those too are quite dried up; and then the effluvia that arise are al- most quite insupportable. At this season the winds blow so hot from the land, that they may be compared to the heat proceeding from the mouth of an oven, and they bring with them an intolerable smell. The wolves, tigers, lions, and other wild beasts, then re- sort to the river, sleeping their body under water, and only their snout above it for the sake of breathing. The birds soar to an immense height in the air, and fly a vast way over the sea, where they continue till the wind changes, and comes from the west. NEGROES WHITE. See HELIOPHOBIA and ALBINOS. NEGROMANCY. See NECROMANCY.

NEGROPONT

Pages 865-865

anciently Euboea, an <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of the Archipelago, stretching along the eastern <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Achaia <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIVADIA">Livadia</a>, from which it is separated by a narrow channel called the Euripus. This strait is so narrow, that the island is joined to the continent by a Negropont <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> thrown over it; and here, it is thought, there was formerly an isthmus. The irregularity of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIDES">tides</a> in the Euripus hath from the remotest antiquity been very remarkable, and this irregularity is found to be connected with the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MOON">moon</a>. From the three last days of the old moon to the eighth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> of the new moon, and from the 14th to the 20th day inclusive, they are regular; but on the other days they are <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a>, flowing 12, 13, or 14 times in the space of 24 hours, and ebbling as often. The island is 90 miles <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a> and 25 <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> in the widest <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a>; and pro- duces corn, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, fruit, and cattle, in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> abundance. The only <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the island worth notice is the capi- tal, which is also called Negropont; and which is walled, and contains about 15,000 inhabitants; but the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> are said to be much more numerous than the Turks. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASHAW">bashaw</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a>, who is also governor of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CITY">city</a>, the island, and the adjacent continent of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, resides here; and the harbour, which is very safe and spacious, is seldom without a fleet of galleys, ready to be put to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SEA">sea</a> against the pirates and the Maltese. A part of the bridge between the city and the coast of Greece, con- sists of a drawbridge no longer than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> to let a galley <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through.

NIUM

Pages 196-196

marshmoss; a genus of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> order of mosses, belonging to the cryptogamia class of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. The anthera is operculate; the calyx smooth; the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPITULUM">capitulum</a> naked and powdery, remote. There are 18 <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, of which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> are natives of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>; but none have any remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> except the two following. 1. The fontanum is an elegant moss, frequent in bogs, and on the borders of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLD">cold</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>. It is from two to four inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>: the stalks are simple at the base, and covered with a rusty <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DOWN">down</a>; but higher up are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RED">red</a>, and divided into several round, single, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAPER">taper</a> branches, which proceed nearly from the same point. The leaves are not more than 1/4th of an inch <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a>, lanceolate and acute, of a whitish green <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>; and so thinly set, that the red stalk appears between them. This moss, as it may be seen at a considerable distance, is a good mark to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> to the discovery of clear and cold springs. Linnaeus informs us, that the Laplanders are well acquainted with this sign. Mr Withering informs us, that wherever this moss grows, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> of fresh <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WATER">water</a> may be found without much <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DIGGING">digging</a>. 2. The hygrometricum grows in woods, heaths, garden-walks, walls, old trees, decayed wood, and where coals <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> cinders have been laid. It is stemless, hath tips inversely <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-EGG">egg</a>-shaped, nodding, and bright <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the fruit-stalk is moistened at the base with a little water or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-STEAM">steam</a>, the head makes three or four revolutions; if the head is moistened, it turns back again.
